title: An Elucidation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: The Platform Sutra is the only work of indigenous Chinese Buddhism honored with the title of a sutra. Its appearance marks the formal establishment of Chinese Chan Buddhism, and it shines with boundless light.

inline.s: Course
Textbook

The Platform Sutra is the only work of indigenous Chinese Buddhist literature that has been honored with the title of a sutra. It gives a systematic and comprehensive exposition of the theory and practice of the sudden teaching of "seeing one's own nature and realizing Buddhahood by seeing the nature," and its appearance marks the formal establishment of Chinese Chan Buddhism, resplendent with boundless light.

[Seeing one's own nature] Realizing the mind-substance of no-thought. Seeing one's own nature is abbreviated as "seeing the nature." [Mind-substance of no-thought] The self-nature abiding in the state of no-thought.
The Patriarch Bodhidharma first transmitted it to the Second Patriarch Huike; it is precisely this mind-substance of no-thought.
The Patriarch
(Bodhidharma)

first lived in seclusion at Shaolin Monastery for nine years, and in expounding the Dharma for the Second Patriarch taught only this: "Externally still all conditions, internally the mind without panting; when the mind is like a wall, one may enter the Way." Huike discoursed on mind-nature in many ways
(the true wondrous essence of mind)
, but never yet met the principle; the Patriarch merely negated his errors
(Bodhidharma simply denied his answers)
without explaining
the mind-substance of no-thought
(he did not openly tell him the answer was the mind-substance of no-thought)
. Huike suddenly said: "I have already stilled all conditions
(I have ceased all manner of clinging — that is, I am abiding in the state of no-thought)
." The Patriarch said: "Have you not fallen into annihilation?" Huike said: "I have not fallen into annihilation
(clear knowing is fully present)
." The Patriarch said: "
This is the mind-substance transmitted by all the Buddhas
(this is the mind-substance of no-thought transmitted by all the Buddhas)
, have no further doubt."
(From the Record of Pointing at the Moon)
[Externally still all conditions] External: cease all manner of clinging. [Internally the mind without panting] Internal: the mind does not give rise to thought.

[Realizing Buddhahood by seeing the nature] See one's own nature, then, in reliance on that nature, cultivate and perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way. [The sudden teaching] The teaching that "points directly to the source, without passing through any stages, and realizes Buddhahood by seeing the nature." Its aim is: sudden enlightenment to self-nature, originally pure, originally complete — self-nature itself is Buddha. [Without passing through any stages] Ordinarily a bodhisattva, from an ordinary person through to Buddhahood, must pass through fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transfers of merit, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment, over three great asamkhya kalpas. The practice of Chan, however, is far, far swifter, without going through each of these stages one by one. [Asamkhya kalpa] Rendered in Chinese as "a kalpa of countless eons."

Master Qisong's "Eulogy on the Platform Sutra" says: "How great is this work, the Platform Sutra! Its root is upright, its traces efficacious, its cause true, its fruit without error. Sages past, sages future — thus it raises them, thus it reveals them, thus it restores them. Vast and overflowing, like a great river in spate, like the unobstructed flow of emptiness, like the brightness of sun and moon, like the unhindered unity of form and shadow, like the ordered progress of a swan in flight."
[Ordered progress of a swan] Like a swan soaring from low to high, advancing step by step.

Master Deyi's "Preface to the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch's Dharma Jewel" says: "As for the Platform Sutra, the words are simple and the meaning rich, the principle clear and the matters complete, fully endowed with the immeasurable Dharma-gates of all the Buddhas. Each and every Dharma-gate is endowed with immeasurable wondrous meaning; each and every wondrous meaning unfolds the immeasurable wondrous principle of all the Buddhas. It is within the tower of Maitreya and within the pores of Samantabhadra; he who enters well is like Sudhana, and in a single thought perfects merit, equal to Samantabhadra, equal to all the Buddhas."
[Tower of Maitreya] The Avatamsaka (Flower Garland) Sutra

volumes seventy-eight and seventy-nine, says: "At that time, the great Bodhisattva Maitreya, having thus praised the manifold merits of the youth Sudhana and caused immeasurable hundreds and thousands of beings to arouse the bodhi-mind, said to Sudhana: 'Excellent! Excellent! Good man, because you seek to benefit all the world, because you seek to rescue all beings, because you seek with diligence all the Buddha-dharma, you have aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.……Good man, as you have asked: How does a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva-conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva-path? Good man, you may enter this great tower of the Majestic Treasury of Vairocana and observe it all around; then you will be able to know how to learn the bodhisattva-conduct, and having learned it, to accomplish immeasurable merit.' At that time the youth Sudhana, having reverently circumambulated the great Bodhisattva Maitreya, said to him: 'I pray that the Great Sage open the tower's door so that I may enter.' Then the Bodhisattva Maitreya went up to the tower, snapped his fingers, and the door opened at once, bidding Sudhana enter. Sudhana rejoiced, and having entered, the door closed behind him. He saw that the tower was vast and immeasurable, like empty space,……" [Vairocana] That is, Vairocana Buddha, the Dharma-body of Śākyamuni Buddha.
[Pores of Samantabhadra] The Avatamsaka (Flower Garland) Sutra

volume eighty, says: "At that time the youth Sudhana at once saw the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, in the assembly before the Tathagata, seated upon a lion-throne of jeweled lotuses, surrounded by the host of bodhisattvas, most supreme and excellent, unequaled in the world; his wisdom-realm was immeasurable and boundless, hard to fathom and hard to conceive, equal to the Buddhas of the three times, such that no bodhisattva could observe it. He saw in each and every pore of Samantabhadra's body clouds of light as numerous as the dust-motes of all worlds, pervading the Dharma-realm, the space-realm, and all worlds, dispelling the afflictions of all beings and causing the bodhisattvas to be filled with great joy; he saw in each and every pore clouds of various-hued incense-flames as numerous as the dust-motes of all Buddha-lands, pervading the Dharma-realm, the space-realm, and the assemblies and daises of all the Buddhas, universally perfuming them; he saw in each and every pore clouds of manifold flowers as numerous as the dust-motes of all Buddha-lands, raining manifold wondrous flowers throughout the assemblies of all the Buddhas; he saw in each and every pore clouds of incense-trees as numerous as the dust-motes of all Buddha-lands, raining manifold wondrous incense; he saw in each and every pore clouds of wondrous garments as numerous as the dust-motes of all Buddha-lands, raining manifold wondrous garments; he saw in each and every pore,……"
The Platform Sutra is the great practice of the Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra.

The Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra speak of the reality of all dharmas, while the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, in accordance with the Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra, uses concrete practice to realize the reality of all dharmas, to accomplish the patience of non-arising dharmas, and then, contemplating clearly and brightly, to forever leave all marks and directly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

The core of practice in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch is what the Diamond Sutra says: "All marks are false and vain. If you see that the marks are not marks, then you see the Tathagata." "You should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, scent, taste, touch or dharmas; you should give rise to a mind abiding nowhere." "Know that all dharmas are without self, and attain the patience (the patience of non-arising dharmas)." "To be free of all marks is to be called a Buddha." This is likewise what the Heart Sutra says: "These dharmas are empty of marks, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing." "There is no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, the bodhisattva, relying on Prajñā-paramita, has no hindrance in the mind. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear, and, far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, he attains ultimate nirvāṇa." Therefore the Platform Sutra takes no-thought, no-mark and no-abiding as its guiding principles of practice. The Sixth Patriarch said: "This Dharma-gate of mine, from the past down to the present, first establishes no-thought as the doctrine, no-mark as the substance, and no-abiding as the root." (Chapter Four, on Samādhi and Wisdom)

The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch is a complete system of practice and study, whose thread is "you should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, scent, taste, touch or dharmas; you should give rise to a mind abiding nowhere," "know that all dharmas are without self, and attain the patience (the patience of non-arising dharmas)," and "to be free of all marks is to be called a Buddha."

[Patience of non-arising dharmas] Abbreviated as the patience of non-arising. Realizing that all dharmas are illusions, which from the very beginning never arose and therefore never cease (neither arising nor ceasing), and abiding in this principle unmoved. "Patience" means abiding, that is, the mind abides in the principle without wavering. In the Great Nirvāṇa Sutra, volume forty
the Kaundinya chapter, the Buddha said: "All dharmas are false and vain." The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom,

volume fifty, says: "The patience of non-arising dharmas is, within the reality of dharmas that neither arise nor cease, to believe, accept, penetrate and be unimpeded and unregressing — this is called the patience of non-arising."

Therefore, one who reads the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch cannot but read the Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra, and one who reads the Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra cannot but read the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. When a practitioner, receiving and upholding the Diamond Sutra, the Heart Sutra and the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, gains attainment, he will surely give voice from the heart: "Destroy my inverted thoughts of incalculable kalpas; without passing through an asamkhya of kalpas, gain the Dharma-body." Thus the monk Deyi said in his "Preface to the Platform Sutra": "As for the Platform Sutra, the words are simple and the meaning rich, the principle clear and the matters complete, fully endowed with the immeasurable Dharma-gates of all the Buddhas." Master Taixu, in his "A New Beat of Caoxi Chan," says: "In whatever Caoxi (the Sixth Patriarch) spoke to awaken others, it all flowed from his own state of self-awakening."

The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch has theory, method and examples, and establishes a complete and ultimate system of practice and study — the essential mind of all the Buddhas, the precious boat of the sea of enlightenment, the bright torch of the long night, the guide along the bodhi-path. The Sutra tells us concretely how to go about it; if only we put it into practice one by one, advancing understanding and practice together, the effort will naturally gain power, and before long we too shall say: "In this disciple's own mind wisdom is constantly arising; without departing from self-nature, this is the field of merit." May all readers arouse a deep resolve and strive onward, and not let this great opportunity fly past before our eyes and beneath our feet!

The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, whose full title is the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch's Dharma Jewel, abbreviated as the Platform Sutra, records the words and deeds throughout the life of Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, compiled by his disciple Fahai. It is divided into ten chapters: The Account of His Conduct, Prajñā, Resolving Doubts, Samādhi and Wisdom, Sitting in Meditation, Repentance, Conditions and Opportunities, Sudden and Gradual, Protecting the Dharma, and Entrustments. The Platform Sutra is not only a treasure of Chan Buddhism, but has also had a vast and profound influence on the whole of Buddhism, on Chinese culture and thought, and indeed on the development of the culture and thought of all humanity.

Eleven versions of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch are extant; the widely known ones are the circulating edition, the Caoxi original and the Dunhuang edition, with the circulating edition and the Caoxi original the most widely circulated. The content of the circulating edition is essentially consistent with the Caoxi original; in order to make it easier for later generations to study, some alterations were made in the division of chapters. This book adopts the text of the circulating edition.
Question: The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch is truly a treasure of practice, yet the episodes concerning supernormal powers in the Sutra confuse me — were they added by later generations?

Answer: In fact, what is called supernormal power, also known as the six supernormal powers, is the sixfold, unimpeded, sovereign wondrous function manifested by the sages of the three vehicles in reliance on the power of samādhi and wisdom. All beings likewise possess this potential, but are unable to reveal it because of deluded thoughts and attachments. There are indeed far too many records of cultivators who possessed supernormal powers; reading such works as the Biographies of Wondrous Monks will make this known. Master Miaoshan of modern times (1852–1935) is one example: because he stayed at Jinshan Monastery in Zhenjiang for several decades, using supernormal powers in play to ferry and save the world, his contemporaries called him the Jinshan Living Buddha. His deeds are recorded in the Record of the Wondrous Deeds of the Jinshan Living Buddha, which is an account personally seen and heard by the Dharma-master Leguan. As for the small measure of supernormal power mentioned in the Platform Sutra, measured against the Sixth Patriarch's state, it is truly of no account.

[Six supernormal powers] The supernormal powers attained by the sages of the three vehicles number six in all: First, the divine eye, able to see the beings of the six realms, dying here and reborn there, the marks of suffering and joy, and to see all the various forms and colors of the world, without obstruction. Second, the divine ear, able to hear the suffering, joy, sorrow, happiness and speech of the beings of the six realms, and the various sounds of the world. Third, the power of knowing others' minds, able to know what the beings of the six realms are thinking in their minds. Fourth, the power of knowing past lives, able to know one's own past lives, one life, two lives, three lives, up to a hundred thousand myriad lives, and the deeds performed; also able to know the past lives of the beings of the six realms, each and every one, and the deeds they performed. Fifth, the power of psychic transformation: the body can fly, mountains and seas offer no obstruction; vanishing from this world it emerges in that world; vanishing in that world it emerges in this world; the great can be made small, the small can be made great, changing at will. Sixth, the power of the extinction of defilements: the visional and reflective delusions are exhausted, and one no longer undergoes the birth and death of the three realms. [Three vehicles] The vehicle of the Listeners (shravakas), the vehicle of the Self-enlightened (pratyekabuddhas), and the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas.

The doctrine is the aim, and the aim the direction. The scope and aim are the methods of practice that carry out the doctrine — what is called seeking the doctrine and returning to its aim. The aim of the Platform Sutra is: see one's own nature, and realize Buddhahood by seeing the nature. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Now, at the Great Brahma Monastery, I preach this sudden teaching, and universally pray that beings throughout the Dharma-realm, upon hearing the words, may see the nature and realize Buddhahood." Its core is: recognize one's own mind, and see one's own nature. The Sutra says: "If you do not recognize your own mind, studying the Dharma is without benefit. If you recognize your own mind and see your own nature, you are then called a great man, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha."

The scope and aim of the Platform Sutra is this: to speak solely of seeing the nature, to accomplish the patience of non-arising dharmas, and to perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood. This is the key to interpreting the Platform Sutra. The Sixth Patriarch said: "I speak solely of seeing the nature, and not of dhyana and liberation." "Neither arising nor ceasing is the Tathagata's pure dhyana; the emptiness and stillness of all dharmas is the Tathagata's pure sitting.……I say that neither arising nor ceasing is: originally there was no arising, and now too there is no ceasing.……If you wish to know the essential mind, simply do not think at all of good or evil; you will then naturally enter the pure mind-substance, serene and ever still, its wondrous function like the Ganges' sands."

Its essential instruction in practice is: contemplate with wisdom, within and without clear and bright, recognize one's own mind and see one's own nature as neither arising nor ceasing. In the Sutra the Fifth Patriarch said: "Supreme bodhi requires that upon the hearing of the words one recognize one's own mind and see one's own nature as neither arising nor ceasing, and at all times, in every thought, see it oneself, so that all dharmas are without obstruction." The Sixth Patriarch said: "Do not give rise to deception; using one's own true-suchness nature, with wisdom contemplate, not grasping and not rejecting any dharma — this is to see the nature and realize the Buddha Way." "In thought after thought, see the purity of one's own nature, cultivate and practice oneself, and oneself realize the Buddha Way." Thereby one attains "no mark of self, no mark of a person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life-span," attains "you should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, scent, taste, touch or dharmas; you should give rise to a mind abiding nowhere," attains "know that all dharmas are without self, and attain the patience (the patience of non-arising dharmas)," and attains "to be free of all marks is to be called a Buddha."

The Platform Sutra is a gate of the sudden teaching. In comparing the sudden and the gradual teachings, the Essential Mind of the Transmission of Mind says: "Yet the realization of this mind may be swift or slow. There are those who, upon hearing the Dharma in a single thought, attain the mind of no-mind; there are those who attain the mind of no-mind only after the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices and the ten transfers of merit; and there are those who attain it only at the ten grounds. Whether long or short, having attained the mind of no-mind one dwells there; there is nothing further to cultivate or realize. Truly there is nothing attained; it is real, not false. One who attains it in a single thought and one who attains it at the ten grounds have exactly the same function; there is no depth or shallowness — it is only that, passing through kalpas, one has vainly endured toil.……It is like the strong man who, deluded about the jewel within his forehead, seeks for it without, journeying through all the ten directions and never finding it; a wise man points it out to him, and he sees it at once, the original jewel as before.……And when he realizes the Way, he only realizes the Buddha of his own mind; the toils of the kalpas were all vain cultivation. As when the strong man gained the jewel, he only gained the jewel that was in his forehead — it had nothing to do with the strength spent in seeking outside."

[The jewel in the forehead] A mighty strong man, wrestling with another strong man, struck heads, and the vajra-jewel on his forehead sank into his skin, hidden within a swelling. He rushed about in all four directions, searching everywhere for the jewel but unable to find it. A skilled physician later told him, and only then did he know that the vajra-jewel was right within his forehead — what need was there to seek it without? Here the jewel in the forehead is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature that every person innately possesses.
Question: What does "seeing one's own nature" as spoken of in the Platform Sutra mean?
Answer: "Seeing one's own nature" as spoken of in the Platform Sutra means, when both coarse thoughts and subtle thoughts have ceased (that is, what is commonly called no-thought), to realize the
mind-substance of no-thought

. Its method of practice is: first, see one's own nature; then, maintain and guard it while eradicating residual habits. The Sixth Patriarch, through the Fifth Patriarch's transmission of the Dharma at the third watch of the night, saw his own nature. Afterwards he mixed among a band of hunters for fifteen years, and that was maintaining and guarding it while eradicating residual habits. Then, the Way accomplished, he came down from the mountain. So the Platform Sutra speaks of sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation: seeing the nature, subduing afflictions, eradicating afflictions (eradicating the visional and reflective delusions), attaining the patience of non-arising, and perfectly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood.

[Eradicating afflictions] Eradicating the visional delusions and the reflective delusions. Visional delusions are the misunderstandings and errors of ordinary people in their views, such as the five wrong views: the view of a self, extreme views, perverse views, the view of grasping views, and the view of grasping precepts and prohibitions. Reflective delusions are the misunderstandings and errors of ordinary people in their thoughts, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride and doubt. These two delusions are the root cause of beings' falling into the three realms and vainly undergoing birth and death; eradicating them, one can end birth and death and escape the three realms. Among the ten grounds, the bodhisattva of the first ground (the Ground of Joy)
breaks the visional delusions
, and the bodhisattva of the second ground (the Ground of Freedom from Defilement)
eradicates the reflective delusions

[Patience of non-arising] That is, the patience of non-arising dharmas: true wisdom abides in the principle that "all dharmas originally never arose, and therefore never cease," and no longer regresses.

The patience of non-arising dharmas is the bodhisattva's realization of the complete emptiness of all dharmas; when the bodhisattva's practice reaches the seventh ground, he attains the patience of non-arising dharmas. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says: "Subhuti! The great bodhisattva, abiding in the
seventh ground
, should not be attached to twenty dharmas.
There are moreover twenty dharmas that should be fully perfected. What are the twenty? First, perfect emptiness; second, the realization of the markless;……; ninth,
the Dharma of the patience of non-arising
[The Platform Sutra speaks of sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation] It was said earlier that what the Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted was sudden enlightenment (
realizing the mind-substance of no-thought
) and gradual cultivation. In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, "Chapter Eight, Sudden and Gradual," the section "Shenhui pays his respects" records:
"the Master
(the Sixth Patriarch)

again said: If your mind is deluded and you do not see, ask a good teacher for the path; if your mind is enlightened, you then see your own nature yourself and practice in accordance with the Dharma."

(The Sixth Patriarch instructed Shenhui: If you have not yet seen the nature, you should seek a good teacher to point the way so that you may see the nature; if you have already seen the nature, you should then practice in accordance with the Dharma.) From this it can be seen that what the Sixth Patriarch transmitted is "first enlightenment (seeing the nature), then, in reliance on the nature, cultivation" — sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation. The Annotated Record of the Chan Garden's Jade Forest records:

Long ago, when Lan'an visited the Chan Master Baizhang, he bowed and asked: "I have come wanting to recognize Buddha — what is it?" Baizhang said: "It is very much like riding an ox and seeking the ox
(your own self-nature is Buddha; why speak of coming to recognize Buddha)
." He said: "After recognizing it, what then
(after recognizing Buddha — seeing the nature — what then)
?" Baizhang said: "Like a man riding the ox home
(causing self-nature to return to the source)
." He said: "I do not know, from beginning to end, how to maintain and guard it
(I do not know how, on the way home, from start to finish, to maintain and guard it)
?" Baizhang said: "Like a cowherd who, staff in hand, watches over it and does not let it harm the crops
(amid circumstances and conditions, eradicating residual habits)
From this it can be seen that what the First Patriarch of Chan, the Patriarch Bodhidharma, transmitted, what the Sixth Patriarch Huineng transmitted, and what

the Sixth Patriarch's descendant, the Chan Master Baizhang, transmitted (the Sixth Patriarch transmitted to Huairang, Huairang transmitted to Mazu, and Mazu transmitted to Baizhang), were all sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation.
Question: The Sixth Patriarch transmitted the sudden teaching — why does it speak here of gradual cultivation?

Answer: The sudden teaching is the teaching that "points directly to the source, without passing through any stages, and realizes Buddhahood by seeing the nature." With this teaching one realizes Buddhahood without passing through the stages, hence it is called "sudden." Gradual cultivation, however, refers to the cultivation, after seeing the nature, in reliance on that nature, to perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way. So the "sudden" of the sudden teaching does not mean that after seeing the nature there is no further cultivation needed. In fact, a great portion of the Platform Sutra deals with how to cultivate in reliance on the nature. As for the principle of sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation, it is set forth very clearly in the Essential Mind for Cultivation; see
An Elucidation of the Essential Mind for Cultivation

[Without passing through any stages] Ordinarily a bodhisattva, from an ordinary person through to Buddhahood, must pass through fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transfers of merit, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment, over three great asamkhya kalpas. The practice of Chan, however, is far, far swifter, without going through each of these stages one by one. [Realizing Buddhahood by seeing the nature] See one's own nature, then, in reliance on that nature, cultivate and perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way. [Asamkhya kalpa] Rendered in Chinese as "a kalpa of countless eons."
Question: Why sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation? What is wrong with first gradual cultivation and then sudden enlightenment?

Answer: In point of fact, there is also gradual cultivation before sudden enlightenment, though it is usually called the preliminary practice to sudden enlightenment. When one already has the initial skill of a single thought not arising, one should then see one's own nature. Then, cultivating in reliance on the nature, is the correct path. If one sets aside seeing one's own nature and merely keeps cultivating gradually, then the path becomes circuitous. The Platform Sutra says: "If you do not recognize your own mind, studying the Dharma is without benefit." This is because, without having awakened to one's own nature, practice is always seeking within the dharmas of arising and ceasing, and runs counter to the Way; hence the patriarchs rebuke it as "blind practice and deluded cultivation." This principle
is set forth very clearly in the Essential Mind for Cultivation; see
An Elucidation of the Essential Mind for Cultivation
The essence of the Sixth Patriarch's Chan is:
to awaken directly within seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing
(contemplation with prajñā)
, so as to attain the lively, vibrant state of being undefiled by the myriad realms and ever free
(passing through a garden of a myriad flowers without a single leaf clinging to the body)
The Sixth Patriarch said:

"When true-suchness self-nature gives rise to thought, though the six faculties possess seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing, they are undefiled by the myriad realms, and the true nature is ever free. Therefore the Sutra says: able to well discriminate the marks of all dharmas, yet unmoved within the first principle."

When true-suchness self-nature gives rise to thought, one is making contemplation with prajñā: when the false comes, one crosses it over with the upright; when delusion comes, one crosses it over with enlightenment; when ignorance comes, one crosses it over with wisdom; when evil comes, one crosses it over with good — until both extremes are left behind and the mind of false thoughts is cast away. This is the dharma of the Sixth Patriarch's Chan.
The Sixth Patriarch said:
"Do not give rise to deception; using one's own true-suchness nature, with wisdom contemplate, not grasping and not rejecting any dharma — this is to see the nature and realize the Buddha Way."
Therefore, no-thought does not mean that thought is forbidden, but that one is undefiled.
The Sixth Patriarch said:
"No-thought is: within thought, to be without thought. The mind not defiled by any state is called no-thought.
In one's own thoughts, always apart from all states, not giving rise to a mind upon the states.

If one only thinks of nothing at all, and eradicates thought entirely, then when a single thought is cut off one dies and is reborn elsewhere — this is a great error." "There are also deluded people who, emptying the mind and sitting still, thinking of nothing at all, call themselves great; these people should not be conversed with, because of their wrong views." "What is called no-thought? If one sees all dharmas and the mind is not defiled or attached to them, that is no-thought.

Good teachers! One who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought penetrates all dharmas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought sees the realms of all the Buddhas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought reaches the stage of Buddhahood."
Mazu said:

"Thoroughly understanding the mind and the realms, deluded thoughts no longer arise. Since deluded thoughts no longer arise, this is the patience of non-arising dharmas. It was there originally and is here now, without need of cultivating the Way or sitting in dhyana. Without cultivating and without sitting, this is the Tathagata's pure dhyana. If now you see this principle as truly real, do not create any karma, pass your life according to your lot, with a single robe and a single sitting, standing and sitting together, the conduct of precepts ever accumulating incense, amassing pure karma. If only you can be thus, why worry that you will not penetrate?
(From the Extensive Record of the Chan Master Mazu Daoyi)
Question: Why is there no mention of the "huatou" (topic of meditation) in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch?
Answer: In this regard, the old master Xuyun instructed:

"The meditation school focuses on meditation; meditation lies in 'clarifying the mind and seeing the nature,' that is, in penetrating to one's original countenance, the so-called 'clearly awakening to one's own mind and entirely seeing one's own nature.' This Dharma-gate, from the Buddha's twirling of the flower down to when the Patriarch Bodhidharma brought it to the East, has undergone many changes in the initial practice. The Chan worthies before the Tang and Song dynasties mostly awakened through a single word or half a phrase; the transmission between teacher and disciple was but mind-sealing mind, with no actual concrete dharma. Daily questioning and repartee were merely unbinding the knots according to the occasion, giving medicine according to the illness. After the Song dynasty, people's faculties grew inferior: they were told to do something but could not accomplish it. For instance, told to 'let go of everything' and 'think neither of good nor evil,' they were yet unable to let go — if not thinking of good, then thinking of evil. At this juncture the patriarchs had no recourse but to adopt the method of counteracting poison with poison, teaching students to meditate on a gong'an. At first it was contemplating the huatou, indeed to the point of biting fast hold of a dead huatou, teaching you to bite it tightly, not relaxing for an instant, like a mouse gnawing a coffin, biting fast at one place, not stopping until it goes through
if it cannot bite through, it can only die inside)
; the goal is to use one thought to counteract a myriad thoughts. This is truly a last resort, like a virulent poison in the body that cannot be cured unless one cuts and treats it."
(From the Old Master Xuyun's Expedient Instructions
"The Prerequisite for Meditation")
The great master Hanshan instructed:

"From the past Buddhas and patriarchs, people were only taught to awaken to their own mind and recognize themselves; there had never been any talk of gong'an or huatou. Down to the masters after Nanyue and Qingyuan, the patriarchs gave expedient instructions, mostly striking at the places of doubt, causing people to turn their heads and then stop. Should there be those who could not grasp it, even though the mallet and tongs were brought down, they simply left it to the season and to conditions. It was only with Huangbo that people were first taught to look at a huatou, and it was only the great master Dahui who vigorously advocated it, teaching students to meditate on an ancient person's gong'an, taking it as a handle, calling it a huatou, urging one to hold it up intently. Why is this? Only because in students' eighth consciousness the evil habitual seeds of incalculable kalpas have been perfuming within, thought after thought, flowing on in continuous stream, with deluded thoughts unceasing, and there is no other remedy. Therefore a phrase without flavor is given for you to bite fast hold of
, first setting down all the deluded thoughts of inner and outer realms, the whole of mind and circumstances at once. Because one cannot set them down, one is taught to raise this huatou
to use this one thought to counter a myriad thoughts)

, like cutting tangled silk — one cut severs it all at once, no longer continuous; cutting off the consciousness, never letting it go again. This is precisely the rule of Bodhidharma's externally stilling all conditions, internally the mind without panting, the mind like a wall. Unless one makes this beginning, one will never see one's own original countenance. It is not teaching you to ponder over the phrases of a gong'an, taking it as a case of doubt and hoping to get an answer from it."
(For the annotations see
The Essentials of Chan and Pure Land
the chapter 'The Essentials of Meditation'.)
[Handle] Meaning a place to grasp hold of.
[The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch's Dharma Jewel]

The title of this Sutra is: The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch's Dharma Jewel. "Sixth Patriarch" refers to Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of the Chan lineage, posthumously conferred the title of Great Mirror Meditation Master in the tenth year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong of Tang. The origin of the name "Dharma Jewel Platform Sutra" is this: before Master Huineng passed away, he instructed his disciples, saying: "I have expounded the Dharma at the Great Brahma Monastery, and up to the present day it has been copied and circulated, titled the 'Dharma Jewel Platform Sutra.' You should guard it, transmitting it to one another, to ferry across the many beings; if you speak only in accordance with this, it is called the right Dharma."

[Titled the 'Dharma Jewel Platform Sutra'] Named the 'Dharma Jewel Platform Sutra.' [Dharma Jewel] One of the three jewels (the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel and the Sangha-jewel). The wondrous Dharma spoken by all the Buddhas is treasured like the treasures of this world, hence it is called the Dharma Jewel. [Platform Sutra] The compiler of this Sutra (the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch), the Dharma-master Fahai, in his "Preface to the Platform Sutra" says: "In the first year of the Yifeng era, the year bingzi (676), on the eighth day of the first month, Master Huineng met the Dharma-master Yinzong, and they debated the profound and mysterious truths; Yinzong awakened and conformed to the Master's intent (awakened to the intent of Master Huineng). On the fifteenth day of that month, the fourfold assembly was gathered and the Master's head was shaved. On the eighth day of the second month, the renowned virtuous ones were gathered and the full precepts were conferred. The Vinaya-master Zhiguang of the Western Capital was the precept-master; the Vinaya-master Huijing of Suzhou was the karmadana; the Vinaya-master Tongying of Jingzhou was the instructor; the Master Jiduo of Central India proclaimed the precepts; and the Tripitaka-master Miduo of the Western Lands was the witness of the precepts. The precept-platform was created by the Tripitaka-master Gunabhadra of the Song dynasty (the Liu Song, 420–479 CE), who erected a stele saying, 'Later there will be a bodhisattva in the flesh who will receive the precepts here.' Moreover, in the first year of the Tianjian era of the Liang (502 CE), the Tripitaka-master Zhiyao came by sea from the Western Lands of India, and, planting a bodhi tree by the side of this platform, likewise foretold: 'One hundred and seventy years later, a bodhisattva in the flesh will, beneath this tree, expound the supreme vehicle, ferrying across immeasurable beings — the king of the Dharma who truly transmits the Buddha's mind-seal.' The Master then shaved his head (received the tonsure) and received the precepts, and thereupon expounded to the fourfold assembly the essential purport of the single transmission, exactly as the ancient prophecies had foretold." These prophecies were each and every one fulfilled: Master Huineng received the precepts upon this precept-platform, and again beneath the bodhi tree by its side he propagated the transmission of the Buddha's mind-seal; therefore his recorded words of teaching are called the "Platform Sutra." [King of the Dharma] The Buddha, being sovereign and free within the Dharma, is called the King of the Dharma. The Lotus Sutra, "Chapter Three, The Parable" says: "I am the King of the Dharma, sovereign and free within the Dharma." The same Sutra, "Chapter Twenty-three, the Medicine King" says: "The Tathagata is the king of all dharmas." The Vimalakirti Sutra, "Chapter One, The Buddha Land" says: "Having already attained sovereignty over the Dharma, therefore I bow to this King of the Dharma." [Prophecy] A prediction that is to come true in the future.
[Recorded by the disciple Fahai]

Menren", that is, a disciple. The Dharma-master Fahai was a monk of the Tang dynasty and a great disciple of Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, a native of Qujiang in Guangdong. When he first met the Sixth Patriarch, he asked the meaning of "this very mind is Buddha," and instantly awakened. Later he became the senior seat among the disciples and compiled the Sixth Patriarch's sermons into the Dharma Jewel Platform Sutra, whose principle is profound and which was widely current in the world, serving as the fundamental sutra of Chan Buddhism.
[Senior seat] A monastic office, positioned only below the abbot (the master of a monastery).

Mind, self-nature, the tathagata-garbha and the eight consciousnesses, as well as the reality of all dharmas, are the most commonly used basic concepts in the Platform Sutra, which speaks of them throughout. In order to better understand the text, a separate chapter is here established to present them
See
"Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-Garbha"
for the full essay.
See
"The Reality of All Dharmas"
for the full essay.

blocks.text: Chapter One: The Account of His Conduct

inline.s: A "pin" is a chapter. "Chapter One, The Account of His Conduct" is equivalent to "Chapter One: The Account of His Conduct." The subheadings within each chapter, such as the "1. Opening the Occasion and Preaching the Dharma" below, were added by the annotator for ease of understanding and reference, and do not belong to the sutra text.
[Account of His Conduct] The circumstances and origin of his practice.

blocks.text: 1. Opening the Occasion and Preaching the Dharma

inline.s: At that time the Master arrived at Baolin. The Prefect Wei of Shaozhou and his officials entered the mountains to invite the Master to come forth, and at the lecture hall of the Great Brahma temple in the city he opened the occasion and preached the Dharma for the assembly.

At that time, Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch, came from Faxing Temple in Guangzhou to take up residence at Baolin Temple on Caoxi Mountain in Qujiang County. The Prefect of Shaozhou, Wei Qu, along with his subordinate officials and aides, entered the mountains and respectfully invited the Master to come forth. There, in the lecture hall of the Great Brahma temple in the city of Qujiang County (seat of the Shaozhou prefecture), he opened the Buddha-karmic occasion and preached the Dharma for all present.

[The Master] Here this refers to Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of the Chan lineage. Fahai's "Preface to the Platform Sutra" says: "The Master's name was Huineng. His father was surnamed Lu, named Xingtiao, and his mother was of the Li family. The Master was born in the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang, the year wuxu [

on the eighth day of the second month, at the hour of the rat [midnight]. At that time a radiant light shot into the sky and a rare perfume filled the room. At dawn, two unusual monks came to call, and said to the Master's father: 'A son was born last night; we have come especially to name him. His first name should be Hui, and his second name Neng.' His father asked: 'Why the names Hui and Neng

The monks said: 'Hui means to bestow the Dharma upon sentient beings; Neng means to be able to do the work of a Buddha.' Having spoken, they went out, and no one knew where they went." [Taking up residence] A monk residing in a certain place. Xi, the pilgrim's staff. [Prefect Wei] Surnamed Wei, named Qu; the prefect was the chief administrator of a prefecture in the Tang dynasty. [Baolin Temple] Located on Caoxi Mountain, thirty-five kilometers south of Qujiang County, Guangdong; today it is known as Nanhua Temple.

When the Master ascended the seat, more than thirty officials, including the Prefect, more than thirty Confucian scholars, and more than a thousand monks, nuns, and lay followers made obeisance together, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma.

The Master ascended the Dharma seat. More than thirty officials and aides of the Prefect, along with Confucian masters and scholars, as well as more than a thousand monks, nuns, and lay practitioners, simultaneously bowed in homage to the Master, wishing only to hear the essential marrow of the Dharma.

[Seat] That is, the seat of honor; here "ci" indicates a place, as in "a traveler's lodging" or "a boat's berth." [Confucian master] A master of the Confucian school; after the Han dynasty it came also to refer generally to scholars held in esteem by readers. [Clergy and laity] The renunciates and the householders. Those who have left home are called "the wayfarers"; those who remain at home are called "the laity." [Bowing in homage] Kneeling, with both palms on the ground and the head touching the feet of the person venerated — this is the most sublime form of reverence.
The Master said to the assembly: Good friends! The self-nature of bodhi is originally pure. Only use this mind, and directly realize Buddhahood.

The Master said to all: Good friends! The awakened self-nature is originally pure. Only use this mind, set down deluded thoughts and attachments, recover the original purity of self-nature, and, without passing through any stage, directly accomplish Buddhahood.
The Platform Sutra speaks of the sudden teaching. The characteristic of the sudden teaching is precisely this: only use this mind, and directly realize Buddhahood.
"The self-nature of bodhi is originally pure; only use this mind, and directly realize Buddhahood." This line is extremely important; it is the guiding principle of the whole work.

[Good friends] Those who can teach sentient beings to turn away from evil dharmas and practice good dharmas; here it is the Master's respectful form of address for the audience. [Bodhi] Rendered in Chinese as "awakening." [Self-nature of bodhi] The awakened self-nature, that is, one's original nature. [Directly realize Buddhahood] Without passing through any stage, directly accomplish Buddhahood. This is the singular excellence of the Chan school. In ordinary Dharma-gates, realizing Buddhahood requires passing through the fifty-two stages of the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transfers of merit, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment.
The path of practice of the Chan school is this: not relying on written words, see one's own nature, and realize Buddhahood by seeing the nature.

[Not relying on written words, see one's own nature] Without establishing written theories or pondering over words (transcending speech and thought), one directly works on stilling delusions in one's own mind, returning to the source. Yet "not relying on written words" does not mean to utterly reject words; the value of written theories is still esteemed by the Chan patriarchs. The Patriarch Bodhidharma, for instance, used the Lankavatara Sutra to confirm later students, and both the Fifth Patriarch Hongren and the Sixth Patriarch Huineng advocated the Diamond Sutra. [Realize Buddhahood by seeing the nature] This means: first see the nature, and after seeing it, cultivate in reliance on the nature to perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way. The Platform Sutra says: "Do not give rise to deception; using one's own true-suchness nature, with wisdom contemplate, not grasping and not rejecting any dharma — this is to see the nature and realize the Buddha Way."
Question: The sutra text above says, "Only use this mind, and directly realize Buddhahood." What is this mind?

Answer: This mind is the single thought-mind of the present moment. The Sutra of the Buddha's Five Karmic Verses says: "The mind takes up hell, the mind takes up the hungry ghosts, the mind takes up the animals, the mind takes up the gods and humans; all the forms of appearance are made by the mind. He who can subdue the mind and walk the Way has the greatest power. I struggled with the mind for countless kalpas, and only now have I become a Buddha, treading alone throughout the three realms — all done by the mind." The Mahayana Sutra of Contemplation of the Mind-Ground of Essential Nature says: "The Buddhas take the Dharma as the great teacher; the bodhi-path is realized through cultivation of the mind." A former worthy said: "The raging mind never ceases; when it ceases, that is bodhi."

blocks.text: 2. Seeking the Dharma at East Mountain

inline.s: Good friends! Listen to the account of how Huineng won the Dharma.
Good friends! Listen to the circumstances and origin of how Huineng practiced and obtained the Dharma.
Huineng [638

] was a high monk of the Tang dynasty and the Sixth Patriarch of the Chan lineage, of the common surname Lu. The First Patriarch, the great master Bodhidharma, came from South India to China, bringing a single kashaya as the token of the Dharma, and transmitted it to Huike (the Second Patriarch); Huike transmitted it to Sengcan (the Third Patriarch); Sengcan to Daoxin (the Fourth Patriarch); Daoxin to Hongren (the Fifth Patriarch); and Hongren to Huineng (the Sixth Patriarch) — six generations of succession. From the Sixth Patriarch Huineng onward, Chan was greatly developed, branching into the five schools of Caodong, Linji, Yunmen, Weiyang, and Fayan — the so-called "one flower with five petals" — and sweeping the whole world. [The Patriarch Bodhidharma] Bodhidharma, the third son of the Fragrant King of South India, understood both the Greater and Lesser Vehicle Dharma, and was the twenty-eighth patriarch of the Chan lineage in India. Sensing that the karma-conditions in the East were ripe, he came to China to spread the teaching. He arrived by sea at Guangzhou during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang, and the emperor welcomed him to Jianye (present-day Nanjing). Finding no rapport with Emperor Wu, he crossed the river into Wei, and sat facing a wall for nine years at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song, transmitting the mind-Dharma of Chan to Huike — and so became the first patriarch of Chinese Chan. Because he saw that Chinese Buddhists mostly started from written words, and that the preachers of the sutras mostly explained in accordance with the letter without actual cultivation, not conforming to the profound purport of the sutras, he founded a school of his own: not relying on written words, seeing one's own nature, and realizing Buddhahood by seeing the nature.

The Sixth Patriarch respectfully addressed the audience as good friends, while calling himself Huineng; his attitude was extremely humble, and the bearing of a great master can be glimpsed in this. What follows is the Master's personal account, in which the point lies beyond the words — most instructive and most splendid.

Huineng's honorable father was originally of Fanyang, but was demoted and banished to Lingnan, becoming a commoner of Xinzhou. This body of mine was unfortunate: my father died early in grief, leaving my old mother widowed and alone. We moved to Nanhai, and in hardship and poverty I sold firewood at the market.

My father was originally a man of Fanyang in Hebei, but was stripped of his official post and banished as a commoner to Xinzhou in Lingnan, Guangdong. My life was most unfortunate: my father, in grief and indignation, passed away early. My widowed mother and I, an orphan, moved to the region of Nanhai to survive. Life was hard and poor, so I made a living selling firewood.

[Guan] Place of birth: native place. [Demoted] Deposed from office. [Lingnan] The region south of the Nanling Mountains. [Nanling] The collective name for the range of mountain chains running through the borders of Hunan, Jiangxi, Guangdong, and Guangxi. [Xinzhou] Present-day Xinxing County, Guangdong. [Orphan and widow] An orphan and a widow. [Nanhai] On the authority of Ding Fubao's Annotated Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch: "Nanhai" is a commandery name, now changed to a county, in the Yuehai circuit of Guangdong.

At that time there was a guest who bought firewood and had it delivered to a guesthouse. After the guest took the firewood and Huineng received the money, he went out the door and saw a guest chanting a sutra. The moment Huineng heard the words of the sutra, his mind became awakened.

One day, as I was selling firewood on the street, a customer bought it and had me carry it to his shop. He took the firewood and I received the money; as I went out the door, I saw a guest reciting a sutra. The moment I heard the words of the sutra, my mind awakened. (This awakening here is an understanding-awakening. Huineng received the robe and bowl from the Fifth Patriarch at twenty-four, so at this point he should have been twenty-three.)
The corresponding passage in the Caoxi original reads: "Seeing a guest reciting a sutra, Huineng, upon hearing the words 'should give rise to a mind abiding nowhere,' instantly awakened his mind."

Because the Dharma was then widespread, though Huineng was illiterate, he had planted spiritual roots in past lives and had long nurtured his practice. This can be seen from his later answers to the Fifth Patriarch — "Though people are from north and south, the Buddha-nature is fundamentally without north or south; though the body of a southern barbarian differs from that of a monk, what difference is there in the Buddha-nature?" and "never apart from self-nature, this is the field of merit."
The great master Hanshan said:
"Before the Sixth Patriarch appeared in the world
(before he succeeded to the patriarchate)

he was only a firewood-seller of Xinzhou. Because he had planted spiritual roots in past lives and long nurtured his practice, the moment he heard the Diamond Sutra's phrase 'should abide nowhere' he at once severed the birth and death of countless kalpas and clearly awakened to his own mind, and so obtained the robe and bowl at Huangmei."
(From the Collected Works of Dream Wandering
"Instruction for the Abbot Angtang of Baolin, Caoxi")

At the time Huineng was mulling over what the essential instruction of practice really was, and thought of a hundred answers without finding one. So the moment he heard this passage of the Diamond Sutra,

"All the great bodhisattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this manner: not giving rise to a mind dwelling in form, not giving rise to a mind dwelling in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas — giving rise to a mind abiding nowhere."

his obstruction was suddenly opened, and he understood: so this is it! From then on, in all places and times, he was aware of his own thoughts, never giving rise to a mind dwelling in form, sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas; and further, in his own thoughts constantly apart from all states, never giving rise to a mind upon any state.

During the more than thirty days on the road seeking the Dharma and the more than eight months splitting wood and treading the pestle, Huineng worked earnestly upon this very passage. In less than ten months he had great awakening and succeeded to the patriarchate.

I then asked the guest: What sutra are you reciting? The guest replied: The Diamond Sutra. Again I asked: From where did you come bringing this sutra? The guest said: I came from East Chan Temple in Huangmei County, Qizhou. There the Fifth Patriarch, the great master Ren, presides and teaches, with more than a thousand disciples. I went there to bow before him, and to hear and receive this sutra. The Master constantly urges the clergy and laity: only uphold the Diamond Sutra, and you will see your own nature and directly realize Buddhahood.

So I asked the guest: What sutra are you reciting? The guest answered: The Diamond Sutra. I asked again: From where have you obtained this sutra? The guest said: I obtained this sutra from East Chan Temple in Huangmei County, Qizhou in Hubei (read as qi). The Fifth Patriarch of Chan, the great master Hongren, presides there, with more than a thousand disciples. I went there to bow to the Master and hear and receive this sutra. The Master constantly urges the clergy and laity: only maintain the Diamond Sutra, and you will see your own nature by yourself; then, cultivating in reliance on that nature, untainted by any state, you will be free and liberated, and, without passing through any stage, directly accomplish Buddhahood.

The Platform Sutra is the sudden teaching, whose central thought is realizing Buddhahood by seeing the nature. "Realizing Buddhahood by seeing the nature" means first see the nature, then, cultivating in reliance on that nature, thoroughly eradicate residual habits and realize Buddhahood; it does not mean that upon seeing the nature one is already a Buddha. Seeing the nature gives one fundamental wisdom (the wisdom of non-discrimination) — this is the Buddha of the causal ground; thoroughly eradicating residual habits gives one acquired wisdom, with blessing and wisdom both fully rounded — this is the Buddha of the fruitional ground.

[Wisdom of non-discrimination] When the realm and wisdom are not two, and no discrimination arises, this is called "fundamental wisdom," also called the mind of non-discrimination. [Acquired wisdom] Able to well discriminate the marks of all differences, clear and bright in contemplative knowing — this is called "acquired wisdom."

Concerning the suddenness and gradualness of attaining the Way, the Master of the Essence of Mind Transmission, the Chan Master Huangbo Duanji, in his Essential Mind of the Transmission of Mind, says: "One who attains in a single thought and one who attains at the ten grounds have exactly the same function; there is no depth or shallowness — it is only that, passing through kalpas, one has vainly endured toil." Here is the passage from the Essential Mind of the Transmission of Mind, quoted in full: "Being free of all marks, the beings and the Buddhas have no difference; only be able to be without mind, and that is the ultimate. A student of the Way who does not at once become without mind, even though he cultivates through many kalpas, will never accomplish the Way, being bound by the functions and conduct of the three vehicles and unable to attain liberation. Yet the realization of this mind may be swift or slow. There are those who, upon hearing the Dharma in a single thought, attain the mind of no-mind; there are those who attain the mind of no-mind only after the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten transfers of merit; and there are those who attain it only at the ten grounds. Whether long or short, having attained the mind of no-mind one dwells there; there is nothing more to cultivate or realize. Truly there is nothing attained; it is real, not false. One who attains in a single thought and one who attains at the ten grounds have exactly the same function; there is no depth or shallowness — it is only that, passing through kalpas, one has vainly endured toil."
Only uphold the Diamond Sutra, and you will see your own nature and directly realize Buddhahood." Master Huineng personally verified this famous saying.

When Huineng heard this, he knew that karma from past lives had ripened, and so was favored by a guest who gave him ten taels of silver to provide for his old mother's clothing and food, and urged him to go at once to Huangmei to bow before the Fifth Patriarch. Having settled his mother, Huineng took leave of her without delay. In not more than thirty-odd days he reached Huangmei and bowed before the Fifth Patriarch.

Hearing these words, I was greatly moved and longed to go to Huangmei to seek the Dharma, yet I was worried that my old mother had no clothing or food. Fortunately, by the karma of a past life, a guest presented me with ten taels of silver as living expenses for my mother, and told me to set out at once for Huangmei to pay my respects to the Fifth Patriarch. Having settled my mother and taken leave of the old lady, I set off immediately. Traveling by day and resting by night, in little more than thirty days I reached Huangmei and bowed before the Fifth Patriarch.

For Huineng, who made a living selling firewood, ten taels of silver were no small sum. It must have been that, having awakened upon hearing the sutra, he spoke out his understanding, and everyone there was unstinting in praise, seeing that, though so young, he had such insight and such awakening — a rare talent — and so a guest generously assisted him.

The Patriarch asked: Who are you, and what is it you seek? Huineng replied: Your disciple is a commoner of Xinzhou in Lingnan. Having come from afar to bow before the Master, I seek only to become a Buddha, and seek nothing else.

The Fifth Patriarch asked: What place are you from? What do you seek? I replied: Your disciple is a commoner of Xinzhou in Lingnan. I have come from afar to bow before the Master; I seek only to become a Buddha, and nothing else.

The Patriarch said: You are a man of Lingnan, and moreover a southern barbarian — how can you possibly become a Buddha? Huineng said: Though people may be from north and south, the Buddha-nature is fundamentally without north or south; though the body of a barbarian differs from that of a monk, what difference is there in the Buddha-nature? The Fifth Patriarch wished to converse further, but seeing that the assembly was all around, he told Huineng to go and work with the others.

The Fifth Patriarch said: You are an unenlightened man of Lingnan, and a barbarian besides — what claim have you to become a Buddha? I replied: Though people have a division of north and south, the Buddha-nature has no north or south; though a barbarian and a Master are far apart in standing, what difference is there in the Buddha-nature? (The implication: Since you, Master, can become a Buddha, I too can become a Buddha.) Seeing that my words were out of the ordinary, the Fifth Patriarch wished to talk further with me; but seeing the assembly all around, and fearing that someone might, out of jealousy, do me harm, he said no more and told me to go and work with the others.

[Southern barbarian] A contemptuous term for the southern minorities. [How can] How could. [Claim] Equal to, sufficient for. [Master] Meaning my teacher; a respectful term used by monks for their own master. [The assembly all around] The disciples all around. Here "always" has the sense of "all."

When the Fifth Patriarch heard Huineng say, "I seek only to become a Buddha, and nothing else," he knew the words were out of the ordinary, and so used a taunting remark to test him: "You are a man of Lingnan, and moreover a southern barbarian — how can you possibly become a Buddha?" Huineng's answer — neither servile nor overbearing, and hitting the very point — indeed showed real insight, and the Fifth Patriarch inwardly rejoiced.

Huineng was a native of Guangdong, and in his era the Dharma had already flourished. The Dharma came to China by two routes: one from the Western Regions to Chang'an, and one by sea to Guangzhou. At the time Huineng grew up in Lingnan where the Dharma flourished, so before he came to bow before the Fifth Patriarch he had already had the opportunity to hear the Dharma, and had practiced and realized something of it.

Huineng said: Huineng makes this request of the Master. In this disciple's own mind wisdom is constantly arising; never apart from self-nature, this is the field of merit. I do not know what work the Master would have me do? The Patriarch said: This barbarian's keen faculties are too great! Say no more; go to the stable.

I then said: Huineng reports to the Master that in this disciple's own mind wisdom is constantly arising; never apart from self-nature, this is the field of merit. I do not know what work the Master would have me do? The Fifth Patriarch said: This fellow's faculties are too keen! Say no more — go to the stable in the back courtyard and work.

[Never apart from self-nature, this is the field of merit] No longer delusorily grasping the five aggregates and the body-mind as a self, one has found the master — "he who awakens to this and guards it sits in one thusness, unmoved and liberated" — this is to be planting the greatest field of merit. Ordinarily, what people never leave is the "self" of the five aggregates and the body-mind. When you leave that "self" and are never apart from self-nature, that is the state of clear awareness. To never be apart from the "self" of the five aggregates and the body-mind is to be creating karma; and to cast aside that "self" and never be apart from self-nature is to be planting the field of merit. The Essential Mind for Cultivation says: "He who awakens to this and guards it sits in one thusness, unmoved and liberated; he who is deluded about this and turns away from it goes into the six destinies and revolves in samsara through long kalpas." [Faculties] The capacity to understand the Dharma. [Too keen] Extremely sharp. Here the character "da" was anciently interchangeable with "tai" and should be read "tai." [Stable] The horse barn; the work of splitting wood and pounding rice was also done there.

Since Huineng heard "All the great bodhisattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this manner: not giving rise to a mind dwelling in form, not giving rise to a mind dwelling in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas — giving rise to a mind abiding nowhere" and awakened, he had obtained the secret of practice, treasuring it like a precious jewel. On the road he ate when hungry and drank when thirsty, traveling under the stars, yet not for a moment setting down his practice, his state growing daily in freshness. Now that he had finally seen the Patriarch, he seized the opportunity to seek the Patriarch's confirmation, and said, "In this disciple's own mind wisdom is constantly arising; never apart from self-nature, this is the field of merit." The Fifth Patriarch confirmed it: "This barbarian's keen faculties are too great!" At this the Fifth Patriarch was all the more certain of his judgment: here was one to carry on the line. In the more than eight months that followed, the Fifth Patriarch observed Huineng covertly, and seeing that the time for transmitting the Dharma had ripened and wishing to settle the matter, he had his disciples each present a verse, publicly testing and selecting.
"I do not know what work the Master would have me do?" is a double entendre. On the surface it asks what work I should do; beneath the surface it asks: the disciple's present state is that of
never apart from self-nature, this is the field of merit
— what should the next step be? To this, since the assembly was present and he feared Huineng might be harmed, the Fifth Patriarch did not reply, but only said:
say no more — go to the stable in the back courtyard and work!
"Never apart from self-nature" — this is to recognize the Dharma-body and not the physical body; to recognize clear knowing and not deluded thought.

The "self" of the five aggregates and the body-mind is precisely what the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment calls the mark of one's own body and the mark of one's own mind. In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha said: "All sentient beings from beginningless time, in all manner of inversion, are like a deluded man who mistakes the four quarters: deludedly taking the four elements as the mark of one's own body, and the shadow-images of the six sense-objects as the mark of one's own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in space and a second moon. Good man! There are in truth no flowers in space; it is the sick man's deluded grasping. Because of this deluded grasping, not only is one confused about the nature of this void, but one is also deluded about the place where real flowers arise. From this delusion there is revolving birth and death, and so it is called ignorance."

The Surangama Sutra says: "You should know that all sentient beings, from beginningless time, have been born and dying in a continuous stream, all because they do not know the everlasting true mind, the pure and bright substance of nature, and instead use all manner of deluded thought; this thought is not true, and so there is revolving."

This is to say: all sentient beings, from beginningless time, revolve in birth and death because they do not know the ever-dwelling, pure and luminous original nature, and instead give rise to deluded thoughts, taking the five aggregates and the body-mind as a self, and so pursue external states and create karma; this deluded thought is not true, and so there is birth and death and revolving. Now, in seeking liberation in practice, one must go against this: dwell in the original nature, and cast aside deluded thought — this is the fundamental program of practice. Huineng practiced in accordance with "not giving rise to a mind dwelling in form, not giving rise to a mind dwelling in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas — giving rise to a mind abiding nowhere," fully conforming to this program, and so his results were outstanding. He had already reached the state of
never apart from self-nature, this is the field of merit
Huineng withdrew to the back courtyard. There was a certain lay-worker who assigned Huineng to split wood and tread the pestle, and this continued for more than eight months.

I withdrew to the back courtyard, and a certain lay-worker assigned me to split firewood and tread the pestle to pound rice; and so it was for more than eight months. (The passage above says that East Chan Temple had more than a thousand disciples alone, so one can see that the daily demand for firewood and rice was very great.)
[Lay-worker] A person who lives at a monastery but retains his hair and practices.

One day the Patriarch suddenly saw Huineng and said: I think your insight is useful, but I feared that evil men might do you harm, so I did not speak to you. Do you know this? Huineng said: Your disciple also knows the Master's intent, and so dared not go before the hall, so that no one might notice.

One day the Fifth Patriarch suddenly saw me and said: I consider your insight quite commendable, but I feared that evil men, out of jealousy, might do you harm, so I have not spoken plainly to you. Do you know this? I replied: Your disciple too knows the Master's intent, and so has not dared to come before the Dharma hall, so that no one might take notice. (The teacher and disciple were of one accord, concealing their brightness and nurturing their practice. How lamentable!)
[Dharma hall] Other schools call it the lecture hall; the Chan school calls it the Dharma hall — the hall where the great Dharma is expounded
Question: What is the "insight" of which the Fifth Patriarch spoke when he said, "I think your insight is useful"?

Answer: It is precisely: "I seek only to become a Buddha, and nothing else." "Though people are from north and south, the Buddha-nature is fundamentally without north or south; though the body of a barbarian differs from that of a monk, what difference is there in the Buddha-nature?" "In this disciple's own mind wisdom is constantly arising; never apart from self-nature, this is the field of merit."

One day the Patriarch summoned all his disciples together. I tell you: for people in this world the matter of birth and death is great. You spend all day only seeking merit, and do not seek to escape the sea of birth-and-death suffering. If the self-nature is deluded, how can merit save you?

One day the Fifth Patriarch summoned all his disciples, and instructed them: "I tell you, ending birth and death is the foremost concern of life. But you all, day and night, practice grasping at marks, and what you gain is only human and heavenly blessings. If the self-nature is deluded, how can the merit you cultivate save you from the sea of birth-and-death suffering?"

"If the self-nature is deluded, how can merit save you?" Therefore the essential point of practice is awakening, is seeing the nature and eradicating residual habits — this is the road to ending birth and death.

Go each of you and contemplate your own wisdom, and, taking the prajñā-nature of your own mind as your theme, make for yourselves a verse and bring it to show me. If you have awakened to the general purport, I will transmit you the robe and the Dharma, and make you the Sixth Patriarch. Go quickly, and do not delay
To produce it by conscious reflection is useless. A man who sees the nature must see it on the instant
For one such as this, even in the midst of drawing a sword in battle, he can see the nature.

You each go back and contemplate your own wisdom, and, with the nature (the prajñā-nature of the original mind) as your subject, each compose a verse and bring it to show me. If any has awakened to the essential purport of the Dharma, I will transmit to him the robe and the Dharma, making him the Sixth Patriarch of the Chan lineage. Go quickly, do not tarry! When composing the verse, pondering and deliberating over it is of no use: one who sees the nature, when it is said, sees it immediately (he must see it on the instant). Such a person, even in the midst of advancing into battle, can see the nature.

[If you have awakened to the general purport] If you have awakened to the general purport of the Buddha-Dharma. "The general purport of the Buddha-Dharma," like "the Patriarch's meaning in coming from the West," "the meaning of coming from the West," and "the Patriarch's meaning," all express the profound purport of the Buddha-Dharma and the true marrow of Chan principle. [The Patriarch's meaning in coming from the West] The First Patriarch of Chan, Bodhidharma, came from the West to China to transmit Chan; this is the mind-seal of the Buddhas and patriarchs, called "the Patriarch's coming from the West." [Mind-seal] Mind is the Buddha-mind; seal means confirmation and affirmation. Chan does not rely on written words or on speech; it transmits mind with mind, sealing the minds of beings with the Buddha-mind, so that the non-dual mark is realized. [Robe and Dharma] "Robe" refers to the monk's kashaya; "Dharma" refers to the right Dharma. Inwardly it transmits the Dharma to confirm the Buddha-mind purport of the school; outwardly it transmits the robe to signify the truthfulness of the lineage. [Must see it on the instant] When one can see, one sees — that is, one can see at any moment. Later the Fifth Patriarch said to Shenxiu: "Supreme bodhi requires that upon the hearing of the words one recognize one's own mind, see one's own nature as neither arising nor ceasing, and at all times, in every thought, see it oneself, so that all dharmas are without obstruction." [The prajñā-nature of one's own mind] One's original nature. [Prajñā] A Sanskrit word meaning wisdom, but not the cleverness of the world — rather, the wondrous wisdom that penetrates to the true nature of life and the universe; the right wisdom of self-nature. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom
volume seventy-four, says: "Prajñā is the mother of all the Buddhas; abiding in this prajñā, one is able to fulfill all the Buddha-dharmas." [On the instant] At a single word; instantly.
Question: What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West?

Answer: It is what Huineng's verse below says: "originally there was not a single thing." The great master Hanshan said: "Therefore Huangmei (the Fifth Patriarch Hongren) used this (the Diamond Sutra) to seal the mind, because it establishes not a single dharma — this is the right eye of the school." (From his Inscription to the Diamond Sutra, Resolving Doubts.)

The assembly having received the instruction, withdrew and said among themselves: We people have no need to clarify our minds and use our intention to compose verses to present to the Master; what use would it serve? The senior seat Shenxiu is now our professor; surely he will obtain it. If we recklessly make verses, we only waste our energy. Hearing these words, everyone altogether abandoned the idea, all saying: From now on we will rely on Master Shenxiu — why bother composing verses?

When the assembly heard the Fifth Patriarch's instruction, they withdrew and discussed it together, saying: We have no need to clarify our minds and deliberately compose verses to submit to the Master, because it would be wasted effort. The senior seat Shenxiu is at present our professor; he will surely be the one to obtain the robe and the Dharma. If people such as we, lacking discretion, recklessly composed verses, it would be a futile exertion of mind. Hearing these reports, they all cast aside the intention of composing verses, and said: We shall rely on Master Shenxiu from now on — why labor to compose verses?
[Professor] The instructor of deportment and rites who teaches the disciples. [From now on] The same as "hereafter."

Shenxiu reflected: The reason the others do not present verses is that I am their professor. I must compose a verse and present it to the Master; if I do not present it, how will the Master know whether my insight is deep or shallow? If I present a verse and my intent is to seek the Dharma, this is good; if my intent is to seek the patriarchate, then it is evil — and how would that differ from an ordinary man who covets the holy seat? Yet if I do not present a verse, I shall never obtain the Dharma. How hard! How hard!

Shenxiu reflected alone: The reason the others do not present a verse is that they hold me in esteem as their professor. I must compose a verse and present it to the Master; if I do not present it, how can the Master know the depth or shallowness of my insight? If I present a verse and my intent is to seek the Dharma, that is right; if my intent is to gain the patriarchate, then it is most evil — what difference would there be between that and an ordinary person's coveting the holy seat? Yet if I do not present a verse, the Master will not know my insight, and how could I ever receive the Master's teaching? How hard! How hard! (The purity of Shenxiu's virtue can be glimpsed in this.)

[To seek the Dharma is good] Here "good" means an action that is wholesome. [Evil] Here "evil" means an action that is most unwholesome. [How hard] Too difficult. Here the character "da" was anciently interchangeable with "tai" and should be read "tai."

Before the Fifth Patriarch's hall there was a corridor of three rooms, and he intended to have the court painter Lu Zhen paint the illustrated scenes of the Lankavatara Sutra and the lineage-chart of the five patriarchs, so that they might be circulated and honored.

Before the Fifth Patriarch's Dharma hall there was a corridor of three rooms. He intended to have the court painter Lu Zhen paint the illustrated scenes of the Lankavatara Sutra, as well as the lineage-chart of the five patriarchs of the Chan school, so that they might be circulated and honored.

[Corridor] A covered walkway. [Court painter] One who serves the emperor with a particular craft. [Lankavatara Sutra] There are three Chinese translations of the Lankavatara Sutra: First, the four-volume Lankavatara Sutra translated by Gunabhadra of the Liu Song

) (full title, the Lankavatara Ratna Sutra), also called the four-volume Lankavatara Sutra or the Song translation. Second, the ten-volume Lankavatara Sutra translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei
(roughly the fifth
-sixth
centuries), also called the ten-volume Lankavatara Sutra or the Wei translation. Third, the seven-volume Mahayana Lankavatara Sutra translated by Siksananda of the Tang

), also called the seven-volume Lankavatara Sutra or the Tang translation. Of these, the four-volume Lankavatara Sutra translated by the Tripitaka master Gunabhadra of India during the Liu Song is the one the First Patriarch Bodhidharma entrusted to the Second Patriarch Huike, and so from ancient times it has been particularly esteemed by the Chan school. The Patriarch Bodhidharma said: "I see that in the land of Han there is only this sutra; if the good rely upon it and practice, they will themselves attain liberation." Thus the Lankavatara Sutra became the essential mind of Chan.
