But later people, concerning the Lankavatara Sutra, "entered the sea to count the sand and did not seek the treasure," searching among the numerous names and terms instead of practicing earnestly; and since the Fifth Patriarch began expounding the Diamond Sutra, Chan gradually took the Diamond Sutra as its essential mind of practice.
[Liu Song] (

) was a regime of the Southern dynasties during the Northern and Southern period, historically called the Liu Song or Southern Song to distinguish it from the later Song of the Zhao family (the Zhao Song). [India] In ancient times India was called "India." [Illustrated scenes] Rendering the stories of the sutras in the form of painting, relief, or sculpture. [Lineage-chart] A chart of the transmission-lineage of the successive patriarchs.

Shenxiu, having composed his verse, several times wished to present it. He walked up to the front of the hall, his mind in a daze, sweat streaming over his body; though he wished to present it, he could not. In all, over four days, thirteen times, he failed to present it. Shenxiu then reflected: It would be better to write it on the corridor wall, and let the Master see it for himself. Should he happen to praise it, I will come forth and bow, saying it was I who wrote it; but if he says it is not acceptable, then I have but wasted these years cultivating in the mountains, and been revered by people besides — then what Way is there further to cultivate?

Shenxiu, having finished his verse, went several times to present it. But each time he reached the front of the Dharma hall, his mind was in a daze, and sweat streamed over his whole body, so that he could not present it. After four days in all, having gone thirteen times, he hesitated and turned back each time without presenting it. Then he thought to himself: better to write it on the wall of the corridor, and let the Master see it for himself. If he says it is good, I will come out, bow, and acknowledge that I made it; if the Master says this verse is not acceptable, then I have wasted these years studying on East Mountain and been honored by people besides — what Way am I then cultivating?
[Sweat streaming] The same as "streaming everywhere."

That night, at the third watch, without letting anyone know, he took up a lamp himself and wrote the verse on the south wall of the corridor, presenting what his mind had seen. The verse said: The body is the bodhi tree, the mind a bright-mirror stand; ever diligently wipe and dust it, and let no dust alight.

That night at the third watch, without anyone knowing, Shenxiu quietly took up a lamp and wrote his verse on the south wall of the corridor, presenting what his own mind had seen. The verse says: The body is the bodhi tree, the mind a bright-mirror stand; ever diligently wipe and dust it, and let no dust alight.

The meaning of this verse is: the body (conduct) should be upright and bright like the bodhi tree, and the mind (thought) should be crystal-bright like the bright mirror on the dressing stand; at all times and places one should wipe away the evil of body, speech, and mind, and not let oneself be defiled by worldly toil.

[Bodhi tree] Originally named the "pippala tree," so called because Śākyamuni Buddha realized the Way beneath it, hence also the "bodhi tree." [Mirror stand] A dressing stand on which a mirror is mounted.

Having written his verse, Shenxiu went back to his room, and no one knew anything of it. Shenxiu reflected further: If tomorrow the Fifth Patriarch sees the verse and is pleased, then I have a connection with the Dharma; if he says it is not acceptable, then it is I who am still deluded, and the karma of past lives weighs heavy — I am not fit to obtain the Dharma. The holy mind of the patriarch is hard to fathom! Thinking thus in his room, he was restless sitting and lying, until the fifth watch.

Shenxiu finished writing the verse and returned to his quarters; none of the assembly knew of it. He reflected alone again: If tomorrow the Fifth Patriarch sees the verse and is delighted, then I have an affinity with the Dharma; if the Patriarch says this verse is no good, then I am still deluded and unawakened, and the evil karma I created in past lives is a heavy hindrance — I am not worthy to attain the Dharma. The holy mind of the patriarch is hard to fathom, and I do not know how it will turn out! Thinking it over in his room, he was restless sitting and lying, until the fifth watch.
[Not acceptable] No good. "Khan," able. [Karma of past lives] The karma created in past lives.

blocks.text: 4. The Fifth Patriarch Sees the Verse

inline.s: The Patriarch already knew that Shenxiu had not yet entered the gate and had not seen his own nature. At daybreak, the Patriarch summoned the Painter Lu, intending to have him paint the illustrated scenes on the south wall of the corridor and the lineage-chart of the five patriarchs; then he suddenly noticed this verse on the wall, and abandoning the idea of painting, said to the Painter Lu: Painter! There is no need to paint now; I am sorry for the trouble of your long journey. The Sutra says: "All marks are false and vain." Let this verse remain, for people to recite and uphold. Practicing in accordance with this verse, one avoids falling into evil destinies; practicing in accordance with this verse brings great benefit. He then had his disciples: burn incense and bow in reverence, and said: recite this verse with all your hearts, and you will see the nature. The disciples recited the verse, all exclaiming: Excellent!

The Fifth Patriarch had already known that Shenxiu had not entered the gate, not seen his own nature. At daybreak, the Fifth Patriarch summoned the Painter Lu, intending to have him paint the illustrated scenes of the Lankavatara Sutra and the lineage-chart of the five patriarchs on the south wall of the corridor. Then he suddenly saw this verse on the wall, and gave up the plan to paint, saying to the Painter Lu: Painter! There is no need to paint now; I am indeed sorry that you have come such a distance on my account. The Diamond Sutra says: "All marks are false and vain." Let this verse stay on the wall, and have the assembly recite and uphold it. Practicing in accordance with this verse, one avoids falling into evil destinies; practicing in accordance with this verse brings great benefit. Thereupon he bade the disciples burn incense and bow in homage, and said, carefully recite this verse, and you will see the nature. The disciples all recited the verse and exclaimed: how well it is written!

With all their hearts recite this verse, and you will see the nature" — this is what the Fifth Patriarch said expediently in accordance with the faculties of the disciples, making them recite and uphold it so that they would not fall into evil destinies.

At the third watch that night the Patriarch summoned Shenxiu into the hall and asked: Is this verse yours? Shenxiu said: It was indeed made by Shenxiu. I dare not vainly seek the patriarchate; I only hope the Master will be compassionate and see whether this disciple has a little wisdom.

The Fifth Patriarch knew in his heart what state Shenxiu was in, and knew that this verse was made by Shenxiu. So that night at the third watch he summoned him into the Dharma hall and asked: Is this verse yours? Shenxiu replied: Indeed it was made by your disciple. Your disciple dares not vainly seek the patriarchate; I only hope the Master, in his compassion, will see whether this disciple has any wisdom at all.

The Patriarch said: In writing this verse you have not yet seen the nature; you have only reached the door, not yet entered within. With such an understanding, seeking supreme bodhi is utterly in vain. Supreme bodhi requires that upon the hearing of the words one recognize one's own mind and see one's own nature as neither arising nor ceasing, and at all times, in every thought, see it oneself, so that all dharmas are without obstruction. One truth, then all is true; all realms are as they truly are. The mind of suchness is itself the real. If you see in this way, this is the self-nature of supreme bodhi. Go and reflect for a day or two, and make another verse, and bring it for me to see. If your verse has entered the gate, I will transmit you the robe and the Dharma.

The Fifth Patriarch said: This verse you have made has not yet seen the nature; you have reached only the door, not yet entered within. With such an understanding to seek supreme bodhi is utterly impossible! To seek supreme bodhi, one must in the present instant penetrate the state of the original mind, see one's own nature as neither arising nor ceasing, and at all times see it thus in thought after thought. Hence, with regard to all things, one is not deluded or attached (all dharmas without obstruction). When self-nature awakens (one truth), one clearly sees the true state of all dharmas (all is true) — all are illusions. When the myriad realms appear, the mind naturally is thus, still and unmoved; and this thus-mind is the real. If one sees it thus in thought after thought, this is the thoroughly awakened self-nature (the self-nature of supreme bodhi). Go back, and for a day or two carefully contemplate my words, then make another verse and bring it for me to see. If your verse has entered the gate (seen the nature), I will transmit you the robe and the Dharma.

[Neither arising nor ceasing] What Buddhism means by "neither arising nor ceasing" is that all things are illusory and never existed at all. This was already explained in the earlier chapter on "Fundamental Knowledge." [Supreme bodhi] That is, anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, rendered in Chinese as the supreme right and equal awakening, the supreme wisdom that truly and equally awakens to all truths. [All dharmas without obstruction] Here "obstruction" means taking the illusory and unreal dharmas (things and phenomena) to be real and being deluded within them. "All dharmas without obstruction" means passing through every realm and circumstance, not being turned by marks; not abiding in, not defiled by, any dharma. In the Sutra of the World-Holding, chapter three, the Eighteen Natures, the Buddha said: "Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions, without reality, without root." In the Great Prajñā-paramita Sutra, volume 341, the Buddha said: "All dharmas are empty." [All dharmas] Also called "the various dharmas"; the general name for all things, matters, principles, and phenomena. [Recognize one's own mind, see one's own nature] The Record of the Mirror of the School says: "A student asked: What is called 'recognizing the mind and seeing the nature'? Answer: It is like a dream of night, in which one sees good and evil. If one knows the body is sleeping soundly in bed, with not a trace of sorrow or joy, this is 'recognizing the mind and seeing the nature.'" [One truth, then all is true] That is: one truth, therefore all is true. "One truth" means seeing the nature; "all is true" means that one who sees the nature clearly sees the true state of all things.
This instruction of the Fifth Patriarch is in fact the essential mind of Chan; it is a pity that Shenxiu did not awaken.
Shenxiu bowed and withdrew. Several days passed, and he made no verse; his mind was in a daze and his spirit uneasy, as if in a dream, unhappy whether sitting or walking.

Shenxiu bowed and withdrew. After several more days of effort, he still had not seen the nature and could not compose a verse; his mind was in a daze, his spirit restless and ill at ease, as if in a dream, unhappy whether walking or sitting.

According to records, in his youth Shenxiu read widely in the classics and histories. At nineteen he received the full precepts at Tiangang Temple in Luoyang, and at fifty he went to East Chan Temple at Huangmei in Qizhou to pay his respects to the Fifth Patriarch Hongren, engaging in such labors as chopping firewood and drawing water. He sought the Dharma with bitter toil, diligent and unremitting, and the Fifth Patriarch likewise held him in deep esteem, making him the professor; because he ranked first among the disciples, he was called the Senior Shenxiu.

With Shenxiu's learning and more than thirty years of cultivation, he could of course understand the Fifth Patriarch's instruction, and making a verse accordingly was no difficulty. The problem lies in the fact that "recognizing one's own mind and seeing one's own nature" is not intellectual understanding but immediate perception, a state, a skill. Shenxiu was absolutely unwilling to make a verse from mere understanding (making a verse with a thieving mind, claiming realization when one has not realized, is a great taboo for a cultivator); what the verse spoke of had to be a state personally realized. "Several days passed, and he made no verse" means that though Shenxiu received the Fifth Patriarch's instruction and exhausted his efforts, he was still unable to see his own nature accordingly; hence "he made no verse; his mind was in a daze and his spirit uneasy, as if in a dream, unhappy whether sitting or walking."
[Immediate perception] Direct knowing is called "immediate perception"; inferential knowing is called "inferential perception."
Question: The passage above is the Sixth Patriarch relating the dialogue between the Fifth Patriarch and Shenxiu, and Shenxiu's state of mind at the time — how could the Sixth Patriarch know it?

Answer: The Sixth Patriarch knew it all through the supernormal power of knowing past lives. Judging from the principles, methods, and states of practice set forth in the Platform Sutra, the Sixth Patriarch's own attainment, and the achievements of the disciples, the Sixth Patriarch had realized the fruit of Buddhahood, so all six supernormal powers were operative.

Two more days passed, when a young boy passed by the rice-hulling shed, intoning this verse. The moment Huineng heard it, he knew this verse had not seen the nature. Though he had not yet been taught by the Fifth Patriarch, he had long recognized the general purport. Then he asked the boy: What verse is it you are reciting?

Two more days passed, when a young boy passed by the rice-hulling shed, singing Shenxiu's verse. The moment I heard it, I knew this verse had not seen the nature; though I had not yet been taught by the Fifth Patriarch, I had long recognized the essential purport of the Dharma. So I asked the boy: What verse is it you are reciting?

The boy said: You southern barbarian do not know. The Master said: For people in this world the matter of birth and death is great; wishing to transmit the robe and the Dharma, he had the disciples make verses for him to see. If any had awakened to the general purport, he would transmit him the robe and the Dharma, making him the Sixth Patriarch. The Senior Shenxiu wrote a markless verse on the south wall of the corridor, and the Master has everyone recite it. Practicing in accordance with this verse, one avoids falling into evil destinies; practicing in accordance with this verse brings great benefit.

The boy said: You southern barbarian, you do not know. The Fifth Patriarch said: for people in this world the matter of birth and death is great; wishing to transmit the robe and the Dharma, he had the disciples make verses for him to see; if any had awakened to the essential purport of the Dharma, he would transmit him the robe and the Dharma, making him the Sixth Patriarch of the Chan lineage. This is the markless verse that the Senior Shenxiu wrote on the south wall of the corridor, and the Master has commanded everyone to recite it, saying: practice in accordance with this verse, and you avoid falling into evil destinies; practice in accordance with this verse, and you gain great benefit.

Huineng said: I too wish to recite this, to form a bond for a future life, and to be born together in the Buddha-land. Teacher! In these more than eight months treading the pestle, I have never walked to the front of the hall; I hope the Teacher will lead me before the verse to bow.

I said: I too wish to recite this verse, to form an affinity for a future life and be born together in the Buddha-land. Teacher! In the more than eight months I have been here treading the pestle to hull rice, I have never come before the Dharma hall, and do not know the way; I ask the Teacher to lead me before the verse to bow.
[Teacher] A person of superior virtue. In the Buddha-gate, it is the respectful appellation for a bhikkhu. That Huineng here addresses a young novice as Teacher shows his humility and respect.

The boy led him before the verse to bow. Huineng said: Huineng cannot read; I ask the Teacher to read it for me. At the time there was a Vice-Magistrate of Jiangzhou, surnamed Zhang, named Riyong, who read it aloud in a loud voice.

The boy led me before the verse to bow. I said: Huineng cannot read; I beg the Teacher to read it for me. At that time there was a Vice-Magistrate of Jiangzhou, surnamed Zhang, named Riyong, who read it aloud.
[Vice-Magistrate] An assistant official to a prefectural governor.

Huineng, having heard it, then said: I also have a verse, and I hope the Vice-Magistrate will write it for me. The Vice-Magistrate said: You too can make a verse — a rare thing indeed! Huineng said to the Vice-Magistrate: If you would learn supreme bodhi, you must not slight a beginner. A person of the very lowest station may have the highest wisdom; a person of the very highest station may be stunted in wisdom. If you slight others, you commit immeasurable, boundless offenses. The Vice-Magistrate said: Just recite your verse, and I will write it for you. If you obtain the Dharma, you must be the first to ferry me across; do not forget these words.

Having heard this verse, I then said: I too have a verse, and I hope the Vice-Magistrate will write it on the wall for me. Vice-Magistrate Zhang said: You can make a verse too — a rare thing indeed! I then said to Vice-Magistrate Zhang: One who would learn supreme bodhi must not slight a beginner. A person of the very lowest, humblest station may yet possess the highest wisdom; a person of the very highest, most noble station may yet be dull and deluded. If you slight people, you commit immeasurable, boundless offenses. Hearing this, Vice-Magistrate Zhang was at once startled into awareness, and said: Now recite your verse, and I will write it for you. If you obtain the Dharma, you must be the first to ferry me across; do not forget today's words.
[Stunted] Without reason, senseless.
Huineng's verse said: Bodhi is originally without a tree; the bright mirror is no stand either; originally there is not a single thing; where could dust alight?

Then I recited: Originally there was no bodhi tree, and no bright-mirror stand either; originally there is not a single thing — where could dust alight? (The bodhi tree is a metaphor for the body, the bright-mirror stand for the mind.)

Bodhi is originally without a tree; the bright mirror is no stand either" is an inverted construction, to strengthen the tone. Its normal order is: originally there is no bodhi tree, and no bright-mirror stand either. The meaning is: body and mind are illusions, they do not exist at all; how could there be any defilement of body and mind? The Diamond Sutra says: "All marks are false and vain." In the Sutra of the Buddha-Treasure

chapter two, the Buddha-recitation chapter, the Buddha said: "What are called the real marks of all dharmas? So-called the various dharmas, ultimately empty, nothing at all." So "originally there is not a single thing" is precisely the real mark of all dharmas. When the mind does not vainly move, all realms cease.

What the Fifth Patriarch asked for was a verse taking "the prajñā-nature of one's own mind (one's original nature)" as its theme, but Shenxiu, not having seen the nature, had written a verse depicting the state of one who has not yet seen the nature. Huineng's verse, aimed at where Shenxiu's verse fell short, reveals the state of seeing the nature. The Diamond Sutra says: "If you see that the marks are not marks, then you see the Tathagata." (If, upon seeing the marks, you know they are illusion and at once leave them, then the realm is still and the mind empty, and in the present instant you see the nature.)

Comparing these two verses, one knows that the general purport of the Buddha-Dharma (the essential purport) is: awaken to and break through the dream of delusion. The reason there is "defilement" is delusion and inversion, vainly seeing flowers in the sky. Hence the fundamental method of liberation is not to remove defilement, but to awaken to and break through the dream of delusion — this is the sudden method. This is to cultivate at the root, like felling a poisonous tree: cut its root directly, rather than plucking its leaves. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "Knowing it is illusion, you are at once free, without need of expedient means; free of illusion, you are at once awakened, with no gradual steps." The Song of Realizing the Way of the Great Master Yongjia says: "Directly severing the root is what the Buddha seals; plucking leaves and seeking branches I cannot do." "Awaken, and it is done, with no effort applied." So the sudden teaching is to awaken to the fact that body, mind, and the dusty realms are illusion, and not to be turned by them! It is not, within the dream of delusion, to remove defilement and seek purity.

[Inverted construction] A rhetorical device that reverses the word order to strengthen the tone, harmonize the rhythm, or complicate the syntax. [Flowers in the sky] In Buddhism a common metaphor for illusions. "Flowers in the sky" means flowers in the air. A person with an eye disease sees flowers in the sky; the void originally has no flowers, they are only the diseased eye's hallucination. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "Deludedly taking the four elements as one's own body, and the shadow-images of the six sense-objects as one's own mind — like that diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon." The Transmission of the Lamp says: "When a single film covers the eye, the flowers in the sky fall in confusion."

The verses of Shenxiu and Huineng represent the two great paths of practice: the gradual teaching and the sudden teaching. The gradual teaching is "ever diligently wipe and dust it" — purifying defilement within concrete marks, gradually liberating oneself. The sudden teaching is awakening to the fact that all dharmas are illusion ("originally there is not a single thing"), and not being turned by them, thus liberating oneself at once.

The sudden teaching has sudden awakening with sudden cultivation, and sudden awakening with gradual cultivation. Of these, sudden awakening with sudden cultivation is fit only for those of the highest faculties (those whose delusions and habitual tendencies are very thin), who take it up directly; ordinary people should use sudden awakening with gradual cultivation, that is, take the principle of sudden awakening ("originally there is not a single thing") as the power of contemplation, to break attachments and eradicate habits, refining the mind amid circumstances. Like felling a poisonous tree: cut its root directly, rather than plucking its leaves. Its guiding principle is: "see one's own nature, and realize Buddhahood by seeing the nature." (Note: "realize Buddhahood by seeing the nature" means first see the nature, then cultivate in reliance on the nature, so as to accomplish the Buddha Way; it does not mean that upon seeing the nature one is at once a Buddha.) The advantage of "first see the nature, then cultivate in reliance on the nature" is: one clearly sees the road (so as not to practice blindly), the power of cultivation is great (because it is the functioning of the bodhi self-nature), it is direct and straightforward, and one transcends in a single leap. In the Platform Sutra the Sixth Patriarch systematically sets forth the principle and method of sudden awakening with gradual cultivation; this is the point to grasp in studying the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch!
Nothing originally at all" is speaking of the real mark of all dharmas. In the Sutra of the Buddha-Treasure

chapter two, the Buddha-recitation chapter, the Buddha said: "What are called the real marks of all dharmas? So-called the various dharmas, ultimately empty, nothing at all." In the Sutra of the Buddha-Treasure
chapter one, the Real Marks of All Dharmas, it says: "All dharmas have no nature; empty, nothing at all." In the Sutra of the World-Holding
chapter three, the Eighteen Natures, the Buddha said: "Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions, without reality, without root." In the Great Prajñā-paramita Sutra
volume 341, the Buddha said: "All dharmas are empty."

Nothing originally at all" is the contemplation of emptiness on the very substance. Body and mind, and the dusty realms, are all matters within the dream of ignorance, empty on the very substance. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "All sentient beings from beginningless time, in all manner of inversion, are like a deluded man who mistakes the four quarters: deludedly taking the four elements as the mark of one's own body, and the shadow-images of the six sense-objects as the mark of one's own mind. It is like that diseased eye seeing flowers in space and a second moon." The Diamond Sutra says: "All marks are false and vain; if you see that the marks are not marks, then you see the Tathagata."

Body and mind are illusion" is the very basis of practice for escaping the three realms. If one does not break through this barrier and yet speaks grandiosely of cultivation, it all becomes idle talk; the patriarchs call this blind practice and deluded cultivation. If after many years of bitter practice the effort still gains no power, and there is not a trace of progress, one should begin here.
Question: It is said that the verse "originally there is not a single thing" is the annihilationist view of the emptiness of all dharmas. Is that so?

Answer: That view is mistaken. This sutra writes that the Fifth Patriarch "had the disciples make verses for him to see; if any had awakened to the general purport, he would transmit him the robe and the Dharma, making him the Sixth Patriarch." Huineng's verse was made in accordance with the requirement to "awaken to the general purport (the essential purport of the Buddha-Dharma)," and was confirmed by the Fifth Patriarch, who at the third watch transmitted the Dharma. One must pay special attention to the two words "originally" and "at all" in "originally there is not a single thing" — this says that dharmas have a mark but no substance, and does not so much as deny their having a mark. How then can it be called an annihilationist view?
In the Sutra of the Buddha-Treasure

chapter two, the Buddha-recitation chapter, the Buddha said: "What are called the real marks of all dharmas? So-called the various dharmas, ultimately empty, nothing at all." And "originally there is not a single thing" is saying: "all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing at all." So "originally there is not a single thing" is speaking of the real mark of all dharmas: though the dharmas are a myriad and manifold, in the final analysis they do not truly exist — "ultimately empty, nothing at all." The real mark is the seal transmitted from Buddha to Buddha from the beginning, and so it is called the real-mark seal. All the lesser-vehicle sutras are sealed with the three dharma-seals (the seal that all compounded things are impermanent, the seal that all dharmas are without self, and the seal that nirvāṇa is still); all the greater-vehicle sutras are sealed with this real-mark seal. The Lotus Sutra
chapter one, the Introductory chapter, says: "I adorn my body with marks, and illuminate the world with light; revered by immeasurable beings, I expound the real-mark seal to them."
Moreover, "all dharmas are empty," "the various dharmas are empty" — these are the Buddha's own words. How then can they be called an annihilationist view?! In the Great Prajñā-paramita Sutra

volume 341, the Buddha said: "Again, Subhuti (the Chinese rendering of Subhuti), if the great bodhisattva studies thus, he is studying inner emptiness; he is studying outer emptiness, both-inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, supreme emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, ultimate emptiness, beginningless emptiness, scattered emptiness, unvarying emptiness, original-nature emptiness, self-mark emptiness, common-mark emptiness,
all-dharmas emptiness

(i.e. emptiness of all dharmas), unattainable emptiness, natureless emptiness, self-nature emptiness, natureless self-nature emptiness. If the great bodhisattva studies inner emptiness, outer emptiness, up to natureless self-nature emptiness, he is studying the all-knowledge" In the Sutra of the World-Holding
chapter three, the Eighteen Natures, the Buddha said: "Know that
all dharmas are empty
(the emptiness of all dharmas), like illusions, without reality, without root."
In the Lotus Sutra

chapter fourteen, the Peaceful Conduct chapter, the Buddha said: "The great bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, in accord with the real mark — not inverted, not moving, not regressing, not turning." The Buddha further said: "
all the various dharmas, empty, nothing at all
" — "there is not a single thing that is permanent, nor arising nor ceasing; this is called the place the wise draw near."

Having written this verse, the assembly was all astonished, none not sighing in admiration, and each said to the other: How strange! One must not judge people by their looks. In so short a time he has become a bodhisattva in the flesh. The Patriarch, seeing the assembly marvel and wonder, and fearing that harm might befall the boy, wiped the verse away with his shoe, saying: this too has not seen the nature. The assembly took this to be so.

Vice-Magistrate Zhang having written this verse, the disciples were all taken aback, and none failed to sigh. They said to one another: What a wonder! We truly should not have judged him by his appearance — in only a few months he has become a bodhisattva in the flesh. The Fifth Patriarch, seeing the assembly marvel and wonder, and fearing that I might be harmed by evil people, wiped the verse away with the sole of his shoe, saying: he too has not seen the nature. The assembly all took the Fifth Patriarch's word to be right — how could it be so easy to see the nature!
[Bodhisattva in the flesh] A person who, with the present physical body, reaches a deep stage of bodhisattvahood.

In fact, Huineng's verse did see the nature, and was acknowledged by the Fifth Patriarch; otherwise there would have been no secret visit the next day and transmission at the third watch, for the Fifth Patriarch announced at the outset that the requirement of this verse-making was "if you have awakened to the general purport, I will transmit you the robe and the Dharma, making you the Sixth Patriarch." The reason the Fifth Patriarch wiped the verse with his shoe and falsely said, "this too has not seen the nature," was to protect Huineng from harm by evil people (the sutra text says "fearing that harm might befall him"). And so, after transmitting the Dharma, he told Huineng: "You must go quickly, for I fear others may do you harm." This was not unfounded worry on the Fifth Patriarch's part; in fact, after Huineng fled, several hundred people gave chase, and even set fire to the mountain.

blocks.text: 6. Transmitting the Dharma at the Third Watch

inline.s: The next day, the Patriarch came secretly to the rice-hulling shed, and seeing Huineng pounding rice with a stone bound to his waist, said: One who seeks the Way should forget his body for the sake of the Dharma — is it not so! Then he asked: Is the rice ready yet? Huineng said: It has long been ready! It only awaits sifting. The Patriarch tapped the pestle three times with his staff and left.

The next day, the Fifth Patriarch came secretly to the rice-hulling shed. Seeing a large stone bound to my waist as I pounded rice, he could not help sighing and saying: One who seeks the Way, forgetting his body for the Dharma, could go to such bitter lengths! Then he asked: Is the rice ready yet? (A veiled question: is your practice ripe?) I replied: It has long been ready! It still needs the husks sifted away. (A veiled answer: I am long since ripe; please, Master, lead me up to the next stage.) The Fifth Patriarch then tapped the pestle three times with his staff and left. (A veiled direction: come to me at the third watch of night!)

Huineng's state at this time was that of seeing the nature and breaking through the first barrier: he recognized true emptiness and spoke of "originally there is not a single thing," breaking through the "having" (existence); but there was still something obstructing him, hence "it still awaits sifting." At the third watch, when the Fifth Patriarch expounded the Diamond Sutra for him, he had great awakening on the spot, recognized wondrous existence, and spoke of "how unexpected that self-nature can give rise to all dharmas," and so emptiness and existence merged together, and he broke through the second barrier. Later he took refuge among the hunters, and after fifteen years of refining his mind amid circumstances, when the Way was accomplished and he came down from the mountain, he was already in non-dual stillness and illumination, with emptiness and existence no obstruction — he had broken through the final barrier.

[Rice-hulling shed] The workshop where rice is hulled. "Dui," a tool of wood and stone for pounding rice; when the pestle falls it strikes the grain in the stone mortar, separating the kernel from the husk. [Pounding rice with a stone bound to his waist] In ancient times hulling large quantities of rice made use of the lever principle: at one end the pestle, at the other a person stepping on it. Huineng bound a large stone at his waist to add weight, so that the counterweight at the pestle end could be heavier, thus increasing the efficiency of hulling.

Huineng immediately understood the Patriarch's intent, and that night at the third watch entered the room. The Patriarch, covering the windows with his kashaya so that no one might see, expounded the Diamond Sutra for him. When he came to "should give rise to a mind abiding nowhere," Huineng had great awakening on the spot: all the myriad dharmas are without departing from self-nature.

I at once understood the Master's intent, and so that night at the third watch entered the Master's room (the abbot's quarters). The Fifth Patriarch completely covered the windows with his kashaya so that no one could see, and expounded the Diamond Sutra for me. When he came to "should give rise to a mind abiding nowhere," I suddenly had great awakening: it turns out that all the myriad dharmas are the functioning of self-nature.

[The third watch] That is, midnight. [All the myriad dharmas are without departing from self-nature] All the myriad dharmas are the functioning of self-nature. For example, chapter six, the Repentance chapter, says: "The nature of people is originally pure; all dharmas arise from self-nature. Thinking of all evil things, one gives rise to evil conduct; thinking of all good things, one gives rise to good conduct." In chapter ten, the Entrustment chapter, the Sixth Patriarch says: "If (self-nature) gives rise to thinking, that is the turning of consciousness; it gives rise to the six consciousnesses, issues through the six gates, and perceives the six objects; and in this way the eighteen realms all arise from the functioning of self-nature."

Huineng's great awakening was not only upon the phrase "should give rise to a mind abiding nowhere" in the Diamond Sutra, but from the beginning of the sutra through to "should give rise to a mind abiding nowhere." What did he awaken to? He awakened to this: it turns out it was all a dream of ignorance; the myriad dharmas are like illusions, all arising from the mind. How to get out of the dream? Leave the marks! How to leave the marks? "You should give rise to a pure mind in this manner: not giving rise to a mind dwelling in form, not giving rise to a mind dwelling in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas — giving rise to a mind abiding nowhere." The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch sets forth these points and indicates how to practice them.

Then he addressed the Patriarch, saying: How unexpected that self-nature is originally pure! How unexpected that self-nature is originally neither arising nor ceasing! How unexpected that self-nature is originally complete! How unexpected that self-nature is originally without movement! How unexpected that self-nature can give rise to all dharmas!

Thereupon I reported to the Fifth Patriarch: How unexpected that self-nature is originally pure! How unexpected that self-nature is originally without arising or ceasing! How unexpected that self-nature is originally endowed with all virtues! How unexpected that self-nature is originally without movement! How unexpected that self-nature can give rise to all dharmas! At this, Huineng had awakened to true emptiness and also conformed to wondrous existence, clearly understanding the substance and reaching its function — a great and complete awakening.

The five "how unexpected" show that Huineng awakened to the fact that self-nature is also an illusion of true-emptiness-wondrous-existence (substance without mark, with mark). "How unexpected that self-nature is originally pure," "How unexpected that self-nature is originally neither arising nor ceasing," and "How unexpected that self-nature is originally without movement" describe the true emptiness of self-nature (without substance), while "How unexpected that self-nature is originally complete" and "How unexpected that self-nature can give rise to all dharmas" describe its wondrous existence.

[How unexpected] Who would have thought. Meaning one did not expect it. [Self-nature is originally neither arising nor ceasing] This says self-nature has a mark but no substance, and is an illusion. In chapter two, the Prajñā chapter, the Sixth Patriarch says: "self-nature is true emptiness." As for "neither arising nor ceasing" meaning originally not existing, the Sixth Patriarch, in chapter nine, the Dharma-Protection chapter, clearly instructs: "What I call neither arising nor ceasing is: originally there was no arising, and now too there is no ceasing."

[How unexpected that self-nature can give rise to all dharmas] This speaks of the function of self-nature — the mind; the mind can give rise to all dharmas. As at the end of this sutra, when the Sixth Patriarch took leave of the assembly, he instructed: "Your own mind is Buddha; do not harbor further doubt. There is not a single thing outside that can establish; it is all the original mind giving rise to all manner of dharmas. Therefore the sutra says: 'When the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of dharmas cease.'"

[When the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of dharmas cease] "When the mind arises" means: when ignorance arises, the alaya consciousness generates the various discriminating consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and manas consciousnesses), and thereupon the marks of realms appear (all manner of dharmas arise); if ignorance ceases, then the various discriminating consciousnesses cease (the mind ceases), and the marks of realms accordingly cease (all manner of dharmas cease). The Record of the Mirror of the School says: "Because when the mind arises all manner of dharmas arise — through the power of ignorance, without knowing the mind stirs, and can manifest all realms; then the mind follows the perfuming and stirs, and so it is said to arise. If ignorance ceases, the realms cease along with it, and the various discriminating consciousnesses all cease without remainder; hence it is said, when the mind ceases all manner of dharmas cease. This is the mind's source returning to purity, and so it is said to cease."

These five lines are Huineng's report to the Fifth Patriarch of the realm he had realized upon his great awakening. The first four describe the fundamental condition of the intrinsic nature, and so each carries the word “originally.” As Master Huineng describes the intrinsic nature in the tenth chapter, the Chapter of Entrustment: “Only recognize your own original mind; see your own intrinsic nature—without movement or stillness, without arising or ceasing, without coming or going, without right or wrong, without abiding or departing.” The fifth line speaks of the function of the intrinsic nature—the mind.

The intrinsic nature is originally pure” and “the intrinsic nature is originally free of arising and ceasing” tell us that the fundamental nature is serene and ever still; “the intrinsic nature is originally complete in itself” tells us that this nature is fully endowed with everything and no different from a Buddha; “the intrinsic nature is originally unmoving” tells us that this nature is ever thus and never shaken.

When Huineng composed the verse on “originally there is not a single thing,” he had only realized the essence of the intrinsic nature; now he has realized the essence, the characteristics, and the function of the intrinsic nature in full. “The intrinsic nature is originally pure” and “the intrinsic nature is originally free of arising and ceasing” speak of its essence; “the intrinsic nature is originally complete in itself” and “the intrinsic nature is originally unmoving” speak of its characteristics; “the intrinsic mind gives rise to all dharmas” speaks of its function.

“The Patriarch knew that I had awakened to the intrinsic nature and said to Huineng: If you do not recognize the original mind, studying the Dharma will be of no benefit. If you recognize your own original mind and see your own intrinsic nature, you are then called a great man, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.”

The Fifth Patriarch knew that I had fully awakened to the intrinsic nature, and so he said to me: If you do not recognize the original mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit. If you recognize your own original mind and clearly see your own intrinsic nature, you are then called a taming master, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.

Husband: that is, the Taming Master, one of the ten epithets of the Tathagata. Teacher of gods and humans: one of the ten epithets of the Tathagata. The ten epithets of the Tathagata: The Buddha has ten honored titles: first, Tathagata, one who comes by the path of reality and attains perfect enlightenment; second, Worthy of Offerings, one who rightly deserves the offerings of gods and humans; third, Rightly All-knowing, one who truly and completely knows all dharmas; fourth, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, one fully endowed with the three clear knowledges and the five practices; fifth, Well-gone, one who goes freely and well, entering nirvāṇa; sixth, Knower of the World, one able to understand all the worldly principles and their causes; seventh, Supreme Man, one unsurpassed and supreme; eighth, Taming Master, a great man able to tame and guide those on the correct path; ninth, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha as teacher of all gods and humans; tenth, Buddha the World-honored One, the Buddha respected by all beings in the world. Three clear knowledges: the knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of defilements. Five practices: the holy practice, the pure practice, the heavenly practice, the infant practice, and the sick practice. The holy practice is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the threefold discipline of precepts, concentration, and wisdom; the pure practice is the bodhisattva’s application of compassion with a pure mind, removing suffering and bestowing joy on beings; the “heaven” of the heavenly practice means the principle of naturalness, and the bodhisattva’s following this natural principle to accomplish wondrous practice is called the heavenly practice; the “infant” of the infant practice is a simile for gods, humans, and the lesser vehicle, and the bodhisattva, out of compassion, manifests the practices of gods, humans, and the lesser vehicle, which is called the infant practice; the sick practice is the bodhisattva’s sharing with all beings, out of great compassion, the afflictions and the sickness of suffering in order to liberate them.

“At the third watch I received the Dharma, and no one knew of it. He then transmitted the Sudden Teaching and the robe and bowl, saying: You are the sixth-generation patriarch. Guard your own thought well, widely liberate sentient beings, let the teaching be handed down in the future, and never let it cease.”

That I received the Dharma at the third watch was known to no one. The Fifth Patriarch then transmitted to me the doctrine of the Sudden Teaching together with the robe and bowl, saying: I transmit to you the sixth-generation patriarchate of the Chan school. You must guard your own thought well, broadly liberate sentient beings, and let the Sudden Teaching be widely spread in days to come—do not let it be cut off.

Guard your own thought well: keeping external wrong from entering is “guarding,” and giving rise to inner good is “thought.” “Guard your own thought well” means: protect yourself well so that you are not enticed and disturbed by circumstances, that your resolve for the Way remains ever pure, and that your power of practice advances steadily.

At this time Huineng was only twenty-four years old, could not read, and had not yet been ordained. Since arriving at the monastery he had not even had the opportunity to enter the lecture hall to hear the Dharma. The Fifth Patriarch nonetheless unreservedly transmitted the patriarchate to him, and because of this the Chan cause flourished throughout the world and blessed later generations. One cannot but admire the Fifth Patriarch’s unique discernment—a true connoisseur of men!
“Hear my verse: Sentience plants the seed; in the ground the fruit is born. Without sentience there is no seed either; without nature there is no birth.”
Hear my verse: With compassionate mind sow the Buddha-seed; when the ground-conditions ripen, the Buddha-fruit is born. This too is a matter of dreaming; there is no nature and no fruit that is born.

Sentience, without sentience: In this line “sentience” refers to the compassionate mind. In the following line “without sentience” means: in the ultimate sense there is no such thing as “sentience.” Buddha-seed: the seed that can give rise to the fruit of Buddhahood.
The original text of the verse is explained as follows:

Sentience plants the seed; in the ground the fruit is born”—the compassionate mind (sentience) sows the Buddha-seed, and the seed, ripening in the causal ground, gives rise to the fruit of Buddhahood. Causal ground: from the first arousing of the mind to seek Buddhahood while still on the level of an ordinary being, up to the point just before full Buddhahood is realized, this whole process is called the “causal ground.”

Without sentience there is no seed either”—in reality there is neither a sentient being nor a sentient being sowing the Buddha-seed, nor the ripening of the seed into the fruit of Buddhahood, because all of these are illusions. The Diamond Sutra says: “All that has form is false and illusory.” In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra
chapter three, the Chapter on Practice and Response, the Buddha says: “There is no Buddha, and likewise no Buddha-path.”

“Without nature there is no birth”—in reality there is neither a self-nature (for the self-nature is illusory) nor the matter of sentient beings attaining Buddhahood. The Buddha-treasury Sutra, chapter two, the Chapter on Buddha-recitation, says: “What is called the real characteristics of all dharmas? Namely, all dharmas are ultimately empty, having nothing at all.” The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, roll forty, says: “All dharmas are false and unreal.” The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says: “All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky,” and again: “Samsara and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are alike nothing but the forms of flowers in the sky (illusions).”

With this verse the Fifth Patriarch admonished Huineng to practice compassion and emptiness together, mutually interpenetrating and fusing. This is the same idea as the Buddha’s saying in the Diamond Sutra: “Thus, though I liberate immeasurable, numberless, and boundless sentient beings, in truth there is no sentient being who is liberated” (in other words, though one thus liberates immeasurable, numberless, and boundless beings into Buddhahood, in truth there is no matter of a being being liberated).
Liberating sentient beings: leading sentient beings to Buddhahood.

The meaning this verse sets forth (that self-nature, sentient beings, Buddhahood, and nirvāṇa are all affairs within the dream of ignorance) is explained at length in the Exegesis of the Diamond Sutra. Let it be especially noted that although self-nature, sentient beings, Buddhahood, and nirvāṇa are all affairs within the dream of ignorance, to emerge from that dream one must still use illusion to cultivate illusion, taking as one’s aim the attainment of Buddhahood and the liberation of sentient beings!

In the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra the Buddha says: “All bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age should remain far from all illusory and false realms. Because they firmly uphold this mind of distance, they come also to be far from the mind that is itself illusion; being far is itself illusion, and they are far from that too; being far from the far that is illusion, they are far from that as well; and when they reach that which there is nothing to be far from, then all illusion is swept away. It is like drilling for fire: the two pieces of wood depend on each other, and when the fire breaks out the wood is consumed and the ashes fly away and vanish. To use illusion to cultivate illusion is likewise so; when all illusion has been exhausted, one does not fall into annihilation.”

All illusion exhausted, one does not fall into annihilation: When the dream of ignorance ends, the dreamer attains perfect enlightenment. The Sutra on the Inconceivable Realms of the Tathagatas, the Great and Vast, says: “All Tathagatas, relying on this samādhi, accomplish immeasurable great powers, even realizing that all dharmas are empty (all dharmas are illusions), and can display various sovereign deeds in all Buddha-lands of the ten directions. It is as when a person dreams various changing events, and upon waking sees that none of what was seen exists. Ordinary beings are likewise; because they are in the dream of ignorance, they wrongly conceive of dharmas as having real substance. Once Buddhas are awake, they are attached to nothing, and so they can, in a single thought, display immeasurable Buddha-deeds in all worlds of the ten directions, sovereign and unhindered, benefiting and perfecting all sentient beings, leading them all to awaken to the immeasurable and profound gates of liberation.”

Question: I believe the meaning of the verse “Sentience plants the seed; in the ground the fruit is born. Without sentience there is no seed either; without nature there is no birth” should be: to sentient beings one sows the seed of the Dharma, and in time they will become Buddhas; since insentient beings have no Buddha-nature, to them one cannot sow the seed of the Dharma, and they will never become Buddhas.

Answer: This verse was spoken by the Fifth Patriarch in the course of transmitting the Dharma, after Huineng had been greatly awakened by hearing an explanation of the Diamond Sutra. It is a summation of the supreme truth of the first meaning: it neither leans toward emptiness nor clings to existence, but is the Middle Way of perfect harmony without obstruction, bidding Huineng to practice compassion and emptiness together, mutually interpenetrating and fusing, and to liberate all beings universally. This is the essential heart of the Buddhas! The Fifth Patriarch would never, at so critical a moment, have been discussing whether blocks of wood or stones could become Buddhas.

“The Patriarch said further: In the past, when the great master Bodhidharma first came to this land, people did not yet believe in it, and so he transmitted this robe as a token of faith, handed down from generation to generation. As for the Dharma, it is transmitted from mind to mind, in every case leading one to awaken and understand by oneself. From of old the Buddhas have transmitted only the essential nature, and each patriarch has secretly handed on the original mind. The robe is a cause of contention; let it stop with you and be transmitted no further. If this robe is handed on, your life will hang by a thread. You must leave quickly, for I fear people may harm you.”

The Fifth Patriarch said further: When the great master Bodhidharma first came to China, the transmission of the Dharma of the Chan school was not yet believed in by the world, and so he transmitted this kashaya as a token of the attainment and the transmission of the Dharma, passed down from generation to generation. As for the Dharma, it is transmitted from mind to mind, in every case leading one to awaken and understand by oneself. From of old the Buddhas have transmitted only the essential nature, and each past patriarch has secretly handed on the original mind. This kashaya is the cause of strife over the patriarchate; to you let it stop, and do not transmit it further. If you transmit it again, there will surely be danger to your life. You must leave quickly, for I fear that evil people may harm you.

Transmitting the robe: The first patriarch, the great master Bodhidharma, transmitted the kashaya as a token of the Dharma, first giving it to Huike (the second patriarch); Huike transmitted it to Sengcan (the third); Sengcan to Daoxin (the fourth); Daoxin to Hongren (the fifth); Hongren transmitted it to Huineng (the sixth). It passed through six generations without interruption, down to Huineng. Essential nature: that is, the intrinsic nature. Transmitted from mind to mind: transmitted from mind to mind. The Chan school does not rely on written words or on sutras and commentaries, but solely on direct face-to-face instruction between teacher and student, with mind and mind mirroring each other in the transmission of the great meaning of the Dharma; this is called transmitting from mind to mind, also known as “sealing mind with mind.” A life hanging by a thread: “hanging by a thread” is a fine silk thread from which a heavy object hangs, and which may snap at any moment. “A life hanging by a thread” describes being in an extremely perilous situation, in danger of losing one’s life at any time.
“Huineng asked: Where shall I go? The Patriarch said: When you reach Huai, stop; when you meet Hui, conceal yourself.”
I asked my teacher: To what place shall I go? The Fifth Patriarch said: First go to Huaiji County in Guangxi, and then go quietly to Sihui County in Guangdong and hide yourself there.

That Huineng received the patriarchate was personally conferred by the Fifth Patriarch, an entirely upright and proper matter, and yet he had to flee for his life; and this flight was not simply a matter of running away and being done with it, but required feinting east while striking west and laying down a trail of confusion. How far the harm of selfish desires and emotional attachments can go! Even those cultivating the Way cannot escape such vulgarity: how deplorable!

“Huineng received the robe and bowl at the third watch and said: I am a man of the south and have never known these mountain paths—how can I get out to the river crossing? The Fifth Patriarch said: You need not worry; I myself will see you off.”

I received the robe and bowl at the third watch and said: Your disciple is a southerner and has never known these mountain paths here—how am I to get out of the mountains and reach the ferry at the river? The Fifth Patriarch said: Do not be troubled; I will personally see you off.

“The Patriarch escorted me all the way to the post station at Jiujiang. He had me board the boat and took the oar himself, rowing. Huineng said: Please sit, Master; your disciple should take the oar. The Patriarch said: It is proper that I should ferry you across. Huineng said: When deluded, the master ferries one; when awakened, one ferries oneself. Though the word ‘ferry’ is the same, its use differs. Huineng was born in a border region and my speech is not correct; yet I received the Dharma through your kindness. Now that I have awakened, I should ferry myself by my own self-nature.”

The Fifth Patriarch escorted me all the way to the post station at Jiujiang and, having me board the boat, rowed the oar himself. I said: Please sit, Master; your disciple should be the one to take the oar. The Patriarch said: It is proper that I should ferry you across. I said: When deluded, the master ferries one; when awakened, one ferries oneself. Though these are both “ferrying,” their use is each different. Huineng grew up in a remote border region and my speech is impure, yet I received the Dharma through my honored teacher. Now that I am already awakened, I should ferry myself with the awakened self-nature.

“The Patriarch said: So it is! So it is! In days to come the Dharma will flourish greatly through you. Three years after you leave, I shall pass away. Go now, and make your way south with diligence. You should not speak of the Dharma too soon; the Dharma is hard to flourish.”

The Fifth Patriarch said: So it is! So it is! In days to come the Dharma will flourish greatly in the world through you. Three years after you depart I shall leave this world (the Fifth Patriarch had already attained mastery over birth and death). Go well now, and hurry on your way south. You should not come forth to teach the Dharma too soon; the Dharma is hard to rouse, and you must wait for the right time and conditions.

Question: Huineng could not read and was young; moreover, after attending on the Fifth Patriarch he had not heard a single lecture from the Dharma hall, and even the novice monks looked down on him. It is very hard to understand why the Fifth Patriarch would avoid everyone and transmit the patriarchate to him at night.

Answer: In fact, judged by his spiritual faculties, in merely a little over nine months Huineng made four leaps, which shows that he not only had extremely keen awakening but also had a considerable foundation of practice. These four leaps are: first, he heard a guest chant the Diamond Sutra, and upon hearing a single line his mind was instantly awakened. Second, after more than thirty days of enduring wind and exposure, when he paid homage to the Fifth Patriarch at Huangmei he was already able to say: “Your disciple’s own mind constantly gives rise to wisdom, never apart from the self-nature; this is itself the field of blessings.” Third, after more than eight months of treading the pestle, he composed the verse “originally there is not a single thing.” Fourth, when the Fifth Patriarch explained the Diamond Sutra to him at the third watch, up to “should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere,” Huineng was greatly awakened on the spot and uttered the five “how unexpected” lines. As for ascetic practice, Huineng husked rice with a stone tied at his waist, so that even the Fifth Patriarch sighed with emotion: “One who seeks the Way and forgets his body for the Dharma—should he not be like this!” Huineng possessed both keen awakening and ascetic practice, and he cultivated in accordance with the mind-dharma of the one Buddha-vehicle taught in the Diamond Sutra, so that becoming a Buddha and a patriarch was inevitable. That is why the Fifth Patriarch prophesied: In days to come the Dharma will flourish greatly through you. Later Huineng indeed fulfilled these expectations, and with his one flower opening into five leaves he greatly flourished the Chan school throughout the world, blessing later generations, proving that the Fifth Patriarch was a true connoisseur of men!

Further, an illiterate person very often has surpassing memory and comprehension, and the Sixth Patriarch was such a person. In chapter seven, the Chapter of Conditions and Opportunities: “At the time there was a Confucian scholar, Liu Zhilue, who honored him with great respect. Liu had an aunt who was a nun, named Wujin Zang, who constantly recited the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra. The Master, having heard it but once, instantly knew its wonderful meaning, and thereupon explained it for her. The nun then held up the text and asked him about characters. The Master said: I do not recognize the characters; ask me about the meaning. The nun said: Not even recognizing the characters, how can you grasp the meaning? The Master said: The wondrous principle of all Buddhas has nothing to do with written words.” In chapter eight, the Chapter of Sudden and Gradual: “The Master said: The Nirvāṇa Sutra—I once heard the nun Wujin Zang recite it through once, and I then explained it, not a single word or single meaning departing from the scripture.” Even the great master Shenxiu, who had read widely in the scriptures, admired him, saying: “He has gained the wisdom that is without a teacher, deeply awakened to the supreme vehicle—I am not his equal. Moreover, our master the Fifth Patriarch personally transmitted the robe and Dharma to him: could it have been in vain? I regret only that I cannot go far away to draw near to him and have vainly received the nation’s favors. Do not linger here, all of you; you may go to Caoxi to seek his judgment.” When the emperor and the empress dowager invited the two great masters Hui’an and Shenxiu into the palace, they both declined, saying: “In the south there is the Chan master Huineng, who received in secret the robe and Dharma of the master Hongren and transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal; you may ask him.”

For the educated, written words are of the utmost importance; without them they can scarcely move a step, and to them an illiterate person seems blind to everything. Yet the purpose of the Chan school is: not to rely on written words, to see one’s own intrinsic nature, and to attain Buddhahood by seeing one’s nature. “The wondrous principle of all Buddhas has nothing to do with written words.” Precisely because the Sixth Patriarch could not read, he was spared from pondering and measuring over words, from wasting years, from counting the sand of the sea, from looking at the finger instead of the moon; instead, knowing one thing he used one thing, and all his effort was spent at the very point. That is why the Sixth Patriarch’s sayings are always concise yet true to the principle, and cut straight to the bone.

“After Huineng had taken leave of the Patriarch, he set out on foot toward the south, and in the course of two months he reached Dayu Ridge. Behind him several hundred men pursued him, wanting to seize the robe and bowl. A monk of the secular name Chen, named Huiming, formerly a general of the fourth rank, was of coarse conduct, but he sought with utmost zeal and ran ahead of the others, catching up to Huineng. Huineng threw the robe and bowl down upon a stone and said: This robe is a token of faith—can it be taken by force? I then hid myself in the deep grass.”

After I had taken leave of my teacher, I pressed on southward and in less than two months reached Dayu Ridge. Several hundred men came chasing after me, wanting to seize the robe and bowl. A monk of the Chen family surname named Huiming, formerly a general of the fourth rank, though crude in character and conduct, was zealous in seeking the Way and most eager to find me and inquire of me, so he ran ahead of the crowd and was the first to overtake me. Seeing him come after me, I threw the robe and bowl down upon a rock and said: This robe is the token of the transmission of the patriarchate—how can it be fought for by force? So I concealed myself in the deep thicket.

Dayu Ridge: situated south of Dayu County in Jiangxi, forming the border with Nanxiong County in Guangdong. It is one of the Five Ridges and commands the strategic passage between Jiangxi and Guangdong, extremely steep. Five Ridges: the collective name for the Yuecheng Ridge, the Dupang Ridge, the Mengzhu Ridge, the Qitian Ridge, and the Dayu Ridge. Coarse: rough and rude. Coarse: same as “crude.”

“Huiming came and tried to lift it but could not move it. He then called out: Ascetic! Ascetic! I have come for the Dharma, not for the robe. Huineng then came out and sat upon a flat rock. Huiming made obeisance and said: I beg the ascetic to speak the Dharma for me. Huineng said: Since you have come for the Dharma, set aside all conditions and let not a single thought arise, and I shall speak the Dharma for you. Huiming was silent for a long while. Huineng said: Think not of good and think not of evil—at just this moment, what is the original countenance of the venerable Huiming? Huiming was greatly awakened at these words.”

Huiming rushed to the stone and tried to lift the robe and bowl but could not move them, and so he called out loudly: Ascetic! Ascetic! I have come for the Dharma, not to snatch the robe and bowl. So I came out and sat upon a great rock. Huiming made obeisance and said: I beg the ascetic to speak the Dharma for me. I said: Since you have come for the Dharma, set aside all conditions and let not a single thought arise (this is the key!), and I shall speak the Dharma for you. Huiming sat cross-legged, clearing his mind and calming his thoughts, and after quite some time had passed I said to him: Think not of good and think not of evil—at just this very moment (the state in which not a single thought has arisen), which is your original countenance? Huiming was greatly awakened at that very moment.

Ascetic: At this time Huineng had not yet been ordained, so Huiming called him an ascetic. Flat rock: same as “bedrock,” a great boulder. Venerable Huiming: this is an honorific way of addressing Huiming, just as earlier the little novice monk was addressed as “venerable.” Think not of good and think not of evil: to think of nothing at all. Original countenance: the intrinsic nature, that is, the condition of the self-nature in which even the subtlest thought is absent.

This case is the first investigative koan in the history of the Chan school. It points out the path to seeing the mind and realizing the nature (that is, the “upward turning key” spoken of by the great master Huangbo, incomparably precious): in this thought-free state of neither good nor evil (at just this moment), turn the light back and reflect: which is your original countenance?
Seeing the mind and realizing the nature: when the subtle thoughts momentarily subside, one clearly sees the intrinsic nature. Turning key
(liè)

the mechanism that sets a device in motion; used as a metaphor for the key and crucial point. For example, in the Tales Old and New, “Song the Fourth Man causes havoc in the Soul-Snatching Zhang’s house”: “A paper figure, holding in its hand a silver ball (same as ‘ball’), had beneath it that turning key; when one stepped on the turning key, the silver ball dropped to the ground.”
The “upward turning key” spoken of by the great master Huangbo
The great master Huangbo said:
“Just as the Great Master Niutou, under the Fourth Patriarch
(that is, the Chan master Farong, first patriarch of the Niutou school under the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin)
, spoke at length in many ways, he did not yet know the upward turning key.”
(from the Transmission of the Lamp)
Investigating
, the preceding work of practice is: first, bring a myriad thoughts to one, then bring the one to nothing, and be able to abide stably in the thought-free state (
“think not of good and think not of evil, at just this moment”
); then investigate before a single thought has sprung (
which is your original countenance
). Xiangyan’s awakening upon the sound of a bamboo strike was just this (see the article
Xiangyan Strikes the Bamboo
for details).
Question: Why was Huiming unable to lift the robe and bowl?

Answer: Because guardian spirits protected them. Marvelous events have existed from ancient times; in the three realms there are dragons and gods and good spirits that guard the Dharma, and one should not lightly dismiss them as superstition.

Dragons and gods: of the eight classes of beings, the dragon class and the god class are the good spirits that guard the Dharma (see the Thousand-armed Avalokitesvara Sutra). Eight classes of beings: the god class, the dragon class, the yaksha (translated as the brave and strong ghost), the gandharva (translated as the incense spirit), the asura (translated as the godless), the garuda (translated as the golden-winged bird), the kinnara (translated as the non-human), and the mahoraga (translated as the great python spirit, or the great-bellied earth dragon). Because the eyes of humans cannot see these eight classes, they are also called the “eight classes of invisible beings.”
Question:

The Sixth Patriarch said, “Think not of good and think not of evil—at just this moment, which is the original countenance of the venerable Huiming?” Here, is the word “which” a demonstrative pronoun or an interrogative?

Answer: The original countenance refers to the intrinsic nature, that is, the condition of the self-nature in which even the subtlest thought is absent. At the moment of “think not of good and think not of evil,” there are no coarse thoughts and no fine thoughts, but subtle thoughts remain, and so it is not the original countenance. Therefore, the “which” in “which is the original countenance of the venerable Huiming” is an interrogative, equivalent to “which one” in present-day Chinese, and it rouses Huiming to doubt and investigate.

Coarse thought, fine thought, subtle thought: One’s thoughts are of three kinds: coarse, fine, and subtle. For example, for a person who recites the Buddha’s name, wandering thoughts are coarse thoughts, and the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is a fine thought. Subtle thoughts are the subtle arising and ceasing and flowing of the conscious mind, the characteristics of the alaya consciousness. When subtle thoughts momentarily subside, one sees the mind and realizes the nature; when subtle thoughts cease forever, one fully realizes Buddhahood. No-thought: ordinarily, when both coarse and fine thoughts subside, this is called no-thought, which is the commonly spoken no-thought. Further, if subtle thoughts also cease, this is the ultimate no-thought. Thus the meaning of the term “no-thought” must be determined according to context.
Question: The scripture says: “Huiming was greatly awakened at these words.” What did Huiming awaken to?
Answer: For one who truly cultivates, the key lies in
recognizing the entrance to the path
“There is no other way to cultivate: one need only know the entrance to the path; if the entrance to the path is recognized, birth and death both come to rest.”
“Huiming was greatly awakened at these words”—he awakened to the fact that this is how one investigates and thereby sees the mind and realizes the nature
The great master Hanshan said:
“When the Sixth Patriarch returned south, he showed Daoming
(that is, Huiming)
and said: ‘Think not of good and think not of evil—at just this moment, which is the original countenance of the venerable Huiming?’ This is the first true instruction the Sixth Patriarch gave
for instructing one in the investigation of Chan
(from the Dream-Wandering Collection
Showing the Essentials of Investigating Chan)
A na ge: the syllable “a” (na) used in a question to strengthen the tone. True instruction: the most genuine and excellent instruction.

“He asked again: Apart from the secret words and secret meaning spoken above, is there yet more secret meaning? Huineng said: What I tell you is not secret. If you turn the light back, the secret is on your side.”

Huiming again asked: Apart from the secret words and secret meaning above, is there any further secret instruction? I said: What can be told to you is not a secret instruction; if you turn the light back upon yourself, the secret is in your own place.

Above: that is, the foregoing, what has been said. The secret words and secret meaning above: the passage given above by which Huiming was greatly awakened: “Think not of good and think not of evil—at just this moment, which is the original countenance of the venerable Huiming?” This single saying broke open the mysterious gate and the lock of consciousness, so that Huiming seemed to wake from a dream, rejoicing for a lifetime, and so sought further instruction. Mysterious gate: the gate of entry into the wondrous Way.

“Huiming said: Huiming, though at Huangmei, has in truth never been aware of his own countenance. Today, through your instruction, it is like water drunk by one who knows for himself whether it is cold or warm; now the ascetic is Huiming’s teacher! Huineng said: If you are so minded, you and I share the same teacher Huangmei; guard and maintain yourself well.”

Huiming said: Although Huiming studied there with the Fifth Patriarch, I have in truth never awakened to my own original countenance. Today, through your instruction, I have at last come to recognize the entrance to the path; it is like water drunk by one who knows for himself whether it is cold or warm. From now on, the ascetic is Huiming’s teacher. I said: If you have this mind, then you and I both take the Fifth Patriarch as our teacher; guard and maintain yourself well, not entangled by conditions, and advance diligently in practice.

Huangmei: refers to the Fifth Patriarch. The fifth patriarch of the Chan school, Hongren, lived at the Dongchan Temple in Huangmei County, Qizhou, in Hubei, and so was called Huangmei. To refer to a person by the place he dwelt in is an ancient way of showing respect; this is the so-called “avoiding the name and citing the residence to show reverence.”
“Huiming asked again: Whither shall Huiming go from now on? Huineng said: When you reach Yuan, stop; when you meet Meng, dwell. Huiming made obeisance and took leave.”
Huiming again asked: Whither shall Huiming go from now on? I told him: When you reach Yuanzhou in Jiangxi, dwell at Mengshan. Huiming made obeisance and took leave of me.

According to the Transmission of the Lamp, the Pointing at the Moon, and other records: Huiming regarded Huineng as his honored teacher, and in order to avoid the taboo of the character “Hui” in his teacher’s name, he changed his name to Daoming, residing at Mengshan in Yuanzhou, where he greatly proclaimed the Chan breeze.

“Later Huineng came to Caoxi. He was again pursued and sought after by evil men, and so at Sihui he took refuge among a band of hunters, passing through fifteen years there. At times he spoke the Dharma to the hunters as opportunity allowed. The hunters often had him watch the nets, and every time he saw living creatures he released them all. At mealtimes he would have vegetables cooked in the pot of meat. Someone asked about this, and he answered: I only eat the vegetables beside the meat.”

Later I arrived at Caoxi, south of Qujiang County in Guangdong. I was again pursued and sought by evil men, and so I fled to Sihui and took refuge among a band of hunters, passing fifteen years there. At times I would speak the Dharma to the hunters as the occasion allowed. The hunters often had me watch the nets, and every creature I saw caught in the nets I released completely. Whenever it was time to cook, I would have my vegetables boiled in the pot of meat; if someone asked me why I did this, I would answer: My stomach is weak, so I can only eat the vegetables at the side of the meat.

Later Huineng came to Caoxi... he took refuge among a band of hunters at Sihui: The detailed circumstances of this passage are recorded later in chapter seven, the Chapter of Conditions and Opportunities: “After the Master received the Dharma at Huangmei and returned to the Caohou village of Shaozhou, no one knew of him. There was a Confucian scholar, Liu Zhilue, who honored him with great respect. Liu had an aunt who was a nun, named Wujin Zang, who constantly recited the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra. The Master, having heard it but once, instantly knew its wonderful meaning and thereupon explained it for her. The nun then held up the text and asked him about characters. The Master said: I do not recognize the characters; ask me about the meaning. The nun said: Not even recognizing the characters, how can you grasp the meaning? The Master said: The wondrous principle of all Buddhas has nothing to do with written words. The nun was astonished and told the village elders: This is a man of the Way; you should invite him and make offerings to him. Then Cao Shuliang, a descendant of the Marquis of Wei, and the villagers all came to pay their respects. At that time the ancient Baolin Temple had been ruined by the fires of war at the end of the Sui dynasty, and so a sanctuary was rebuilt upon its old foundation and the Master was invited to dwell there; in a short time it became a precious monastery. The Master dwelt there for a little over nine months, and was again pursued and sought by an evil band. The Master then fled into the mountain before him, and they set fire to the grass and trees; the Master hid himself, pressing into the rock, and so escaped. To this day the rock bears the marks of the Master’s crossed legs and robe, and so it is called the Refuge-from-disaster Rock. The Master recalled the Fifth Patriarch’s instruction to ‘stop at Huai and conceal oneself at Hui,’ and so went into hiding in those two counties.”

blocks.text: 9. The Way Accomplished, Leaving the Mountain

inline.s: “One day it occurred to me: The time for spreading the Dharma has come; I can never hide away forever. So I set out and came to the Faxing Temple in Guangzhou, finding there the Dharma Master Yinzong lecturing on the Nirvāṇa Sutra. At that time the wind was blowing and a banner was waving. One monk said: The wind is moving. Another said: The banner is moving. They argued back and forth without ceasing. Huineng stepped forward and said: It is not the wind that moves, it is not the banner that moves; it is the minds of you, virtuous ones, that move. The whole assembly was astounded.”

One day I reflected by myself: The time is ripe, and now I should spread the Dharma; I can never hide away forever in the mountains and forests. So I left the mountain and arrived at the Faxing Temple in Guangzhou, where I happened upon the Dharma Master Yinzong lecturing on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra. At that moment the wind was blowing a banner about, and one monk said: This is the wind moving the banner. Another monk said: It is the banner moving by itself. They argued endlessly. Then I stepped forward and said: It is not the wind that moves, and it is not the banner that moves itself—it is the minds of you two that move. When the people heard this, they were all greatly astonished.

To flee: same as to escape. Dharma Master Yinzong: a native of Wu Commandery (Wu County, Jiangsu); he left home under a teacher and excelled in the Nirvāṇa Sutra. In the first year of the Xianheng era of the Tang dynasty he reached the capital and was commanded to reside at the Great Jing’ai Temple. He firmly declined and went to Qichun to pay respects to the master Hongren.
