Later, at the Faxing Temple in Guangzhou, he lectured on the Nirvāṇa Sutra; when he met the Sixth Patriarch, master Huineng, he first awakened to the profound principle and made Huineng his teacher of the Dharma. He also gathered the words of the eminent ones of various places from the Liang to the Tang dynasties and composed the Essentials of the Mind, which circulated widely in the world. On the twenty-first day of the second month of the second year of the Xiantian era he passed away at the Miaoxi Temple on Kuaiji Mountain, aged eighty-seven. Banner: a long, narrow flag raised on a bamboo pole and hung straight up. Virtuous ones: a Buddhist term, an honorific for others. Virtuous one: originally meaning a person of virtue, or a person of kindness. The whole assembly: the assembly of people.

It is not the wind that moves, it is not the banner that moves; it is the mind of the virtuous one that moves: The wind moving and the banner moving—these are matters within the dream of ignorance. That the vulgar in the world should dispute over whether the wind or the banner moves is not beyond reason, for they are already sunk in the dream of ignorance; but the cultivator is meant to awaken from the dream of ignorance, and so should firmly grasp that “all that has form is false and illusory” and “dwell not on forms so as to give rise to the mind; dwell not on sounds, scents, tastes, touch, or dharmas so as to give rise to the mind,” guarding the original mind so that it is not turned by conditions, and only then can one be delivered from birth and death. In the Surangama Sutra the Buddha says:
“You should know that all sentient beings, from time without beginning, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind, the pure and bright essence of the nature
(all because they do not know the pure and bright essence of the nature that abides in the true mind)
, and use various false thoughts
(and so give rise to false thoughts)
; this thought is not true, and therefore there is transmigration.”

Thus in their arguing over whether the wind or the banner moved, these two monks were clinging to forms as real, allowing the mind to follow conditions, and using false thoughts—not at all the conduct of a cultivator. “It is not the wind that moves, and it is not the banner that moves” means: seen from the standpoint of enlightenment (gathering forms back into the nature), “all that has form is false and illusory,” “originally there is not a single thing.” What wind-moving or banner-moving is there? And the saying “it is the mind of the virtuous one that moves” speaks to the root:
“Because the mind arises, all sorts of dharmas arise; because the mind ceases, all sorts of dharmas cease.”
(from the Sutra of Divining the Wholesome and Unwholesome Karma) The great master Hanshan said:
“All dharmas exist only in dependence on false thoughts and so are differentiated. If the mind and thoughts are apart, then there are no characteristics of any realm at all.”

(from the Record on Contemplating the Lankavatara) Because the mind arises, all dharmas arise; because the mind ceases, all dharmas cease: “Because the mind arises, all dharmas arise” means: when the mind rises (the first stirring of thought) one enters the dream of ignorance, and so all sorts of dharmas appear; “because the mind ceases, all dharmas cease” means: when the mind ceases (the subtle thoughts cease) the dream of ignorance ends, and the various dharmas seen in the dream cease.

With this Huineng settled the dispute at its very root, which shows how high his attainment was. (What is meant by the height of attainment is not any abstruse words and fine phrases, but the actual skill of remaining ever thus and unmoved when the sense-faculties meet their objects.) Hence “the whole assembly was astounded.” The saying “It is not the wind that moves, it is not the banner that moves; it is the mind of the virtuous one that moves” is truly earth-shattering! In the serene birthlessness, sentient beings see only arising and ceasing; in the manifest arising and ceasing, the Buddhas see only birthlessness.

“Yinzong invited me to the seat of honor, questioning me on the profound meaning. Seeing that Huineng’s words are concise and true to the principle, not relying on written words, Yinzong said: The ascetic is certainly no ordinary man. I have long heard that the Dharma and robe of Huangmei have come south—could it be you, the ascetic? Huineng said: I dare not. Yinzong then made obeisance and requested that the robe and bowl that had been transmitted be shown to the assembly.”

Hearing this, the Dharma Master Yinzong knew I was no ordinary person, and respectfully invited me to the seat of honor (the seat of respect), repeatedly investigating the profound meaning of the Dharma. Seeing that my answers were concise and to the point, clear in principle and accurate and exact, without multiplying empty technical terms and formulaic platitudes, the Dharma Master Yinzong said to me: The ascetic is certainly no ordinary man; such superb discourse could never be gained from notes and commentaries—unless one had personally realized it, how could one be so penetrating! I have long heard that the Fifth Patriarch’s successor has come south—could it be you yourself? I said: I dare not presume! Then the Dharma Master Yinzong made obeisance to me and asked me to show the robe and bowl transmitted by the Fifth Patriarch to the assembly, to make plain that I am truly the sixth-generation patriarch of the Chan school.

[Names and characteristics] Buddhist technical terms. [Platitudes] the formulaic talk current in a craft. [Robe and bowl] “robe” refers to the kashaya, “bowl” is the vessel used by monastics to hold the food offered by almsgivers; both are important Dharma-objects of the monastic and may serve as the credential of a master’s transmission. The conferral of the robe and bowl represents the conferral of the mind-Dharma and of the patriarchate. [I dare not] I dare not presume. This is a modest expression of acknowledgement in ancient usage.

Looking over the Platform Sutra as a whole, it is indeed “concise in words and true to the principle, not relying on written words”; from this one can see in part how precious the Treasure Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch is. How fortunate are those who are able to uphold and recite it!

“Yinzong again asked: In the transmission from Huangmei, how did he instruct and bestow it? Huineng said: There is no instruction and bestowal as such; it only discusses seeing the nature, and does not discuss meditative concentration and liberation. Yinzong said: Why not discuss meditative concentration and liberation? Huineng said: Because these are two dharmas and not the Buddha-Dharma; the Buddha-Dharma is the Dharma of non-duality.”

The Dharma Master Yinzong asked again (which shows his humility and his eagerness for the Way): When the Fifth Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to you, how did he instruct and bestow it? I answered: There is no specific instruction and bestowal; it only stresses seeing the nature (clearly seeing the real characteristics of all dharmas), and does not advocate attaining liberation through meditative concentration. The Dharma Master Yinzong asked: Why do you not advocate attaining liberation through meditative concentration? I answered: Because liberation is relative to bondage, and so the two are two dharmas; two dharmas are not the Buddha-Dharma. The Buddha-Dharma is the Dharma of non-duality.

In chapter nine, the Chapter of the Dharma-Protectors, Xue Jian, the envoy sent by Empress Wu and Emperor Zhongzong, said: “The Chan virtuosos of the capital all say: If one wishes to comprehend the Way, one must sit in meditation and practice concentration; there has never been anyone who attained liberation apart from meditative concentration.” This shows that the common practice of that time was to attain liberation through meditative concentration.

[Only discusses seeing the nature] In chapter five, the Chapter of Sitting Meditation, the Sixth Patriarch said: “Good friends! In thought after thought, see your own intrinsic nature as pure, cultivate yourself and practice yourself, and by yourself accomplish the Buddha Path.” [Only discusses seeing the nature, does not discuss concentration and liberation] Liberation is relative to bondage, whereas seeing the nature has already transcended both liberation and bondage; it is a state with neither bondage nor liberation. [The Dharma of non-duality] Non-duality means no duality. The real characteristics of all dharmas, all ever thus and equal, with no distinction of self and other—this is called non-duality. If a bodhisattva awakens to this principle of the one reality and equality, it is called “the gate of non-duality.”

“Yinzong asked again: What is the Buddha-Dharma of non-duality? Huineng said: The Dharma Master is lecturing on the Nirvāṇa Sutra, which makes clear that the Buddha-nature is the Buddha-Dharma of non-duality. For example, the noble King of Virtue bodhisattva said to the Buddha: Those who commit the four grave offenses, the five heinous offenses, and the icchantikas—do they cut off the root of good and the Buddha-nature? The Buddha said: The root of good is twofold: one is eternal, the other is impermanent; the Buddha-nature is neither eternal nor impermanent, and so it is not cut off; this is called non-duality. Again: one is good, the other is not good; the Buddha-nature is neither good nor not good, and this is called non-duality. The aggregates and the realms, the ordinary man sees as two; the wise, having understood, know that their nature is not two. The nature that is not two is the Buddha-nature.”

The Dharma Master Yinzong asked again: Then what is the Buddha-Dharma of non-duality? I said: The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra that the Dharma Master is now lecturing on makes clear that the Buddha-nature is the Buddha-Dharma of non-duality. For example, the King of Virtue bodhisattva asked the Buddha: For those who commit the four grave offenses, the five heinous offenses, and the icchantikas, is the root of good and the Buddha-nature cut off? The Buddha answered: The root of good (the good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind) has two opposed states: one is eternal, the other impermanent. Therefore the root of good is a dual dharma, and so it has arising, abiding, change, and ceasing, and so can be cut off. The Buddha-nature has no opposed states; it is neither eternal nor impermanent, but eternal and absolute, and so it cannot be cut off; this is called the Dharma of non-duality. Again, speaking through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, there are also two opposed states: one is good, the other not good; a dual dharma, with arising, abiding, change, and ceasing, and so can be cut off. The Buddha-nature has no opposed states; it is neither good nor not good, but eternal and absolute, and so cannot be cut off; this is called the Dharma of non-duality. The five aggregates and the eighteen realms—the ordinary man sees these illusions and thinks they each have two opposed states; the awakened one, having clearly seen the nature of dharmas, knows that they are in reality not two. The nature that is not two is the Buddha-nature.

[Root of good] the good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind is firm and not to be uprooted, and so is called a root; again, good can give rise to wonderful fruits and give rise to further good, and so is called a root. The Vimalakirti Sutra, chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Conduct, says: “Not grudging body and life, plant all roots of good.” [Four grave offenses] committing the precept against lust, the precept against stealing, the precept against killing a human, and the precept against lying greatly. [Great lying] speech that is not truthful and deceives others is called “false speech.” Within the path of the sages, claiming attainment when there is none, claiming realization when there is none, or saying that one receives the offerings of dragons, gods, ghosts, and spirits, in order to deceive fools and seek fame, gain, and offerings—all these are called “great lying,” a grave offense; after death one falls into the great hell. [Five heinous offenses] five kinds of gravely unjust crimes: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, drawing blood from a Buddha’s body, and destroying the harmony of the sangha. Because these five are acts of extreme wickedness, committing any one of them causes one to fall into the hell of unremitting suffering, and so they are also called “the karma of unremitting suffering.” [Icchantika] meaning without faith. Such a person is said to negate causes and effects (not believing in the principle of karmic retribution), to hold inverted false views, not to believe in the karmic retribution of the present and the future, not to draw near to the good and to good-knowing teachers, not to heed the Buddha’s teachings and admonitions; such a one will fall into hell and have no way out.

[Aggregates] refers to the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. [Realms] refers to the eighteen realms. The six sense-faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind), the six objects (form, sound, scent, taste, touch, Dharma), and the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness) together are called “the eighteen realms.” [The nature that is not two is the Buddha-nature] The Avatamsaka Sutra, roll thirty-nine, says: “The Buddha-nature is the profound true Dharma-nature, quiescent and without characteristics, the same as empty space.”

In this passage the Sixth Patriarch borrows the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra that the Dharma Master Yinzong was lecturing on to make clear the Dharma of non-duality. Among the methods of awakening in the Chan school, one of the most distinctive is the gate of non-duality (doing away with the discriminating mind). The Third Patriarch Sengcan’s Inscription of Faith in the Mind says: “The ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. If one neither loves nor hates, it is clear and bright. With a hair’s-breadth of difference, heaven and earth are set apart.” (The supreme wonderful Way is not difficult; the difficulty is in one’s own discriminating mind. As long as there is neither love nor hate, the ultimate Way is clear and bright. If there is even a hair’s-breadth of love or hate, then there is a distance of heaven and earth from the ultimate Way.) In the Platform Sutra the Sixth Patriarch points out that “the Buddha-Dharma is the Dharma of non-duality” and “the nature that is not two is the Buddha-nature.” The gate of non-duality upheld by the Chan school—speech and silence not-two, small and great not-two, self and other not-two, arising and ceasing not-two, defilement and purity not-two, good and evil not-two, clarity and ignorance not-two, form and emptiness not-two, and so forth—is the state reached by carrying the spirit of the Middle Way through to the full. Everything that arises through conditions is a dual dharma, that is, an opposed dharma; the gate of non-duality is the method that dissolves all distinctions and brings them back to the one characteristic of perfect, equal harmony—gathering forms back into the nature.

[The gate of non-duality] refers to the teaching that reveals the truth of absolute equality that transcends all relativity and discrimination. The Vimalakirti Sutra, chapter nine, the Chapter on Entering the Gate of Non-duality, records thirty-three gates of non-duality. The Teaching of Vimalakirti, chapter nine, the Chapter of Non-duality, says: “Arising and ceasing is dual; if bodhisattvas know that all dharmas are originally unarisen and also unceasing, and realize this tolerance of the unarisen dharmas, this is entering the gate of non-duality.”

[The Middle Way] neither leaning toward emptiness nor leaning toward existence; neither empty nor existent, both empty and existent, not falling into either extreme, perfectly harmonious and unobstructed—this is called the Middle Way. [Emptiness] dharmas that arise through conditions and are ultimately without real substance are called empty. The Vimalakirti Sutra, chapter on the disciples, says: “All dharmas are ultimately without anything at all; this is the meaning of emptiness.” Therefore “emptiness” refers to illusion—having form but no substance, like the affairs of a dream. But sometimes “emptiness” means mere nothingness. Whether “emptiness” refers to illusion or to nothingness must be judged according to context. For example, when above it explained “the Middle Way” saying “neither leaning toward emptiness nor leaning toward existence; neither empty nor existent, both empty and existent, not falling into either extreme, perfectly harmonious and unobstructed—this is called the Middle Way,” there “emptiness” means nothingness, that is: neither leaning toward nothingness nor leaning toward existence; neither nothing nor existent, both nothing and existent, not falling into either extreme, perfectly harmonious and unobstructed—this is called the Middle Way. [Neither nothing nor existent] “nothing” says form is present, “existent” says substance is absent. [Both nothing and existent] “nothing” says substance is absent, “existent” says form is present.

“Yinzong, having heard this, joyfully joined his palms and said: This one’s lecturing on the sutra is like tiles and pebbles; the virtuous one’s discussion of the meaning is like real gold. He then shaved Huineng’s head, wishing to serve him as his teacher. Huineng thereupon opened the East Mountain gate of the Dharma beneath the bodhi tree.”

Hearing this discussion, the Dharma Master Yinzong joyfully joined his palms and said: This one (a humble self-referential phrase) lecturing on the sutra is like tiles and pebbles; the virtuous one’s discourse on the profound meaning of the Dharma is like real gold. He then shaved my head, wishing to take me as his teacher. And so beneath the bodhi tree I opened and spread the Fifth Patriarch’s Sudden Teaching.

At that time the Dharma Master Yinzong was already the abbot and lecturing teacher of the Faxing Temple in Guangzhou. He was Huineng’s ordination teacher, since it was he who shaved Huineng’s head; and yet, after shaving his head, he in turn took Huineng as his teacher and even yielded his teaching seat to Huineng. This spirit of forgetting oneself for the Dharma is admirable, and cannot be spoken of in the same breath as those who praise themselves and disparage others.

[Tiles and pebbles] fragments of broken tile and stone, a metaphor for things of no value. [East Mountain gate of the Dharma] refers to the Dharma of the Fifth Patriarch of the Chan school, so called because the fifth patriarch, the Chan master Hongren, dwelt at the Twin-peak Mountain in Huangmei County, Qizhou. The mountain was in the eastern part of the county, and so it was called East Mountain.

“Huineng received the Dharma at East Mountain and endured every hardship, with his life as if hanging by a thread. Today, being able to join with the governor, the officials, monks, nuns, and laypeople alike in this one assembly—unless it is from the conditions of many past kalpas, it must be from having made offerings to the Buddhas and planted the same root of good in past lives, that one is able to hear the causes of receiving the Dharma of this Sudden Teaching as above. This teaching was transmitted by the former sages; it is not the wisdom of Huineng himself. Let those who wish to hear the former sages’ teaching each purify their minds; and having heard it, each should remove his doubts, and so be no different from the sages of former times.”

I received the Dharma at East Mountain, under the Fifth Patriarch, enduring every hardship, my life in peril as if hanging by a thread. That I am able today to join the governor, the officials, monks, nuns, and laypeople alike in this same Dharma assembly—unless it were the conditions of many past kalpas, it must be from having made offerings to the Buddhas and planted the same root of good in past lives that I am able to hear the causes of receiving this Sudden Teaching as above. The Sudden Teaching was transmitted by the former sages; it is not something attained by my own wisdom. Let those who wish to hear the former sages’ Sudden Teaching each purify their minds; and having listened earnestly, let each remove his doubts and truly believe, and so be no different from the sages of former times.

[Removing doubts] All the Buddha-Dharma springs from faith. It is said that “faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit, nourishing all roots of good.” And again: “The Buddha-Dharma is a great ocean; faith is what enables one to enter it.” Hence faith is the foremost prerequisite for entering the Buddha-Dharma. The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says: “If one meets the right path of practice of the Tathagata’s supreme bodhi, regardless of whether one’s faculties be great or small, one can accomplish Buddhahood.” Therefore for those who are fortunate enough to hear the Sudden Teaching, removing doubt is especially important.

The Verse on Cultivating the Mind says: “May those who seek the Way not give rise to timidity, but must arouse a courageous mind. The good causes of past kalpas are not yet fully known. If one does not believe in the supreme and wonderful, is content to be lowly and inferior, and gives rise to thoughts of difficulty and obstruction, then if now one does not cultivate, even though one has roots of good from past lives, by cutting them off now the difficulty becomes even greater, and one drifts ever farther away. Now that one has arrived at the place of treasure, one must not return empty-handed; once the human body is lost, in ten thousand kalpas it is hard to regain. Be careful of this! Would a wise person, knowing the place of treasure, turn away and not seek it, forever lamenting loneliness and poverty? If you wish to obtain the treasure, let go of the skin-bag!”
“The whole assembly, hearing the Dharma, rejoiced, made obeisance, and withdrew.”
Having heard my discourse, the people rejoiced and praised, and respectfully made obeisance and withdrew.
This chapter is the very heart of the whole sutra, and one must read it thoroughly until it is familiar; then the sutras before and after it will be easy to understand and grasp.
“The next day, Governor Wei requested instruction. The Master ascended the seat and said to the assembly: All of you purify your minds. Recite together: Mahāprajñāpāramitā.”

The next day, Governor Wei respectfully invited the Sixth Patriarch to give further instruction on the essential purport of the Dharma. The Master ascended the Dharma seat and said to the assembly: All of you put down your thoughts and purify your minds; now follow me and recite “Mahāprajñāpāramitā.”

Mahā] great. [Prajñā] this is a phonetic transcription of a Sanskrit word; it means wisdom, but this wisdom is not the cleverness of the world, but the wondrous wisdom that fully perceives the truth of life and the universe, the right wisdom of the self-nature, and so it is rendered by transliteration. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom

volume seventy-four says: “Prajnā is the mother of all Buddhas; dwelling in this prajnā, one is able to completely fulfill the Buddha-Dharma.” [Pāramitā] also translated as “pāramitā,”? no—also rendered “pāramitā,” meaning reaching the other shore. [Prajñāpāramitā] also translated as “prajñāpāramitā,”? Meaning: with the right wisdom of the self-nature, ferrying across to the other shore of nirvāṇa.

“He said again: Good friends! The wisdom of bodhi and prajnā that the people of the world originally possess within themselves is something all persons have; only because their minds are deluded they cannot awaken to it by themselves, and so must rely on a great good-knowing teacher to point it out and guide them to see their nature. You should know that the Buddha-nature of the foolish and the wise is originally without difference; only because of the difference between delusion and awakening is there foolish and wise. I now speak for you the Dharma of Mahāprajñāpāramitā, to enable you all each to attain wisdom. With all your mind, listen attentively; I will now speak it for you.”

After they had recited “Mahāprajñāpāramitā,” the Master continued his instruction: Good friends! The great wisdom of awakening (the wisdom of bodhi and prajnā) that people of the world originally possess, they have within themselves; only because their minds are deluded they cannot awaken by themselves, and so must rely on a great good-knowing teacher to reveal and guide them to see their nature. You should know that the Buddha-nature of foolish and wise is originally without difference; only because of the difference between delusion and awakening is there foolish and wise. Today I speak for you the Dharma of Mahāprajñāpāramitā, so that you may each attain the great wisdom of awakening (the wisdom of bodhi and prajnā). Set your minds to listen attentively; now I will speak it for you.

“Good friends! The people of the world all day long merely recite prajnā with their mouths, yet do not recognize the prajnā of their own self-nature; it is like talking about food without being satisfied. Speaking only of emptiness with the mouth, for ten thousand kalpas they do not see their nature, and in the end there is no benefit.”

Good friends! The people of the world all day long merely recite prajnā with their mouths, yet do not recognize the prajnā of their own self-nature, and do not use it to guide their daily life and their practice. It is like speaking of fine food and yet not filling the belly. They only keep saying “emptiness, emptiness, emptiness” with the mouth, without acting on it to be free from forms, so that when they meet a circumstance they take it as real and are turned by it; going on deluded in this way, for ten thousand kalpas they do not see their nature, and in the end there is no benefit.

The Sixth Patriarch first of all stresses the importance of practice—one must put it into practice oneself; otherwise, a painted cake cannot satisfy hunger. Therefore, reciting sutras and hearing the Dharma must be investigated and carried out within one’s own mind-practice to be of benefit.
[Emptiness] having form but no real substance (like the affairs of a dream) is called “empty.” In the Sutra of Holding the Worlds

, the third chapter, the Chapter on the Eighteen Natures, the Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions without reality, without any root.” In describing the existence of things, besides “existence” and “nonexistence,” there is another case, namely illusion; for example, the affairs of a dream are not truly existing—they have form but no substance—and so the concept of “emptiness” is used to describe them. The Vimalakirti Sutra

chapter three, the Chapter on the Disciples, says: “All dharmas are ultimately without anything at all; this is the meaning of emptiness.” In this sentence, “all dharmas” says form is present, “without anything at all” says there is truly nothing; this situation of form present yet nothing real (illusion) is called emptiness. Note well that the word “emptiness” is used very widely in Buddhist learning, in the hundred schools, and in works of literature, and its meaning differs in each; for instance, “emptiness” also has the sense of mere nothingness, and so on. Hence it should be carefully distinguished in context.

“Good friends! Mahāprajñāpāramitā is Sanskrit; in this language it means “the great wisdom that reaches the other shore.” This must be practiced in the mind, not merely recited with the mouth. Reciting with the mouth while not practicing in the mind is like illusion, like transformation, like dew, like lightning; reciting with the mouth and practicing in the mind, then mind and mouth are in accord. The intrinsic nature is the Buddha; apart from the nature there is no other Buddha.

Good friends! Mahāprajñāpāramitā is Sanskrit; this means “with great wisdom, ferrying across to the other shore of nirvāṇa.” This must be practiced in the mind, and not consist in reciting with the mouth. If one recites with the mouth but does not practice in the mind, it is like illusion, like transformation, like dew, like lightning—false and unreal, and one receives no benefit; if one recites with the mouth and practices in the mind, then mind and mouth are in accord, and one ferries across the sea of birth and death to the other shore. The intrinsic nature is the Buddha; apart from the nature there is no other Buddha.

[Mind-practice] to apply effort in the mind. The Chan school takes “that very mind is the Buddha” as its foundation, and so everything must be accomplished through effort in the mind. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “The liberation of all Buddhas is to be sought in the mind-practice of sentient beings.” The Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “This one mind alone is the Buddha; the Buddha and sentient beings are no different. It is only that sentient beings, clinging to characteristics, seek outside; seeking, they only lose it the more, so that a Buddha seeks a Buddha, the mind seizes the mind; exhausting kalpas and ending their lives, they never attain it. They do not know that when thought is stilled and reflection is forgotten, the Buddha of itself appears.” [Like illusion, like transformation] false and unreal. [Like dew, like lightning] like morning dew and lightning, a metaphor for fleeting transience. [The intrinsic nature is the Buddha; apart from the nature there is no other Buddha] this reveals the path to Buddhahood—returning the consciousness-nature to the intrinsic nature.

The sutra text that follows explains respectively the “Mahā,” the “prajñā,” and the “pāramitā” in the term “Mahāprajñāpāramitā”: a mind vast as empty space, without attachment and without discrimination, is Mahā; knowing that all dharmas are empty is prajnā; being free from the objects is pāramitā.

“What is Mahā? Mahā is great. The measure of the mind is vast, like empty space, without any border, without round or square, great or small, without blue, yellow, red, or white, without up or down, long or short, without anger or joy, without right or wrong, without good or evil, without head or tail.”

What is Mahā? Mahā means great; the measure of the mind must be vast, like empty space, without border, without round or square, great or small, and also without color, up or down, long or short, anger or joy, right or wrong, good or evil, beginning or end, and so forth—without attachment, without discrimination, pure and natural.

This passage says: a mind vast as empty space, without attachment and without discrimination, is Mahā (great). And as the text later says: “If you see all people, whether evil or good, you neither grasp nor reject them, and are also without attachment; the mind like empty space is called great, and so it is called Mahā.”

Having no characteristic at all, empty and without a single thing—this is called great, and the mind-practice should be like this. This is the pure mind. The Song of Certification says: “Clearly seeing, not one thing, neither a person, nor a Buddha. The great chiliocosm, the realms as numerous as the dust, the bubbles in the sea; all sages and saints, like a flash of lightning, are swept away.” The Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “If one views the Buddha as having the characteristics of pure, bright, and liberated, and views sentient beings as having the characteristics of defiled, dark, and of birth and death, one who holds this understanding, even through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, will never attain bodhi, because of clinging to characteristics.”

[The measure of the mind vast like empty space] the measure of the mind should be vast, like empty space, containing all things, yet equal and unmoving, pure and natural. In his Records of Instruction, the Dharma Master Huiming says that the measure of the mind should be vast, and compares it to the great earth, which has the same effect: “If our mind-measure could be as great as the earth, and benefit others as the earth does, without the self-clinging of grasping, rejecting, or anger, with everything unmoving, then it would not be difficult to be in accord with the true-such original mind—could there be anything unaccomplished?”

That the mind-measure is vast is a very crucial link in the practice of prajnā, and so this passage of instruction from the Dharma Master Huiming is excerpted as follows: “Our own mind is originally immeasurable and all-pervading, able to give rise to all dharmas; and it is also like the earth, which has the virtue of being broad and deep, able to give rise to all things, and so the earth is used as a comparison. The reason the earth can give rise to all things is that it can act spontaneously in accord with the seasons, doing without doing, wholly without knowing, still and unmoving. But sentient beings, deluded about the truth and pursuing the false, give rise to a mind when they see a circumstance, and move as soon as they meet an object, and so they obscure their own luminous spirit and only add to their obstructions. Those who study the Buddha, using the false to cultivate toward the true, should take the earth as their model. Yet the mountains, rivers, and great earth all arise through the false, and have their formation and destruction—why must we take the false as our model? It must be known that although the earth is false, its virtue is immeasurable. The earth can give rise to all things, can carry all things, can contain all things. And in giving rise to all things, it is nourishing sentient beings, without selfishness; in carrying all things, it accepts the great and the small alike, defilement and purity as one, without any view of grasping or rejecting, of discrimination; in containing all things, it lets people defile it and dig it, still and unmoving, without any thought of aversion or anger—and so it is called the great earth. If our mind-measure could be as great as the earth, and benefit others as the earth does, without the self-clinging of grasping, rejecting, or anger, with everything unmoving, then it would not be difficult to be in accord with the true-such original mind—could there be anything unaccomplished? We who study the path of the mind-ground speak daily of ‘mind-ground without wrong, benefiting others without self’; but in the end, is our mind as great as the earth? Can it nourish sentient beings? Can it accept all together and contain, letting people defile it without moving? Not to speak of letting people defile it—I fear it cannot even contain a single empty word; not to speak of nourishing sentient beings—I fear toward one’s own relatives one still cannot avoid self-interest. If so, what is meant by ‘mind-ground without wrong’? Those who study the path of the mind-ground, at every moment, must compare their own mind with the earth, to see whether it can truly compare! As I see it, not to speak of being as great as the great earth—even as small as a single acre of land it does not compare. Why? A single acre of land can still give rise to many things in the four seasons to nourish sentient beings, and also has the capacity to bear offenses without retaliation. I ask you: how does our mind-measure compare with the nourishing capacity of this acre of land? If you do not reflect on this and apply effort here, then no matter what, you will gain no benefit.”

“The Buddha-lands are all the same as empty space. The wonderful nature of people of the world is originally empty; there is not a single Dharma to be attained. The self-nature’s true emptiness is likewise so.”

All Buddha-lands are the same as empty space. The wonderful being of people of the world has a nature that is originally empty; there is not a single Dharma to be attained. The self-nature is likewise so; its nature is originally empty, and there is not a single Dharma to be attained.

The Buddha-lands are all the same as empty space” means that the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are illusions; “the wonderful nature of people of the world is originally empty” means that the “self” people speak of (the five aggregates of body and mind) and what is “mine” are illusions; “the self-nature’s true emptiness” means that the self-nature is also an illusion. The ordinary man falsely clings to the five aggregates of body and mind as real; the two-vehicle practitioners falsely cling to the self-nature and nirvāṇa as real. Here the Sixth Patriarch reveals: everything is illusion; nothing exists at all; nothing can be attained.

[The self-nature’s true emptiness] “true emptiness” means form present yet substance absent; “the self-nature’s true emptiness” means the self-nature has form present yet substance absent—it is an illusion. The self-nature is the consciousness-spirit, the dreamer within the dream of ignorance, and so it too is an illusion. Hence it is said: “The wonderful nature of people of the world is originally empty; there is not a single Dharma to be attained. The self-nature’s true emptiness is likewise so.” “The empty space of the world can contain all forms of things, the sun, moon, stars, mountains, rivers, the great earth, springs and streams, grasses, trees, forests, evil people and good people, evil dharmas and good dharmas, heaven and hell, all the great oceans, all the mountains of Sumeru—all are in the empty space. The emptiness of the nature of people of the world is likewise so.” In the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra the Buddha says: “The perfect-enlightenment self-nature: it is not a nature, yet has nature, arising in accord with all natures, with nothing grasped and nothing realized. In the real characteristic, there are in truth no bodhisattvas and no sentient beings. Why? Because bodhisattvas and sentient beings are all transformation; since the transformation ceases, there is no one who grasps or realizes.”

[The perfect-enlightenment self-nature: not a nature, yet has nature, arising in accord with all natures] The great master Hanshan, in his Direct Explanation of the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra, says: “The self-nature has no nature, and so it is said ‘not a nature’; ordinary and holy alike possess it, and so it is said ‘has nature’; it manifests following conditions, and so it is said ‘arising in accord with all natures.’” Here “all” is like “of,” for example: “Can he manage it?” [No nature] nature means substance; all dharmas have no substance, and this is called no nature. The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that all dharmas are eternally without nature.” The Surangama Sutra says: “All illusions become without nature.”

In the ultimate sense, the Buddha-lands, the body and mind of people of the world, and the self-nature are all like empty space—empty and without anything at all. The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says: “Within it, the Buddha-worlds as many as hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asamkhyeya, inexpressible, as many as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky, springing up confusedly and ceasing confusedly.” To awaken to the emptiness of all dharmas, holding not a single thing, without attachment—this is called great.
[Asamkhyeya] translated as “innumerable,” meaning so many that there is no number by which to count them.
Question: The sutra text above says “the self-nature’s true emptiness.” Is the alaya consciousness then also an illusion?
Answer: Yes, the alaya consciousness is an illusion. Since this question has historically been quite controverted, a brief citation is added.
The Teaching of Vimalakirti

volume six, discussing “no alaya,” the Buddha says: “Though one delights in observing no alaya, yet he does not abandon the pure treasury of Dharma; though he observes that all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, yet he constantly bears the burden of benefiting sentient beings.” The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra

volume five hundred seventy-six also speaks of “no alaya.” Manjushri (the bodhisattva of wonderful auspiciousness) says: “All sentient beings can be established in the Buddha’s wonderful Dharma, awakening wisdom without movement, knowing the Dharma-nature to be empty, without name and without characteristic, without reliance and without abiding, without grasping and without attachment, without obstruction and without clinging, like empty space, with no alaya, no niryantika? (no niryanti, the name for greed, meaning insatiable),? the supreme stillness, the most extreme stillness, without arising and without ceasing, without defilement and without purity, without becoming and without destruction, neither existent nor nonexistent. Thereby within it one accomplishes the deep tolerance, never far from the Buddha’s wonderful Dharma.”
[Niryanti] another name for greed, meaning its extreme and insatiable.
All the passages above say that the alaya consciousness is not real, but an illusion.

In the Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahayana, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu classifies all dharmas into five great categories. The alaya consciousness belongs to the mind-dharma category among all dharmas. The Buddha says: “All dharmas are like illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a flame.” (The Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra
volume ten.) The Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusions without reality, without any root.” (The Sutra of Holding the Worlds

chapter three, the Chapter on the Eighteen Natures.) Since all dharmas are like illusions without reality, then the alaya consciousness, being one dharma among all dharmas, is of course likewise like an illusion without reality.
Question: Why does the Buddha say in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra: “The true self spoken today by the Tathagata is called the Buddha-nature”?

Answer: Here “the true self” is spoken relative to the false self of the five aggregates of body and mind. In chapter ten, the Chapter of Entrustment, the Sixth Patriarch says: “Only recognize your own original mind; see your own intrinsic nature—without movement or stillness, without arising or ceasing.” And “without arising or ceasing” means that originally there was nothing; as the Sixth Patriarch, explaining “without arising or ceasing” in chapter nine, the Chapter of the Dharma-Protectors, says: “Originally there is no arising, and now there is also no ceasing.” In the Buddha-treasury Sutra the Buddha says: “All dharmas are without arising and without ceasing, without characteristic and without action.” This shows that the intrinsic nature (that is, the tathagatagarbha, the Buddha-nature) is likewise an illusion. In the Lankavatara Sutra the Buddha says: “Great Wisdom, in order to be free from the views of the heterodox, one should rely on the Tathagata-garbha of no-self.” In the Mahayana Lankavatara Sutra the Buddha says: “Therefore, the Buddhas speak of the tathagatagarbha, which is different from the self spoken of by the heterodox. If one wishes to be free from the views of the heterodox, one should know the meaning of the no-self tathagatagarbha.” (See the section on “the no-self tathagatagarbha” in
The Annotated Lankavatara
Question: If this is so, is the Dharma-body also an illusion?

Answer: The Contemplation of the Mind-ground Sutra of the Mahayana says: “Always contemplate the wonderful Dharma-body of all Buddhas; its essence-nature is like empty space, unattainable.” The Mahayana Lankavatara Sutra says: “The Dharma-body is like illusion and a dream—how can it be praised? To know that there is no nature and no arising is what is called praising the Buddha.”

“Good friends! Do not, upon hearing me speak of emptiness, then cling to emptiness. Above all, do not cling to emptiness! If one empties the mind and sits in quiet, one falls into the emptiness of non-memory.”

Good friends! Do not, upon hearing me speak of emptiness, then cling to emptiness, thinking that there is nothing at all (clinging to nothingness). The cultivator of the Way, above all, must not cling to emptiness, thinking that there is nothing at all. If one empties the mind and sits in quiet, still but without illumination, one falls into the emptiness of non-memory, which obscures the mind-nature.

[Clinging to nothingness] All dharmas have form but no substance and are illusions. Here there are two extreme views (each holding to one side): first, clinging to existence, thinking these dharmas truly exist, having form and substance; second, clinging to nothingness, denying even the form of these dharmas, thinking there is nothing at all, even negating cause and effect. Clinging to existence belongs to the eternalist heterodox; clinging to nothingness belongs to the nihilist heterodox. The correct attitude is: to know for certain that these dharmas have form but no substance and are illusions, and therefore to treat them as: let the form serve me, and not be turned by it; use illusion to leave illusion; when illusion is exhausted, the dream ends. [Emptying the mind and sitting in quiet] what is called here “emptying the mind and sitting in quiet” is being still without illumination, falling into the emptiness of non-memory. The master Yongjia says: “Clear and tranquil is right; clear and (given to) random thought is wrong; tranquil and clear is right; tranquil and non-memory is wrong.” [Clear] the mind lucid and alert. [Non-memory] without false thoughts and also without right thoughts, still without illumination.

When sitting in meditation, one should neither scatter (random thoughts) nor sink into drowsiness. It should be still and yet illuminating, illuminating and yet still. The master Yongjia, in his Collected Sayings of Yongjia, says: “Stillness” means not thinking of matters external, such as good and evil of the objects; “lucidity” means not giving rise to the characteristics of drowsiness, dullness, non-memory, and so forth... Using stillness to treat scattering, using lucidity to treat drowsiness. “Clear and tranquil is right; non-memory and tranquil is wrong; tranquil and clear is right; random thought and clear is wrong.” Therefore within stillness there must be no non-memory (still without illumination), and within lucidity there must be no random thought (illuminating without stillness).

Emptying the mind and sitting in quiet is being still without illumination—the so-called having concentration without wisdom; a concentration without wisdom is not true concentration, and cannot cut off afflictions or escape birth and death; the patriarchs compared it to soaking a stone in cold water. Such a concentration, though body and mind are at ease and happy, sinks and stalls on the path of cultivation, and is a pitfall on the Bodhi path, from which one should stay far away. At a small gathering, a student said: “When right thought is let go, there are no false thoughts either; pure and free.” To this, the old master Xuyun explained: “This purity and freedom is laziness and negligence, soaking a stone in cold water; even cultivating for a thousand years is but a waste. One must surely lift up right thought, bravely investigate, and see just who it is who is reciting the Buddha’s name, only then can one break through. It is necessary that you apply effort diligently.” (From the Dharma-dharmas of the old master Xuyun: the instruction of the old great-grandmaster.)

In order to prevent sinking and stalling on the path of cultivation, in the Dream-Wandering Collection, “to the guest-in-charge, the Venerable Xiuliu,” the great master Hanshan says: “I know that you dwell in quiet, your body and mind at peace, and that false thoughts have long since vanished away of themselves. But among this vanishing of false thoughts you find yourself light, at ease, and happy; you must not take this ease and happiness as something to be enjoyed. If you regard it as attainment, from then on you fall into the sickness of mere letting-be, thinking only of a dim, tranquil state, taking doing nothing as excellent. Little do you know that this sickness is the most poisonous; if you cling to it long, there is no progress at all. Secretly growing are the flowing karmic consciousness of ignorance, and the life-root is never cut off. In the end it is like using saliva to polish dead water-silver; it is of utterly no use. At this very time when false thoughts vanish, it is exactly right to take hold of the head-utterance, investigate it earnestly, and arouse a deep doubt. If the doubt takes effect, and you hold fast to the head-utterance, investigating day and night, the deeper you investigate the more profound it becomes, and there will at last be a time when the beans burst in cold ashes. If you settle for doing nothing without arousing a doubt, it is never true effort.”

[The sickness of mere letting-be] The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says: “The second is the sickness of mere letting-be. If another person speaks thus: ‘We now do not cut off birth and death, nor seek nirvāṇa; for nirvāṇa and birth and death have no thought of arising or ceasing; let all things be, following the nature of each dharma,’ wishing to attain perfect enlightenment—since that perfect-enlightenment nature is not possessed through mere letting-be, it is called a sickness.” To this the great master Hanshan commented: “This shows the sickness of mere letting-be. This sickness of mere letting-be belongs to those with wild interpretations, who drift along at ease, indulging and letting go body and mind, calling themselves free of things and without obstruction, having attained great liberation. They in turn use as an excuse that originally there is no birth and death to cut off, and originally no nirvāṇa to realize, and make this a basis for indulgence. They are not people with true insight or good-knowing teachers. If one follows such persons, one falls into wildness; therefore doing as one pleases is spoken of as a sickness.” (From the Direct Explanation of the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra.) [Using saliva to polish dead water-silver] this is the so-called “secret prescription” of the elixir of immortality, with no actual effect; hence the great master Hanshan uses it here as a metaphor for something of utterly no use.

The people of the world all cling to existence, and so give rise to delusion, create karma, and wander in birth and death. But the cultivator of the Way, knowing that nothing whatsoever can be attained, after passing the stage of clinging to existence, very often goes to the other extreme and clings to nothingness. If one falls into one-sided emptiness (thinking there is nothing at all) or even into non-memory, the consequences are to be feared. So, to dance along with circumstances is indeed muddled; but if one becomes cold and solitary, that too is not the Bodhi path.

“Good friends! The empty space of the world can contain all forms of things, the sun, moon, stars, mountains, rivers, the great earth, springs and streams, grasses, trees, forests, evil people and good people, evil dharmas and good dharmas, heaven and hell, all the great oceans, all the mountains of Sumeru—all are in the empty space. The emptiness of the nature of people of the world is likewise so.”

Good friends! The empty space of the world contains all sorts of things with their forms. The sun, moon, stars, mountains, rivers, the great earth, springs and streams, grasses, trees, forests, evil people and good people, evil dharmas and good dharmas, heaven and hell, all the great oceans, and the mountains such as Sumeru—all are within empty space. The true emptiness of the self-nature of people of the world is likewise able to contain all dharmas.
[Forms] the various things with their forms. “Form” refers to matter; “image” refers to shape.

“Good friends! That the self-nature can contain all dharmas is great; all dharmas exist in the natures of all people. If you see the evil and the good of all people and neither grasp nor reject them, and are free of attachment, the mind like empty space is called great, and so it is called Mahā.”

Good friends! That the self-nature can contain all dharmas is great; all dharmas are in the self-nature of each person. If you see the evil and the good of all people and are without desire, without aversion, and also free of attachment, the mind like empty space is called great, and so it is called Mahā.
[Neither grasping nor rejecting] without desire, without aversion.

Here again it is stressed: the mind like empty space, not giving rise to a mind toward any circumstance-conditions (neither grasping nor rejecting), without moving of thought (without attachment)—this is called great. The mind-practice should be like this!
What is great? The mind like empty space, without border, without grasping or rejecting, without attachment—this is called great (Mahā).

“Good friends! The deluded speak with the mouth; the wise practice with the mind. And there are deluded people who empty the mind and sit in quiet, thinking of nothing at all, and call themselves great; such people one cannot speak with, because of their wrong views.”

Good friends! As for emptiness, the deluded speak with the mouth, while the wise practice with the mind. And there are foolish, deluded people who empty the mind and sit in quiet, thinking of nothing at all, and take this as ultimate, calling themselves great; such people cannot be reasoned with, because they hold wrong views.

Emptying the mind and sitting in quiet, thinking of nothing at all” does not take awakening as its purpose, but seeks quiet stillness and ease, mistakenly believing this to be the right path. In truth it is a side-road on the path of cultivation, and so it met with the Sixth Patriarch’s rebuke. The Sixth Patriarch said earlier: “Good friends! Do not, upon hearing me speak of emptiness, then cling to emptiness. Above all, do not cling to emptiness! If one empties the mind and sits in quiet, one falls into the emptiness of non-memory.”

“Good friends! The measure of the mind is vast, penetrating the whole Dharma-realm. When used, it is clear and distinct in everything; when applied, one knows all. All is one; one is all. Coming and going freely, the mind-substance without obstruction—this is prajnā.”

Good friends! The measure of the mind should be vast, penetrating the whole Dharma-realm. When used, it is clear and distinct in everything; when applied, one knows all. All is the mind (all is one); the mind is all (one is all). The mind, in the six dust-objects, coming and going freely, without attachment and without clinging—this is prajnā.
[Dharma-realm] all-inclusively embracing all things is called the Dharma-realm.

“Good friends! All prajnā-wisdom arises from the self-nature and does not come from outside. Do not misuse your mind—this is called the self-use of the true nature; one truth, all truths. The measure of the mind is a matter of great things; it does not practice the small path. Do not all day long speak of emptiness with the mouth while not practicing this course in the mind—it is exactly like an ordinary person who calls himself a king; in the end it cannot be so. Such a one is not my disciple.”

Good friends! All prajnā-wisdom arises from the self-nature and does not come from outside; do not misunderstand, thinking that prajnā-wisdom lies outside the self-nature. This is called the self-use of the true nature; one truth, all truths. In a matter of great things, the measure of the mind does not practice the small path. (The small path is the “emptying the mind and sitting in quiet, thinking of nothing at all” spoken of above.) Do not all day long speak of emptiness with the mouth while not practicing this course in the mind—it is exactly like an ordinary person who calls himself a king and thinks he is a king, when in truth what king is he? Such a person is not my disciple.

[One truth, all truths] this was already explained in the first chapter: “one truth, all truths” means that one truth, and so all truths. “One truth” means seeing the nature; “all truths” means that one who sees the nature clearly sees the true characteristics of all things: all are illusions having form but no substance. The Buddhas, with their self-nature awakened, in the manifest arising and ceasing see only birthlessness; sentient beings, with their self-nature deluded, in the serene birthlessness falsely see arising and ceasing. [The measure of the mind] the arising of the mind that measures external objects. The mind-measure of the ordinary man is all manner of reckoning and clinging; the mind-measure of the Tathagata is to be free of all that is depended upon and of all dependence, and to abide in non-mind. The Lankavatara Sutra says: “Observing all conditioned dharmas, free of the reliance and the relied-upon, the mind-measure that is without mind—this I call the mind-measure.”

“Good friends! What is prajnā? Prajnā is a Tang [Chinese] word meaning wisdom. In all places, at all times, in thought after thought not to be foolish, always to practice wisdom—this is the practice of prajnā. With one thought of folly, prajnā is cut off; with one thought of wisdom, prajnā is born. The people of the world, foolish and deluded, do not see prajnā; they speak of prajnā with the mouth while their minds are ever foolish; they constantly say that they practice prajnā, reciting ‘emptiness’ every thought without recognizing true emptiness. Prajnā has no form or characteristic; the mind of wisdom is it. If you understand it thus, this is called prajnā-wisdom.”

Good friends! What is prajnā? Prajnā, translated into Chinese, is “wisdom.” One must, in all places, at all times, in thought after thought not be foolish and deluded, always practice wisdom—this is the practice of prajnā! With one thought of folly and delusion, prajnā is cut off; with one thought of wisdom and illumination, prajnā is born. The people of the world, foolish and deluded, do not see prajnā; they speak of prajnā with the mouth while their minds are ever foolish. They constantly say that they practice the practice of prajnā, yet reciting ‘emptiness’ every thought, they do not recognize true emptiness. Prajnā has no form or characteristic; the mind of wisdom is prajnā. If one understands it thus, one has prajnā-wisdom.
What is prajnā? “Prajnā has no form or characteristic; the mind of wisdom is it.” Here the Sixth Patriarch gives a clear definition of prajnā.

[Not recognizing true emptiness] The people of the world, foolish and deluded, speak of emptiness with the mouth. In fact, they either fall into existence or fall into non-existence, and do not understand that the true meaning of “emptiness” is illusion—form present yet substance absent. Hence to practice the practice of prajnā is to be free from forms—knowing illusion, one is free of it—not to negate the existence of forms, and still less to speak of emptiness with the mouth while clinging to forms every thought (taking them as real). For example, there is this case: long ago a Chan master loved eating beef, yet made the excuse: “This is eating yet not eating.” After death he entered the womb of an ox and became an ox to repay his debt. On the road he met the Venerable Baozhi. Baozhi took one look: “Oh! Is this not such-and-such a Chan master? Did you not say ‘eating yet not eating’? You should not have become an ox—how is it that you became an ox to repay a debt?” The ox, tears streaming down its face, banged, banged, banged itself to death. This sort of thing is all “spoken prajnā,” “reciting ‘emptiness’ every thought without recognizing true emptiness”—speaking of illusion with the mouth, taking it as real in fact.
Question: To go against the principle is called foolish; to accord with the principle is called wise. Then concretely, what is the principle?

Answer: The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch is the great practice of the Diamond Sutra, and so the principle of the Platform Sutra is exactly what the Diamond Sutra says: “All that has form is false and illusory. If you see that all forms are not forms, then you see the Tathagata.” “Dwell not on form so as to give rise to the mind; dwell not on sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas so as to give rise to the mind; give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.” “Being free from all forms is called the Buddha.” “Grasping not at characteristics, ever thus and unmoved.” Therefore the Platform Sutra takes no-thought, no-form, and no-abiding as its program of practice. The Sixth Patriarch says: “My gate of Dharma, from the beginning onward, establishes no-thought as its aim, no-form as its essence, and no-abiding as its foundation.” (Chapter Four, the Chapter of Concentration and Wisdom.)

“What is pāramitā? This is a Sanskrit word; in Chinese it means “reaching the other shore,” and its meaning is to be free of arising and ceasing. Clinging to the objects, arising and ceasing arises, like water with waves—this is called this shore; being free of the objects, there is no arising and ceasing, like water ever flowing—this is called the other shore. Hence it is called pāramitā.”

What is pāramitā? This is a Sanskrit word, meaning “reaching the other shore,” and its meaning is to be free of arising and ceasing. Clinging to the objects, the thoughts of arising and ceasing arise—like water with waves, called this shore; being free from the objects, the thoughts are without arising and ceasing—still and yet illuminating, illuminating and yet still, like water ever flowing without waves (not a still pool of dead water)—called the other shore. Hence being free from the objects is called pāramitā.

Being free from the objects is the being free from forms in the Diamond Sutra. The Diamond Sutra says: “Being free from all forms, one is called a Buddha.” Mahāprajñāpāramitā is using the great wisdom to be free from the objects, free from all the dust-objects.

The wind of objects blows on the sea of the mind, and karma uniting gives rise to the waves of consciousness. “Objects” include external objects and internal objects. The external objects are the dusts of form, sound, scent, taste, and touch; the internal object is the dust of dharmas. The so-called “being free from the objects” is not that one must leave the surroundings, but that when meeting objects one neither grasps nor rejects and is also free of attachment, not being turned by them, and so within the conditions of objects one removes habitual tendencies and refines the mind.

In his Notes on the Diamond Sutra, the Sixth Patriarch says: “The mind of sentient beings is originally without abiding. Because objects come and touch [it], it then gives rise to the mind. It does not know that touching objects is empty, and takes the worldly dharmas as real, and so abides the mind upon objects—just as a monkey grasps at the moon (seizing the moon in water), an ailing eye sees flowers (seeing flowers in the sky). All the myriad dharmas arise from the mind. If one awakens to the true nature, then there is no abiding. A mind that abides nowhere is wisdom, without all afflictions, like the great void, with no obstruction. A mind that abides somewhere is false thought; the six dusts vie in arising, like the drifting clouds coming and going unfixed.”

“Good friends! The deluded recite with the mouth; at the time of reciting there is falsehood and dispute. If in thought after thought one practices [in the mind], this is called the true nature. One who awakens to this Dharma practices the Dharma of prajnā; one who cultivates this practice is in the practice of prajnā. Not to cultivate is to be ordinary; with one thought of such cultivation one is equal to the Buddha.”

Good friends! The deluded recite pāramitā with the mouth, and at the time of reciting there are false thoughts and disputes. If in thought after thought one practices in the mind (being free from the objects), without false thoughts or disputes, this is the true nature. One who awakens to this Dharma is in the Dharma of prajnā; one who cultivates this practice is in the practice of prajnā. Not to cultivate is to be ordinary; with one thought of such cultivation one is equal to the Buddha.

“Good friends! The ordinary man is the Buddha; affliction is bodhi. With a previous thought of delusion, one is an ordinary man; with a later thought of awakening, one is a Buddha. With a previous thought clinging to the objects, one is in affliction; with a later thought free of the objects, one is in bodhi.”

Good friends! The ordinary man and the Buddha are in truth both the self-nature—only in different states; affliction and bodhi are in truth both the mind—only in different states. With a previous thought of delusion, one is an ordinary man; with a later thought of awakening, one is a Buddha. With a previous thought clinging to the objects, one is in affliction; with a later thought free of the objects, one is in bodhi.

[The ordinary man is the Buddha] the self-nature deluded is the ordinary man; the self-nature awakened is the Buddha. [Affliction is bodhi] the mind clinging to the objects is affliction; the mind free of the objects is bodhi (awakening). [Affliction] there are six kinds: greed, anger, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong views.
“Good friends! Mahāprajñāpāramitā is the most honorable, the most supreme, the very first; without abiding, without going, and also without coming; the Buddhas of the three times all issue from it.”

Good friends! Mahāprajñāpāramitā is the most honorable, the most supreme, the very first; within the dust-objects it does not abide (without attachment), does not go (without chasing), and also does not come (not approaching the objects). The Buddhas of the three times all practice Mahāprajñāpāramitā and realize Buddhahood.
[Without abiding, without going, and without coming] not defiled by the dust-objects, ever thus and unmoved.

“One should use the great wisdom to break through the five aggregates, affliction, and the toils of the dust. Cultivating thus, one will surely accomplish the Buddha Path, transforming the three poisons into precepts, concentration, and wisdom.”

You should use this great wisdom to break through clinging to body and mind (the five aggregates), and to break through affliction and the toils of the dust. Cultivating thus, one will surely accomplish the Buddha Path, transforming the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion into precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
[Toils of the dust] the mind toiling in the dust-objects.

In cultivation there are all sorts of methods to break through the five aggregates, affliction, and the toils of the dust, and transform greed, anger, and delusion into precepts, concentration, and wisdom. The Platform Sutra uses Mahāprajñāpāramitā, and, like felling a poisonous tree, cuts directly at its root rather than picking off branches and plucking leaves; hence it is called the Sudden method.

“Good friends! My gate of Dharma, from one prajnā, gives rise to the eighty-four thousand wisdoms. Why? Because the people of the world have eighty-four thousand toils of the dust. If there were no toils of the dust, wisdom would ever be present, not apart from the self-nature. One who awakens to this Dharma is in no-thought, in no-memory, in no-attachment. Not giving rise to falsehood, using one’s own true-such nature, contemplating with wisdom, neither grasping nor rejecting any dharma—this is seeing the nature and accomplishing the Buddha Path.”

Good friends! My gate of Dharma, the Sudden Teaching, from one prajnā, gives rise to the eighty-four thousand wisdoms. Why? Because the people of the world have eighty-four thousand sorts of toils of the dust, and so prajnā can liberate [one from] all the toils of the dust. If the mind does not cling to characteristics nor grasp at objects (if there is no toil of the dust), then wisdom is ever present, not apart from one’s own nature. One who awakens to this Dharma is in no-thought, no-memory, no-attachment. Not being deluded by illusions, but using the awakened self-nature, contemplating with wisdom, neither grasping nor rejecting any dharma—this is seeing the nature and accomplishing the Buddha Path.

[Not giving rise to falsehood] The people of the world see all things through the karma-mirror formed by their own karmic power, forming karmic images (the images of karma), and cling to them as real. “Not giving rise to falsehood” is not to look at the myriad dharmas through the karma-mirror—not to deceive oneself—but to use the bodhi self-nature to contemplate the myriad dharmas with wisdom, seeing clearly that all dharmas are illusions, and so pay no heed to them (without love or hate, like or dislike). This is the path of seeing the nature and accomplishing Buddhahood. In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra the Buddha says: “All dharmas are false and unreal.” [The karma-mirror] the so-called “karma-mirror” is like the glasses one wears when watching a three-dimensional film; it is originally a flat image, but seen through these glasses it becomes a lifelike “real body,” and the “real bodies” seen by those of different karmic powers differ from one another.

[To neither grasp nor reject any dharma] Grasping is greed, rejecting is anger; the mind then continually reckons amid grasping and rejecting—constant deliberation. When the wild mind does not rest, resting is bodhi. The master Guifeng says: “Awakening to the emptiness of all forms, the mind is of itself without thought. When thought arises, one is aware of it; when aware, it is gone. The wonder of cultivation lies only in this.” [This is seeing the nature and accomplishing the Buddha Path] this is the path of seeing the nature and accomplishing Buddhahood. Here the Sixth Patriarch explains clearly how to see the nature: “not giving rise to falsehood (not deluded by illusions), using one’s own true-such nature, contemplating with wisdom, neither grasping nor rejecting any dharma.” This is not only the path to seeing the nature, but also the standard by which to test whether one has seen it—practicing thus, one can see the nature; only when one has done so is it seeing the nature.

“Good friends! If one wishes to enter the profound Dharma-realm and the samādhi of prajnā, one must practice the practice of prajnā. Reciting and holding the Diamond Prajnā Sutra, one is able to see the nature. Know that the merit of this sutra is immeasurable and boundless; the sutra itself clearly praises it, and cannot be fully stated. This gate of Dharma is the supreme vehicle, spoken for people of great wisdom, spoken for people of superior faculties; people of small wisdom and small faculties hearing it give rise in their minds to unbelief.”

Good friends! If one wishes to enter the profound Dharma-realm and the samādhi of prajnā, one should practice the practice of prajnā. Reciting and holding the Diamond Sutra, one is able to see the nature. Know that the merit of this sutra is immeasurable and boundless; the sutra itself clearly praises it, and one cannot speak of it item by item. This gate of Dharma, the Sudden Teaching, is the supreme vehicle, spoken for people of great wisdom, spoken for people of superior faculties; people of small wisdom and small faculties, upon hearing it, cannot give rise to belief in their minds.

[Samādhi] translated into Chinese as “concentration,” meaning the mind fixed in one place. [Diamond Prajnā Sutra] that is, the Diamond Sutra, whose full name is the Diamond Prajnāpāramitā Sutra. [The supreme vehicle] the supreme and unsurpassed teaching, that is, the perfect Sudden Teaching, that is, the one Buddha-vehicle.

“People of small wisdom and small faculties hearing it give rise in their minds to unbelief.” Therefore the difference between the people of great wisdom and superior faculties and the people of small wisdom and inferior faculties lies solely in whether they can give rise to faith in this prajnā gate of Dharma, and has nothing to do with the level of cultural knowledge or cleverness. The Diamond Sutra says: “Those who delight in the lesser dharmas, clinging to the view of self, the view of persons, the view of sentient beings, and the view of a life, are unable to hear, receive, recite, or explain this sutra for others.”

“Why? For example, when the dragons and gods rain upon the Jambudvipa, the cities, towns, and villages all drift away, like floating date leaves; but if it rains on the great ocean, it neither increases nor decreases. If a Mahayana person, if a person of the supreme vehicle, hears the Diamond Sutra spoken, his mind opens and he awakens and understands.”

Why? For example, when the dragon king sends down a great rain from heaven upon this world, the floodwaters burst forth and destroy the cities and villages, like floating little leaves; if this great rain falls upon the great ocean, the surface of the water does not rise or fall. If a Mahayana person, if a person of the supreme vehicle, hears the Diamond Sutra spoken, his mind opens and he awakens and understands.

This passage uses a simile to show that the supreme Way (the great rain) can only correspond to those of great wisdom and superior faculties (the great ocean), and only then can they open their minds and awaken and understand.
[Jambudvipa] also called southern Jambudvipa, also called the southern continent, translated into Chinese as “the continent of surpassing gold,” that is, the Saha world in which we dwell.

“Therefore know that the self-nature originally possesses the wisdom of prajnā; using one’s own wisdom to contemplate constantly, one is able to see it without relying on written words. For example, the rain: it does not come from heaven of itself, but a dragon is able to call it forth, causing all sentient beings, all grasses and trees, the sentient and the insentient, to be moistened; the hundred rivers and many streams all flow into the great ocean and become one body. The wisdom of prajnā in the self-nature of sentient beings is likewise so.”

Therefore know that the self-nature originally possesses the wisdom of prajnā; using one’s own wisdom to contemplate constantly, one attains it without relying on written words. For example, the rain: it is not that it comes from heaven, but that the dragon king sends it down (here, the Master uses the then-current notion of the “dragon king bringing rain” as a simile), causing all sentient beings, all grasses and trees, the sentient and the insentient, to be moistened; the hundred rivers and many streams all flow into the great ocean and become one body. The wisdom of prajnā in the self-nature of sentient beings is likewise so.

Here the sky is a simile for written words, the dragon king for the self-nature, the rain for the wisdom of prajnā, and “all sentient beings, all grasses and trees, the sentient and the insentient” for the sentient beings within the mind (that is, the various thoughts that arise when meeting conditions and touching objects; see chapter six).

[Without relying on written words] The Five Lamps Merged, the chapter on the World-honored One, says: “The World-honored One, at the assembly on Mount Grdhrakuta, held up a flower and showed it to the assembly. At that time, the millions of gods and humans were all at a loss (completely at a loss what to do); only the golden-colored ascetic (Mahakasyapa) broke into a smile. The World-honored One said: I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wonderful mind of nirvāṇa, the real characteristic that is without characteristic, the subtle gate of Dharma, not established on written words, transmitted separately outside the scriptures; this I entrust to Mahakasyapa (that is, Mahakasyapa).” The Sutra of the Brahman Heavenly King Asking the Buddha to Resolve Doubts, chapter two, the Chapter of the Flower: “At that time the lord of the Saha world, the Great Brahman king, by name Fangguan, took the root of the accomplishment of the three-thousand great thousand worlds, the wonderful Dharma lotus of gold, the light and radiant great Brahman flower, and held it up to the Buddha. Stepping back, he made obeisance, and said to the Buddha: ‘World-honored One, the Buddha has now accomplished the right enlightenment; for fifty years he has spoken various Dharmas, given various teachings, and transformed and saved all classes of sentient beings. If there be yet a supreme great Dharma not spoken, for my sake and for the bodhisattva-practitioners of the last age, and for the ordinary sentient beings who wish to practice the Buddha Path, let it be revealed and proclaimed.’ Having said this, he relinquished his own body to become a seat, adorned with heavenly garments, and had the Tathagata sit upon it. At that time the Tathagata sat upon this precious throne, received this lotus flower, and, without speaking, without saying anything, only held up the flower and entered the great assembly, the eighty-four thousand gods and humans. At that time the whole assembly all stopped and were silent. Then the elder Mahakasyapa, seeing the Buddha hold up the flower and show it to the assembly, immediately became free and broke into a smile. The Buddha then declared: ‘It is so. I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wonderful mind of nirvāṇa, the real characteristic that is without characteristic, the subtle gate of Dharma, not established on written words, transmitted separately outside the scriptures, held and upheld, by which the ordinary man becomes a Buddha—the supreme truth of the first meaning; now this is entrusted to Mahakasyapa.’” (From the Newly Compiled Continuation of the Tripitaka, vol. 1, no. 0027, the Sutra of the Brahman Heavenly King Asking the Buddha to Resolve Doubts.)

[The treasury of the true Dharma eye] The Buddha’s mind-eye clearly sees the true Dharma—this is called “the true Dharma eye”; being deep and vast and containing all virtues is called “the treasury.” [The treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wonderful mind of nirvāṇa] abbreviated as “the true Dharma wonderful mind”—that is, the truth, profound and inconceivable, realized by the World-honored One; this state of great awakening is the recondite and subtle Buddha-mind, which can neither be expressed in words nor grasped by scriptural teaching. [Transmitted separately outside the scriptures] “scriptures” means the scriptural teaching; “transmitted separately outside the scriptures” is the special transmission apart from the scriptural teaching. [Not established on written words] Those awakened in the Chan school do not touch written words or phrases, but transmit from mind to mind. The Blue Cliff Record says: “Bodhidharma, seeing from afar that this land had the faculties and vessels of the Mahayana, crossed the sea and came with great effort. He transmitted solely the mind-seal, revealing [the way] out of confusion. Not established on written words, clarifying the mind and seeing the nature, seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha.”

“Good friends! People of small faculties hearing this Sudden Teaching are like plants and trees of small root-nature: if drenched by the great rain, they all fall over of themselves and cannot grow. People of small faculties are likewise. They originally possess the wisdom of prajnā, without any difference from people of great wisdom. Why is it that, hearing the Dharma, they do not awaken of themselves? Because their wrong views are heavy and their obstructing karma deep, and the root of affliction is strong—like a great cloud covering the sun, and without the wind to blow it away, the sunlight does not appear.”

Good friends! Sentient beings hearing this Sudden Teaching are like plants and trees meeting the rain.
