The little grasses and small trees (similes for those of small root-nature) meeting the great rain (a simile for this Sudden Teaching, the supreme vehicle) all fall over and cannot grow; while the giant trees (similes for those of great root-nature) meeting the great rain flourish and thrive. People of small faculties hearing this Sudden Teaching are like the little grasses and small trees meeting the great rain; they cannot give rise to faith, and even slander it. In fact, the wisdom of prajnā originally possessed by people of small faculties is without any difference from that of people of great wisdom. Then why is it that, hearing the Dharma, they do not awaken of themselves? This is because their wrong views are firmly fixed, their obstructing karma is deep, and the root of affliction is deep and firm—like the densely dark clouds covering the sun; without the wind to blow it away (a simile for not removing doubt and dissolving karma), the sunlight does not appear (the light of the wisdom of the self-nature cannot shine forth).

“The wisdom of prajnā is also without great or small; it is only that the delusion or awakening in the self-minds of all sentient beings differs. A deluded mind seeking outside, cultivating to seek a Buddha outside, without awakening to one’s own self-nature—this is having small faculties; if one awakens to the Sudden Teaching, does not cling to external practice, but within one’s own mind constantly gives rise to right views, so that affliction and the toils of the dust cannot defile one—this is seeing the nature.”

The wisdom of prajnā is originally without great or small; it is only that the degree of delusion or awakening in the self-minds of all sentient beings differs, and so the wisdom they manifest is sometimes great and sometimes small. A deluded mind seeking the Dharma outside, practicing outside to seek a Buddha, without awakening to one’s own self-nature—this is having small faculties; if one awakens to the Sudden Teaching, does not cling to practice outside the mind, but within one’s own mind constantly gives rise to right views, so that affliction and the toils of the dust cannot defile one—this is seeing the nature.

Here the Master reveals what “seeing the nature” is: “but within one’s own mind constantly gives rise to right views, so that affliction and the toils of the dust cannot defile one—this is seeing the nature.”

“Good friends! Abiding neither within nor without, coming and going freely, able to remove the clinging mind, penetrating without obstruction. One who can cultivate this practice is without any difference from the Prajnā Sutra.”

Good friends! The practice of prajnā is to follow neither the turning of thoughts within nor to be pulled by objects without; within the six dust-objects, coming and going freely, able to remove the mind of clinging to falsehood, without attachment and without grasping or rejecting, penetrating without obstruction. One who can cultivate this practice of prajnā is without any difference from what the Diamond Sutra says.
[Prajnā Sutra] refers to the Diamond Sutra, whose full name is the Diamond Prajnāpāramitā Sutra

“Good friends! All the sutras and all written words, the greater and lesser vehicles, and the twelve divisions of scripture, are all established for people, and can only be established in dependence on the nature of wisdom. Without the people of the world, all the myriad dharmas would originally not exist. Hence know that the myriad dharmas are originally set up by people, and all scriptures come into being because of people’s speaking. And since among these people there are the foolish and the wise—the foolish are the small people, the wise are the great people—the foolish ask the wise, and the wise speak the Dharma for the foolish. When the foolish one suddenly awakens and understands and his mind opens, he is no different from the wise.”

Good friends! All the sutras and all written words, the greater and lesser vehicles, and all scriptures (the twelve divisions of scripture), are all established in dependence on people; because the natures of wisdom and faculties differ, they can only then be established. Without the people of the world, all the Buddha-Dharma would originally not exist. Hence know that the various gates of the Dharma were originally established to teach and transform sentient beings; all the scriptures come into being because they must instruct sentient beings. This is because among sentient beings there are the foolish and the wise; the foolish are the small, the wise are the great. The foolish ask the wise, and the wise speak the Dharma for the foolish; when the foolish one suddenly awakens and understands and his mind opens, he is no different from the wise.

[Sutra] translated into Chinese as “sutra text” or “accordant scripture.” [Twelve divisions of scripture] The Buddhist scriptures, according to their style and the matters they set forth, are divided into twelve categories, and so are called the twelve divisions of scripture. “The twelve divisions of scripture” here means all the scriptures.

“Good friends! Without awakening, the Buddha is a sentient being; with one thought of awakening, sentient beings are Buddha. Hence know that all the myriad dharmas are wholly within one’s own mind. Why not, from within one’s own mind, suddenly see the true-such self-nature? The Bodhisattva Precept Sutra says: I am originally of a pure self-nature; if you recognize your own mind and see the nature, you all accomplish the Buddha Path. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: Instantly and suddenly clear, one again attains the original mind.”

Good friends! Without awakening, the Buddha is a sentient being; with one thought of awakening, sentient beings are Buddha. Hence know that all the Buddha-Dharma is wholly within one’s own mind—why not, from within one’s own mind, suddenly see the true-such self-nature? The Bodhisattva Precept Sutra says: “I am originally (original source) of a pure self-nature; if you recognize your own mind and see the nature (recognize your own original mind and see your own intrinsic nature), you all accomplish the Buddha Path.” The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “Instantly and suddenly clear (totally thoroughly awaken at that moment), one again attains the original mind.”
This passage of instruction collects the thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises all together into awakening to one’s own original mind and intrinsic nature.

[The Vimalakirti Sutra] another name for the Sutra Spoken by Vimalakirti. The Sutra Spoken by Vimalakirti has had seven Chinese translations, of which three survive: first, the Buddha-speak Vimalakirti Sutra in three scrolls translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty of the Three Kingdoms period; second, the Sutra Spoken by Vimalakirti in three scrolls translated by Kumarajiva of the Later Qin; third, the Teaching of Vimalakirti in six scrolls translated by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty. Of these, Kumarajiva’s translation has circulated most widely and has never declined. In the Eastern Jin dynasty, Sengzhao; in the Liang dynasty of the southern dynasties, Zhiyi (the Tiantai master of wisdom); Huiyuan; in the period from the end of the Sui to the beginning of the Tang, Jizang of Jixiang; and in the Tang dynasty, Kuiji of Cien all wrote commentaries on this sutra.

“Good friends! I, at the place of the master Ren [Hongren], upon hearing a single [line], immediately awakened, and suddenly saw the true-such self-nature. Therefore I have handed down and spread this teaching, causing those who study the Way to suddenly awaken to bodhi. Let each of you contemplate your own mind and see your own nature.”

Good friends! I, at the place of the Fifth Patriarch, upon first hearing this principle, was immediately awakened, and suddenly saw the true-such self-nature. Therefore I have handed down and spread this gate of Dharma, the Sudden Teaching, causing those who study the Way to suddenly awaken to bodhi. Let each of you contemplate your own mind and see your own nature.

The path of practice in the Platform Sutra is “to know your own original mind, and to see your own original nature.” The point at which one sets to work is the contemplation of the mind—turning the light back upon one’s own mind. Thus the Sixth Patriarch, in an earnest and weighty tone, exhorted: each of you should gaze into your own mind and see your own nature.
The method of turning the light back upon one’s own mind is this:
When a thought arises, know it and do not follow it; when a thought subsides, be still and yet clearly aware.

To contemplate and thereby attain samādhi—this is the samādhi of true reality (tathata), king of samādhis, and is therefore called the supreme samādhi. The Treatise on the Awakening of the Bodhi Mind says: “When a deluded thought arises (i.e. when a thought rises), know it and do not follow it; when the delusion subsides (i.e. when the thought is stilled), the mind-source is empty and still, all virtues are complete, and its wondrous functions are inexhaustible.”

[Know it and do not follow it] Gaze upon the thought without adding judgments. The key to “know it and do not follow it” lies in doing the work upon “knowing”—watching as a cat keeps watch over a mouse’s hole: the moment a thought rises, you know it. Once “knowing the instant a thought rises” is achieved, “not following” becomes easy. [Stillness with bright awareness] This is no-thought, clearly knowing that it is no-thought. The Treatise on Cutting Off Delusion says: “The still, calm extinction of the mind-nature is samādhi; the constant understanding of that extinction is prajñā.” This is to say: when the mind-nature abides in the state of still extinction, this is called samādhi; and when one knows clearly and unceasingly that at this moment the mind-nature is in that state of extinction, this is called prajñā. Thus, stillness with bright awareness is the even upholding of samādhi and prajñā. [Mind-source] The mind is the source of the myriad dharmas, and so it is called the mind-source. [All virtues complete] All virtues are then complete. “Then” (si) means “then, thereby.” Example sentence: With preparedness, one then has no calamity.

The Treatise on Destroying Delusion says: “The single dharma of contemplating the mind gathers up all dharmas and is the most essential and concise.” The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: “To be able to contemplate the mind-nature is called the supreme samādhi.”

The Fourth Patriarch Daoxin said: “All the hundred and thousand Dharma-gates alike return to this single square inch; the boundless, river-sand-like wondrous virtues all rest in the mind-source. All the gates of precepts, of samādhi, and of wisdom, together with the powers of spiritual transformation, are all inherently complete, and do not depart from your mind.”
Therefore the root of the Buddha-Dharma lies in the mind, and the root of practice lies in contemplation.
To turn the light back upon oneself constantly—this is prajñā fumigating ignorance. The moment ignorance is broken, the dharmakaya manifests at once.

In a single leap one enters directly the ground of the Tathagata, and without passing through asankhya kalpas one attains the dharmakaya. The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says: “All Tathagatas, from the causal ground in which they first arose, all rely on the perfect illumination of the pure, clear knowing-nature, and only by eternally cutting off ignorance do they accomplish the Buddha-way.”

The core of practice after awakening is to remove habitual tendencies in order to cut off afflictions; and contemplation of the mind is the keen instrument for removing those habits. So one must use the contemplation of the mind to remove habits and to do the “three no’s” work (see the section “The Three No’s Work” in “Chapter Four, Samādhi and Prajñā”).

[If you cannot awaken by yourself, you must seek out a great good-knowing friend (kalyanamitra), one who understands the supreme Dharma-vehicle, so that he may directly point out the right path. This good-knowing friend bears a great karmic connection, being one whose teaching and guidance cause you to see your nature. All good dharmas are set in motion because the good-knowing friend can arouse them. The twelve sections of the scriptures of the Buddhas of the three times are inherently complete within the nature of beings. If you cannot awaken by yourself, you must seek the pointing of a good-knowing friend to see; if you can awaken by yourself, then you need no seeking outside.]

If one cannot awaken by oneself, one must seek out an illuminating teacher (the great good-knowing friend who understands the supreme Dharma-vehicle) to directly point out the right path. Because of a great karmic connection with him from past lives, his teaching and guidance can cause one to see one’s nature. All the wondrous dharmas that guide practice toward realization are set in motion precisely because the good-knowing friend can arouse them. The twelve sections of the scriptures of the Buddhas of the three times are inherently complete within the nature of sentient beings. Yet one who cannot awaken by himself must seek the instruction of a good-knowing friend to see his nature; if one can awaken by oneself, then no seeking outside is needed.

[If one obstinately clings to the notion that one must rely upon a good-knowing friend, and from him expects to gain liberation, there is no such principle. Why? Because within one’s own mind there is a good-knowing friend able to cause self-awakening. If one gives rise to deviant confusion and inverted, delusive thoughts, then even though a good-knowing friend without should teach, one cannot be saved. If one raises the true and correct contemplation of prajñā, in a single instant all delusive thoughts are extinguished; if one recognizes one’s own nature, in one awakening one reaches the ground of Buddhahood.]

If one obstinately insists that one must rely upon a good-knowing friend, hoping through him to gain liberation, there is no such principle. Why? Because within one’s own mind there is a good-knowing friend able to guide one to awakening. If one gives rise to deviant confusion and inverted, delusive thoughts, then even though a good-knowing friend without should teach, one still cannot be saved; if one raises the true prajñā contemplation, in a single instant all delusive thoughts vanish and one can awaken; if one recognizes one’s own original nature, in one awakening one reaches the ground of Buddhahood.

arising in deviant confusion” and “arising in the true contemplation of prajñā” have utterly different results; therefore the practitioner must at all times and everywhere be alert to whether he is “arising in deviant confusion” or “arising in the true contemplation of prajñā.”

[Within one’s own mind there is a good-knowing friend] Within one’s own mind there is a good-knowing friend—what is commonly called the “inner teacher.” To rouse one’s own “inner teacher” is truly a most vital matter.
Q. How does one rouse one’s own “inner teacher”?
A. “Still your thoughts and forget your deliberations, and the Buddha appears before you of itself.” (Essentials of Mind Transmission)

[Good-knowing friends! Contemplate with prajñā wisdom, so that within and without are clearly illumined, and you know your own original mind. If you know your original mind, you are fundamentally liberated. If you attain liberation, that is the samādhi of prajñā, that is “no-thought.”]

Good-knowing friends! Contemplate with prajñā wisdom (that is, the “true contemplation of prajñā” spoken of above), so that within and without are clearly illumined, and you know your own original mind. If you know your own original mind, you attain the fundamental liberation. If you attain the fundamental liberation, that is the samādhi of prajñā, that is no-thought.

[Know your own original mind] This is to realize within oneself the mind’s original state—luminous, clear, and deeply still. The Mahayana Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground says: “If one can contemplate that the nature and essence of the mind is empty, then the delusions and obstructions do not arise, and one is liberated.” [Fundamental liberation] The mind being empty, the realms are empty of themselves; the myriad dharmas bind nothing, and are fundamentally liberated.

[What is called no-thought? If, upon seeing all dharmas, the mind does not become defiled by grasping, this is no-thought. In its functioning it reaches everywhere, yet it does not grasp at any place. Only purify your original mind, causing the six consciousnesses to issue out through the six gates, and amid the six dusts to be without defilement and without mixture, coming and going freely, functioning universally without obstruction—this is the samādhi of prajñā, ease and liberation, called the practice of no-thought. If one ceases to think of the hundred things and causes thought to be utterly cut off, that is bondage to dharmas, and is called a biased view.]

What is called “no-thought”? If, upon seeing the myriad things (all dharmas), the mind does not become defiled by grasping (that is, does not discriminate and reckon, does not indulge in delusive imaginings and clinging, is without love and hate, liking and disliking), this is no-thought. The mind, in functioning, reaches everywhere, yet does not grasp at any place. Only purify your original mind, causing the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness) to issue out through the six gates (that is, the six sense-organs: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), and amid the six dusts
(form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharma)

—neither mingled with greed, hatred, and delusion, nor defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion—coming and going freely, functioning universally without obstruction, this is the samādhi of prajñā, ease and liberation, called the “practice of no-thought.” If one thinks of nothing whatsoever and suppresses thought so that it does not arise, that is bondage to dharmas, and is called a biased view.

Therefore “no-thought” is not to be without thoughts at all; rather it is: upon seeing all dharmas, the mind does not cling, has no delusive imaginings or clinging, no love and hate, no liking and disliking. As the Diamond Sutra says: “Think not with a mind dwelling on form, think not with a mind dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma; think with a mind that dwells nowhere.” That is to say: merely keep one’s own thought free from the realms, and do not let the mind be born upon a dharma.

[Cause thought to be utterly cut off] Not permitting thought to arise. [Bondage to dharmas] A one-sided clinging to dharmas, taking passages out of context and not knowing how to apply them flexibly—so that one is fettered by them and cannot be liberated. [Biased view] An evil view that leans to one side (rushing off to an opposite extreme).
This sutra says:
“If one ceases to think of the hundred things and causes thought to be utterly cut off, that is bondage to dharmas, and is called a biased view.”

Therefore correct practice is not to cease thinking of the hundred things, but rather to awaken at the place of seeing, hearing, and knowing. The “seeing, hearing, and knowing” that arises when the six sense-organs contact the six dusts, though the root of delusive thought, is also the essential gate for awakening and entering the Way. The difference between “delusion” and “awakening” lies solely in whether, at the place of seeing, hearing, and knowing, one can turn delusion into awakening and consciousness into wisdom. As a later passage says:
“The true-suchness self-nature gives rise to thought; though the six sense-organs have seeing, hearing, and knowing, they are not defiled by the myriad realms.”

[Awakening] To see all dharmas with a mind that does not become defiled by grasping (that does not discriminate and reckon, does not indulge in delusive imaginings and clinging, is without love and hate, liking and disliking).

[Good-knowing friends! One who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought penetrates all the myriad dharmas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought sees the realms of all the Buddhas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought reaches the stage of Buddhahood.]

Good-knowing friends! One who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought reaches through all the Buddha-Dharmas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought sees the realms of all the Buddhas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought reaches the stage of Buddhahood.
How I praise the Dharma of no-thought!

[Good-knowing friends! Those in later ages who gain my Dharma, let them, toward those of like view and like practice, vow to receive and hold this Sudden-Teaching Dharma-gate. Because in so doing they serve the Buddha, those who to the end of life never retreat will surely enter the stage of the sages. Yet one must transmit the silent transmission and charge handed down from the patriarchs of old, and must not conceal the true Dharma. If they are of unlike view and unlike practice, dwelling in another Dharma, one must not transmit and entrust it to them; for that would injure the common-goods of those former worthies, and in the end be of no benefit. I fear that foolish people, not understanding, will slander this Dharma-gate, and for a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives cut off the seed of Buddhahood.]

Good-knowing friends! Those in later ages who gain my Dharma should, together with those of like view and like practice, vow to receive and hold this Sudden-Teaching Dharma-gate. Because receiving and holding the Sudden Teaching is like serving the Buddha, those who persist to the end of life without retreat will surely enter the stage of the sages. But to them (those of like view and like practice) one must transmit the silent transmission and charge handed down through all the successive patriarchs, and must not conceal the true Dharma of the Sudden Teaching. If they are of unlike view, unlike practice, and dwell in other Dharma-gates, one must not transmit and entrust it to them; because this would injure the reputations of their former ancestors and masters, and in the end be harmful and profitless both to them and to oneself. In particular, I fear that foolish people, not understanding the Sudden Teaching, will slander this Dharma-gate and incur the grave retribution, over a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives, of cutting off the seed of Buddhahood.

“No-marks” means not clinging to marks (not grasping characteristics as real). Why must one not cling to marks? Because “all marks whatsoever are false.” From beginningless kalpas, we, precisely because we clung to marks, were enticed, coerced, and bound by marks, and so created karma and received retribution—hence there is birth and death, and the wheel of transmigration. Now, in order to end birth and death and escape the three realms, we must depart from marks and no longer cling to them. The Verse of No-Marks tells us how not to cling to marks. If one can recite it again and again, realize it again and again, practice it again and again, and test it again and again, the results will surely be great.

[Good-knowing friends! I have a Verse of No-Marks; each of you must recite and take it up. Both lay and monastic, simply practice according to it. If you do not practice it, but only bear in mind my words, it will likewise be of no benefit. Listen to my verse:]

Good-knowing friends! I have a Verse of No-Marks; each of you must recite, receive, and hold it. Both lay and monastic, simply practice according to it; if you do not actually practice it yourself, but only bear in mind my words, there is also no benefit. Listen to my verse:
[Through speech and through the mind, as the sun that dwells in the empty sky, so to transmit the Dharma of seeing nature, I have come forth from the world to destroy the false sects.]

Through speech and through the mind—like a radiant sun at the zenith illuminating the whole world. To transmit the Sudden-Teaching Dharma of seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha, I have come into this world to destroy the false sects.

[Through speech (shuo-tong)] One who is well versed in the scriptures and, responding to the capacities of sentient beings, speaks the Dharma with skillfully appropriate means, is called one who is through in speech; one who can awaken to the essential purpose, knowing his own original mind and seeing his own original nature, is called one who is through in the essential. The Lankavatara Sutra says: “All sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have two kinds of throughness—the throughness of the essential and the throughness of speech.” [Through the essential] This is the throughness of the essential (zong-tong). [False sects] The Chan school calls all sects that do not take seeing one’s nature as their essential aim “false sects.” Why? Because these sects hold that there is Dharma outside the mind, and so they cling to marks. For this reason the verse is named “No-Marks.” [No-marks] Amid all marks, to be free of all marks.
[The Dharma has neither sudden nor gradual, but confusion and awakening are slow or quick. Only this gate of seeing one’s nature—the foolish cannot fully know it.]

The Dharma originally has neither sudden nor gradual; rather, sentient beings’ confusion and awakening are slow or quick. But this Dharma-gate of seeing one’s nature is something that foolish and deluded people cannot comprehend.
[Speaking is of a myriad kinds, yet being in accord with principle it returns to one. In the dark dwelling of affliction, ever must be born the sun of wisdom.]

Though the teachings are many and varied, their principle is one: in the dark dwelling of affliction, one must at all times contemplate with the principle of prajñā (let the sun of wisdom be born). (This is what was said above: “Contemplate with prajñā wisdom, so that within and without are clearly illumined, and you know your own original mind.”)

[In the dark dwelling of affliction, ever must be born the sun of wisdom] By contemplating with the principle of prajñā (the contemplation of wisdom), deviant thoughts naturally cannot stain it, just as when the sun is in the sky the mountain-sprites sink away unnoticed.
[When the deviant comes, afflictions arrive; when the right comes, afflictions are removed. When deviant and right are both put aside, purity is reached with nothing left over.]
When a deviant thought arises, afflictions arrive; when a right thought arises, afflictions are removed; when neither a deviant nor a right thought is used, then one reaches complete purity.
[Bodhi is intrinsically self-nature; to stir the mind is to be false. To purify the mind amid the false—only uprightness, and the three hindrances are gone.]

Bodhi is the awareness inherently complete in self-nature; to stir the mind gives rise to illusions. To purify the mind amid illusion, one need only maintain right thought, and then there are no three hindrances (the hindrance of afflictions, the hindrance of karma, and the hindrance of retribution).

[The three hindrances] There are three that veil the right Way: the hindrance of afflictions, the hindrance of karma, and the hindrance of retribution. The hindrance of afflictions is the obstacle caused by the delusions of greed, hatred, and ignorance; the hindrance of karma is the obstacle caused by karmic actions; the hindrance of retribution is the obstacle caused by the fruits of retribution.
[If people of the world would cultivate the Way, nothing whatever obstructs them. Ever seeing one’s own faults—this is to be in accord with the Way.]
If people of the world cultivate the Way, nothing at all obstructs them; ever aware of one’s own faults, one is in accord with the Way.
[Ever see one’s own faults] Here “fault” does not mean a mistake in one’s doing, but rather becoming defiled by the dust-realms and following the emotions to create karma.

Regarding the faults of one’s own mind, the Great Master Hanshan said: “Those who in ancient times studied the Way, the very first thing was that the mind concerning birth and death must be earnest—not that they sought some profound and mysterious principle. What is this ‘birth and death’? It is precisely our common, present-day experience: amid the many states of worldly dust and toil, when one meets a circumstance or encounters a condition, whether adverse or favorable, the inner habitual tendencies call forth manifested activity, giving rise to such discriminating, delusive minds as love and hate, grasping and rejecting, and so forth. Because thought after thought clings and attaches, and gives rise to karma of many kinds, good and evil, all of these become the very root of future birth and death. Since delusive thought is boundless, so birth and death is without end. Hence sentient beings, through long kalpas revolving in the bitter sea of birth and death, have no moment of getting out—this is wholly because they do not know the faults of their own mind.” (Dream Journey Collection
[Beings possessed of color each have their own Way, and should none hinder or trouble the other. To leave the Way and seek another way—to the end of life one never sees the Way.]

Sentient beings each have their own Way; let each cultivate and not hinder or trouble the other. To leave the Way of one’s own mind and seek the Way outside—to the very end of life, one will not see the Way.

The Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “Only this one mind—there is not so much as a particle of Dharma to be obtained; this very mind is Buddha. Now those who study the Way, not awakening to the essence of this mind, generate a mind upon the mind and seek Buddha outside; practicing while clinging to marks—all these are unwholesome Dharmas, not the Way of bodhi.” “Only this one mind is Buddha; Buddha and sentient beings are in no way different. It is only that sentient beings, clinging to marks, seek outside, and the more they seek the more they lose—making the Buddha seek the Buddha, using the mind to catch the mind, through kalpas without number and throughout life never obtaining it. They do not know that by stilling thoughts and forgetting considerations, the Buddha appears before them of itself.”

[Beings possessed of color] Sentient beings who have a body of form. [Seeing the Way] Seeing the Way, cultivating the Way, and the Way of no-more-learning are together called the three Ways. In the Mahayana, the first stage (bhumi) is called seeing the Way; the second through the ninth stages are called cultivating the Way; and the tenth stage up to Buddhahood is called the Way of no-more-learning. To see one’s original nature completely is the first stage, and is called seeing the Way.

[Drifting to and fro for a whole lifetime, at the end still wearying oneself. If you would see the true Way, conduct that is upright is itself the Way. If you yourself have no mind for the Way, walking in darkness you will not see the Way.]

One who does not polish and realize one’s own mind upon the states and conditions, but thinks the Way is elsewhere, rushes about in all directions for a lifetime searching, and at the end still is vexed that he has not seen the Way; if you would see the true Way, conduct that is upright (not clinging) is itself the Way. If you yourself have no mind for the Way, it is like walking a road at night—you cannot see the Way.
[Drifting to and fro (bo-bo)] Rushing about.
This passage says that the Way lies right in one’s own present place, not to be turned by the states and conditions; conduct that is upright (not clinging) is itself the Way.

[One who truly cultivates the Way does not see the faults of the world. If one sees the wrongs of others, one’s own fault is then the wrong. Another’s wrong I do not make my wrong; if I make a wrong, that is my own fault.]

If one is a true cultivator of the Way, one will not see the faults of the world. If one sees that others are wrong and censures them in one’s own mind, then one has oneself erred. Another’s wrong—I must not take it as wrong; if I take it as wrong (censuring others in my own mind), then I myself have a fault.

Removing the discriminating mind is most crucial for cultivating the Way. So the Sixth Patriarch, in “Chapter Eight, Sudden and Gradual,” instructs: “The ground of mind without wrong—this is the precept of self-nature.” (When the ground of mind does not give rise to right and wrong, self and other, that is the precept of self-nature.)
[Only put aside the mind that censures—strike and break through afflictions. With love and hate unheeded in the mind, stretch out both feet and lie down.]

As long as one puts away the mind that censures others, one will break through many afflictions; when the feelings of love and hate no longer rise in the mind, then at all times and in all places one is at ease and free.

[With love and hate unheeded in the mind, stretch out both feet and lie down] The mind being empty, the realms are empty of themselves; the myriad dharmas bind nothing, and one is fundamentally liberated.
[If you would transform others, you yourself must have the skillful means. Do not let them have doubt—this is the manifestation of self-nature.]
If you would use the Sudden Teaching to transform others, you yourself must have the skillfully appropriate means; to not cause them to have doubt—this is the manifestation of self-nature.
[The Buddha-Dharma is in the world, and is not separate from the world’s awakening. To seek bodhi apart from the world is like seeking the horn of a rabbit.]

The Buddha-Dharma is in the world; to awaken, one cannot be apart from the world. To seek bodhi apart from the world is exactly like seeking the horn of a rabbit, which does not exist at all—for there is no awakening apart from the world!

[Not separate from the world’s awakening] The Platform Sutra especially emphasizes testing the mind amid the states of affairs. One must examine and temper oneself upon the states of affairs; these states of affairs are the tongs and the hammer. Apart from the tempering of the states of affairs, one cannot cut off afflictions and escape the three realms—much less realize the Way and become Buddha!

“The world” refers to the three realms: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness. The Buddha-Dharma is the teaching that leaves the false and realizes the true; it is a transcendent Dharma. This is the watershed between the Buddha-Dharma and the way of Confucius and Mencius, the externalist schools, and the externalists attached to Buddhism. Yet the Buddha-Dharma exists within the world, and one must in the world test the mind amid the states of affairs, so as to break clinging and remove habits—to subdue afflictions and cut off afflictions, and so transcend the world. (The Pure Land method, by only subduing afflictions and reciting the Buddha’s name with the aim of rebirth in the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss, suffices to end birth and death and escape the three realms; other methods must cut off afflictions in order to end birth and death and escape the three realms.)

This says that one must work at the very place of meeting affairs and objects, rather than fleeing from the states of affairs. A cultivator who leaves the grinding and polishing of the world is like the flowers and plants of a hothouse, unable to withstand wind and rain—how could he realize the Way and become Buddha?

[The tempering of the states of affairs] Tempering is the ancient method by which raw iron is turned into steel—the so-called “a hundred refiner’s hammerings make steel.” The method is: raw iron, by repeated high-temperature hammering, is freed of its impurities and reduced in its carbon content, and so becomes steel. “The tempering of the states of affairs” is the grinding and polishing upon the states of affairs by which one removes affliction and ignorance. [Externalists attached to Buddhism] Sects that, by latching onto Buddhism, distort and tamper with its doctrines.
[Right view is called transcending the world; wrong view is called the world. When both wrong and right are struck down, the nature of bodhi stands revealed.]
Right view is called transcending the world, and wrong view is called the world; when both wrong view and right view are struck down, the bodhi-nature stands clearly revealed.
[This verse is the Sudden Teaching, and is also called the great Dharma-boat. The confused, hearing it, pass through many kalpas; the awakened, then, is in an instant.]

This Verse of No-Marks is the Sudden-Teaching mind-Dharma, and is the great Dharma-boat that conveys beings to the other shore of nirvāṇa; the confused, hearing it, do not awaken through many kalpas, while sudden awakening is in but a moment.

[The Master again said: Today, in the Great Brahma Temple, having spoken this Sudden Teaching, I pray that all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm may, upon these words, see nature and become Buddha. At that time Prefect Wei, together with the officials and the religious and lay followers, hearing what the Master taught, all without exception came to awareness. They all at once made obeisance, and all exclaimed: Well done! Whoever would have thought that in Lingnan a Buddha had appeared in the world.]

The Master again said: Today, in the Great Brahma Temple, I have spoken this Sudden Teaching, and pray that all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm may, at this very moment, see nature and become Buddha. At that time Prefect Wei, together with the officials and the religious (those gone forth) and the lay (those at home), hearing the Master’s instruction, all without exception came to awareness, and together made obeisance to the Master. All praised it, saying: How well spoken! We never thought that in Lingnan a Buddha had appeared in the world.

[One day, Prefect Wei prepared for the Master a great assembly-feast. When the feast was finished, the Prefect asked the Master to ascend the seat, and together with the officials, scholars, and commoners, with solemn mien, made obeisance again, asking: Your disciple, having heard the Reverend speak the Dharma, finds it truly inconceivable. Now I have a small doubt, and beg the Teacher, in great compassion, to explain it for me. The Master said: If you have a doubt, ask, and I shall speak it for you.]

One day, Prefect Wei set up for the Master a great unrestrained assembly. When the feast was done, the Prefect invited the Master to ascend the Dharma-seat, and together with the officials and the gathered community, with solemn mien, made obeisance again, asking: The disciple, having heard the Reverend speak the Dharma, finds it profound, subtle, and penetrating—truly inconceivable. The disciple now has a few small doubts, and begs the Teacher, in great compassion, to set them forth. The Master said: If you have a doubt, ask, and I shall speak it for you.

[Great assembly-feast] Also called the unrestrained assembly, in which, from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas above down to the hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals below, and likewise to people in this world, without distinction of wise and foolish, sage and ordinary, high and low, religious and lay, all are equally offered gifts of wealth and gifts of Dharma. [Scholars and commoners (shi-su)] Scholars (the lettered) and commoners (the ordinary). Shi-su also generally denotes the people, the common multitude, or the community without office. [Reverend (he-shang)] This is a Sanskrit term meaning “my teacher”; it is the respectful title that a monastic uses toward his own personal preceptor. [Inconceivable] Either the profound subtlety of principle, or the marvellous rarity of events, cannot be grasped by thought nor expressed in words.

Lord Wei said: Is that which the Reverend speaks not the essential aim of the Grand Master Bodhidharma? The Master said: It is. Lord Wei said: Your disciple has heard that when Bodhidharma first converted Emperor Wu of Liang, the Emperor asked: “In this life I have built monasteries, ordained monks, given alms, and made offerings—what merit is there?” Bodhidharma said: “There is no merit at all.” Your disciple has not grasped this principle, and begs the Reverend to explain it.]

Prefect Wei said: Is that which the Reverend has disclosed not the essential aim of the Grand Master Bodhidharma? The Master said: It is. Prefect Wei said: Your disciple has heard that when the Grand Master Bodhidharma first converted Emperor Wu of Liang, the Emperor asked: “In this life I have built monasteries, ordained monks, given alms, and made offerings—how much merit is there?” The Grand Master Bodhidharma answered: “There is not a single bit of merit.” Your disciple does not understand this principle, and begs the Teacher to explain it for me.

[Emperor Wu of Liang] The first emperor of the Liang, the southern dynasty. In the third year of the Tian-jian era (504 CE) he issued an edict declaring Buddhism the state religion; thereafter he gave himself four times into monasteries as a servant, and constantly held the unrestrained assembly, the great equanimity assembly, and the Ullambana assembly, and widely built monasteries and stupas. In the capital Jian-kang (today’s Nanjing) alone there were more than five hundred Buddhist monasteries and over a hundred thousand monks and nuns—this was the most flourishing era of Southern-dynasty Buddhism. [Zhen] The emperor’s style of self-designation. [There is no merit at all] The Grand Master Bodhidharma, in the eighth year of the Putong era of Liang (527 CE), crossed the sea and arrived in Nan-hai (today’s Guangzhou, Guangdong). The governor of Guangzhou received him with full ceremony; Emperor Wu sent a messenger to invite him to Jin-ling (today’s Nanjing, Jiangsu). Emperor Wu was a devoutly believing sovereign who, after taking the throne, built monasteries, copied sutras, ordained monks, and made images in great number, and so asked the Grand Master with self-satisfaction: “I have done so many Buddhist works—how much merit is there?” The Grand Master Bodhidharma said: “There is no merit at all.” The Emperor asked again: “Why is there no merit?” The Grand Master said: “These are conditioned activities, not true merit.” The Emperor did not comprehend; whereupon Bodhidharma crossed the river and entered Wei.

[The Master said: There is indeed no merit at all! Doubt not the words of the earlier sages. The Emperor’s mind was deviant, and he did not know the true Dharma. Building monasteries and ordaining monks, giving alms and making offerings—these are called seeking blessings; you must not take the blessings to be merit. Merit lies in the dharmakaya, not in cultivating blessings.]

The Master said: Though Emperor Wu built monasteries, ordained monks, gave alms, and made offerings in great number, there is indeed not a single bit of merit! Doubt not the words of the earlier sages, thinking the Grand Master Bodhidharma was mistaken. The Emperor harbored a deviant mind and did not know the true Dharma. Building monasteries and ordaining monks, giving alms and making offerings—this is cultivating blessings; you must not take these blessings as merit. Merit lies in one’s self-nature, and does not lie in cultivating blessings.

[Merit] To wipe out the inner ignorance is the meritorious work; for wisdom to come forth is the virtue. [Blessings (fude)] This refers to the meritorious bliss reaped from cultivating the good deeds of humans and heavenly beings. Blessings and merit are different: to cultivate the conditioned good that has outflows is blessings; only to realize within the Buddha-nature the wisdom that has no outflows is merit. Moreover, in cultivation, to cultivate while clinging to marks is blessings; to cultivate free of marks is merit. Emperor Wu cultivated good while clinging to marks, and so had only blessings and no merit. [Outflow (lou)] Another name for afflictions, carrying the two meanings of “leaking out” and “falling down.” The afflictions of greed, hatred, and ignorance, day and night, leak and flow out through the gates of the six sense-organs without ceasing, and so are called outflows. Also, afflictions cause one to fall down into the three evil destinies, and so are also called outflows. All dharmas that have afflictions are called “dharmas with outflows”; dharmas without afflictions are called “dharmas without outflows.” [Dharmakaya] This is the body of self-nature, the true body of the Buddha.

[The Master again said: Seeing nature is the meritorious work; evenness is the virtue. In thought after thought without obstruction, always seeing the true, marvellous function of one’s original nature, this is called merit. Inward humility is the meritorious work; outward practice of propriety is the virtue. Self-nature establishing the myriad dharmas is the meritorious work; the mind-essence free from thought is the virtue. Not departing from self-nature is the meritorious work; in application without defilement is the virtue. If you seek the merit-dharmakaya, but act according to this, that is true merit.]

The Master again said: Seeing nature is the meritorious work; the mind’s evenness is the virtue. In thought after thought, without pollution and without attachment, always seeing the true, marvellous function of one’s original nature, this is called merit. Inward humility is the meritorious work; outward practice of propriety is the virtue. Self-nature, taking the lead, establishing the myriad dharmas is the meritorious work; the mind-essence free from thought is the virtue. Not departing from self-nature is the meritorious work; in application without defilement is the virtue. If you would seek the merit-dharmakaya, merely practice according to this—that is true merit.

[Evenness] With no difference of high and low, noble and mean, deep and shallow—this is called evenness. The Records of the Five Lamps says: “Heaven is even, and so constantly covers; earth is even, and so constantly bears; sun and moon are even, and so the four seasons are constantly bright; nirvāṇa is even, and so sage and ordinary are not two; the human mind is even, and so high and low have no contention.” [Propriety (li)] The norms of conduct that accord with the overall interest of the community. [Self-nature establishing the myriad dharmas is the meritorious work] This is self-nature, taking the lead, establishing the myriad dharmas—that is, as Chapter Four states: “The true-suchness self-nature gives rise to thought; though the six sense-organs have seeing, hearing, and knowing, they are not defiled by the myriad realms, and the true nature is always free.” [Merit-dharmakaya] The Tathagata, taking the merits of the myriad practices as the cause, accomplishes the fruit of the dharmakaya; hence it is called the merit-dharmakaya.

[One who cultivates merit, his mind does not disparage, and he constantly practices universal respect. If the mind constantly disparages people, and self and pride are not cut off, then naturally there is no meritorious work; if self-nature is false and unreal, then naturally there is no virtue. Because of self-glorifying greatness, one constantly disparages all things.]

One who would cultivate merit should have a mind that does not disparage, and constantly practice universal respect. If the mind constantly disparages others, always taking the self as the very center, with self, self, self unbroken—then naturally there is no meritorious work; if self-nature is false and unreal, then naturally there is no virtue. This is because, proud and self-glorifying, one constantly disparages all.

[Good-knowing friends! In thought after thought without break is the meritorious work; the mind’s conduct even and upright is the virtue. Cultivating one’s own nature is the meritorious work; cultivating one’s own body is the virtue.]

Good-knowing friends! In thought after thought, seeing nature without break, is the meritorious work; the mind’s conduct even and upright is the virtue. Cultivating one’s own mind-nature is the meritorious work; cultivating one’s own body-conduct is the virtue.

[Good-knowing friends! Merit must be seen within one’s self-nature, and is not what gift-giving and offerings seek, therefore blessings and merit differ. The Emperor did not know the true principle—it is not that our patriarch had any fault.]

Good-knowing friends! Merit must be seen within one’s own self-nature, and is not attained by outward gift-giving and offerings; therefore blessings and merit are different. Emperor Wu did not know the true principle of how merit is made, and so though his good deeds were many, in truth he had no merit—it is not that our patriarch spoke wrongly.

Q. When Bodhidharma first met Emperor Wu of Liang, the Emperor asked: “What is the highest meaning of the holy truths?” Bodhidharma said: “Vast and empty, there is no holy.” Then the Emperor went on to ask: “Who is it that confronts me?” Bodhidharma said: “I do not know.” The Emperor did not fall in with it, and so Bodhidharma crossed the river and went to the Wei. How should this exchange be understood?

Answer: This is the first case among the hundred cases of the Blue Cliff Record, and it is extremely famous. It is how Patriarch Bodhidharma, using the most ultimate reality of all dharmas, brought Emperor Wu of Liang to liberation, transmitting the mind-seal of the Buddha. A pity that although the emperor believed in the Buddha, his delusion about objects and attachment to marks ran so deep that he could not enter into it; so the Patriarch crossed the river on a single reed and went off to the state of Wei, letting the encounter slip by. After Bodhidharma passed into nirvāṇa, the emperor recalled this and composed a stele inscription himself, saying: Alas! Seen yet not seen, met yet not met, encountered yet not encountered; of the present and the past, I grieve and I regret. He further eulogized: When the mind has something, one is mired as an ordinary being through countless eons; when the mind has nothing, one ascends to wondrous awakening in an instant.

The teaching schools say: the ultimate truth reveals the not-existing, and the conventional truth reveals the not-nonexistent; the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional is the foremost meaning of the holy truth. This is where the scholastic tradition reaches the utmost subtlety and exhausts the profound. Emperor Wu of Liang, at this very ultimate point, asked Bodhidharma, 'What is the foremost meaning of the holy truth?' The Patriarch replied, 'Fundamentally there is no holy one (vast and complete, nothing holy),' answering with the reality of all dharmas. The Sutra of the Buddha's Treasury says: 'All dharmas have no existence; ultimately they are empty.' This is also what the Sixth Patriarch meant by, 'Originally there was not a single thing.' Where, then, is there any ordinary being or holy one?

Emperor Wu then asked again, 'Who is it that faces me?' His meaning was: they call you, Bodhidharma, a holy one, yet you just said, 'Fundamentally there is no holy one (vast and complete, nothing holy)'; if there is no holy one, then what are you? The Patriarch replied, 'I do not know,' and this too was an answer grounded in the reality of all dharmas. The Sutra of the Buddha's Treasury says: 'Because the holy one has attained the reality of all dharmas, he does not discriminate whether one is man or woman, deva or naga, nor even whether a thing is dharma or non-dharma. Because he does not discriminate, he does not grasp at various dharmas.'
Kuoran (vast and complete): the aspect of empty stillness.

What the Sixth Patriarch reveals here is the dharma-body Pure Land state of 'mind-only Pure Land and the intrinsic Amitābha.' Beginners may set this section aside for the time being; when they have attained some skill and realize that the intrinsic nature is itself Amitābha, they may return to read it and will find it deeply intimate and beneficial. As the Zhongfeng Threefold Contemplation Service says: 'Amitābha Buddha is my mind, and my mind is Amitābha Buddha; the Pure Land is this very place, and this very place is the Pure Land.' One enters the mindfulness of principle from the mindfulness of practice, holding to both principle and practice.

[The prefect again asked: Disciples often see monks and laypeople reciting Amitābha Buddha's name, wishing to be reborn in the West. May the master tell us whether they will be reborn there? I wish you would resolve this doubt.]

Prefect Wei again asked: Disciples often see monks and laypeople reciting Amitābha Buddha's name, seeking rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. May the master tell us whether they can attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss? I hope the master will resolve my doubt.

[The master said: Good Sir, listen well! Huineng will explain it for you. The World-Honored One, in the city of Shravasti, spoke the scripture that leads beings onward to the West, making it clear that it is not far from here. If we speak of the distance in terms of marks, there are one hundred and eight thousand li, which is the ten evil acts and eight wrong paths within the body; this is speaking of it as far. To speak of far is for those of inferior faculties; to speak of near is for those of superior wisdom.]

The master said: Good Sir! Listen carefully, and I will tell you. The World-Honored One, in the city of Shravasti, spoke of how the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss receives and guides beings; the scripture states it clearly: the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far from here. (The Sutra of the Buddha of Measureless Life on the Contemplation of the Land of Ultimate Bliss says: 'At that time the World-Honored One told Queen Vaidehi: Do you know now that Amitābha Buddha is not far from here?') If we speak of the distance in terms of relative marks, then it is one hundred and eight thousand li; to speak of cultivation, it is the ten evil acts and eight wrong paths within the body; this is speaking of it as far. To speak of far is from the standpoint of relative marks, for those of inferior faculties; to speak of near is from the standpoint of principle: 'Amitābha Buddha is my mind, and my mind is Amitābha Buddha; the Pure Land is this very place, and this very place is the Pure Land.' Therefore the scripture says the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is clearly not far from here, and this is spoken for those of superior wisdom.

One hundred and eight thousand li: In ancient times people often used one hundred and eight thousand li to describe something extremely distant; it is not an actual distance. For example, the Record of Zen Master Fayan: 'When he ascended the hall, he said: What is Zen? The jambu tree is on the far side of the southern sea; near, it is not apart from the square inch; far, it is one hundred and eight thousand li. After all, what is it? Zen! Zen!' The Sixth Patriarch uses 'one hundred and eight thousand' here partly to describe something extremely distant, and partly to set it against the ten evil acts and eight wrong paths within the body for an illustrative explanation. Ten evil acts: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, idle talk, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, anger, and ignorance. Eight wrong paths: the eight wrong paths opposite to the Eightfold Right Path, namely wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong endeavor, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. Eightfold Right Path: also called the Eightfold Noble Path, the eight paths of the noble ones: 1. Right view, correct understanding. 2. Right thought, correct thinking. 3. Right speech, proper words. 4. Right action, proper conduct. 5. Right livelihood, proper occupation or way of life. 6. Right endeavor, proper effort. 7. Right mindfulness, correct awareness. 8. Right concentration, correct meditation. Cultivating this Eightfold Right Path, one can realize the fruit of arhatship. To speak of near is for those of superior wisdom: The Zhongfeng Threefold Contemplation Service says: 'Amitābha Buddha is my mind, and my mind is Amitābha Buddha; the Pure Land is this very place, and this very place is the Pure Land. Is it not that delusion and awakening differ by themselves, so how can there be sages and ordinary beings, this and that?' 'The journey of a hundred thousand is not parted by a mote of dust; do not let delusion and awakening keep you near or far; when in an instant you have exhausted the Buddha-thought of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you are a person in the land of the lotus flower.'

[People are of two kinds, but the Dharma is not two; delusion and awakening differ, and their insight is quick or slow. Deluded people recite the Buddha's name seeking rebirth there; awakened people purify their own minds. Therefore the Buddha said: 'When the mind is pure, the Buddha land is pure.']

People are of two kinds, deluded and awakened, but the Buddha Dharma is one; delusion and awakening differ, so the attainment of right view is quick or slow. The deluded do not purify their own minds but hope, by reciting the Buddha's name, to be reborn there, in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the awakened purify their own minds, and the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is right before them. Therefore the Buddha said: 'When the mind is pure, the Buddha land is pure.'

This says: when the mind is pure, it accords with the Pure Land; when the mind is defiled, it accords with the defiled land. Therefore those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land should first of all purify their own minds.

As the mind is pure, the Buddha land is pure. The Buddha said: 'If a bodhisattva wishes to attain a pure land, he should purify his mind; when his mind is pure, the Buddha land is pure.' (Vimalakirti Sutra
Chapter on the Buddha Land, part one)

[Good Sir! A person of the East, so long as his mind is pure, is without offense; though a person of the West, if his mind is impure, still has guilt. An Easterner who commits offenses recites the Buddha's name seeking rebirth in the West; a Westerner who commits offenses, reciting the Buddha's name, seeks rebirth in what land? Ordinary and foolish people, not understanding their own nature and not recognizing the Pure Land within their own bodies, wish for East and wish for West; but for the awakened, wherever they are it is the same. Therefore the Buddha said: 'Wherever you abide, there is constant peace and joy.']

Good Sir! A person of the East, so long as his mind is pure, is without offense; though he is a person of the West, if his mind is impure he still has guilt. An Easterner who commits offenses recites the Buddha's name seeking rebirth in the West; then a Westerner who commits offenses, reciting the Buddha's name, seeks rebirth in what land? Ordinary and foolish people, not understanding their own nature and not recognizing the Pure Land within their own body, therefore wish for East and wish for West; but for the awakened, wherever they are it is the same. Therefore the Buddha said: 'Wherever you abide, there is constant peace and joy.'

What the Sixth Patriarch sets forth here is the meaning of 'mind-only Pure Land': 'When the mind is pure, the Buddha land is pure.' This is also what the later text says: 'So long as the mind is pure, that is the intrinsic Western Land.' Realizing the dharma of non-arising, Amitābha Buddha is my mind, and my mind is Amitābha Buddha; the Pure Land is this very place, and this very place is the Pure Land. Master Yuanying said in the Preface to the Essence of Master Yinguang's Collected Writings: 'Only when one knows that the intrinsic nature is itself Amitābha can one discuss the mind-only Pure Land: when the mind is pure, the Buddha land is pure.' (Note: the whole of the Platform Sutra is about the intrinsic Amitābha, real-mindfulness recitation of the Buddha.)

Non-arising dharma: The Diamond Sutra says: 'All that has form is illusory.' All dharmas are illusions; originally they were never born, and so they are never extinguished. Buddhas, amidst the seeming arising and ceasing, see only non-arising; sentient beings, amidst the still non-arising, see only arising and ceasing. Vimalakirti Sutra

Chapter on Entering the Non-Dual Dharma Door says: 'Arising and ceasing are two. The dharma is originally unborn, and now it is unceasing. Attaining this patience with the non-arising dharma is entering the non-dual Dharma door.'

Patience with non-arising: that is, the patience with the non-arising dharma, where true wisdom abides in the principle that 'all dharmas were originally never born, and so are never extinguished,' never again falling back. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says: 'All dharmas are all false.' The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra says: 'Thus this non-retrogressing bodhisattva-mahasattva, by the emptiness of self-marks, contemplates all dharmas, having entered the positive nature of the bodhisattva which transcends birth, until he sees no dharma at all to be obtained. Because nothing can be obtained, there is no making. Because there is no making, ultimately there is no birth. Because ultimately there is no birth, it is called the patience with the non-arising dharma. Because he has attained this patience with the non-arising dharma, he is called the non-retrogressing bodhisattva-mahasattva.'
Question: Is what the Sixth Patriarch says here contrary to the three Pure Land sutras?

Answer: No. The three Pure Land sutras speak from the standpoint of relative marks, while the Sixth Patriarch speaks from the standpoint of principle. The Twelfth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, said in his essay The Explanation of the West: 'By "West having" is meant that the West truly exists, only that it contains such varied principle-aspects as the relative and the absolute, emptiness and being. If one says it is a fixed, truly existing place that cannot be moved, this is the ordinary clinging of the common mind to what is always there. Moreover, the serene adornments of the West, both the main land and the surrounding ones, are all originally inherent in the nature of sentient beings; it is only that they are specially manifested by relying on Amitābha's great vows as the dominant condition, so how could there be any dharma newly obtained? In this light, "West having" is the having of the truly good and wondrous being inherently present in one's own nature.' The Platform Sutra is the sudden teaching, spoken for people of great wisdom faculties, so its explanation never departs from the self-nature. In 'Chapter Eight, Sudden and Gradual,' the Sixth Patriarch says: 'The Dharma I speak never departs from the self-nature; to speak of dharma apart from the essence is called speaking of marks, and the self-nature is ever deluded.'

[Good Sir! So long as the ground of the mind is without what is unwholesome, the West is not far from here; but if one harbors an unwholesome mind, rebirth through reciting the Buddha's name is hard to reach.]

Good Sir! So long as the ground of the mind is without what is unwholesome, the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far away; but if one harbors an unwholesome mind, reciting the Buddha's name to seek rebirth is also hard to reach.
Good: to accord with principle is called good; to oppose principle is called evil.

[Now I urge you, good teachers: first rid yourself of the ten evil acts, and you will have traveled a hundred thousand; then rid yourself of the eight wrong paths, and you will pass beyond eight thousand. In every thought see your nature, always practice equanimity and uprightness, and in a snap of the fingers you will see Amitābha. Good Sir! If you only practice the ten good deeds, why still wish for rebirth? If you do not cut off the mind of the ten evil acts, what Buddha will come to welcome you? If you awaken to the sudden dharma of non-arising, you see the West only in an instant; if you do not awaken, and recite the Buddha's name seeking rebirth, how can you reach the end of such a long road?]

Today I urge you, good teachers: first rid yourself of the ten evil acts, and you will have traveled a hundred thousand li (above, one hundred and eight thousand li is used to describe the distance from here to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss); then rid yourself of the eight wrong paths, and you will pass beyond eight thousand li, arriving at the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. In every thought see your nature, always practice equanimity and uprightness in conduct, and you will be in sympathetic resonance with Amitābha Buddha, reaching the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss in a snap of the fingers and seeing Amitābha Buddha face to face. Good Sir! If you only put effort into the ten good deeds, why still wish for rebirth? If you do not cut off the mind of the ten evil acts, what Buddha will come to welcome you? If you can awaken to the sudden dharma of non-arising, you see the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss only in an instant; if you do not awaken and recite the Buddha's name seeking rebirth, how can you reach the end of such a long road?

Ten good deeds: the ten wholesome acts: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking idly, not being greedy, not being angry, and not being ignorant. Sudden dharma of non-arising: that is, the 'non-arising dharma' spoken of earlier, the method of swift accomplishment of the One Vehicle, hence it is called 'sudden.' Realizing the dharma of non-arising, Amitābha Buddha is my mind, and my mind is Amitābha Buddha; the Pure Land is this very place, and this very place is the Pure Land. Hence it says: 'If you awaken to the sudden dharma of non-arising, you see the West only in an instant.' This principle is fully set forth in the instruction of the Zhongfeng Threefold Contemplation Service

First Period Service. At the opening of the instruction, a verse says: 'All suffering arises from craving, yet who knows where craving arises? Because one forgets the self-nature Amitābha Buddha, and scattered thoughts fly this way and that, all is a devil.' The concluding verse says: 'Arising and ceasing, non-arising, in non-arising nothing is born; how would the Land of Bliss forbid people from walking there? Who would know that within the ten thousand fathoms of the red dust, the lotus flower blooms while the moon is bright?'

[Huineng, in an instant, can move the West here for you all; you will see it before your eyes. Do each of you wish to see it? The assembly all bowed their heads and said: If we see it here, why still wish for rebirth? We beg the master, in his compassion, to manifest the West so that all of us may see it.]

I can, in an instant, move the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss here for you all; you will see it the moment you open your eyes. Do each of you wish to see it? The assembly all bowed their heads and said: If we see the Land of Ultimate Bliss right here, why still wish for rebirth? We beg the master, in his compassion, to manifest the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss so that the whole assembly may see it.

[The master said: Good assembly! The physical body of worldly people is a city, and its eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are the gates. Outside there are five gates, and within is the gate of the mind. The mind is the land, and the nature is the king, and the king dwells on the land of the mind. When the nature is present, the king is present; when the nature departs, the king is gone. When the nature is present, body and mind exist; when the nature departs, body and mind are destroyed. Seek Buddhahood within your nature, do not seek outside the body; when the self-nature is deluded, that is the sentient being, and when the self-nature is awakened, that is the Buddha. Compassion is Avalokitesvara, and joyful renunciation is Mahasthamaprapta; what can purify is Śākyamuni, and equanimity and uprightness is Amitābha. Self and others is Mount Sumeru, the deluded mind is the ocean waters, afflictions are the waves, malice is the evil dragon, falsehood is the ghosts and spirits, worldly defilements are the fish and turtles, greed and anger are the hells, and ignorance is the animals.]

The master said: Good assembly! The physical body of each worldly person is a city, and the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are its gates. Outside there are five gates (the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and the limbs), and within is the gate of the mind. The mind is the city's ground, and the self-nature is the king of the city. The king dwells on the ground of the mind; when the nature is present, the king is present; when the nature departs, the king is gone. When the self-nature is present, body and mind exist; when the self-nature departs, body and mind are destroyed. To become a Buddha, work within your self-nature; do not seek it outside the body. When the self-nature is deluded, that is the sentient being, and when the self-nature is awakened, that is the Buddha. Compassion is the bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, and joyful renunciation is called the bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta; what can purify is Śākyamuni Buddha, and equanimity and uprightness is Amitābha Buddha. The view of self and others is Mount Sumeru, the deluded mind is the ocean waters, afflictions are the waves, malice is the evil dragon, absurdity is the ghosts and spirits, worldly defilements are the fish and turtles, greed and anger are the hells, and ignorance is the animals.
Here Mount Sumeru, the ocean waters, the waves, the evil dragon, and so on are metaphors for the obstacles to being reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Malice: the mind that harms others.

Here the Sixth Patriarch makes an extremely important exhortation on mind and nature: 'The mind is the land, and the nature is the king, and the king dwells on the land of the mind. When the nature is present, the king is present; when the nature departs, the king is gone. When the nature is present, body and mind exist; when the nature departs, body and mind are destroyed. Seek Buddhahood within your nature, do not seek outside the body; when the self-nature is deluded, that is the sentient being, and when the self-nature is awakened, that is the Buddha.' This says that the self-nature has two states, delusion and awakening; when the self-nature is deluded, that is the sentient being, and when the self-nature is awakened, that is the Buddhas. To become a Buddha is for the self-nature to turn from delusion to awakening. In the later 'Chapter Eight, Sudden and Gradual,' the Sixth Patriarch again says: 'The Dharma I speak never departs from the self-nature; to speak of dharma apart from the essence is called speaking of marks, and the self-nature is ever deluded. Know that all dharmas function from the self-nature, and this is the true Dharma of precepts, meditation, and wisdom. Listen to my verse: The ground of the mind without wrong is the self-nature precepts; the ground of the mind without ignorance is the self-nature wisdom; the ground of the mind without disturbance is the self-nature meditation; neither increasing nor decreasing, it is the diamond; body gone and body come, it is originally samādhi.' This says: the ground of the mind determines the self-nature's delusion or awakening. Therefore cultivation is cultivating the mind. The Mahayana Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground says: 'The Buddhas take the Dharma as their great teacher; the bodhi path is realized by cultivating the mind.' The Sutra of the Five Suffering Paragraphs says: 'The mind takes hold of hell, the mind takes hold of the hungry ghosts, the mind takes hold of the animals, the mind takes hold of the devas and humans; what creates forms and appearances is all the work of the mind. The one who can subdue the mind for the sake of the Way has the greatest power. I struggled with the mind for countless eons, and only now attained Buddhahood, treading alone through the three realms; all this is the work of the mind.' The Platform Sutra says: 'Simply use this mind, and directly realize Buddhahood.' The Record of the Dharma-Mirror says: 'Becoming a Buddha is not apart from this very thought.'

Ground of the mind: the mind can give rise to all dharmas just as the earth can give rise to all things, therefore it is called the ground of the mind. The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground says: 'Within the three realms the mind is the master; one who can contemplate the mind attains ultimate liberation, and one who cannot contemplates ultimate sinking. The mind of sentient beings is like the great earth: the five grains and five fruits grow from the great earth; thus this mind-dharma gives rise to the wholesome and unwholesome of the world and beyond, the five destinies, the trainees and the untrained, the solitary realizers, the bodhisattvas, and the Tathagatas. For this reason the three realms are mind-only, and the mind is called the ground.'

[Good teachers! Always practice the ten good deeds, and heaven will arrive at once; remove self and others, and Mount Sumeru collapses; cast away the deluded mind, and the ocean waters run dry; when afflictions are gone, the waves subside; when malice is forgotten, fish and dragons cease. On the ground of your own mind, the Tathagata of the awakened nature emits great light, illuminating the six gates and purifying them, able to break through the six desires of the various heavens. Turning the light within upon the self-nature, the three poisons are at once removed, and the offenses of hell and the rest are all destroyed in a single moment. When inside and outside are wholly bright, it is no different from the West. If you do not cultivate in this way, how can you reach there?]

Good teachers! Always practice the ten good deeds, and heaven arrives at once; remove the view of self and others, and Mount Sumeru collapses; cast away the deluded mind, and the ocean waters run dry; when afflictions are gone, the waves subside; when malice is gone, fish and dragons cease. At this time, on the ground of your own mind, the Tathagata of the awakened nature emits great light, illuminating the six gates (the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and purifying them, able to break through the various temptations of form, sound, scent, taste, touch, and dharmas (the six desires) that are everywhere. Turning the light within upon the self-nature, the three poisons are at once removed, and the offenses of hell and the rest are all destroyed in a single moment. When inside and outside are wholly bright, it is no different from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. If you do not cultivate in this way, how can you reach the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?

Able to break through the six desires of the various heavens: this phrase links back to the previous line, 'illuminating the six gates and purifying them,' so it should not be read as destroying the heavens of the six desires (the six heavenly layers of the realm of desire). The six desires: the desire of sight, the desire of hearing, the desire of scent, the desire of taste, the desire of touch, and the desire of mind. But in the Sixth Patriarch's teaching, 'able to break through the six desires of the various heavens' links back to the previous line, 'illuminating the six gates and purifying them,' so the six desires here refer to form, sound, scent, taste, touch, and dharmas that tempt the mind. The word 'heaven' has several meanings. For example, in 'the people take food as their heaven,' 'heaven' refers to the foremost matter that cannot be parted from for a moment; and in 'able to break through the six desires of the various heavens,' 'heaven' means everywhere.

[The assembly, hearing this, fully understood and saw their nature, and all bowed in reverence. Together they sighed, 'How good!', and proclaimed: 'May it be that all sentient beings in the dharma-realm, whoever hears this, awaken and understand at once.']

The assembly, hearing this exhortation, were suddenly enlightened, turned the light within to see their nature, and joyfully bowed in reverence. Together they exclaimed: How wonderful! They proclaimed: May it be that all sentient beings in the dharma-realm, whoever hears this, awaken and understand together.

[The master said: Good teachers! If you wish to cultivate, it can be done at home as well; it does not depend on being in a monastery. If one can practice at home, it is like the person of the East whose mind is good; if one does not cultivate in the monastery, it is like the person of the West whose mind is evil. So long as the mind is pure, that is the intrinsic Western Land.]

The master said: Good teachers! If you wish to cultivate, it can be done at home as well; you do not have to leave home and enter a monastery. If one can practice at home as described above, it is like the person of the East whose mind is good; if one leaves home to enter a monastery but does not cultivate this way, it is like the person of the West whose mind is evil. So long as the mind is pure, that is the intrinsic Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Mr. Wei again asked: How should one cultivate at home? We wish you would teach us. The master said: I will speak for you the Verse of No-Marks; if you but cultivate according to it, you will always be with me without difference. If you do not cultivate in this way, then even shaving your head and leaving home, what benefit will it bring to the Way? The verse says:]

Prefect Wei again asked: Master! How should one cultivate at home? Please teach us. The master said: I will speak for you the Verse of No-Marks; if you but cultivate according to this verse, it is as though you were constantly together with me. If you do not cultivate in this way, then even if you shave your head and leave home, what benefit will it bring to the Way? The verse says:
[When the mind is even, why trouble to observe the precepts? When conduct is upright, what need to cultivate meditation?]
If one holds the mind in evenness, why trouble to observe the precepts? If conduct is upright, what need to cultivate meditation?

[With gratitude, one dutifully supports one's parents; with righteousness, high and low cherish one another. With deference, the honored and the humble live in harmony; with forbearance, no evil clamors.]

With gratitude, one shows filial devotion to one's parents; with righteousness, high and low love and cherish one another. With deference, the honored and the humble live in harmony; with forbearance, the various evils do not arise.
Righteousness: a fair and proper principle or action. Cherish: to love and hold dear.
[If one can rub wood to bring forth fire, in the mud a red lotus is sure to grow.]
If one can cultivate with the constancy and perseverance of rubbing wood to make fire, a red lotus is sure to grow out of the mud.

[Bitter to the mouth, it is good medicine; harsh to the ear, it must be loyal counsel. Correcting one's faults will surely give rise to wisdom; shielding one's shortcomings, the heart within is not wise.]

Bitter to the mouth is indeed good medicine; harsh to the ear must be loyal counsel. Correcting one's faults will surely give rise to wisdom; shielding one's shortcomings, one's heart within is not wise.
[In daily life always act to benefit others; attaining the Way does not come from giving money. Bodhi is to be seen only in the mind; why trouble to seek the mysterious outside!]

In daily life you should always benefit sentient beings; attaining the Way does not come from giving money (giving wealth is merit of fortune, not merit of virtue; if one can give without marks, then it is merit of virtue). To awaken only requires cultivating the mind within; why trouble to go outside seeking the subtle and the mysterious!
