[Hear this and cultivate accordingly; heaven is only before your eyes.]
Hear what I say and cultivate accordingly, and the Pure Land is only before your eyes.

[The master again said: Good teachers! All of you must cultivate according to this verse, see for yourselves your own nature, and directly accomplish the Buddha Way; the Dharma does not wait for anyone. Let the assembly disperse now; I am returning to Caoxi. If you have doubts, come and ask me.]

The master again said: Good teachers! All of you must cultivate according to this verse, see for yourselves your own nature, and directly realize the fruit of Buddhahood; the Dharma does not wait for anyone, so you must earnestly cultivate and make the most of your time. The assembly is now dismissed; I am returning to Caoxi. If you have doubts, please come to Caoxi and ask.
[At that time, the prefect, the officials, and the good men and faithful women present each attained awakening, believed, received, and practiced it.]
At that time, Prefect Wei, the officials, and the good men and faithful women present each attained awakening, believed, received, and practiced it.

blocks.text: 1. Meditation and Wisdom as the Foundation

inline.s: [The master instructed the assembly: Good teachers! This Dharma door of mine takes meditation and wisdom as its foundation.]

The master instructed the assembly: Good teachers! This sudden-teaching Dharma door of mine takes meditation and wisdom as its foundation. (Therefore the whole sutra revolves around the core of holding meditation and wisdom in equal cultivation.)

Meditation and wisdom: when objects do not disturb the mind, that is meditation; when conduct accords with the Way, that is wisdom. (The meditation spoken of in the Platform Sutra, as said in 'Chapter Five, Sitting Meditation': 'If one sees all objects and the mind is not disturbed, that is true meditation.')

[Do not be deluded, assembly, saying that meditation and wisdom are separate; meditation and wisdom are one essence, not two. Meditation is the essence of wisdom, and wisdom is the function of meditation. At the very moment of wisdom, meditation is within wisdom; at the very moment of meditation, wisdom is within meditation. If you understand this meaning, that is the equal cultivation of meditation and wisdom.]

Do not be deluded, everyone, thinking that meditation and wisdom can be separated; meditation and wisdom are always together and inseparable. Meditation is the essence, and wisdom is the function. At the moment of wisdom, meditation is within wisdom; at the moment of meditation, wisdom is within meditation. If you understand this meaning, that is the equal cultivation of meditation and wisdom.

At the moment of wisdom, meditation is within wisdom: at the moment of wisdom one is not deluded and is not turned by objects, so the mind is not disturbed, and at this time meditation is within wisdom. At the moment of meditation, wisdom is within meditation: at the moment of meditation the mind is not disturbed and does not follow objects, so one is not deluded, and at this time wisdom is within meditation.

[Scholars of the Way! Do not say: 'First meditation produces wisdom, or first wisdom produces meditation, and each is separate.' One who holds this view sees the Dharma as having two marks. Speaking good words with the mouth while the mind within is unwholesome, one merely has the empty name of meditation and wisdom, and meditation and wisdom are not equal; if both mind and mouth are wholesome and inside and outside are one, then meditation and wisdom are equal.]

Scholars of the Way, do not say: 'First meditation produces wisdom, or first wisdom produces meditation, and meditation and wisdom are each separate.' One who holds such a view sees the Dharma as having two marks. Speaking good words with the mouth while the mind within is unwholesome, that is merely empty talk of meditation and wisdom and is not holding meditation and wisdom equally; if both mind and mouth are wholesome and inside and outside are one, that is holding meditation and wisdom equally.

[Self-awakened cultivation is not about debating; if one argues about which comes first, one is just like the deluded. Not cutting off the mind of victory and defeat only increases self and dharmas, and one does not leave the four marks.]

Self-awakened cultivation is not about debating; if one argues about superior and inferior, high and low, one is just like the deluded. Not cutting off the mind of victory and defeat only increases self-attachment, which shows one has not left the four marks (the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings, and the mark of a life span). The Diamond Sutra says: 'If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings, and the mark of a life span, he is not a bodhisattva.'

What the Platform Sutra teaches is the sudden teaching, the supreme vehicle, which is different from the rest; 'meditation and wisdom as one essence' is one example, and it easily gives rise to debate. (Because, in the three studies of precepts, meditation, and wisdom, it is said that 'from precepts one attains meditation, and from meditation wisdom arises.') Therefore the master in the sutra repeatedly admonishes his disciples: 'Self-awakened cultivation is not about debating; if one argues about which comes first, one is just like the deluded.'

[Good teachers! To what are meditation and wisdom like? They are like a lamp and its light. With a lamp there is light; without a lamp there is darkness. The lamp is the essence of the light, and the light is the function of the lamp. Though the names are two, the essence is originally one. This Dharma of meditation and wisdom is the same.]

Good teachers! To what are meditation and wisdom like? They are like a lamp and its light. With a lamp there is brightness; without a lamp there is darkness. The lamp is the essence and the light is the function, just as meditation is the essence and wisdom is the function. Though the names are two, their source is the very same thing and they are inseparable.
[The master instructed the assembly: Good teachers! The one-action samādhi is, in all places, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, always practicing a single upright mind.]
The master instructed the assembly: Good teachers! The one-action samādhi is, in all places, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, always practicing a single upright mind.

'One-action samādhi' means: single-mindedly devote yourself to one practice, cultivating right concentration. So what is this 'one action'? The master instructed: the upright mind — without seeking and without attachment, that is, 'One should not give rise to a mind that abides in form; one should not give rise to a mind that abides in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.'

Right concentration: correct meditation, one of the eight right paths. Upright mind: also called the pure mind, the mind unstained by selfish desire and emotional consciousness, without seeking and without attachment, that is, the mind of uprightness and sincerity. The Diamond Sutra says: 'The bodhisattva-mahasattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to a mind that abides in form; they should not give rise to a mind that abides in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.'

[As the Vimalakirti Sutra says: 'The upright mind is the place of practice, and the upright mind is the Pure Land.' Do not practice flattery and crookedness in mind while merely speaking of uprightness with the mouth — mouthing the one-action samādhi without practicing the upright mind. Just practice the upright mind, and do not cling to any dharma.]

As the Vimalakirti Sutra says: 'The upright mind is the place of practice, and the upright mind is the Pure Land.' Do not practice flattery and crookedness in mind while merely speaking of uprightness with the mouth — that is a one-action samādhi on the lips only, without practicing the upright mind. Be certain to practice an upright and pure mind and not to cling to any dharma.

In the Shurangama Sutra, volume one, the Buddha said: 'Because the Tathagatas of the ten directions follow the same Way, they all depart from birth and death by means of the upright mind; since mind and speech are upright, thus even from beginning to end in every stage, never in between are there any crooked marks.' The reason sentient beings have crooked marks, with mind and speech not upright and mind practicing flattery, is entirely because of selfish desire and emotional consciousness.

Vimalakirti Sutra: that is, the Vimalakirti-nirdesa Sutra. Flattery: to please and flatter, accommodating oneself to worldly sentiment. Practicing flattery in mind: thoughts and conduct that are flattering and crooked. The root of flattery is selfish desire, so the cultivator must make strenuous effort in removing selfish desire. The Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters says: 'When the World-Honored One had accomplished the Way, he reflected thus: To be free of desire and still, this is the most supreme.' Again it says: 'The Buddha said: A monk who has left home must cut off desire and abandon love, recognize the source of his own mind, reach the profound principle of the Buddha, and awaken to the unconditioned dharma.' 'The Buddha said: One who shaves off hair and beard and becomes a monk, receiving the dharma of the Way, abandons the wealth of the world and begs for his needs. He eats one meal at midday and rests one night under a tree; take heed, no more! What makes people foolish and deluded is love and desire.'

The upright mind is also the utmost sincere mind and the true mind that Master Shandao explained in his Four-Part Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra: 'Utmost means true, and sincere means real. To understand that the understanding and practice cultivated through the body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings must be done with a true mind. One must not outwardly manifest the marks of virtue, goodness, and diligence while inwardly harboring falsity — greed, anger, wrong and falsehood, deceit in a hundred ways; the evil nature is hard to enter, and a person's deeds are like scorpions and snakes. Though one initiates the three karmas, this is called the goodness mixed with poison, and also called the false practice; it is not called true karma. If one settles the mind in this way and thus acts, even if one vexes body and mind, day and night through the twelve hours, hurrying and rushing as though one's head were scorched, this is all, in sum, called the goodness mixed with poison. To wish to turn this practice mixed with poison toward seeking rebirth in that Buddha's Pure Land, this is utterly impossible. Why? Because that Amitābha Buddha, when in his causal stage he practiced the bodhisattva conduct, even the cultivation of the three karmas in a single thought or instant was all done with a true mind; and everything he did and sought was likewise true.'

The two words sincerity and truthfulness are equally possessed by sages and ordinary beings alike. Why is one not sincere and not truthful? All because of selfish desire! In daily use, when the myriad conditions converge, if one is the least bit inattentive, all sorts of thoughts that run contrary to principle will suddenly arise, and one loses the mean and the upright. Therefore the path of uprightness and sincerity must begin with removing selfish desire. Master Yinguang said: 'In daily words and actions, always maintain awareness, and do not let any thought contrary to principle sprout for even an instant in the mind.' (Preface to the Liao-Fan's Four Lessons)

[The deluded person clings to the mark of the one-action samādhi and says outright: 'Always sitting without moving, with no false thoughts arising in the mind, that is the one-action samādhi.' One who understands it this way is the same as an inanimate thing, and is in fact creating the cause for obstructing the Way.]

The deluded person clings to the mark of the one-action samādhi and says: 'Always sitting without moving, with no false thoughts arising in the mind, that is the one-action samādhi.' One who holds such a view is like a witless stone or a withered tree, and such cultivation in fact becomes the cause for obstructing the Way.
Inanimate thing: sentient beings without consciousness.

The Sixth Patriarch's Chan teaching, as Master Mazu said: 'When one understands the mind and the objects of experience, false thought no longer arises. Since false thought no longer arises, that is the patience with the non-arising dharma. It is originally present and now present, not depending on cultivating the Way or sitting in meditation. Without cultivating and without sitting, that is the Tathagata's pure meditation. If one now sees this principle as truly real, does not create any karma, and passes through life according to one's lot, with a single robe and a single patched undergarment, sitting and rising together, the precept practice ever increasing in influence, accumulating pure karma. If one can simply be like this, how could one fail to be penetrated by it?' (The Extensive Record of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi) At the same time, the Sixth Patriarch holds that the one-action samādhi is a living, vital great function: responding to affairs and meeting objects without being stained by the myriad objects. Therefore he criticizes 'always sitting without moving' and 'contemplating the mind and observing stillness, not moving and not rising.'

Great capacity and great function: 'great capacity' means awakening to one's own nature; 'great function' means responding to affairs and meeting objects without being stained by the myriad objects. Guishan said: 'Many people obtain only the great capacity and not the great function.' (The Record of Chan Master Guishan Lingyou of Tanzhou)

The Elder Master Xuyun said: 'Cultivation must take place amid activity; it is not necessary to sit down and close one's eyes to be considered cultivating. One should, within the four demeanors of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, use the three studies of precepts, meditation, and wisdom to remove the three poisons of greed, anger, and ignorance, and rein in the six senses as one tends a cow, not allowing it to trample the young crops.' As for precepts, meditation, and wisdom, the Elder Master said: 'What are precepts, meditation, and wisdom? Preventing wrong and stopping evil is called precepts; when the six senses meet objects and the mind does not follow the conditions (the mind does not climb after objects) is called meditation; when mind and objects are both empty, and one illuminates and discerns without confusion is called wisdom.' (The Autobiographical Chronicle of Elder Master Xuyun)

A person of no affairs is not about closing the eyes and stopping the ears, not about cutting oneself off from the world, but rather about maintaining an ordinary mind, and with an even, inclusive, easeful state of mind facing everything and bearing everything, far from the dualistic picking and choosing. A monk asked: 'When the six gates (a metaphor for the six senses) are all closed, what then?' The master said: 'Hold them wide open.' He asked: 'After they are held wide open, what then?' The master said: 'The red dust never reaches them.'
When the six gates are all open and yet the red dust does not enter, this is the true person of no affairs.

In this public case, 'when the six gates are all closed' speaks of the work of guarding having already been accomplished, so he asks for instruction: what should the next step of the work be? So the Chan master taught him

'Hold them wide open' and 'the red dust never reaches them' — this is the work of letting go. As for the work of guarding and letting go, see in detail the section on 'Wolun Cutting Off Thought' in 'Chapter Seven, Conditions and Associations.'

One should note that the Platform Sutra is the sudden method, and it often speaks of the work of letting go. If the method it speaks of is something one cannot begin from, that shows one's foundation is insufficient, and in that case one should still begin with the guarding work of 'always be diligent in wiping it, do not let it gather dust' and 'contemplating the mind and observing stillness, with no false thoughts arising.'

[Good teachers! The Way must flow freely; why should it be blocked? If the mind does not abide in dharmas, the Way flows on; if the mind abides in dharmas, it is called binding itself. If one says that always sitting without moving is right, that is just like Sariputra sitting quietly in the forest, only to be scolded by Vimalakirti.]

Good teachers! The Way must flow freely; why should it be made to stagnate? If the mind does not abide in dharmas, the Way flows on; if the mind abides in dharmas, this is binding oneself. If one says that always sitting without moving is right, then it is just like Sariputra sitting silently in the forest, being scolded by Vimalakirti. (See the Vimalakirti Sutra
Chapter on the Disciples, part three)
Sitting quietly: sitting in silent stillness.

[Good teachers! Again some people teach sitting: contemplating the mind and observing stillness, not moving and not rising, and setting forth to make the work from there. Deluded people do not understand, and cling to it until it becomes an upside-down view; such people are many. Teaching one another in this way, therefore know it is a great error!]

Good teachers! Again some people teach sitting in meditation: contemplating the mind and observing stillness, not moving and not rising, saying one must do the work in this way. Deluded people do not understand how to cultivate properly, and cling to this method as the ultimate end; there are many such people. Therefore know, to teach in this way the one-action samādhi is a great error, and a great error indeed!

The three non's — no-thought, no-marks, and no-abiding — this is the core skill of the Platform Sutra. No-thought: within thought there is no thought. No-marks: within marks there is separation from marks. No-abiding: in objects there is no thinking. Achieve the inner mind not being turned by thoughts, and the outer mind not being pulled by objects. No-thought is great concentration, no-marks is great precepts, and no-abiding is great wisdom.

[The master instructed the assembly: Good teachers! The genuine teaching originally has neither sudden nor gradual, yet the natures of people are themselves quick and dull. The deluded cultivate gradually; the awakened penetrate suddenly. Recognizing your own mind and seeing your own nature, there is no difference. Therefore the provisional names of sudden and gradual are established.]
The Sixth Patriarch

instructed the assembly: Good teachers! The genuine teaching originally has neither sudden nor gradual, yet the natures of people are themselves quick and dull. The deluded cultivate gradually and enter; the awakened penetrate suddenly and accord. As long as one recognizes one's own mind and sees one's own nature, there is no difference between them. Therefore the provisional names of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation are established.
Provisional name: a name that is not real. All dharmas are without reality; originally they have no name, and it is people who give them assumed names. The Lotus Sutra
Chapter on Skill in Means, part two says: 'But with provisional names, beings are led along.'

[Good teachers! This Dharma door of mine, from the founding teachers onward, first establishes no-thought as the principle, no-marks as the substance, and no-abiding as the basis. No-marks means: within marks, separate from marks. No-thought means: within thought, without thought. No-abiding means: the human nature, in the world amid good and evil, beauty and ugliness, even enmity and kinship, when words pierce and deceive and contend, treats it all as empty, not thinking of requital, and within thought after thought does not think of the previous objects. If past, present, and future thoughts join one another without break, that is called being tied; in dharmas, thought after thought not abiding, then there is no bondage. This is taking no-abiding as the basis.

Good teachers! This sudden-teaching Dharma door of mine, from Patriarch Bodhidharma onward, first establishes no-thought as the principle, no-marks as the substance, and no-abiding as the basis. No-marks means: within marks, separate from marks, not being turned by marks. No-thought means: within thought, without thought, not giving rise to thought on top of thought, not being pulled by thought. No-abiding means: this is the human nature; for the world's good and evil, beauty and ugliness, even enmity and kinship, at the time of words piercing and deceiving and contending, one knows they are all illusions (treating them as empty), not thinking of requital or revenge, and within thought after thought not thinking of the present objects (in objects, no thinking). If past thought, present thought, and future thought join one another without break, giving rise to thought on top of thought, that is called being tied; in dharmas, thought after thought not abiding in objects and giving rise to mind, without stain and without attachment, then there is no bondage and one obtains ease. This is taking no-abiding (in objects, no thinking) as the basis.
No-marks: no clinging to marks; within marks, separate from marks.

Clinging to marks: taking marks as real, and so loving and hating, picking and rejecting. Separating from marks: realizing that marks are all illusory, and so no loving and hating, picking and rejecting. The Diamond Sutra says:
'Whatever has marks, all is illusion. If one sees all marks as no marks
(if one sees that all marks are not real)
, then one sees the Tathagata
(then one sees the Buddha of one's own nature)
(For the full explanation see
The Diamond Sutra Explained

Within thought without thought: do not suppress thought so that it does not arise, but rather: when a thought arises, know it and do not follow it. Suppressing thought so that it does not arise not only makes the whole body tense, but once one stops suppressing, false thoughts become all the more active. No-abiding
is the human nature

The human nature is no-abiding; knowing that all dharmas are empty, therefore it does not climb after and is not stained. The human propensity is to abide, wrongly holding all dharmas to be real, therefore it climbs after and is stained. Not thinking of previous objects: not thinking of the present objects (in objects, no thinking); looking is just looking, listening is just listening, the mind vast and unhindered, without attachment.
The Diamond Sutra says:
'One should not give rise to a mind that abides in form, nor a mind that abides in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.'
Among these, 'one should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere'

is to practice the upright mind without being influenced by objects and conditions (temptation, distress, coercion). Therefore one should make the work on the present thought; this is the wondrous method of mastering the mind within the midst of objects.
[Good teachers! Externally separating from all marks is called no-marks. Being able to separate from marks, then the dharma-substance is pure. This is taking no-marks as the substance.]

Good teachers! Externally separating from all marks, not being turned by them, is called no-marks; being able to separate from marks, then the dharma-substance of one's own nature is pure. This is taking no-marks as the substance.

[Good teachers! In all objects the mind not being stained is called no-thought. On one's own thought, always separating from all objects, not giving rise to mind on objects. If it is only that one does not think of the hundred things, and all thought is completely removed, then when one thought ceases one dies and is reborn elsewhere — this is a great error. Those studying the Way should think on this! If one does not recognize the meaning of the Dharma, one's own error is tolerable, but also to counsel others, one's own delusion not seeing the Way, and in addition slandering the Buddha's scriptures. Therefore no-thought is established as the principle.]

Good teachers! On all objects and conditions the mind not being stained, that is called no-thought. No-thought means: on one's own thought, always separating from all objects ('one should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere'), not giving rise to mind on objects ('one should not give rise to a mind that abides in form, nor a mind that abides in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas'). If one takes no-thought to be merely 'not thinking of the hundred things, and completely removing all thoughts,' that is a great error! Because if thought is cut off one dies and is reborn elsewhere, still turning in the cycle of rebirth. Those studying the Way should deeply ponder this principle! If one oneself does not recognize the true meaning of the Dharma, one's own error is tolerable, but if one further counsels others with this wrong method, not only is one oneself deluded and not seeing the Way, but one incurs the offense of slandering the Buddha's scriptures; the consequences are extremely serious. Therefore no-thought must be established as the principle.

On one's own thought, always separating from all objects, not giving rise to mind on objects' — this is: 'One should not give rise to a mind that abides in form, nor a mind that abides in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.' But on one's own thought separating from objects, do not give rise to mind on dharmas.

Question: The Sixth Patriarch says: 'If it is only that one does not think of the hundred things, and all thought is completely removed, then when one thought ceases one dies and is reborn elsewhere — this is a great error.' Yet the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, says: 'The great Way is vast and open, cutting off thought and cutting off deliberation.' These two sayings are contrary; which should one rely on?

Answer: The Sixth Patriarch is speaking against the prevalent error at that time of taking 'not thinking of the hundred things, with all thought completely removed' as the ultimate end. In the later text of this sutra he also criticizes Master Wolun's 'being able to cut off the hundred thoughts,' precisely because Wolun took 'being able to cut off the hundred thoughts' as the ultimate end. Where they were wrong was in taking 'all thought completely removed' and 'being able to cut off the hundred thoughts' as the ultimate end; this is what is meant by knowing only the great death and not the great life.

Master Dahui said: 'This old man always liked what Chan Master Zhenjing said: nowadays people mostly obtain a body and mind that are quiescent and extinguished, with the before and after cut off, resting and stopping, a single thought for ten thousand years, like the incense burner in an old temple, going on cold and dreary, and take this as the ultimate end. They do not realize that they are blocked and veiled by this superior and wondrous object, so that their own right knowledge and right view cannot be present, and their spiritual powers and brightness cannot be revealed.' (The Record of Chan Master Dahui Pujue)
In fact, in the cultivation of one's skill there are two great stages: guarding and letting go. With regard to this, the Fourth Patriarch of the Chan school, Daoxin, has a detailed instruction.

The Fourth Patriarch spoke to Farong, saying: 'The hundred thousand Dharma doors all return to the square inch; the wondrous virtues of the Ganges' sands all reside in the mind-source. All the gates of precepts, gates of meditation, gates of wisdom, and the transformations of spiritual powers are all complete within and do not depart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic hindrances are originally empty and still. All cause and effect are like dreams and illusions. There is no three realms to be transcended, and no bodhi to be sought. Human and non-human, nature and marks are all equal. The great Way is vast and open, cutting off thought and cutting off deliberation. Such a dharma you have now obtained, with nothing lacking; how is it different from the Buddha? (Note: 'Such a dharma you have now obtained' speaks of Farong's guarding work — cutting off thought and cutting off deliberation — already accomplished, therefore the following instruction directs him to do the letting-go work — letting the mind be at ease.) There is no other dharma; you only need to let your mind be at ease, do not perform contemplation, and do not still the mind, do not give rise to greed and anger, do not harbor worry, vast and unhindered, at will and free, not creating the various good and not creating the various evil, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, whatever meets the eye and what conditions arise, all is the Buddha's wondrous function. Happy and free of worry, therefore it is called Buddha.' Farong said: 'Since you do not permit performing contemplation, when objects arise, how does the mind deal with them?' The master said: 'Object-conditions have no good or ugly; good and ugly arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, from where does false feeling arise? Since false feeling no longer arises, the true mind is at liberty to know all. You only need to let the mind be at ease, with no further contending, that is called the eternal dharma-body.' (See the full explanation in the article
The Fourth Patriarch's Instruction to Farong

The Diamond Sutra says: 'One should not give rise to a mind that abides in form, nor a mind that abides in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.' The guarding work is 'one should not give rise to a mind that abides in form, nor a mind that abides in sound, scent, taste, touch, or dharmas.' The letting-go work is 'one should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.'

[Good teachers! Why is no-thought established as the principle? Only because the deluded person, who speaks of seeing the nature, gives rise to thought on objects, and on thought immediately gives rise to wrong views, and all worldly defilements and false thoughts arise from this. The self-nature originally has no dharma to obtain; if there is something obtained, and one falsely speaks of fortune and misfortune, that is worldly defilement and wrong view. Therefore this Dharma door establishes no-thought as the principle.]

Good teachers! Why is no-thought established as the principle? Because the deluded person who speaks of seeing the nature gives rise to thought on objects, and on thought immediately gives rise to wrong views, and all worldly defilements and false thoughts arise from this. And the self-nature originally has no dharma to obtain; if there is something obtained, and one falsely speaks of fortune and misfortune, that is worldly wrong view. Therefore this Dharma door establishes no-thought as the principle.

All dharmas are illusions, so the self-nature, with regard to dharmas, has nothing to obtain. Why give rise to thought on objects? Sentient beings are deluded precisely here. One should regard everything from the standpoint of the reality of all dharmas; this is the Way.

Worldly people are bound up in fortune and misfortune, gain and loss. If they can understand that these are all illusions, with nothing to obtain, the mind becomes empty, without hindrance, and only then can one enter the Way.

[Good teachers! As for non, what thing does it negate? As for thought, what does it think of? Non negates the two marks and the mind of worldly defilement; thought thinks of the true suchness nature. True suchness is the substance of thought, and thought is the function of true suchness. It is the true-suchness self-nature giving rise to thought, not the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body giving rise to thought. True suchness has a nature, therefore it gives rise to thought. If true suchness were without, then the eyes, ears, and objects of form would immediately be destroyed.]

Good teachers! The 'non' of no-thought — what does it negate? The 'thought' of no-thought — what does it think of? The 'non' of no-thought negates the differentiating marks of right and wrong, good and evil, beauty and ugliness, and the mind of the various afflictions; the 'thought' of no-thought thinks of the true suchness nature. True suchness is the substance of thought, and thought is the function of true suchness. It is the true-suchness self-nature giving rise to thought, not the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body giving rise to thought. The true-suchness self-nature functions, therefore it can think; if the true-suchness self-nature did not function, then the eyes could not see forms and the ears could not hear sounds.

[Good teachers! When the true-suchness self-nature gives rise to thought, though the six senses have seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, they are not stained by the myriad objects, while the true nature is ever at ease. Therefore the sutra says: Being able to discriminate the marks of all dharmas well, yet unmoved in the foremost meaning.]

Good teachers! When the true-suchness self-nature gives rise to thought, though the six senses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind) have seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, they are not stained by the myriad objects, while the true nature is ever at ease (unaffected and unstained). Therefore the Vimalakirti Sutra

Chapter on the Buddha Land, part one says: 'Being able to discriminate the marks of all dharmas well, yet unmoved in the foremost meaning.' (Being able to clearly discern all dharmas, while the mind is not moved by these illusions.)

Foremost meaning: the supreme principle, that is, the reality of all dharmas. The Buddha said: 'All dharmas are all deceptive; where they cease, that is called real, called real-mark, called the dharma-realm, called ultimate wisdom, called the foremost meaning truth, called the foremost meaning emptiness.' (The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, volume forty, the Kaundinya chapter)

When the true-suchness self-nature gives rise to thought, though the six senses have seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, they are not stained by the myriad objects, while the true nature is ever at ease. This is 'to give rise to a mind that abides nowhere,' this is 'giving rise to a no-abiding mind.' If one faces objects and thinks of objects and pursues objects, then one is disturbed, deluded, and not at ease.

Being able to discriminate the marks of all dharmas well, yet unmoved in the foremost meaning.' — The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: 'It is like the eye-light knowing the earlier objects; its light is complete, and it obtains no aversion or love.'
Master Hanshan says:
(Sentient beings)
have all along solely taken the false-thinking, arising-and-ceasing mind as true, and therefore with regard to the objects of the six senses, all sorts of illusions, they take them as real.'
(The Collected Writings of the Dream Journey
Reply to Zheng Kunyan, the Vice Censor-in-Chief.) In the Shurangama Sutra the Buddha says:
All sentient beings, from beginnings time, in birth and death endless, all because they do not know the eternal true mind, the nature-pure bright substance
(all because they do not know this nature-pure bright substance abiding in the true mind)
, use the various false thoughts
(and so go on to use false thoughts)
; because these thoughts are not true, therefore there is the turning.

Nature-pure bright substance: the bright and wondrous substance, originally pure in nature. From a grammatical standpoint, 'nature-pure bright substance' is an appositive that modifies the noun 'true mind.' Turning: the birth-and-death by divisions and the birth-and-death by transformation. Birth-and-death by divisions: sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because of the karmic retribution of good and evil deeds, have a limited life span and a segmented body, so their birth and death is called 'birth-and-death by divisions.' One who ends birth-and-death by divisions is freed from the cycle. Birth-and-death by transformation: the sages of the three vehicles have already cut off the delusions of views and thought and ended birth-and-death by divisions; in the process of cultivation the delusive thoughts gradually extinguish and realization gradually increases; this transition from delusion to awakening, each period different, is a move from an earlier period into a later one, exactly like a single birth-and-death, and its transformation is wondrous and unfathomable, inexpressible, so it is called 'birth-and-death by transformation.' One who ends birth-and-death by transformation perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
The self-nature unmoved: not pulled by thought, not turned by objects.
[The master instructed the assembly: This door's sitting meditation, originally does not attach to the mind, nor attach to purity, nor is it not moving.]
The master instructed the assembly: This sudden-teaching Dharma door's sitting meditation, originally does not attach to the mind, nor attach to purity, nor is it not moving.

Originally: from the start. Attach: clinging and not letting go is called 'attach'; attachment is the root of illness. In the Lotus Sutra, Chapter on Skill in Means, part two, the Buddha said: 'Since my becoming a Buddha, through various causes and conditions, various similes, widely expounding the teaching, with countless expedient means, I have led sentient beings and caused them to be free of the various attachments.'
[If one says to attach the mind, the mind is originally false; knowing the mind is like an illusion, therefore there is nothing to attach.]
If one speaks of attaching the mind, the mind is originally false; knowing the mind is like an illusion, therefore there is nothing to attach.

[If one says to attach purity, the human nature is originally pure; because of false thoughts, it covers the true suchness; but only without false thinking, the nature is itself pure. Giving rise to a mind that attaches purity, then one creates a false purity, and false thinking has no abiding place; what attaches is the false thinking. Purity has no form or mark, yet one establishes a purity mark and says this is skill! One who holds this view obstructs his own nature and is bound by purity.]

If one speaks of attaching purity, the human nature is originally pure; because of false thoughts covering the true suchness, one falls into being a sentient being; but only without false thinking, the nature is itself naturally pure, so the key is to be without false thoughts. If one gives rise to a mind that attaches purity, then one creates a false-thought purity; false thinking originally has no fixed abiding place, and what attaches is the false thinking. Purity originally has no form or mark; once the false thought of attaching purity arises, one establishes a purity mark and says this is skill! One who holds this view obstructs his own nature and is bound by 'purity.'
Covers the true suchness: here true suchness refers to the nature (the Tathagata-garbha).
[Good teachers! If one cultivates the unmoved, then in seeing every person, not seeing the rights and wrongs, good and evil, faults and errors of others, that is the self-nature unmoved.]

Good teachers! What is called cultivating the unmoved is not the body not moving, but the self-nature unmoved (not pulled by thought, not turned by objects); one should, upon seeing every person, not see their rights and wrongs, good and evil, faults and errors. This is the self-nature unmoved.

[Good teachers! The deluded person, though his body does not move, as soon as he opens his mouth speaks of the rights and wrongs, merits and shortcomings, good and evil of others — this is contrary to the Way. If one attaches to the mind or attaches to purity, that too obstructs the Way.]

Good teachers! The deluded person, though in his seat he trains his body to be still and unmoved, once off the seat opens his mouth and speaks of the rights and wrongs, merits and shortcomings, good and evil of others — this is contrary to the Way. If one attaches to mind or attaches to purity, this too obstructs the bodhi path.

The Sixth Patriarch emphasizes that the path of liberation must be entered and tempered amid objects and conditions, whereas the prevailing custom at the time was sitting in meditation and cultivating concentration, and the still-sitting skill of most practitioners was quite deep. In practicing meditation concentration there are four stages: first meditation, second meditation, third meditation, and fourth meditation. Before first meditation there are coarse abiding, fine abiding, the concentration of the desire realm, and the concentration before reaching the stage. In first meditation the outer breathing stops and the inner breathing becomes active, as in hibernation. At this time the mind is clear as water, its brightness like a mirror. Compared with first meditation, the concentration skill of the fourth meditation is deeper still. But even if one attains the fourth meditation, at death one can only be born in the four meditation heavens of the form realm and cannot transcend the three realms or end birth and death. Therefore sitting in meditation and cultivating concentration is not the path of liberation. To attain liberation one must cut off the delusions of views and thought, and not give rise to mind upon seeing objects; this must be entered and tempered amid objects and conditions. So in what follows the Sixth Patriarch redefines sitting meditation and meditation concentration.

[The master instructed the assembly: Good teachers! What is called sitting meditation? In this Dharma door, there is no obstruction and no impediment. Externally, in all good and evil objects, the mind-thought does not arise; that is called sitting. Internally, seeing the self-nature unmoved; that is called meditation.]

The master instructed the assembly: Good teachers! What is called sitting meditation? In this sudden-teaching Dharma door there is no obstruction and no impediment, with no restriction of time, place, or environment. Externally, in all good and evil objects, the mind-thought does not arise; that is called sitting. Internally, seeing the self-nature and being thus unmoved (without loving or hating, picking or rejecting); that is called meditation.

Externally, in all good and evil objects, the mind-thought does not arise; that is called sitting. Internally, seeing the self-nature unmoved; that is called meditation: this is mutual composition, meaning that externally, in all good and evil objects, the mind-thought does not arise, and internally, seeing the self-nature unmoved, is called sitting meditation. Mutual composition: also called mutual phrasing, a rhetorical device commonly used in classical Chinese. Its feature is not to be wordy, not to be redundant, not to be flat narration, but to be implicit and concise, with the wording sparing and the meaning preserved, complementing each other to convey the sense, and mutually illuminating. For example, in the Ballad of Mulan, 'The general dies in a hundred battles, the warrior returns after ten years' means: the general and warrior die in a hundred battles, the general and warrior return after ten years. Again, in the Record of Yueyang Tower, 'not rejoicing in things, not sorrowing for oneself' means: not rejoicing in things and in oneself, and likewise not sorrowing in things and in oneself. Here 'things' refers to things outside oneself and the environment one is in, and 'oneself' refers to one's personal circumstances.

[Good teachers! What is called meditation concentration? Externally separating from marks is meditation; internally not being disturbed is concentration. If externally one attaches to marks, the inner mind is then disturbed; if externally one separates from marks, the mind is then not disturbed. The nature is originally pure and originally concentrated; only because one sees objects and thinks of objects, one is disturbed. If one sees the various objects and the mind is not disturbed, that is true concentration.]

Good teachers! What is called meditation concentration? Externally separating from marks is meditation; internally not being disturbed is concentration. If externally one attaches to marks, the inner mind is then disturbed; if externally one separates from marks, the mind is then not disturbed. The nature is originally pure and originally concentrated; only because one sees objects and thinks of objects, one is disturbed. If one sees objects and does not think of them and the mind is not disturbed, then that is true concentration.
The Essentials of the Sudden-Awakening Path of Entering the Way says: 'Without false thought arising is meditation; sitting and seeing the nature is concentration.'

[Good teachers! Externally separating from marks is meditation; internally not being disturbed is concentration. External meditation and internal concentration, this is meditation concentration. The Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra says: 'My original self-nature is pure.' Good teachers! In thought after thought, see the self-nature as pure, self-cultivate and self-practice, and self-accomplish the Buddha Way.]

Good teachers! Externally separating from marks is meditation; internally not being disturbed is concentration. External meditation and internal concentration, this is meditation concentration. The Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra says: 'My original self-nature is pure (my original self-nature is pure).' Good teachers! In thought after thought, see the self-nature as pure (abiding in original awakening), self-cultivate (cultivate, seeing the nature and removing habits) and self-practice (practice, using and examining it in daily life), and self-accomplish the Buddha Way.

In thought after thought, see the self-nature as pure, self-cultivate and self-practice, and self-accomplish the Buddha Way: The Chan-Origin All-Preface says: 'If one suddenly awakens that the self-mind is originally pure, with no affliction originally, and the undefiled wisdom-nature is originally complete, this mind is Buddha, ultimately no different. Cultivating according to this is the supreme vehicle meditation, also called the Tathagata's pure meditation, also called the one-action samādhi, also called the true-suchness samādhi. This is the root of all samādhis. If one can cultivate in thought after thought, one naturally gradually obtains hundreds and thousands of samādhis. What was handed down generation after generation in the school of Bodhidharma is this meditation.' Undefiled wisdom: the pure wisdom free of all affliction; this wisdom has the function of cutting off delusion and realizing truth.

Body and mind are illusions; but whether they are realized, one must at all times examine in daily affairs and objects: is the mind moved? is it turned by karma? — this is cultivation. Master Hanshan said: 'If today one seeks to realize true suchness, it is not to be sought in the ghostly cave of dead eyes and dead brows, but to be sought amid all the myriad daily practices of conditioned existence. So to seek in practice is not to pick out on the matter itself some mysterious-marvelous true Tathagata; it is merely to take the upright mind and right thought and examine in all affairs whether it accords with the upright mind and right thought or not. If every matter and every dharma accords with upright mind and right thought, then not a single dharma or matter before you is not the realm of true suchness. Therefore Mazu and the various disciples of Baizhang, in daily life, carrying firewood, hauling water, hoeing the field, planting the seedling, burning the fire, cooking the rice, examine face-to-face in every matter. An ordinary word, a cold or warm remark, are all to lead disciples into the gate of realizing true suchness.' (The Collected Writings of the Dream Journey
Instruction to Shi Liuru Kungong)

Before the Sixth Patriarch, what people commonly called meditation was meditation concentration, especially the four dhyanas and eight concentrations, taking this as the path of liberation. But the Sixth Patriarch redefined sitting meditation and meditation concentration, shaking the whole of the ancient and present, causing the Chan school to achieve outstanding accomplishments. Here I will give just a few examples of Chan elders who were free in birth and death, to show a glimpse of it:

Chan Master Yinfeng of Mount Wutai, in the Yuanyhe era of the Tang, passing through Huaixi, happened upon the rebellion of Wu Yuanji, with the government army and the rebel army locked in battle, undecided. The master said: 'I should go and put an end to this trouble.' Then he threw his staff into the air and flew across the air, and both armies' officers and soldiers looked up; the matter corresponded with the dream of the night before, and the fighting heart immediately subsided. Since the master had displayed supernatural powers, and feared he would confuse the multitudes, he entered Wutai and, before the Diamond Grotto, was about to pass into cessation. First he asked the assembly: 'The various places (that is, cultivators of the Way in various places) pass into transformation (pass into cessation), sitting or reclining; I have seen this. Is there also a standing transformation?' They said: 'There is.' The master said: 'Is there also a handstand one?' They said: 'We have not seen one.' The master then passed away standing on his head, and his robe hung down along his body. At that time the assembly discussed lifting him to be cremated (to be cremated), but he stood firm and unmoved; those far and near who saw it were astonished and sighing endlessly. The master had a sister who was a nun, also present, and she went up to him and scolded him, saying: 'Elder brother, in the past you did not follow the rules (did not keep the pure regulations, referring to the matter of displaying supernatural powers), and in death you still confuse people!' Thereupon she pushed him with her hand, and he fell over flat. Then he was cremated (to be cremated), and his relics were collected and a stupa built. (The Pointing-at-the-Moon Record
volume nine)

Layman Pang of Xiangzhou, about to take the extinction, told his daughter Lingzhao to go out and watch whether the sun was early or late, and report at noon. The daughter hastily reported: 'The sun is already at the zenith, and there is an eclipse.' The layman went out to the door to look, and Lingzhao immediately ascended her father's seat, and with palms joined sat in death. The layman smiled and said: 'My daughter is sharp! ' So he extended it another seven days. The provincial governor, Lord Yu, came to inquire about his illness, and the layman said to him: 'Only wish to empty all that there is, be careful not to real-ify that which is not. Farewell! The world is all like a shadow and an echo.' When he had spoken, he leaned on the lord's knee and passed away. (The Jingde Transmission of the Lamp
volume eight)
Only wish to empty all that there is, be careful not to real-ify that which is not: empty all that there is, and also do not attach to the nonexistent.

Yangshan, about to pass into cessation, at noon, ascended the seat and took leave of the assembly, then recited a verse: 'Seventy-seven years of age, the impermanent comes today; the sun wheel directly at noon, two hands clasp the bent knees.' When he had spoken, he clasped his knees with his two hands and passed away. (The Pointing-at-the-Moon Record
volume thirteen)

Chan Master Shanzhao of Taizi Temple in Fenzhou, one day, ordered a feast to be prepared and his belongings packed, then told the assembly: 'The old monk is going; who will follow?' A monk came forward and said: 'I will follow.' The master said: 'How many li do you walk in a day?' He said: 'Fifty li.' The master said: 'You cannot follow me.' Again a monk came forward and said: 'I walk seventy li a day.' The master said: 'You too cannot follow me.' The attendant came forward and said: 'I can follow, because wherever the master is, I am there.' The master said: 'You are the one who can follow the old monk.' Then he looked again at the emissary and said: 'I am going ahead.' He laid down his chopsticks and passed away, and the attendant immediately stood there and passed away at his side. (The Pointing-at-the-Moon Record
volume twenty-three)
Prepare a feast: to make a banquet and prepare food; here it means setting up a meal. Pack belongings: to tidy one's luggage.

One day Monk Puhua, in the marketplace, begged people for a long robe (the robe worn by monks). Everyone gave him one, but Puhua refused them all. Chan Master Linji Yixuan (the founder of the Linji school) had the temple superintendent buy a coffin. When Puhua returned, the master said: 'I have made a long robe for you.' Puhua then carried it off himself, and went around the market calling: 'Linji has made a long robe for me; I am going to the east gate to pass into transformation.' The townspeople vied to follow and watch, and Puhua said: 'I am not doing it today; tomorrow I will go to the south gate to pass into transformation.' So it went for three days, and no one believed him. On the fourth day, no one followed to watch, and he went out alone beyond the city wall, entered the coffin himself, and asked a passerby to nail it shut. News spread at once, and the townspeople vied to open the coffin, but his remains were not to be seen; only the sound of a bell in the air was heard, fading away into the distance. (The Record of Chan Master Zhenzhou Linji Huizhao)

Four dhyanas and eight concentrations: that is, the four concentration meditations of the realm of form and the four formless concentrations of the realm of formlessness, together eight concentrations, attained gradually in sequence. The four dhyanas are first meditation, second meditation, third meditation, and fourth meditation; the four formless concentrations are the concentration of the sphere of emptiness, the concentration of the sphere of consciousness, the concentration of the sphere of nothingness, and the concentration of neither-perception-nor-nonperception. The patriarch's Chan does not cultivate the four dhyanas and eight concentrations, but rather sees the self-nature, so that one is not deluded by objects and not shaken by objects; this is the true concentration that neither issues forth nor enters. Patriarch's Chan: the Chan method in the Chan school, so called because it was advocated by the patriarchs, whom later generations named it 'patriarch's Chan.' In fact the patriarch's Chan also came from the Tathagata; it was not invented by the patriarchs. When Śākyamuni Buddha, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, entrusted the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma and the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa to Mahakashyapa, this was the first transmission of the patriarch's Chan.

blocks.text: 1. Transmitting the Incense of the Dharmakaya

inline.s: [At that time, seeing the multitudes of Guangzhou and Shaozhou and the four quarters gathered in the mountains to hear the Dharma, the master ascended the seat and told the assembly: Come! Good teachers! This matter must be taken up from the self-nature. At all times, in thought after thought, purify your own mind, cultivate and practice yourself, see your own dharmakaya, see the Buddha of your own mind, save yourself and observe the precepts for yourself; only then have you not come here in vain.]

At that time, seeing the monks and laypeople of Guangzhou, Shaozhou, and the four quarters gathered in the mountains (Caoxi) to hear the Dharma, the master ascended the Dharma seat and said to the assembly: You have all worked hard! Good teachers! The matter of repentance must be taken up from within the self-nature. At all times, in thought after thought, purify your own mind, cultivate your own practice, see your own dharmakaya, see the Buddha of your own mind, save yourself and observe the precepts for yourself; only then have you not come here in vain.
Ji (ji): meaning and; read ji.

[Since you have all come from afar and gathered here in a single assembly, you all have a common karmic connection. Now each of you may kneel on one knee, and first I will transmit to you the incense of the self-nature's five-part dharmakaya, and then teach you the markless repentance. The assembly knelt, and the master said:]

Since you have all come from afar and gathered here, you all have a karmic connection with one another. Now each of you may kneel on one knee, and first I will transmit to you the incense of the self-nature's five-part dharmakaya, and then teach the markless repentance. Thereupon the assembly knelt down, and the master said:

Kneeling on one knee: an ancient rite of salutation for monks, with the right knee on the ground, the left knee raised and upright; when weary, the two knees would alternate postures. Incense: an object made of fragrant materials and burned in offering to the Buddha. Incense represents the true incense of precepts, meditation, and wisdom; burning incense purifies the air, signifying using the true incense of precepts, meditation, and wisdom to purify one's own body and mind and the environment. Incense of the five-part dharmakaya: the incense of precepts, the incense of meditation, the incense of wisdom, the incense of liberation, and the incense of the knowledge and vision of liberation. This is using incense as a metaphor for the five kinds of dharmakaya virtue. Five-part dharmakaya: accomplishing the Buddha-body with five kinds of meritorious dharmas is called the 'five-part dharmakaya.' 1. The dharmakaya of precepts, meaning the Tathagata's three karmic activities are free of all faults. 2. The dharmakaya of meditation, meaning the Tathagata's true mind is quiescent and free of all false thoughts. 3. The dharmakaya of wisdom, meaning the Tathagata's true wisdom is perfectly radiant and penetrates the nature and marks of all dharmas. 4. The dharmakaya of liberation, meaning the Tathagata's body and mind are liberated from all bonds. 5. The dharmakaya of the knowledge and vision of liberation, meaning the Tathagata possesses the wisdom by which he knows that he has actually already been liberated.
[1. The incense of precepts. That is, in your own mind, having no wrong, no evil, no jealousy, no greed and anger, no violent harm — this is called the incense of precepts.]

1. The incense of precepts: within one's own mind there is no unmoral thought, no evil intention, no jealousy, no greed and anger, no thought of harming others — this is called the incense of precepts.
[2. The incense of meditation. That is, seeing the various wholesome and unwholesome states of objects, and your own mind not being disturbed — this is called the incense of meditation.]
2. The incense of meditation: seeing all the wholesome and unwholesome states of objects, while one's own mind is not disturbed — this is called the incense of meditation.

[3. The incense of wisdom. Your own mind being free of obstruction, always using wisdom to contemplate the self-nature, not creating the various evils, though cultivating the various virtues without the mind clinging to them, respecting those above and showing concern for those below, sympathizing with the orphan and the poor — this is called the incense of wisdom.]

3. The incense of wisdom: one's own mind being free of stain and attachment, penetrating without obstruction, always using wisdom to contemplate the self-nature, not creating the various evils, though cultivating the various virtues without the mind clinging to them, respecting those above and showing concern for those below, sympathizing with the orphan and the poor — this is called the incense of wisdom.
[4. The incense of liberation. That is, your own mind having nothing to climb after, not thinking of good and not thinking of evil, at ease and unhindered — this is called the incense of liberation.]
4. The incense of liberation: one's own mind having nothing to climb after, not thinking of good and not thinking of evil, at ease and unhindered — this is called the incense of liberation.

[5. The incense of the knowledge and vision of liberation. Since your own mind has nothing to climb after in good and evil, you must not sink into emptiness and guard stillness; rather you should study broadly and hear much, know your own original mind, reach the principle of all Buddhas, mingle your light with the world and receive beings, with no self and no person, until bodhi, the true nature unchanging — this is called the incense of the knowledge and vision of liberation.]

5. The incense of the knowledge and vision of liberation: though one's own mind does not climb after good and evil, one must not sink into emptiness and guard stillness; rather one must study broadly and hear much, know one's own original mind, reach the Buddha's principle, mingle one's light with the world and receive beings, with no mark of self and no mark of person, until bodhi, the true nature unchanging — this is called the incense of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Mingling one's light with the world and receiving beings: 'mingling one's light,' that is, harmonizing one's light with the dust of the world; 'receiving beings,' associating with people. 'Mingling one's light with the world and receiving beings' refers to living and relating with people without displaying one's sharpness, contending with no one, humble, courteous, and wise.
[Good teachers! This incense each of you should fumigate within yourselves; do not seek it outside.]
Good teachers! This incense must each of you fumigate within your own mind; do not seek it outside.

[Now I will transmit to you the markless repentance, to extinguish the offenses of the three times, and cause the three karmic activities to be pure. Good teachers! Each of you follow my words and recite together:]

Today I transmit to you the markless repentance, to extinguish the offenses of the past, present, and future, and cause the three karmic activities of body, speech, and mind to be pure. Good teachers! All of you recite together after me:

Repentance: 'repent' means reproving oneself for the past; 'remorse' means resolutely cutting off the future. Three times: past, present, and future. Three karmas: the karma of body, the karma of speech, and the karma of mind.
The reason the markless repentance can extinguish future offenses is that it causes the three karmic activities of body, speech, and mind to be pure, so that one does not create them again.

[We disciples, from past thought, present thought, to future thought, in thought after thought, are not stained by delusion and ignorance; all the past evil karma, the offenses of delusion and ignorance, we all repent, wishing them to be extinguished at once and never to arise again.]

We disciples, from past thought, present thought, to future thought, in thought after thought, are not stained by delusion and ignorance; all the past evil karma, the offenses of delusion and ignorance, we all repent, wishing them to be extinguished all at once and never to arise again.

[We disciples, from past thought, present thought, to future thought, in thought after thought, are not stained by pride and deceit; all the past evil karma, the offenses of pride and deceit, we all repent, wishing them to be extinguished at once and never to arise again.]

We disciples, from past thought, present thought, to future thought, in thought after thought, are not stained by pride and deceit; all the past evil karma, the offenses of arrogance and deceit, we all repent, wishing them to be extinguished all at once and never to arise again.
Pride and deceit: 'pride' is the same as the 'proud' in arrogance; 'deceit' is to cheat and hoodwink.

[We disciples, from past thought, present thought, to future thought, in thought after thought, are not stained by jealousy; all the past evil karma, the offenses of jealousy, we all repent, wishing them to be extinguished at once and never to arise again.]

We disciples, from past thought, present thought, to future thought, in thought after thought, are not stained by jealousy; all the past evil karma, the offenses of jealousy, we all repent, wishing them to be extinguished all at once and never to arise again.

The master here specifically brings up jealousy, because it causes people to lose their reason, and even some of those who have cultivated quite deeply find it hard to avoid; it is a stumbling block on the bodhi path.

[Good teachers! What has gone before is the markless repentance. What is called repentance? What is called remorse? Repentance means repenting of one's former faults; all the past evil karma, the offenses of delusion, pride and deceit, jealousy, and so on, are all entirely repented, never to arise again — this is called repentance. Remorse means remorse for one's later faults; from now on, all the evil karma, the offenses of delusion, pride and deceit, jealousy, and so on, now that one has awakened, are all cut off forever and never again committed — this is called remorse. Thus it is called repentance.]

The master went on to say: Good teachers! What has gone before is the markless repentance. What is called repentance? What is called remorse? Repentance is to beg forgiveness for one's former faults; all the past evil karma, the offenses of delusion, arrogance and deceit, jealousy, and so on, are all begged to be forgiven — this is called repentance. Remorse is to awaken and vow never again to commit these faults; from now on, all the evil karma, the offenses of delusion, arrogance and deceit, jealousy, and so on, today having awakened, are all cut off forever and never again committed — this is called remorse. Since one both repents and is remorseful, it is called repentance.

[Ordinary and foolish people only know to repent of their former faults, not knowing to be remorseful over their later faults. Because they are not remorseful, their former faults are not extinguished, and later faults arise again. Since former faults are not extinguished and later faults again arise, how can this be called repentance?]

Ordinary and foolish people, being deluded and confused, know only to beg forgiveness for their former faults, not knowing to awaken and vow not to repeat them. Because they do not reform, their former faults will not be extinguished, and these faults will be repeated later. Since the former faults are not extinguished and later faults again arise, how can it be called repentance?
Repentance: beg forgiveness for former faults; remorse: never again commit them. This is the gist of repentance.
[Good teachers! Having already repented, together with the good teachers I will make the four great vows; each of you must listen attentively and correctly:]
Good teachers! Having completed the repentance, now together with everyone I will make the four great vows; you must each attend with your whole mind and listen truly and understand correctly:

The four great vows: the Buddhas have general vows and particular vows. The four great vows are the general vows, which every bodhisattva makes when he first gives rise to the resolving mind. Because the vows universally cover all beings, they are called 'great.' The four great vows are: I vow to save the numberless sentient beings; I vow to cut off the endless afflictions; I vow to study the immeasurable Dharma doors; I vow to accomplish the supreme Buddha Way. The Sixth Patriarch here especially emphasizes one's own mind and self-nature.
[The numberless sentient beings of my own mind I vow to save; the endless afflictions of my own mind I vow to cut off;]
I vow to save the numberless sentient beings of my own mind; I vow to cut off the endless afflictions of my own mind;
[the immeasurable Dharma doors of my self-nature I vow to study; the supreme Buddha Way of my self-nature I vow to accomplish.]
I vow to study the immeasurable Dharma doors of my self-nature; I vow to accomplish the supreme Buddha Way of my self-nature.

[Good teachers! Do you all not say that the numberless sentient beings I vow to save? Saying so, it is not that Huineng saves them. Good teachers! The sentient beings in the mind, the so-called deluded mind, the deceitful mind, the unwholesome mind, the jealous mind, the malicious mind — such minds are all sentient beings; each of you must save yourselves with your own self-nature; this is called true saving.]

Good teachers! Do you not say, 'The sentient beings in my own mind are countless, and I vow to save them'? Saying so, then it is not that Huineng can save them. Good teachers! The sentient beings in the mind are the deluded mind, the deceitful and false mind, the unwholesome mind, the jealous mind, the malicious mind, and so on; such minds are all sentient beings. Each person must save himself with the wisdom of his own original nature; this is true saving.
Deluded mind: a mind that falsely sees arising and ceasing within the still non-arising. Deceitful and false mind: a mind of fraud and slander.

The Essentials of the Sudden-Awakening Path of Entering the Way says: 'Sentient beings save themselves; the Buddha cannot save them. If the Buddha could save sentient beings, then the Buddhas of the past, as many as dust motes, would have saved all sentient beings, so why do we to this day wander in birth and death and fail to become Buddhas? You should know that sentient beings save themselves; the Buddha cannot save them.'

[What is called saving oneself by the self-nature? That is, the sentient beings of wrong views, afflictions, and delusion in one's own mind, to save them with right views. Since there are right views, one uses prajñā wisdom to break through these deluded, confused, and false sentient beings, each saving himself. When wrong comes, save it by right; when delusion comes, save it by awakening; when ignorance comes, save it by wisdom; when evil comes, save it by good. Saving in this way is called true saving.]

What is called saving oneself by the self-nature? That is, the sentient beings of wrong views, afflictions, and delusion in one's own mind, to save them with right views. Since there are right views, one uses prajñā wisdom to break through all these deluded, confused, and false sentient beings, each person saving himself. When wrong comes, save it by right; when delusion comes, save it by awakening; when ignorance comes, save it by wisdom; when evil comes, save it by good. Saving in this way, this is true saving.
Question: Why must one save the sentient beings of the mind?

Answer: Because the sentient beings of the mind are the root of one's own birth and death; if they are not saved and removed, how can one end birth and death? Take anger and resentment as an example: if one does not eliminate them, one will surely still turn in the cycle. The Avatamsaka Sutra

Chapter on Cultivating Compassion says: 'If I am much given to anger and resentment, the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones of the ten directions would all see me and think: How is it that this person, seeking bodhi, gives rise to anger and resentment? This deluded person, because of hatred, cannot liberate himself from his own suffering; how could he save all sentient beings?' Moreover, the disturbances and hindrances a cultivator receives come mainly from the sentient beings of his own mind, so saving the sentient beings of the mind is a pressing matter.

Master Hanshan said: 'People of recent times are increasingly far from the sages and do not see the real practice of the ancients, so in the objects that appear before them in daily life, they pass through the boundary of birth and death one by one. Just in this daily use, not apart from one dharma, not abiding in one dharma, letting nothing slip through anywhere, this is true effort. Just in this present object of all sounds and forms, agreeable and disagreeable, love and hate, passing through the place one by one, this is the true gateway of awakening. Just in this awakened place, each and every dharma, this is the true Buddha-dharma. It is not only when one listens to the lecturer strike the bell and beat the drum, ascend the flower-seat and open one's mouth wide to perform the cry of a wild fox, with ears bent, head bowed, eyes closed, and robe donned, that it is the Buddha-dharma. Thus the youth Sudhana, traveling south through the hundred cities, making pilgrimage to the good teachers as numerous as the dust motes of Buddha-lands, therefore awakened to the various liberation Dharma doors in every land and every dust. And yet the Dharma doors are not worth discussing, but even the good teachers, how could there be so many as lands and dusts? Little does he know that the lands and dusts are the defilements of false thought, deliberation, and emotion in our daily use (that is, the sentient beings of our own mind). If one can, at the place where the mind moves in daily use, where the emotional roots are firmly tied, where love and hate intersect and are hard to untangle, where the habitual tendencies of greed, anger, ignorance, and arrogance are hard to wear away, thrust an awl into the very root of the sore spot (the ancient writing is the same as to pierce), and examine and break through each one, pass through each one — this is the true teacher, and in the present moment one ascends the unsurpassed Dharma door of unhindered, self-mastered, great liberation. Apart from this, what other teacher is there to seek? What other extraordinary Dharma door is there to enter?' (The Collected Writings of the Dream Journey
Instruction to Miao Zhan the Lecturer)

The cry of a wild fox: 'wild fox' is a kind of fox. 'The cry of a wild fox' is the opposite of 'the lion's roar,' a metaphor for one who speaks the true principle falsely before his cultivation has matured. The lion's roar: when the Buddha speaks the Dharma, like a lion's roar, the sound shakes the ten directions and all the devils are subdued. The Transmission of the Lamp Record says: 'When Śākyamuni Buddha was born, one hand pointed to the sky and one hand pointed to the earth. He made the lion's roar, saying: In heaven and under heaven, I alone am honored.'
[Again, the endless afflictions I vow to cut off: that is, using the prajñā wisdom of the self-nature to remove the false thinking mind.]
Again, what does 'the endless afflictions of my own mind I vow to cut off' mean? It means using the prajñā wisdom of one's own self-nature to remove one's own false thinking mind.
[Again, the immeasurable Dharma doors I vow to study: one must see the self-nature and always practice the true Dharma; this is called true study.]

Again, what does 'the immeasurable Dharma doors of my self-nature I vow to study' mean? It means one must see one's own original nature and always practice the true Dharma; only this is called truly studying.

[Again, the supreme Buddha Way I vow to accomplish: since one can always humble the mind and practice the true, departing from delusion and departing from awakening, always giving rise to prajñā, removing the true and removing the false, then one sees the Buddha-nature, and in a word accomplishes the Buddha Way.]

Again, what does 'the supreme Buddha Way of my self-nature I vow to accomplish' mean? It means one should always be able to be humble and sincere, practice the true mind and right thought, abide in neither delusion nor awakening, always give rise to prajñā wisdom, remove the discriminating mind of true and false, then see the Buddha-nature, and in the present moment accomplish the Buddha Way.
[Always think: cultivation is the dharma of the power of vows.]
Always muse to yourself: cultivation is the dharma of the power of vows. The power of the mind's vow, its greatness is beyond compare!
[Good teachers! Now that you have made the four great vows, I will further transmit to you the markless three refuges and precepts.]
Good teachers! Now that you have made the four great vows, I will further transmit to you the markless three refuges and precepts.

[Good teachers! Take refuge in awakening, the most honored of the two-fold complete; take refuge in rightness, the most honored of freedom from desire; take refuge in purity, the most honored among all beings.]

Good teachers! Taking refuge in awakening is the supreme honored one complete in both merit and wisdom; taking refuge in rightness is the supreme honored one free of desire; taking refuge in purity is the supreme honored one among all beings.

[From today on, take awakening as your teacher, and no more take refuge in the devils and heterodox creeds; always verify with your own self-nature's three jewels. I urge the good teachers to take refuge in the three jewels of the self-nature: the Buddha is awakening; the Dharma is rightness; the Sangha is purity.]

From today on, you should take awakening as your teacher, no more take refuge in the devils and heterodox creeds, and always use the three jewels of the self-nature (awakening, rightness, purity) to examine whether your own body, speech, and mind accord with the Dharma. I urge all the good teachers to take refuge in the three jewels of the self-nature: the Buddha is awakening; the Dharma is rightness; the Sangha is purity.

The three jewels of the self-nature: the 'three jewels' are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. The Buddha is the awakening of the self-nature; the Dharma is the rightness of the self-nature; the Sangha is the purity of the self-nature. Hence it is called the three jewels of the self-nature.
[My own mind taking refuge in awakening, then evil delusion does not arise, few desires and knowing contentment, able to leave wealth and sex, called the most honored of the two-fold complete.]

My own mind taking refuge in awakening, then evil delusion does not arise, few desires and knowing contentment, able to leave wealth and sex, this is the supreme honored one complete in both merit and wisdom.

[My own mind taking refuge in rightness, then in thought after thought there is no wrong view; because there is no wrong view, therefore there is no self-importance and arrogance, greed, love, and clinging — called the most honored of freedom from desire.]

My own mind taking refuge in rightness, then in thought after thought there is no wrong view; because there is no wrong view, therefore there is no self-importance and arrogance, greed, love, and clinging — this is the supreme honored one free of desire.
[My own mind taking refuge in purity, then in all worldly defilement and the objects of love and desire, the self-nature is not stained — called the most honored among all beings.]
My own mind taking refuge in purity, then in all worldly defilement and the objects of love and desire, the self-nature is not stained — this is the supreme honored one among all beings.

[If one cultivates this practice, this is self-refuge. Ordinary people do not understand, and from day to night, receive the three refuges and precepts. If one says to take refuge in the Buddha, where is the Buddha? If one does not see the Buddha, what does one rely on to take refuge? The words become false.]

If one cultivates this way, this is taking refuge in the three jewels of the self-nature. Ordinary people do not understand self-refuge, and from morning to night, go to receive the three refuges and precepts. If one says to take refuge in the Buddha, where is the Buddha?
