Since you cannot see the Buddha, what do you rely on as the object of refuge? To say so in fact becomes falseness.

[Good teachers! Each of you observe for yourselves, do not misapply your minds. The scripture clearly says to take refuge in one's own Buddha, not to take refuge in another Buddha. If one does not take refuge in one's own Buddha, there is no place to rely on. Now that you have awakened, each of you should take refuge in the three jewels of your own mind: within, harmonize the mind-nature; without, revere others; this is self-refuge.]

Good teachers! Each of you observe well for yourselves, do not misapply your minds. The scripture plainly says: 'Take refuge in one's own Buddha.' It does not say to take refuge in another Buddha. If one does not take refuge in one's own Buddha, then there is no place to take refuge. Now that you have awakened, each of you should take refuge in the three jewels of the self-nature: within, harmonize the mind-nature; without, revere others; strive to achieve awakening, rightness, and purity; this is self-refuge.

Regarding taking refuge in awakening, rightness, and purity, Master Huiming said in his Collected Talks: 'Taking refuge in the Buddha: it is taking refuge in which Buddha? Taking refuge in Śākyamuni Buddha — Śākyamuni Buddha has already passed into extinction. Taking refuge in Amitābha Buddha — Amitābha Buddha is in the West. Taking refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions — the Buddhas of the ten directions are immeasurable. Taking refuge in the Buddha of carved wood, molded mud, and embroidered painting — the carved, molded, and painted Buddhas are merely representations and have no consciousness. Then after all, it is taking refuge in which Buddha? You should know that the Buddha is awakening. Between Buddha and sentient beings there is originally no difference, only the difference between awakening and not awakening. People who study the Buddha use the initial awakening to awaken the original awakening; yet the initial awakening and the original awakening do not depart from one's own mind. Therefore taking refuge in the Buddha is taking refuge in the awakening of one's own mind; it is not taking refuge in a Buddha outside the mind. Then, is there a Buddha outside the mind? One says: Indeed there is. Śākyamuni Buddha, though passed into extinction, has in truth never passed into extinction; Amitābha Buddha, though in the West, together with the dharma-bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions, is immeasurable and all-pervasive. But although the Buddhas are immeasurable and all-pervasive, if our own mind does not awaken, what connection do the Buddhas have with us? One must have one's own mind constantly awake, and only then can one be in sympathetic resonance with the Buddhas of the ten directions, so taking refuge in the Buddha is taking refuge in the awakening of one's own mind. Taking refuge in the Dharma: the Buddha's Dharma doors are immeasurable, and each dharma is equal; in the end, which dharma do we take refuge in? You should know that the Dharma is rightness. Taking refuge in the Dharma is taking refuge in rightness. People studying the Buddha must have right knowledge and right views, and establish right speech and right conduct. What is rightness? Pure compassion is rightness, a mind-ground without wrong is rightness, benefiting others without self is rightness, no-thought and no-marks is rightness. But pure compassion, and even no-marks, and the Buddha's eightfold right path, all do not depart from one's own mind; if the mind is right, all is right, and this is what is meant by 'one is all.' Therefore taking refuge in the Dharma is taking refuge in the rightness of one's own mind. Taking refuge in the Sangha: the original meaning of Sangha is many monks dwelling together in harmony. But the monks of the past cannot be seen, the monks of the present are many, and eminent monks are not few; in the end, in which monk do we take refuge? You should know that the Sangha is purity. Taking refuge in the Sangha is taking refuge in purity. Our own mind is originally pure; only because, over many eons, the defilements of habit have become deep, so that the spiritual brightness is darkened, and we create karma and suffer. From now on, one should sweep away all the seeds of affliction and habit, unstained by the least dust, and restore the original pure countenance. Therefore taking refuge in the Sangha is taking refuge in the purity of one's own mind.'

One-essence three bodies: the dharma body, the reward body, and the transformation body are the essence, the mark, and the function of the self-nature. The self-nature is the dharmakaya Buddha; the mark of the self-nature is the reward-body Buddha; the function of the self-nature is the transformation-body Buddha.

[Good teachers! Having now taken refuge in the three jewels of the self-nature, each of you be of single mind, and I will speak to you of the one-essence three bodies' self-nature Buddha, so that you see the three bodies and clearly realize your own self-nature. Follow my words together: in your own physical body, take refuge in the pure dharmakaya Buddha; in your own physical body, take refuge in the perfect reward-body Buddha; in your own physical body, take refuge in the transformation Buddha of hundreds of thousands of millions.]

Good teachers! Having now taken refuge in the three jewels of the self-nature, each of you attend with your whole mind and listen truly, and I will speak to you of the one-essence three bodies' self-nature Buddha, so that you see the three bodies and clearly realize your own self-nature. Follow my words together: in your own physical body, take refuge in the pure dharmakaya Buddha; in your own physical body, take refuge in the perfect reward-body Buddha; in your own physical body, take refuge in the transformation Buddha of hundreds of thousands of millions.

The later text says: 'The three bodies of the Buddha are in the self-nature.' And the self-nature (the spiritual consciousness) is in the physical body, so the master says: in one's own physical body, take refuge in the three bodies of the Buddha.

Master Qisong's Praise of the Platform Sutra says: 'How great indeed is the work of the Platform Sutra! Its root is upright, its traces are effective, its causes are true, and its fruits are not false. The former sages and the later sages, in this way they arose, in this way they revealed, in this way they restored. Vast and abundant, like the pouring of a great river, like the passing through of empty space, like the brightness of the sun and moon, like the unhinderedness of form and shadow, like the orderly progress of a wild goose.'

[Good teachers! The physical body is a borrowed dwelling, and one cannot speak of taking refuge in it. The three bodies of the Buddha spoken of above are in the self-nature, and all people of the world possess them. Because the mind is deluded, one does not see the inner nature, and seeks the three bodies of the Tathagata outside, not seeing that in one's own body there are the three bodies of the Buddha. You should listen and I will speak, so that you see in your own bodies the three bodies of the Buddha in the self-nature. These three bodies of the Buddha arise from the self-nature, not obtained from outside.]

Good teachers! The physical body is the borrowed dwelling of the self-nature, so one cannot speak of taking refuge in the physical body. The three bodies of the Buddha spoken of just now (the dharmakaya Buddha, the reward-body Buddha, and the transformation Buddha) are in the self-nature, and all people of the world have them. It is only because the mind is deluded that one does not see the inner nature, and seeks the three bodies of the Buddha outside, not seeing that even in one's own body there are the three bodies of the Buddha. You should listen to me speak, so that you see in your own bodies that the self-nature has the three bodies of the Buddha. These three bodies of the Buddha arise from the self-nature, not obtained from outside.

The physical body is a borrowed dwelling: Chan Master Linji Yixuan said: 'Just look at the puppet on the awning; the pulling of all its strings relies entirely on the person within.' (The Blue Cliff Record)

[What is called the pure dharmakaya Buddha? The nature of people of the world is originally pure, and all dharmas arise from the self-nature. Thinking about all evil things, then evil conduct arises; thinking about all good things, then good conduct arises. Thus all dharmas, in the self-nature, are like the sky ever clear, the sun and moon ever bright, covered by drifting clouds, bright above and dark below; suddenly a wind comes and scatters the clouds, and above and below are both bright, and all appearances are manifest. The nature of people of the world is ever drifting, like the clouds in that sky.]

What is called the pure dharmakaya Buddha? The self-nature of people of the world is originally pure, and all dharmas arise from the self-nature. Thinking about all evil things, then evil conduct arises; thinking about all good things, then good conduct arises. Thus all dharmas in the self-nature are like drifting clouds: originally the sky is ever clear, the sun and moon ever bright, but it is covered by them; above the drifting clouds it is bright, below the drifting clouds it is dark. Suddenly a gust of wind comes and scatters the drifting clouds, and above and below are both bright, and everything is seen clearly. The disposition of people of the world is ever drifting and unsettled, just like the drifting clouds of the sky.

All dharmas arise from the self-nature: how do all dharmas arise from the self-nature? By thinking! That is the next sentence: 'Thinking about all evil things, then evil conduct arises; thinking about all good things, then good conduct arises.'

In the passage above, the sky is a metaphor for the self-nature, the sun for wisdom, the moon for prajñā, the drifting clouds for false thoughts, and the sudden gust of wind for meeting a good teacher and hearing the true Dharma: 'Thus all dharmas, in the self-nature, are like the sky (the self-nature) ever clear, the sun (wisdom) and moon (prajñā) ever bright, covered by drifting clouds (the false thoughts born of thinking), bright above and dark below; suddenly a wind comes (hearing the true Dharma and practicing vigorously) and scatters the clouds, and above and below are both bright, and all appearances are manifest.'

[Good teachers! Wisdom is like the sun, prajñā like the moon, wisdom and prajñā ever bright; if one externally attaches to objects, one is covered by the drifting clouds of false thought over the self-nature, and cannot be bright. If one meets a good teacher and hears the true Dharma, and removes one's own delusion and falsehood, then inside and outside are wholly clear, and in the self-nature all dharmas are manifest. The person who sees the nature is likewise so. This is called the pure dharmakaya Buddha.]

Good teachers! Wisdom is like the sun, prajñā like the moon, wisdom and prajñā ever bright, illuminating heaven and earth; if one externally attaches to objects, one is covered by the drifting clouds of false thought over the self-nature, so the light of wisdom cannot shine out. If one meets a good teacher and hears the true genuine Dharma, and breaks through one's own delusion and falsehood, then inside and outside are wholly clear and radiant, and all the Buddha-dharmas in the self-nature are manifest. The person who sees the nature is likewise so. When the self-nature has broken through delusion and falsehood and inside and outside are wholly clear and radiant, this is called the pure dharmakaya Buddha.

[Good teachers! My own mind taking refuge in the self-nature is taking refuge in the true Buddha. Self-refuge means removing the unwholesome mind, the jealous mind, the flattering mind, the self-centered mind, the deceitful mind, the conceited mind, the mind of despising others, the mind of contempt for others, the wrong-view mind, the arrogant mind, and all the unwholesome conduct of every moment; always seeing one's own faults, not speaking of the good and evil of others; this is self-refuge. One should always humble the mind and practice all respect, which is seeing the nature and reaching through, no longer any obstruction; this is self-refuge.]

Good teachers! My own mind taking refuge in one's own nature (the self-nature Buddha) is taking refuge in the true Buddha. Taking refuge in the self-nature Buddha means removing the unwholesome mind, the jealous mind, the flattering mind, the self-centered mind, the deceitful mind, the conceited mind, the mind of despising others, the mind of contempt for others, the wrong-view mind, the arrogant mind, and all unwholesome conduct at every moment; always seeing one's own faults and not speaking of the good and evil of others—this is taking refuge in the self-nature Buddha. One must always be humble and sincere, honoring all with respect; this is seeing the nature and reaching through, with no further defilement or obstruction—this is taking refuge in the self-nature Buddha.
[My ego-mind] A mind centered on the self.

[What is called the Perfect Reward Body? It is like a single lamp that dispels a thousand years of darkness, and a single moment of wisdom that destroys ten thousand years of ignorance. Do not dwell on what is past, for what is gone can no longer be recovered; always think on what is to come, and in every thought be perfectly clear and bright, seeing your own true nature. Good and evil differ, yet the true nature is not two; the nature that is not two is called the real nature. Within the real nature, neither defiled by good nor by evil, this is called the Buddha of the Perfect Reward Body. When a single thought of evil arises in the self-nature, it destroys the karmic causes of good from ten thousand kalpas; when a single thought of good arises in the self-nature, the evil of the Ganges-side sands is exhausted. Even up to supreme bodhi, in every thought see the self-nature, never losing the original thought, and this is called the Reward Body.]

What is called the Buddha of the Perfect Reward Body? For example, lighting a single lamp dispels a thousand years of darkness, and a single flash of wisdom destroys ten thousand years of ignorance. Do not dwell on the past, for what is gone can no longer be recovered; always look to what lies ahead, and in every thought be perfectly bright, seeing your own nature. Good people and evil people are utterly different, yet the true nature is not two; the nature that is not two is called the real nature. Within the real nature one is neither defiled by good nor by evil, and this is called the Buddha of the Perfect Reward Body. When the self-nature gives rise to a single thought of evil, it destroys the karmic causes of good from ten thousand kalpas; when the self-nature gives rise to a single thought of good, the evil deeds of the Ganges-side sands all disappear. Even up to the attainment of Buddhahood, in every thought one should see the self-nature, never losing this thought, and this is the Reward Body Buddha.

[What is called the hundred-thousand-million-fold Transformation Body? If one does not think of the myriad dharmas, the nature is originally like empty space. A single thought of deliberation is called transformation. To think of evil things transforms them into the hells; to think of good things transforms them into heaven; cruelty transforms into dragons and serpents; compassion transforms into bodhisattvas; wisdom transforms into the upper realms; foolishness transforms into the lower realms. The self-nature transforms in countless ways, yet deluded people cannot awaken to this. When thought after thought gives rise to evil, one walks always the evil path; when one turns back to a single thought of good, wisdom is born. This is called the self-nature’s Transformation Body Buddha.]

What is called the Buddha of the hundred-thousand-million-fold Transformation Body? If one does not deliberate on the myriad dharmas, the self-nature is originally like empty space. A single moment of thought gives rise to transformation. To think of evil things, the self-mind transforms into the state of the hells; to think of good things, the self-mind transforms into the state of heaven; to think of cruelty, the self-mind transforms into the state of dragons and serpents; to think of compassion, the self-mind transforms into the state of the bodhisattvas; to think of wisdom, the self-mind transforms into the state of the upper heavens; to think of foolishness, the self-mind transforms into the state of the three evil destinies below. The self-nature can manifest all these countless states, yet deluded people cannot be on their guard, not knowing the great harm of thinking of evil, so that through thought after thought of evil they constantly walk the evil paths. When they turn back and give rise to a single thought of good, wisdom is born. This is the self-nature’s Transformation Body Buddha.

The above explains that sentient beings’ self-nature already possesses the three bodies: when body and mind are completely still, the self-nature is the Dharmakaya Buddha; when every thought sees the self-nature, the self-nature is the Reward Body Buddha; and when thought and deliberation (whether good or evil) arise, it is the Transformation Body Buddha. Therefore the three bodies are three states of the self-nature.
Q: Why is it that when one thinks of evil it is still said to be the self-nature’s Transformation Body Buddha?

A: The Buddha spoken of here is the “Buddha in principle” (li ji fo). Although the self-nature is deluded and thinks of evil, the Buddha-nature is not lost, and from the standpoint of principle it is still Buddha—namely the “Buddha in principle” among the Tiantai school’s Six Identities (liu ji fo).

[Good friends! The Dharmakaya is originally complete; when every thought sees the self-nature, that is the Reward Body Buddha; and when from the Reward Body there is deliberation, that is the Transformation Body Buddha. To awaken oneself and cultivate for oneself the merit of the self-nature is the true refuge. Flesh and skin are the form body, and the form body is but a dwelling; it is not spoken of as a refuge. Only when you awaken to the self-nature’s three bodies do you recognize the Buddha of your own self-nature.]

Good friends! The Dharmakaya is the self-nature’s original state (utter stillness); when every thought sees the self-nature (still yet illuminating), the self-nature is the state of the Reward Body Buddha; and when from the Reward Body there is deliberation (thinking of good or of evil), the self-nature becomes the state of the Transformation Body Buddha. To awaken oneself, and to cultivate for oneself the merit of the self-nature (turning from thoughts of evil to thoughts of good, and turning from thoughts of good to the still-and-illuminating, until finally that which illumines and that which is illumined both vanish) is the true refuge. Flesh and skin constitute the form body, and the form body is only a dwelling; therefore taking refuge does not mean taking refuge in the form body. Only when you awaken to the self-nature’s three bodies (Dharmakaya, Reward Body, Transformation Body) do you recognize the Buddha of your own self-nature.

[I have a Formless Verse; if you can recite and uphold it, in this very present moment it will cause the delusions and offenses you have accumulated over countless kalpas to be extinguished at once. The verse says:]
I have a Formless Verse; if you can recite and uphold it, then in this very present moment the delusions and offenses from beginningless kalpas will be wiped away in an instant. The verse says:

[Deluded beings cultivate merit and not the Way, only saying that cultivating merit is the Way; though almsgiving and offerings bring merit without bound, the mind’s three evils from the very first were made.]

Deluded beings cultivate merit without cultivating the Way, only thinking that cultivating merit is cultivating the Way; even if almsgiving and offerings bring merit to the utmost, the three evils (greed, anger, and delusion) had already created immeasurable offenses in the mind from the very beginning.
[Whoever would use merit to erase his offenses finds, in future lives, the merit yet the offenses remain; only remove the causes of offense within the mind, and in your own nature truly repent.]

If one intends to use the merit one has cultivated to extinguish these offenses, this is impossible; in later lives one may enjoy the merit cultivated, but the offenses remain. Once the reward is exhausted, the retribution appears. Therefore, to extinguish offenses, one must remove the root causes of offense from the mind, and each person must truly repent within their own nature.

[Once you awaken to the Great Vehicle’s true repentance, renouncing evil and walking right, you are no longer offending; learning the Way, ever observe the self-nature, and you are of one kind with every Buddha.]

Once one awakens to the true repentance of the Great Vehicle (that is, the formless repentance described above), and renounces evil and practices good, one is no longer guilty of offenses; one who studies the Way and constantly contemplates with the wisdom of the self-nature is of the same kind as all the Buddhas.

[Our patriarchs transmitted only this Sudden Teaching, vowing that all beings would see their nature and be one in essence; if in the future you seek the Dharmakaya, leave all marks and wash the mind clean.]

What my patriarchs transmitted is precisely this Sudden Teaching; I vow that all beings may see their nature and realize Buddhahood together. If you wish in the future to attain the Dharmakaya, you must be free of every mark and wash the mind clean, unstained by a single thing.
The Diamond Sutra says: “One who is free from all marks is called a Buddha.”

[Strive to see your nature, do not idly wait, for the next thought suddenly ceasing, this life is over; would you awaken to the Great Vehicle and see your nature, reverently with palms together seek it in your own mind.]

Work hard to see your own nature and do not while away the time, because if the next thought does not come, this life is finished; to awaken to the Great Vehicle and personally see your nature, you must sincerely and reverently, with palms joined, seek within your own mind.

[The Master said: Good friends! You must all recite and uphold this, and cultivate according to it. If upon these words you see your nature, then though you be a thousand li away from me, it is as if you were always by my side; if upon these words you do not awaken, then even face to face you are a thousand li away. Why should you trouble yourselves to come so far? Take care, and go well!]

The Master said: Good friends! All of you must recite and uphold this Formless Verse, and cultivate accordingly. If you see your nature in the present moment, then though you are a thousand li from me, it is as if you were always by my side; if you cannot awaken in this present moment, then even face to face with me you are separated by a thousand li. So why undergo the hardship of coming from afar? Let each of you take care, and travel safely.
[The whole assembly heard the Dharma, and there was none who did not awaken; with joy they received and practiced it.]
The great assembly heard the Dharma, and there was none who did not awaken; with joy they received and practiced it.

[After the Master received the Dharma at Huangmei, he returned to Caohou village in Shaozhou, and no one knew who he was. At that time there was a Confucian scholar named Liu Zhilüe who treated him with great respect. Zhilüe had an aunt who had become a nun, named Wujinzang (Endless Treasury), who constantly recited the Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra. The Master listened for a moment and at once understood its sublime meaning, and so explained it for her.]

The Master, having received the Dharma from the Fifth Patriarch at Huangmei, returned to Caohou village in Shaozhou, and no one knew the Master’s true standing. At the time there was a scholar named Liu Zhilüe who treated the Master with great courtesy. Liu Zhilüe had an aunt who had shaved her head and become a nun, named Wujinzang (Endless Treasury), who constantly recited the Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra (the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra). The Master only had to listen once and instantly understood its sublime meaning, and so explained it for her.
[Ru shi (Confucian scholar)] One who reveres and follows the teaching of Confucius. After the Han dynasty it also came to be a general term for scholars and learned men.

[The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters. The Master said: I do not recognize the characters; if you have questions about the meaning, please ask. The nun said: If you cannot even recognize the characters, how can you grasp the meaning? The Master said: The sublime meaning of all Buddhas is not concerned with words and letters. The nun, astonished, told all the venerable elders of the village: This is a man of the Way; we ought to invite and support him.]

The nun then held the sutra and asked about the characters she did not recognize. The Master said: I do not recognize characters, so I cannot tell you; if you have questions about the meaning of the sutra, please ask. Wujinzang said: If you cannot recognize even a single character, how can you grasp the meaning? The Master replied: The sublime meaning of all Buddhas has nothing to do with words and letters; it is all within the self-nature. Wujinzang was most astonished, and told all the elderly and virtuous people of the village: This is a man of the Way; we ought to respectfully invite and support him.
[Qi de (venerable elder)] One of advanced age and high virtue who has long enjoyed the trust and respect of the community.
Q: The Sixth Patriarch said that he could not read. Is this really so?

A: Many people have questioned whether the Sixth Patriarch could read, so I shall answer in some detail. In the Platform Sutra there are several places where the Sixth Patriarch says he could not read, and so it is indeed so, although this is hard for those who are literate to understand.
Master Nan Huaijin (

), in “What the Diamond Sutra Says” (Jingang Jing Shuo Shenme), spoke of a barber surnamed Yang; though illiterate, after he awakened through studying Buddhism his grasp of book learning far surpassed that of any scholar. Master Tanxu (
), in “Memoirs of Life’s Shadows” (Yingchen Huiyilu), tells of a “Candle-Sunning” Master, and Master Huiming (
): these were all, in recent times, illiterate men who nonetheless became great Dharma masters skilled at expounding the sutras.

In truth, as long as one reads the Platform Sutra closely, observes the cultivation of his many disciples and the glorious attainments of the Chan school, one will understand that the Sixth Patriarch is a Buddha. Just as the World-Honored One Śākyamuni manifested as a teacher and founder to deliver sentient beings, and Vimalakirti manifested as a layman to deliver sentient beings, so Master Huineng manifested as a patriarch to deliver sentient beings. The reason the Master manifested himself as illiterate is precisely this: the sublime meaning of all Buddhas is not concerned with words and letters, but is realized through the mind. It is to teach those who study Buddhism not to be trapped in phrases and sentences, not to go in circles among names and concepts, and still less to engage in discussing battle plans on paper, or even to look for a horse from a drawing.

[Yang the Barber] Master Nan Huaijin, in “What the Diamond Sutra Says”, relates: “As far as I know and have seen, there were several great monks who had never studied books, never spent a single day in school, and did not know a single character. After their awakening, their poetry was excellent, their prose was excellent, everything was excellent—truly beyond imagination. Eighty years ago my teacher met a monk who had originally been a barber, carrying a shoulder pole as he traveled about the countryside. In the Qing dynasty the children of barbers were not allowed to take the examinations; the restrictions were extremely strict. Yet this great Chan master who had been a barber, having awakened to the Way, understood everything, with nothing he did not know. He also had a temple, which his supporters had given him when the abbot passed on. Some called him Monk Yang, and some called him Yang the Barber. When the educated went to quiz him, saying, ‘Monk Yang, I have forgotten a line—can you tell me which book it is in?’, he would answer, ‘It is on such-and-such a page of such-and-such a book!’ When my teacher was young he was very mischievous, and deliberately asked him about a line from Dream of the Red Chamber, and he answered it correctly enough—that is extremely strange. There was a wealthy opium smoker who wanted to quit but could not. In the end he had no recourse but to go and ask this Monk Yang: ‘Master Yang, please come and shave my head.’ While he was being shaved his opium craving came upon him, and his nose ran and his tears flowed, in great distress. This Monk Yang patted him on the back and said: ‘Let go!’—that is, liberation—and finished shaving his head. From that day on this man never smoked opium again. These are instances of the textual prajñā (wenzi bore) that arises spontaneously after enlightenment; they are not the product of our cleverness. Cleverness is thought out, and what is thought out is of no use. One who has awakened also has an especially high memory; not only can he remember the affairs of his youth, but he knows the books he read in his former lives. When you hear this, you probably find it very strange, but it is indeed so. That is why Su Dongpo has a verse: “It is already too late to read books in this life.” One should read while young; the books of this life are read for the next life. At the moment of enlightenment, the books one has read in countless past lives all come forth, because the prajñā wisdom has all emerged. Those who are learned have good memories and read ten lines at a glance; those who cannot read pick out one character at a time. Some people, with a single sweep of the eye, finish a page, reading ten lines at a glance and writing a thousand words a day, and to old age do not decline—indeed, the older they grow, the stronger their memory. Of course, this requires concentration and prajñā wisdom; this is the textual prajñā.”

[The “Candle-Sunning” Master] Master Tanxu, in “Memoirs of Life’s Shadows”, relates: There was a Vinaya master surnamed Chi who served as the lamp-keeper in the meditation hall of Jinshan Monastery. He was very dull-witted and illiterate. Others played a trick on him, saying: “Lamp-keeper! Today is the sixth day of the sixth month, when everyone airs their things. Your candles are about to go mouldy! Hadn’t you better take them out to dry?” So he moved out a whole jar of candles and set them one by one at the foot of the wall to dry. The scorching sun melted the candles, and all the wax ran down onto the ground. From then on everyone called him the “Candle-Sunning” Master. The rector (weina) saw this and knew that he had been made a fool of. He thought: This man is too foolish! If I strike him with the incense board it would not be worth it; besides, he has no idea what is going on. So he only shook his head and sighed, and said nothing more. The next day the rector called him over and said before the assembly: “Vinaya Master Chi! With such great wisdom as yours, serving as lamp-keeper and meditating in this hall is a waste of your talent! Now Master Dixian (Master Tanxu’s teacher) is teaching at the Tuotuo Monastery in Wenzhou, specifically training people to spread the Dharma and to become Dharma masters. Since you have such great intelligence, you can go study to become a master under him. When you have completed your studies, you can go everywhere to expound the scriptures and teach the Dharma, benefiting humans and gods, and serving as a model for the three realms. By then I will come serve as your rector, and everyone may share in your light. If you stay here long it would be a great pity to waste such wisdom. Nothing should be delayed; go today!” As for Vinaya Master Chi himself, he did not think this was a joke at his expense, nor that it was revoking his post; he took it as the truth.

He arrived at the Tuotuo Monastery and paid his respects to Master Dixian. The master asked him: “Do you wish to devote yourself to studying the teachings?” “Yes!” Vinaya Master Chi replied. “When I was at Jinshan, they said I had great wisdom, and that meditating there as a lamp-keeper wasted my talent, so they sent me here to study the teachings with you and become a Dharma master; in the future I shall be a model for the three realms and benefit humans and gods!” Master Dixian looked at him, and hearing these words understood in his heart that this was a foolish man who had been made a fool of; but whether of dull or sharp faculties, since he was willing to devote himself to the teachings, one could not refuse him. Master Dixian said to him: “Since you are willing to devote yourself to the teachings, do not be afraid of hardship, and do not be afraid of suffering! First you must do hard service in the monastery, and morning and evening bow before the Buddha and seek wisdom. Take up the scriptures in your spare time and study them slowly; do not be anxious. In time you will naturally become a Dharma master.” After that, Master Chi first served as the cleaner, hauling away the filth, drawing water and sweeping the floor; later he worked in the dining hall, wiping the tables and washing the bowls, and morning and evening bowed before the Buddha, finding time to have someone teach him the five daily liturgies, leaving not a single idle moment. Master Dixian paid close attention to him, and once he had learned the five liturgies, arranged for someone to teach him to memorize the Surangama Sutra and the Lotus Sutra. Since when he first heard the Lotus Sutra he could not understand it, he was also taught to memorize the Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sutra and the Phrase-by-Phrase Comment on the Surangama. At the outset they taught him a few sentences, then a few lines—what is called “Grinding a steel beam into an embroidery needle: when the work is complete the result is achieved of itself.” After more than ten years of effort, he had committed all these scriptures to memory and could bring up any passage with great familiarity. Later he could not only understand the sutras when he heard them, but even hung up the assistant lecturer’s plaque and took the great seat in place of the master; all the doctrines and textual meanings were as familiar and clear to him as though he had attained the eloquence of reality. Yet even up to the time he lectured in the master’s place, he never gave up his single post of service in the dining hall. Often when they went to invite the master they could not find him, and there he would be in the dining hall with an apron tied round him, washing the bowls. Later, when Master Dixian saw that he had become an assistant lecturer and would not let him continue serving in the hall, he insisted and would not agree; every day he still finished his hall service before putting on the red kasaya and ascending the great seat to lecture, and after descending from the seat he would go and set the hall. Sometimes, when Master Dixian went out to lecture in other places, he took him along to take the seat in his stead. The original rector from Jinshan, and those who had mocked him, hearing that the Candle-Sunning Master could now take the great seat and lecture, were all deeply ashamed, acknowledging themselves no match for him. Later they even went to consult him, and when they met him they were covered with shame. Indeed, when Master Chi lectured, that rector humbled himself and served as his rector, and those who had made a fool of him sat in the assembly to listen. In the end, none of their words came to nothing—all of them were fulfilled. When he first went to study under Master Dixian he was only in his thirties, and it was not until he was over fifty that the old master, answering an invitation to lecture on the Lotus Sutra at the Pili Monastery in Nanjing, took him along to take the seat in his stead. Unhappily, it was here that he passed away! At his death he knew the time beforehand, and there were all manner of auspicious signs.

[Master Huiming] Master Leguan, in “In Memory of Master Huiming”, writes: When the abbot of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou, the old Master Huiming, is mentioned, there is no one north or south of the great river who does not know him, and he is especially praised by the wandering Chan monks of every quarter. He was from Fujian, and is said to have left home in his youth. When I drew near to him he was already an old man nearing seventy; he was short of stature, a little over five feet tall, with bronze-colored skin, prominent bone structure and high cheekbones, and his voice when he spoke was as loud and clear as a great bell. When he expounded the sutras in the great hall, his voice shook the bronze bell on the altar until it hummed—a remarkable man. Looking at his outward appearance, he was exactly like the arhat in the “Arhat Hall” who subdues the dragon and tames the tiger, and quite resembled the mummified body of the Sixth Patriarch enshrined in the patriarch hall of Nanhua Monastery in Guangdong. The old Master Huiming had in lay life been a farmer, had never studied, and after leaving home his livelihood was one of bitter ascetic service. In the monastery he labored in the outer service posts, serving as vegetable-head, rice-head, water-head, and cleaner-head—those arduous duty posts—and in his spare time delighted to sit cross-legged in meditation. How did this illiterate ascetic monk come to bear the title of Dharma master? It is truly a strange affair. According to the old seniors of the monastery, when Master Huiming served as the “server” (the post in the dining hall that dishes out the food) at Tiantong Monastery in Ningbo, each day after the meal he would feed the dogs, and this he counted among his regular daily duties. The leftover rice the dogs had not finished, he could not bear to throw away; to conserve merit he would take it up, wash it in water, and eat it himself. And so he did for several years. One day, while eating the dogs’ leftover rice, he suddenly burst out laughing. His cellmates asked him what he was laughing at. He said: “I have often heard people say that dogs have Buddha-nature. Today I have understood this principle, and that is why I laugh.” From that time on he seems to have entered into the Buddha’s understanding. This is exactly what is meant by ‘the lowest of the low have the highest of wisdom.’ Afterwards, Tiantong Monastery invited a Dharma master to lecture on the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment. Though he was a common laborer, he was very earnest, and sat every day with the assembly to hear the sutra. One day, when he heard the teacher explain the principle in the sutra, ‘the perfectly Enlightened self-nature is not a nature, yet there is a nature from which all natures arise; there is nothing to take and nothing to attain,’ he was at once opened and understood, and suddenly saw his own nature. After each lecture he would also explain it to his cellmates, to show his appreciation of the sutra’s meaning. His cellmates all mocked him, saying: “Look at your face in the mirror. With such a miserable appearance, and not knowing a single character, you still fancy yourself a lecturer of sutras?” At the time he could not contain his anger and answered: “You think I cannot become a Dharma master? Very well. From today onward I will make myself a Dharma master to show you. Three years from now I will return to Tiantong and lecture! Just wait and see!” His cellmates, hearing him speak so boldly, all clapped and laughed together. Some said: “With a man of your material to become a lecturer—why, that would take the iron tree to blossom and the waters of the Yellow River to flow backwards.” He did not argue with them, but at once returned to his room, gathered up his robe and bowl, shouldered his bundle, and went out the monastery gate. After leaving Tiantong he wandered everywhere on foot, imitating the story of the fifty-three pilgrimages, calling on every good teacher, and made pilgrimages to the four great mountains of China. Before he knew it, three years had passed. In the spring of the third year he heard that Tiantong Monastery was again holding a sutra assembly, expounding the Mahavaipulya Sutra of the Buddha’s Flower Garland (Avatamsaka Sutra). The thought stirred him, and he shouldered his bundle and returned to Tiantong. When he entered the guest hall and sat down, the guest master saw that he had only a shabby bundle, was small in stature, and had a miserable appearance, so he treated him as a wandering mendicant cloud-and-water monk. With a stern face he asked: “You, master—what business do you have at this monastery?” He answered: “I have come to hear the sutras, and to ask for an auditor’s place.” The guest master laughed inwardly, thinking that such a miserable wretch should come to hear the sutras, and jested: “Do you know what sutra we are expounding here?” He lifted his head and answered: “Why need you ask? Is it not the Mahavaipulya Sutra of the Buddha’s Flower Garland?” The guest master then joshed him: “Do you know how the three characters ‘da fang guang’ are explained? Tell me; if you explain them rightly, I will grant you an auditor’s place.” Seeing that the guest master was deliberately posing a difficulty, he at once dropped his face and pointed at the guest master, saying: “How little you have studied! How can you question the Dharma with a flippant mind? If you want me to give you instruction, you must be reverent and respectful, don the robe and spread the mat, bow to me three times, and then kneel before me with palms together—only then will I explain it to you. Such a child’s-play attitude: is this the way to seek the Dharma?” The guest master, taken aback at this rebuke, felt that although the man’s looks were nothing special, his air was no small matter. So he at once played a trick, saying aloud: “Very well, please sit a moment, I’ll be right back.” The guest master turned and ran to the abbot’s quarters, and with the abbot practiced ‘crossing the sea under cover of heaven’, saying: “Just now an unusual monk came to lodge here. He declares he has come to hear the sutras and to ask for an auditor’s place. I asked him what sutra he wished to hear, and he answered the Mahavaipulya Sutra of the Buddha’s Flower Garland. I asked him how the three characters ‘da fang guang’ were to be explained. His tone was nothing small: he said that to hear the three characters ‘da fang guang’ explained, the abbot would have to don the robe and hold the implements and invite him into the abbot’s quarters, and only then would he explain.” The abbot, hearing these words, was moved by a moment of curiosity, and truly donned the great red kasaya and the implements, went to the guest hall, and invited Master Huiming into the abbot’s quarters. Entering the abbot’s quarters, Master Huiming said to the abbot: “If you want to hear me speak the Dharma, you must lend me your seat.” The abbot agreed and respectfully installed him on the seat. Sitting there, he looked every inch a Dharma master; he slapped the wooden gavel and spoke: “Abbot, the three characters ‘da fang guang’ each have four explanations: broad-within-broad, broad-within-measure, measure-within-broad, and measure-within-measure. If I explain the meaning of broad-within-broad, I could not finish in a lifetime. If I use broad-within-measure and measure-within-broad, that too would take a year or half a year. But if you ask me for the measure-within-measure explanation, I can discuss it with you. Which explanation would the abbot care to hear?” The abbot, hearing this, felt that this wandering monk was no simple man, and dared not treat him lightly. He answered: “Please, then, explain the measure-within-measure!” Thereupon he gave a great lion’s roar. How it is called ‘great’, how it is called ‘square’, how it is called ‘broad’—he discoursed on the threefold profound meaning of essence, mark, and function of these three characters, speaking forth from his own nature, as when the bottom of a bucket falls out and pours forth a thousand miles, and he spoke for a full three hours. The more the abbot listened the more delighted he was, feeling that every principle he spoke flowed from his own nature, not falling into the ruts of earlier men, holding a view of his own, of fathomless wonder and irresistible fascination. At once he bowed in thanks and exclaimed in praise: “The master is sublime! The master is sublime!” And he asked him to take the seat and lecture in his place. This is the origin of the title ‘Dharma master’ given to Master Huiming, and his first time ever lecturing. From that time on, the monasteries of every quarter admired Master Huiming’s fame and vied to invite him to lecture. Each time he lectured the seats were full. Though he bore the name of a lecturer, he did not fuss among words and books; his aim was in Chan contemplation. His lectures were entirely developed from his own insight, unlike other lecturers who relied on commentaries. He held that the principles in the commentaries are the views of earlier men, having nothing to do with oneself; and that to recite the commentaries fluently is no more than counting another man’s treasures. So when he lectured he never classified the teachings, but merely cleared the text and explained its meaning, delighting in relating revealing cases and records. Hence he was joyfully heard by the Chan monks and by lay men and women. As soon as word came that Master Huiming would lecture at some place, the Chan monks and the lay devotees would swarm after him—a spectacle such as ordinary lecturers never had. Although the Master was an illiterate man, his Dharma words were nevertheless very beautiful. That year I was spending the New Year at Lingyin. On New Year’s Eve he ascended the hall and spoke; I remember two lines of his Dharma words: “Flowers bloom, every one lovely; plum petals fall, each one fragrant.” How poetic! How could a man who never drank ink utter such words? It is plain this came from his state of enlightenment. (There is a volume, “The Recorded Sayings of Master Huiming,” recorded by Master Tanyuan of Hunan.)

[There was a descendant of the Marquis Wu of Wei, Cao Shuliang, together with the residents, who vied to come and pay their respects. At that time the ancient Baolin Temple, ruined by the wars and fires at the end of the Sui dynasty, was rebuilt on its old foundations into a monastery, and the Master was invited to reside there. Soon it became a precious shrine.]

Then a distant descendant of the Marquis Wu of Wei, Cao Cao, named Cao Shuliang, together with the residents, came in eager competition to pay their respects to the Master. At that time the ancient Baolin Monastery on the Caoxi stream had been destroyed by warfare at the end of the Sui dynasty and had become a ruin. So on the original foundations they rebuilt the monastery, and respectfully invited the Master to take up residence; very soon the Baolin Monastery became a famous temple.
[The Master dwelt there for more than nine months, and was again pursued by a band of evildoers. The Master then hid himself
(the same character as ‘dun’, to conceal oneself)

in the front mountain. They set fire to the grass and trees, and the Master, concealing himself, squeezed into the crevice of a rock and so escaped. On the rock there are still the traces of the Master’s knees from sitting in meditation and the marks of his robe, and so it is called the Rock of Refuge. The Master remembered the Fifth Patriarch’s charge, “Huai Hui Zhi Cang” (stop at Huai, and hide at Hui), and so he went away and hid himself in the two districts.]

The Master had resided at the Baolin Monastery for only a little over nine months when he was again tracked down by the band of evildoers. The Master then hid himself in the front mountain. When the evil band could not find him they set fire to the mountain (how pitiful!), and the Master squeezed into a crevice in the rock and so escaped death. On the rock there are still the traces of the Master’s knees from sitting in meditation and the marks of his robe, and so it is called the Rock of Refuge. The Master recalled the Fifth Patriarch’s warning, “When you reach Huai, stop; when you meet Hui, hide,” and so he went and hid himself among the company of hunters in the area between the two districts of Huaiji and Sihui.

[The monk Fahai, a native of Qujiang district in Shaozhou, on first seeking instruction from the Patriarch, asked: “Mind is Buddha—I beg you to kindly instruct me.” The Master said: When the previous thought does not arise, that is mind; when the subsequent thought does not cease, that is Buddha. That which forms all marks is mind; that which is free from all marks is Buddha. If I were to explain it fully, even in countless kalpas I should never finish. Listen to my verse:]

The monk Fahai was a native of Qujiang district in Shaozhou. When he first came to see the Sixth Patriarch, he asked: “How should one understand ‘mind is Buddha’ (this mind is Buddha)? I respectfully beg the Master to instruct me.” The Master said: When the previous and subsequent thoughts neither arise (still) nor cease (illuminating), this mind is Buddha; when it forms all marks yet does not attach to them, this mind is Buddha. If I were to explain it in detail, even the time of immeasurable kalpas would not suffice. Listen to my verse:

[Fahai] A great disciple of the Sixth Patriarch; later he became the foremost in the assembly, and collected the Sixth Patriarch’s teachings to form the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. [Mind is Buddha] This mind is Buddha. Here ‘mind’ refers to the self-nature. The Recorded Sayings of Mazu says: “All of you, each trust that your own mind is Buddha; this mind is Buddha.” The Essential Dharma of Mind Transmission says: “Q: What is Buddha? The master said: Your mind is Buddha; Buddha is the mind; mind and Buddha are not different. Hence it is said, ‘mind is Buddha.’ If you separate from the mind, there is no other Buddha.”

[When the previous thought does not arise, this is mind; when the subsequent thought does not cease, this is Buddha; that which forms all marks is mind; that which is free from all marks is Buddha] This is an interchanged expression, meaning: when the previous and subsequent thoughts neither arise nor cease, this mind (self-nature) is Buddha; and when it forms all marks and is free from all marks, this mind is Buddha. [When the previous thought does not arise, this is mind; when the subsequent thought does not cease, this is Buddha] At the moment before a single thought arises, this is called ‘not arising’ (still); not being inflated, not being drowsy, not clinging to stillness, not falling into emptiness—this is called ‘not ceasing’ (illuminating). In this state of neither arising nor ceasing, the mind is Buddha (mind is Buddha). Master Xuyun says: “This moment before a single thought arises is called ‘not arising’; not being inflated, not being drowsy, not clinging to stillness, not falling into emptiness, is called ‘not ceasing.’” (From the Dharma Collection of Master Xuyun.) There is yet a deeper meaning to ‘when the previous thought does not arise, this is mind; when the subsequent thought does not cease, this is Buddha.’ The Essential Dharma of Mind Transmission says: “Those who study the Way, if they wish to become Buddhas, have no need to learn all the Buddha-dharma; they need only learn non-seeking and non-attachment. Non-seeking means the mind is not born; non-attachment means the mind does not cease; when it neither arises nor ceases, that is Buddha.”
[Diao ju (agitation)] An affliction that lifts the mind up and does not let it rest quietly.
[Mind is named wisdom, and Buddha is named concentration; with concentration and wisdom held in equipoise, the mind is pure.]
Forming marks is called wisdom; being free from marks is concentration. With concentration and wisdom held in equipoise (forming all marks yet not attaching to them), the mind is pure.

[Mind is called wisdom, Buddha is called concentration] These two lines, taken together with the passage above, ‘that which forms all marks is mind; that which is free from all marks is Buddha,’ mean: forming marks is called wisdom, and being free from marks is concentration.

[Forming marks] That through which various conditioned factors combine to form the various dharmas—as when rafters and tiles and so forth combine to form a house. [Being free from marks] So-called being free from marks means not attaching to marks: knowing that marks are illusory, not being deluded by marks, and not being turned by marks. The Diamond Sutra says: “If you see that all marks are not marks, then you see the Tathagata.”
Relying on concentration one applies wisdom, and within wisdom one abides in concentration; this is called concentration and wisdom held in equipoise.
[To awaken to this dharma-gate depends on your own habitual nature; the essential function is originally unborn; to cultivate the two together is the right course.]

Awakening to this dharma-gate (mind is Buddha) depends on your own habitual nature (the habit of clinging to “having”); the effort of practice is itself an illusion (the essential function is originally unborn). Nonetheless, only by cultivating concentration and wisdom together does one reach the correct cause of Buddhahood.

[Wu sheng (unborn)] Dharmas are originally unborn, and therefore also unceasing; this is called unborn. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All sentient beings, within the unborn, falsely perceive arising and ceasing, and therefore it is said that they turn in the wheel of birth and death.” The Sutra of the Most Supreme King says: “The unborn is real; arising is false. Foolish people, drowning in birth and death, the Tathagata embodies the real, with nothing false—this is called nirvāṇa.” Hence those who cultivate should contemplate the principle of the unborn in order to destroy the afflictions of arising and ceasing.

This passage—if one understands the principle of the Diamond Sutra that “having delivered all sentient beings to extinction, yet there is not a single sentient being who has actually been delivered”—leads one to appreciate the great compassion and skillful means of the Sixth Patriarch, for the Fahai of that time was “a first-time seeker of the Patriarch.”

A more penetrating way of speaking about mind and Buddha is: not mind, not Buddha (neither mind nor Buddha). Hence the Master’s verse says: “Awakening to this dharma-gate (mind is Buddha) depends on your own habitual nature.” And immediately he points out: “The essential function is originally unborn.” At that time Fahai still had attachments. If his habitual tendencies were entirely spent, he would realize not mind, not Buddha; but as long as his habitual tendencies remained, he had to cultivate concentration and wisdom together. The Transmission of the Lamp

chapter on Mazu says: “A monk asked: Master, why do you say that mind is Buddha? The master said: To stop the infant’s crying. The monk said: When the crying has stopped, what then? The master said: Not mind, not Buddha.” Therefore “mind is Buddha” and “not mind, not Buddha” are two different stages. The phrase “depends on your own habitual nature,” though praising Fahai for being able to realize “mind is Buddha,” also hints that it is not yet the final teaching. Speaking of the expedient means, mind is Buddha; speaking of the ultimate meaning, not mind, not Buddha.

[To stop the infant’s crying] A simile for the expedient teaching (not the final teaching). When a child cries, the elder gives him a yellow poplar leaf, saying: This is a piece of gold; take it and buy some sweets. The child takes it and stops crying. The Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra, chapter twenty, says: “When the infant is crying, the parents give it a yellow poplar leaf and say: ‘Don’t cry! Don’t cry! I will give you gold.’ The infant, seeing this, conceives the thought of real gold and at once stops crying; yet this poplar leaf is not really gold.” [Yue fang bian gu] In terms of the expedient means. “Yue” means to bring something to bear on a particular aspect.
“Mind is Buddha”—this ends the birth-and-death of ordinary life and comes forth from the dream of samsara.
“Not mind, not Buddha”—this ends the birth-and-death of transformation and comes forth from the dream of ignorance.

The Direct Pointing beyond the Gate says: “Funiuxian (Master Zizai) was sent by Mazu with a letter (hurried delivery) to the National Master Zhong of Nanyang (the National Master Huizhong). The National Master asked: ‘What phrases does the master Ma use to show people?’ Funiu said: ‘Mind is Buddha.’ The Master said: ‘What talk is that!’ (The National Master Huizhong did not approve of this state.) After a long while (a long time passed), he asked again: ‘What other phrases are there?’ Funiu said: ‘Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.’ The Master said: ‘That is a little closer (this is about right).’”
Q: Then is the proposition “mind is Buddha” right or wrong?

A: This proposition is of course right, but it is not the final teaching. The “mind is Buddha,” “not mind, not Buddha,” and “not mind, not Buddha, not a thing” spoken of above are three levels of attainment. “Mind is Buddha” means realizing that one’s own mind has always been Buddha, and so no longer seeking Buddha outside the mind, but only awakening to one’s own mind. “Not mind, not Buddha” means realizing that both mind and Buddha are matters within the dream of ignorance; the view of Buddha and the view of Dharma are gone. “Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing” means realizing that “that” which dreams the nameless dream.

[Fahai awakened at once upon these words, and in a verse of praise said: The mind is from the beginning Buddha; not realizing this, one wrongs oneself. I now know that concentration and wisdom are the cause; cultivating them together, I leave behind all things.]

Fahai at once awakened greatly, and praised in verse: The self-mind was from the beginning Buddha; not awakening, one belittles oneself empty. I now know that concentration and wisdom are the right cause of Buddhahood, and so I shall cultivate concentration and wisdom together and leave behind all marks.

The Essential Instructions on Mind-Cultivation says: “A monk asked the master Guizong: What is Buddha? The master said: I will tell you now, but I fear you will not believe. The monk said: The master’s sincere words, how would I dare not believe? The master said: You yourself are. The monk said: How is one to maintain it? The master said: With a single mote in the eye, empty blossoms fall in confusion. The monk thereupon had insight. The former sacred statesmen’s causes of entering the Way given above are clear and plain, and give no trouble. If in this koyan there is a place of faith and understanding (not understood in words, but only by silent accord), then one walks hand in hand with the ancient sages.”

blocks.text: 3. The Head Did Not Touch the Ground

inline.s: [The monk Fahai, a native of Hongzhou, left home at the age of seven and constantly recited the Lotus Sutra. When he came to pay respects to the Patriarch, his head did not reach the ground. The Patriarch reproved him, saying: If your bow does not touch the ground, it is as good as no bow at all! There must be something in your mind. What have you been practicing in?]

A monk named Fahai, a native of Hongzhou, left home at the age of seven and constantly recited the Lotus Sutra. When he came to pay respects to the Patriarch, his head did not touch the ground in his bow. The Sixth Patriarch reprimanded him: You bow and your head does not touch the ground—it would be better not to bow at all! There is surely something in your mind that you think a great deal of. What have you been proudly practicing?

[He said: I have recited the Lotus Sutra and have reached three thousand copies. The Master said: If you recited ten thousand copies and grasped the meaning of the sutra, without thinking it any great achievement, then you might walk with me. Now that you are burdened by this accomplishment and do not even know your own fault! Listen to my verse:]

Fahai replied: I have recited the Lotus Sutra and already reached three thousand copies. The Master said: If you recited to ten thousand copies and grasped the meaning of the sutra, without thinking it any great thing, only then could you walk with me. Now that you have recited three thousand copies and think yourself quite remarkable, you do not even know your own fault! Listen to my verse:
[Bowing is meant to break down the banner of self-conceit; why does your head not reach the ground? Where there is an ego, offenses at once arise; forgetting merit, blessings are immeasurable.]

Bowing is the very sign of crushing one’s self-conceit; why, then, does your head not touch the ground when you bow? When there is an ego in the mind, offenses arise; when one forgets one’s own accomplishments, blessings are immeasurable.
Fahai was self-important and arrogant, clinging to what he had gained, and the Master untied his bonds for him.
[The Master said again: What is your name? He said: Fahai. The Master said: Your name is Fahai (Dharma-Sea), but have you ever reached the Dharma? Again he spoke a verse:]
The Master said again: What is your name? He replied: Fahai. The Master said: Your name is Fahai—have you ever reached the wondrous Dharma? And so he spoke another verse:
[Your name is now Fahai, but you have never reached the Dharma; diligently reciting, you never rest, yet you recite merely following the sound; one who illumines the mind is called a bodhisattva.]

Your present name is Fahai, but in truth you have not reached the Dharma. Though you diligently recite the Lotus Sutra without resting, you only move your mouth while your mind does not recite; you run vainly after the sound. Reciting the sutra means using its meaning to illumine the mind; only this is called a bodhisattva.
[Today you have a karmic connection with me, and so I speak this for you; only believe deeply that the Buddha has no words, and the lotus will bloom from your mouth.]

Today you have a karmic connection with me, and so I speak to you; you need only believe deeply that the Buddha’s teaching has no words, and while you recite the Wondrous Dharma Lotus Sutra the wondrous Dharma lotus will issue forth from your mouth.
[Dan xin fo wu yan (but believe that the Buddha has no words)] The Diamond Sutra

chapter thirteen, “Upholding the Dharma as Revealed”: “Subhuti, what do you think, did the Tathagata preach any Dharma? Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, the Tathagata did not preach anything.” The Diamond Sutra

chapter twenty-one, “What Is not Preached Is Preached”: “Subhuti, do not think that the Tathagata, in so many words, has the thought, ‘I shall preach the Dharma.’ Do not hold such a thought. Why? If anyone says that the Tathagata has preached the Dharma, that is slandering the Buddha, because he does not understand what I teach. Subhuti, as to preaching the Dharma, there is no Dharma that can be preached; this is called preaching the Dharma.” [Miao fa lian hua jing] The full title of the Lotus Sutra.

[Fahai, hearing the verse, repented and thanked him, saying: From now on, I shall be humble and courteous to all. Your disciple has recited the Lotus Sutra but has not understood its meaning; my mind is often full of doubt. The Master’s wisdom is vast; I beg you to explain briefly the meaning of the sutra.]

Fahai, hearing the verse, at once repented and confessed his guilt, saying: From now on, your disciple will be humble and courteous to everyone. Your disciple has recited the Lotus Sutra but has not understood its meaning and my mind is often in doubt. The Master’s wisdom is vast; I beg you to give me a brief explanation of the sutra’s meaning.

blocks.text: 4. The Meaning of the Lotus Sutra

inline.s: [The Master said: Fahai! The Dharma is in fact fully reached; it is your mind that has not reached it. The sutra itself is beyond doubt; it is your mind that doubts. When you recite this sutra, what do you take as its essential teaching? Fahai said: Your student’s faculties are dull and dark; I have always only recited it according to the text—how could I know its essential purport?]

The Master said: Fahai! The Dharma is completely reached; it is your mind that has not reached it. The sutra is originally beyond doubt; it is your mind that doubts. Let me ask you, you have recited three thousand copies of the Lotus Sutra—what does this sutra take as its essential teaching? Fahai said: Your student’s faculties are dull and dark; I have always only recited according to the text—how could I know the essential purport of the sutra?
[Xue ren (student)] One who seeks to learn.

[The Master said: I do not recognize characters; take the sutra and read it aloud once, and I will explain it for you. Fahai then recited the sutra aloud. When he reached the chapter on the Parable, the Master said: Stop! This sutra from the beginning takes the Buddha’s appearance in the world for its essential teaching; although it sets forth many parables, none goes beyond this.]

The Master said: I do not recognize characters; do bring me the sutra and read it once, and I will explain it for you. Fahai then recited the sutra aloud. When he reached the “Third Chapter on the Parable,” the Master said: Stop! This sutra from the beginning takes “the appearance in the world for a single great cause” as its essential teaching; although the sutra sets forth many parables, they are all only to clarify this essential teaching.
The better to understand the Sixth Patriarch’s instruction, the relevant sutra passages are copied out below:

The Lotus Sutra, “Expedient Means Chapter Two,” says: “The Buddha told Shariputra: … the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones appear in the world solely because of a single great cause. Shariputra! What is it called that the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones appear in the world solely because of a single great cause? The Buddhas and World-Honored Ones appear in the world because they wish to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha-knowledge and thereby attain purity; they appear in the world because they wish to show sentient beings the Buddha-knowledge; they appear in the world because they wish to cause sentient beings to realize the Buddha-knowledge; they appear in the world because they wish to cause sentient beings to enter the way of the Buddha-knowledge. Shariputra! This is the single great cause for which the Buddhas appear in the world. The Buddha told Shariputra: The Buddhas and Tathagatas only teach bodhisattvas; whatever they do is always for a single matter, showing and awakening sentient beings only with the Buddha-knowledge. Shariputra! The Tathagata speaks the Dharma for sentient beings only with the single Buddha-vehicle; there is no other vehicle, whether two or three. Shariputra! The Dharma of all the Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise.”
[Yi fo cheng (single Buddha-vehicle)] The only teaching capable of leading one to Buddhahood.

[What is this cause? The sutra says: “The Buddhas and World-Honored Ones appear in the world solely because of a single great cause.” This single great cause is the Buddha-knowledge. Worldly people are deluded on the outside by attachment to marks, and deluded on the inside by attachment to emptiness. If one can be free from marks within marks, and free from emptiness within emptiness, then one is deluded neither within nor without. If one awakens to this Dharma, the mind opens in a single thought; this is opening the Buddha-knowledge.]

What cause? This cause is: for a single great matter. The sutra says: “The Buddhas and World-Honored Ones appear in the world solely because of a single great cause.” What is the great matter? The great matter is the “Buddha-knowledge.” Worldly people either are deluded on the outside, attaching to marks as really existent, or deluded on the inside, attaching to emptiness as absolute nothingness. If one can be free from marks within marks, and free from emptiness within emptiness, then one is deluded neither within nor without. If one awakens to this Dharma, the mind opens in a single thought; this is opening the Buddha-knowledge.

[Buddha means awakening. It is divided into four gates: opening the knowledge of awakening, showing the knowledge of awakening, realizing the knowledge of awakening, and entering the knowledge of awakening. If upon hearing this instruction one can realize and enter, then the knowledge of awakening, the original true nature, comes forth.]

Buddha means awakening. So “causing sentient beings to realize the Buddha-knowledge” is divided into four aspects: opening the knowledge of awakening, showing the knowledge of awakening, realizing the knowledge of awakening, and entering the knowledge of awakening. If, upon hearing the instruction, one can realize and enter the knowledge of awakening, then the original nature appears before one.
[Men (gate)] A division of things. For example: sorting into categories; the five courses of study.

[Take care not to misinterpret the meaning of the sutra. Seeing the Buddha speak of opening, showing, realizing, and entering the Buddha-knowledge, do not think that it is the knowledge of the World-Honored One and the other Buddhas, and that we ordinary beings have no share in it. If you understand it thus, you are slandering the sutra and reviling the Buddha! Since they are already Buddhas and already possess the Buddha-knowledge, what need is there to open, show, realize, and enter it again? You should now believe that the Buddha spoken of as possessing the Buddha-knowledge is only your own self-mind; there is no other Buddha.]

Take care, and do not misinterpret the meaning of the sutra. Seeing the World-Honored One speak of opening, showing, realizing, and entering the Buddha-knowledge, do not think that it is the knowledge of the World-Honored One and other Buddhas, and that we ordinary beings have no share in it. If you understand it thus, you are slandering the sutra and reviling the Buddha! Since they are Buddhas and already possess the “Buddha-knowledge,” what need is there for them to open, show, realize, and enter it again? You should now believe that the Buddha spoken of in the sutra as possessing the “Buddha-knowledge” is only your own Buddha of the self-nature; there is no other Buddha.

[This is because all sentient beings, covering their own light, crave the defiled environment; with external conditions and inner disturbance they willingly let themselves be driven, and so it was that ever the World-Honored One had to rise from samādhi and with every kind of earnest exhortation urge them to cease and rest, not to seek outside; for [the self-nature] is no different from the Buddha. Hence it is said: opening the Buddha-knowledge.]

Because all sentient beings of themselves cover the light of the self-nature, crave the defiled environment, grasp outer conditions and are disturbed by inner thoughts, and willingly allow themselves to be driven about by conditions and deluded thoughts. So the World-Honored One had to rise from samādhi and with every kind of earnest exhortation urge them to cease and rest, not to seek outside; your self-nature is then no different from the Buddha. Hence it is said, “open the Buddha-knowledge” (to open the knowledge of awakening that you already possess).

[I too urge all people to open the Buddha-knowledge constantly within their own minds. Worldly people, with evil minds, deluded and ignorant, commit offenses, speaking good with evil hearts, full of greed, anger, envy, flattery, and conceit, harming others and wronging creatures—these open the knowledge of sentient beings. If one can set the mind right, and constantly give rise to wisdom, contemplating the self-mind, ceasing evil and practicing good, then one opens the Buddha-knowledge.]

I too urge all people to open the Buddha-knowledge constantly within their own minds. Worldly people, with evil minds, deluded and ignorant, commit offenses, speaking good but with evil hearts, full of greed, anger, envy, flattery, and conceit, harming others and creatures—what they open of themselves is the knowledge of sentient beings. If one can set the mind right and constantly give rise to wisdom, contemplating the self-mind, ceasing evil and practicing good, then what one opens is the Buddha-knowledge.

[You must in thought after thought open the Buddha-knowledge, and not open the knowledge of sentient beings. To open the Buddha-knowledge is to transcend the world; to open the knowledge of sentient beings is to be in the world. If you merely toil in clinging thoughts, taking them as your practice, how is this different from the yak’s love of its own tail?]

You must in thought after thought open the Buddha-knowledge, and not open the knowledge of sentient beings. To open the Buddha-knowledge is to transcend the world; to open the knowledge of sentient beings is to remain in the world. If you are busy and toiling, attached to recitation, thinking this is your practice, how is this different from the yak’s doting on its own tail?

[The yak’s love of its tail] Using greed and love to cover oneself, so that one is blind to the suffering, danger, and the way of liberation one faces. The Lotus Sutra, “Expedient Means Chapter Two,” says: “Shariputra, you should know that with the Buddha-eye I see the sentient beings of the six destinies, poor and destitute of merit and wisdom, entering the perilous road of birth and death, their suffering unbroken in succession. Deeply attached to the five desires, like the yak’s love of its tail, covering themselves with greed and love, blind and without sight, they do not seek the great and powerful Buddha, nor the Dharma that ends suffering.” The yak is a kind of long-tailed ox. It is said the yak cherishes its own tail; if the tail-hair becomes caught in a tree branch, even if it sees a hunter coming to kill it, it would rather die than strain the tail-hair off and flee. This is a metaphor for the longing of sentient beings for the five desires, just like the yak’s fondness for its own tail.

blocks.text: 5. Recitation with the Mouth, Practice with the Mind

inline.s: Here the Sixth Patriarch instructs us in what truly constitutes reciting the sutra—to illumine the mind by means of the sutra’s meaning.

[Fahai said: If that is so, then as long as one understands the meaning, one need not recite the sutra? The Master said: What fault has the sutra that it should hinder your recitation? Delusion and awakening rest in the person; gain and loss rest with oneself. Reciting with the mouth while practicing with the mind, that is to turn the sutra; reciting with the mouth while the mind does not practice, that is to be turned by the sutra. Listen to my verse:]

Fahai said: According to that, so long as I understand the meaning, I need not recite the sutra anymore? The Master said: What fault has the sutra that it should tell you not to recite? Only that delusion or awakening rests in each person, and gain or loss rests with oneself. Reciting with the mouth while practicing with the mind, that is to turn the sutra; reciting with the mouth while the mind does not practice, that is to be turned by the sutra. Listen to my verse:
[When the mind is deluded, the Lotus turns you; when the mind is awakened, you turn the Lotus; reciting long without understanding, you become the enemy of its meaning.]

When the mind is deluded, you are turned by the Lotus; when the mind is awakened, you turn the Lotus. If you recite long without understanding its meaning, you become a foe of the meaning—how can you then benefit?
[Without a thought, reciting is right; with a thought, reciting becomes wrong; when you no longer dwell on having or not having, you forever ride the white ox-cart.]
Reciting without a (deluded) thought is right; reciting with a (deluded) thought is wrong; when you no longer cling to whether there is thought or no-thought, that is the single Buddha-vehicle.

[Wu nian (no-thought)] The Sixth Patriarch says: “No-thought means: within thought, no thought.” (Samādhi and Wisdom Chapter Four.) [Bai niu che (white ox-cart)] This is the great white ox-cart. The Lotus Sutra takes the goat-cart to symbolize the Vehicle of the Hearers, the deer-cart the Vehicle of the Solitary Buddhas, and the ox-cart the Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas; these three vehicles are all provisional (expedient teachings). The great white ox-cart symbolizes the Buddha-vehicle, the one true vehicle.

[Fahai, hearing the verse, could not help weeping; he awakened at once upon these words, and told the Master: Fahai from old has never actually turned the Lotus; rather, I have been turned by the Lotus.]

Fahai, hearing the verse, deeply understood its purport, could not help weeping, and at once awakened. He reported to the Master: Since Fahai began reciting, I have never actually turned the Lotus; rather, I have been turned by the Lotus.

[He asked again, saying: The sutra says that the great hearers and even the bodhisattvas all “exhaust their thought and together measure, yet cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.” Now to command ordinary beings merely to awaken to their own minds, and call this the Buddha-knowledge—if one is not of superior faculties, one cannot but doubt and slander this. Moreover, the sutra speaks of three carts—the goat, deer, and ox carts—how are they to be distinguished from the white ox-cart? I beg the Master to bestow instruction again.]

Fahai asked again: The Lotus Sutra says that the great hearers and solitary ones, even up to the bodhisattvas, all exhaust their thought and together measure, yet cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom. Now to command ordinary beings merely to awaken to their own minds and call this the Buddha-knowledge—if it is not a person of superior faculties, he cannot but doubt and slander this teaching. Besides, the sutra speaks of three carts (the goat, deer, and ox carts) and the great white ox-cart—how should these be distinguished? I beg the Master, in his compassion, to instruct me again.

[The Master said: The meaning of the sutra is perfectly clear; it is you who are deluded by going against it. The reason the three-vehicle people cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom is that the fault lies in measuring. Even if they exhaust thought and together infer, that only takes them farther away. The Buddha originally spoke for ordinary beings, not for Buddhas. If anyone will not believe this principle, let him withdraw.]

The Master said: The meaning of the sutra is perfectly clear; it is you who go against it and are deluded. The reason the great hearers and solitary ones, even up to the bodhisattvas, cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom is that the fault lies in deliberation and measuring, for deliberation and measuring use the deluded mind. Even if they exhaust thought and together infer, the more they deliberate and measure, the farther they are from the Buddha’s wisdom.
