The Buddha-knowledge was spoken by the Buddha for ordinary beings, not for Buddhas; ordinary beings are of course able to realize and attain it. As for those who will not believe this principle—they are all of shallow faculties and deep hindrances, self-conceited; let them withdraw.

[Cong ta tui xi (they withdrew)] The Lotus Sutra, “Expedient Means Chapter Two,” says: “Then the World-Honored One told Shariputra: ‘You have already made earnest request three times; how could I not speak? Now listen carefully and think on it well; I shall distinguish and explain it for you.’ When he said this, there were in the assembly bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, upasakas, and upasikas, five thousand in all, who arose from their seats, bowed to the Buddha and withdrew. Why was this? Because these had deep and heavy roots of offense and also great self-conceit; not having attained, they said they had attained; not having realized, they said they had realized. Holding such faults, they could not remain; the World-Honored One remained silent and did not stop them.” “Shariputra! These bhikkhus and bhikkhunis said of themselves that they had attained arhatship, that this was their final body and ultimate nirvāṇa, and so no longer sought Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; you should know that all these are people of great self-conceit.”

[Little did you know that sitting on the white ox-cart, you still seek the three carts outside the gate. Moreover, the sutra clearly tells you: “There is but the single Buddha-vehicle, no other vehicle—whether two or three, and even countless expedient means, with many causes and parables and expressions, all these dharmas are for the sake of the single Buddha-vehicle.” How is it you do not reflect?]

Little did you know that sitting already on the great white ox-cart, you still go outside the gate to seek the goat, deer, and ox carts (the three carts). Moreover, the sutra clearly tells you: there is only the single Buddha-vehicle, with no other two vehicles (the Vehicle of the Hearers and the Vehicle of the Solitary Buddhas) or three vehicles (these two plus the Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas). The Buddha spoke the two vehicles, the three vehicles, and all the other countless expedient means, with many causes, parables, and expressions—all these dharmas are to lead to the single Buddha-vehicle. Why do you still not reflect?

[The three carts are false, because of the time of old; the one vehicle is real, because of the present time. It only teaches you to leave the false and return to the real; and after returning to the real, even the name ‘real’ has no name. You should know that all the precious wealth belongs to you, to be used by you; make no further thought of a father, no thought of a son, and no thought of using—this is called upholding the Lotus Sutra, from kalpa to kalpa the hand never leaves the scroll, from day to night there is not a moment when one is not in recitation.]

The three carts are the provisional teaching, spoken for the time when sentient beings of old were not yet ripe to receive the real teaching. The one vehicle is the real teaching, spoken for the present time when sentient beings are already ripe to receive it. The Lotus Sutra merely teaches you to leave the provisional and return to the real; after returning to the real teaching, even the name of the real teaching no longer exists. You should know that all the treasures in the self-nature belong to you, to be used as you please; make no further thought that the Tathagata is a rich father, no thought that you are a poor son, and no thought of using the treasure; only this is called upholding the Lotus Sutra. In this way, from kalpa to kalpa the hand never leaves the scroll, and from day to night there is not a moment when one is not reciting the Lotus Sutra.

[Quan jiao (provisional teaching) and shi jiao (real teaching)] The provisional is the provisional speech, used for a time and then set aside; the real is the real meaning, the final destination. [Quan] Temporary; expedient adaptation.
Here the Master quotes the parable of the poor son from the Lotus Sutra
chapter four on Faith and Understanding:

There was a poor son who ran away from home in childhood and lived in poverty in another country. By the age of fifty he was more destitute than ever, and ran about in all directions seeking food and clothing. Gradually he came to a city where his father was the wealthiest elder of the city. At that time the poor son reached the side of the gate, and saw his father seated upon a lion’s throne, surrounded respectfully by brahmins and kshatriyas and laymen, adorned with a necklace of real pearls. The poor son did not recognize him, and seeing that he was possessed of great power, was filled with fear, and swiftly ran away.

Then the wealthy elder recognized his son at once and sent men to chase him. The poor son thought to himself: I have committed no offense—why am I being seized? In panic he fainted and fell to the ground. Seeing this from afar, the father knew his son’s will was lowly, and so let him go his way, wherever he would. Released, the poor son again went to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing.

Then, to entice his son, the elder set up an expedient means. First he secretly sent two men to put on a haggard appearance and, through the work of sweeping out the filth, draw near the poor son. He himself also wore soiled and worn clothes, took up the dung-carrying implement, toiled together with the poor son, and by this expedient came near to his son. He then increased his wages and encouraged him to stay. As the days passed, the poor son gradually lost his fear of the elder. The elder then praised his diligence and effort, and his freedom from deceit, idleness, and hatred, and acknowledged him as his adopted son. Though the poor son rejoiced in this meeting, he still thought himself a lowly man, and for twenty years continued to make the work of sweeping out the filth his duty.

The elder fell ill and knew he would die, so he entrusted the storehouses and all their gold, silver, and precious treasures to the poor son. The poor son received them, but had no mind to seek or take the treasures of the storehouses, and could not put away his lowly heart. After a little while longer, the elder knew his mind was gradually opening and that he could accomplish a great purpose; and so at the moment of death he proclaimed that the poor son was in truth his own son, and told how more than fifty years before he had left his father and run away from home. Only then did the poor son awaken, and he was filled with great joy, saying that though he had had no mind to seek it, now this treasure had come to him of itself.
[Fahai, having been awakened by the Master, leapt for joy and praised him in a verse:]
Fahai, enlightened by the Master, was at once freed from his dullness and could not keep from leaping for joy. He praised him in a verse:

[I recited the sutra three thousand times, and one word from Caoxi made them all vanish; not having understood the purpose of appearing in the world, how could I still the madness of my countless lives?]

I recited the Lotus Sutra three thousand times and still remained confused and unenlightened, but a single speech from the Master drove away the darkness of my beginningless kalpas. Without understanding the purpose of the Buddhas’ appearing in the world, how could I still the wild mind of my countless lives?
[Caoxi] A reference to the Sixth Patriarch, a title of respect that uses the place name for the person.

[The goat, deer, and ox were expediently set; the initial, middle, and final good were proclaimed in turn; who would have known that within the burning house were from the beginning the kings of the Dharma!]

The two vehicles and the three vehicles are expedient provisional sayings, and the initial, middle, and final good are the correct Dharma proclaimed in turn. Who would have thought that the sentient beings within the affliction of the burning house were from the very beginning the Buddha (the king of the Dharma)!

[Chu shan, zhong shan, hou shan (initial, middle, and final good)] The initial good is when the Buddha spoke the Dharma of the Four Truths for those seeking the Vehicle of the Hearers; the middle good is when the Buddha spoke the Dharma of the Twelve Conditions for those seeking the Vehicle of the Solitary Buddhas; the final good is when the Buddha spoke the Dharma of the Six Perfections for the bodhisattvas. The Supplemented Wondrous Dharma Lotus Sutra, “Preface Chapter One”: “Preaching the correct Dharma, it is initially good, middlingly good, and finally good; its meaning is deep and far, its words are skillful, pure and single, without mixture, complete with the marks of pure conduct. For those seeking the Vehicle of the Hearers, speaking the Dharma corresponding to the Four Truths, to carry them beyond birth and death to ultimate nirvāṇa. For those seeking the Vehicle of the Solitary Buddhas, speaking the Dharma corresponding to the Twelve Conditions. For the bodhisattvas, speaking the Dharma corresponding to the Six Perfections, to enable them to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and perfect the wisdom of all species.” [Huo zhai (burning house)] Within the three realms there is turmoil and no peace, like a burning house, and so the three realms are likened to a burning house. See the parable of the burning house in the Lotus Sutra, chapter two, “Chapter on the Parable, the third”: There was a great elder of boundless wealth. One day his house caught fire, and the elder’s children, within the burning house, were amused at their games, unaware of it. To save his children from the burning house, the elder set up an expedient means, telling them that outside the house were a goat-cart, a deer-cart, and an ox-cart, which he would give them. After the children had rushed out of the burning house, the elder gave each of them a great white ox-cart.
[The Master said: From now on you may be called a monk who recites the sutra. Fahai from then on grasped the profound purport and did not stop reciting the sutra.]
The Master said: From now on you may be called a monk who recites the sutra. Fahai from then on understood this mysterious purport, and did not cease reciting the Lotus Sutra.

blocks.text: 7. The Three Bodies and the Four Wisdoms

inline.s: [The monk Zhitong, a native of Anfeng in Shouzhou, had first studied the Lankavatara Sutra about a thousand times, but could not understand the three bodies and the four wisdoms, and bowed to the Master to seek an explanation of their meaning.]

The monk Zhitong, a native of Anfeng in Shouzhou, first studied the Lankavatara Sutra more than a thousand times, but could not understand the three bodies and the four wisdoms, so he bowed to the Master and asked him to explain their profound meaning.

[The Master said: As for the three bodies, the pure Dharmakaya is your own nature; the perfect Reward Body is your own wisdom; the hundreds-of-thousands-of-millions of Transformation Bodies are your own conduct. If apart from the self-nature you speak separately of the three bodies, that is called having bodies without wisdom. If you realize that the three bodies have no self-nature, that is called the four wisdoms and bodhi. Listen to my verse:]

The Master said: As for the three bodies, the pure Dharmakaya is your own nature; the perfect Reward Body is your own wisdom; the hundreds-of-thousands-of-millions of Transformation Bodies are your own mind-and-conduct. If apart from the self-nature you speak separately of the three bodies, that is called having bodies without wisdom. If you realize that the three bodies have no self-nature, that is called the four wisdoms and bodhi. Listen to my verse:

[San shen (three bodies)] The Dharmakaya, the Reward Body, and the Response Body. The Dharmakaya is also called the self-nature body or the dharmanature body, which every person originally possesses; only, we sentient beings are deluded and do not manifest it, while the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. The Reward Body is accomplished by the Buddha’s wisdom and merit; it is of two kinds, the self-enjoyment Reward Body and the other-enjoyment Reward Body. The self-enjoyment Reward Body is the Buddha’s own body that enjoys the Dharma joy of inner realization; the other-enjoyment Reward Body is the body the Buddha manifests when speaking the Dharma for the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The Response Body is also called the transformation body, the Buddha-body manifested in response to the conditions and opportunities of sentient beings. To use the moon as a simile: the Dharmakaya is like the moon’s substance, the Reward Body is like the moon’s light, and the Response Body is like the moon’s reflection in water—where there is water it appears, where there is no water it does not appear. This takes water to symbolize the resonance [of sentient beings], and the moon’s reflection for the response; when there is resonance there is communication, when there is no resonance there is no communication. This is what is meant by “a thousand rivers each with a thousand moons.” These three are originally one body; it is only from their function that names are set up. [Wu you zi xing (without self-nature)] Without a self-existing substance; referring to what is illusory. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom

chapter nineteen says: “All dharmas arise from conditions, and so have no self-nature; this is the real emptiness.” [The three bodies have no self-nature] This means that the three bodies (Dharmakaya, Reward Body, Response Body) are illusions. Because the self-nature is illusory, the three bodies that arise from it are of course also illusory. On the question of “the self-nature being illusory,” it has been discussed in detail in the earlier chapter on prajñā (Chapter Two) when explaining “the self-nature’s true emptiness.” For example, as to the Dharmakaya being illusory, the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground of the Great Vehicle says: “Constantly contemplate the wondrous Dharmakaya of the Buddhas; whose substance and nature, like emptiness, cannot be attained.” The Lankavatara Sutra of the Great Vehicle says: “The Dharmakaya is like an illusion or a dream; how can it be praised? Knowing that it is without nature and unborn, one then praises the Buddha.”
[The self-nature possesses the three bodies; being awakened, they become the four wisdoms; without leaving the conditions of seeing and hearing, one transcends and ascends the ground of Buddhahood.]

The self-nature possesses the three bodies; when one awakens, the eight consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, manas-consciousness, and alaya-consciousness) are transformed into the four wisdoms (the wisdom of perfect accomplishment, the wisdom of wondrous observation, the wisdom of equality, and the great mirror wisdom); without leaving the defiled conditions of seeing and hearing, one can transcend and directly ascend to the ground of Buddhahood.

[Si zhi (four wisdoms)] The wisdom of perfect accomplishment, the wisdom of wondrous observation, the wisdom of equality, and the great mirror wisdom. “The wisdom of perfect accomplishment” is accomplished by transforming the first five defiled consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body), and is the wisdom of the Buddha’s successful accomplishment of all that universally benefits sentient beings. “The wisdom of wondrous observation” is accomplished by transforming the sixth defiled consciousness (the mind-consciousness), and is the wisdom of the Buddha in observing the dharmas and the faculties of all sentient beings, giving medicine according to the illness and turning the common into the sage. “The wisdom of equality” is accomplished by transforming the seventh defiled consciousness (the manas), and is the wisdom of the Buddha in penetrating the principle of no-self and equality, and in arousing unconditioned great compassion toward all sentient beings. “The great mirror wisdom” is accomplished by transforming the eighth defiled consciousness (the alaya), and is the wisdom of the Buddha in contemplating all phenomena and principles with nothing ununderstood; this wisdom is pure and perfectly bright, penetrating within and without, like a great mirror that illuminates all things.
[Today I speak this for you; believe it deeply and never be deluded; do not imitate those who rush about seeking, speaking all day of bodhi.]
Today I speak this wondrous principle for you; you must truly believe and never be deluded. Do not imitate those who rush about seeking outside the mind, who only speak of bodhi all day long.

[Zhitong asked again, saying: May I hear the meaning of the four wisdoms? The Master said: Since you already understand the three bodies, you will naturally understand the four wisdoms—why ask further? If apart from the three bodies you speak separately of the four wisdoms, that is called having wisdom without bodies; and this very ‘having wisdom’ becomes no-wisdom. Again he spoke a verse:]

Zhitong asked again: Would the Master be so kind as to explain the profound meaning of the four wisdoms? The Master said: Since you already understand the three bodies, you naturally understand the four wisdoms—why ask further? If apart from the three bodies you speak separately of the four wisdoms, that is called having wisdom without bodies; and this very ‘having wisdom’ turns into no-wisdom. The Master again spoke a verse:

[The nature of the great mirror wisdom is pure; the mind of the wisdom of equality is without affliction; the wisdom of wondrous observation sees without effort; the wisdom of perfect accomplishment is like the great mirror.]

The great mirror wisdom has a pure nature; the wisdom of equality has a mind without affliction; the wisdom of wondrous observation sees and hears without exertion; the wisdom of perfect accomplishment is like a great mirror.

[The great mirror wisdom has a pure nature] The great mirror wisdom is what the eighth consciousness (alaya) is transformed into. The alaya consciousness stores measureless karmic seeds and produces a defiling effect upon feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness. Now that consciousness is transformed into wisdom and no longer defiles, so it is said to be “of a pure nature.” [The mind of the wisdom of equality is without affliction] The wisdom of equality is what the seventh consciousness (manas) is transformed into. The chief function of the manas is discriminatory deliberation, which is the great illness that leads to birth and death; now that consciousness is transformed into wisdom and no longer discriminates and deliberates, so it is said to be “without affliction.” [The wisdom of wondrous observation sees without effort] The wisdom of wondrous observation is what the sixth consciousness (mind-consciousness) is transformed into. The chief function of the mind-consciousness is that when the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body) come into contact with their corresponding objects (form, sound, smell, taste, and touch), it gives rise to discriminating activity; now that consciousness is transformed into wisdom, it only observes and no longer discriminates, so it is said to be “seeing without effort” (when it sees, there is also no activity of discrimination). [The wisdom of perfect accomplishment is like the great mirror] The wisdom of perfect accomplishment is what the first five consciousnesses are transformed into. After the transformation it only reflects the objects before it without discriminating, so it is said to be “like the great mirror.”

[The sixth and seventh transform on the causal ground; the fifth and eighth transform on the fruition. Only the names are used, without real nature; if at the place of transformation one does not linger, amid the bustling world one abides ever in the naga samādhi.]

The sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform on the causal ground, while the first five and the eighth are naturally accomplished on the fruition ground (at the time of Buddhahood). This transformation (of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms) merely changes their names and states, while the substance is not two (without real nature). If at the place where the sixth and seventh transform consciousness into wisdom one does not linger, but transforms decisively and resolutely (this is where the effort is made in daily life), then even amid the rolling red dust one is like a dragon lurking in the deep abyss, still and motionless, always abiding in the dragon samādhi.

The sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform on the causal ground. And this transformation does not lie in meditation practice, but only in transforming at the place where thought arises in daily life. Both the ordinary person and the sage (the bodhisattva above the first ground) transform at the place where thought arises; whether they ultimately transform wisdom into consciousness or transform consciousness into wisdom depends only on whether they linger or do not linger, and hence there is the difference between ordinary and sage, between delusion and awakening. So one should earnestly attend to the point of transformation in daily use, observing carefully whether one is turning rightly (transforming consciousness into wisdom) or turning in reverse (transforming wisdom into consciousness).

[Guo di (fruition ground)] As opposed to the “causal ground”; that is, the position attained by the cultivation of the causal ground. Here the fruition refers to Buddhahood. [If at the place of transformation one does not linger] Like a poisonous snake biting one’s finger, cut it off at once, without the slightest hesitation. [Fan xing (bustling plenty)] Arising in great abundance; here it refers to the confusion of the countless appearances. [Naga samādhi] “Naga” is translated as dragon. “Naga samādhi” is the “dragon samādhi,” like a dragon lurking in the deep abyss. [Amid the bustling world one abides ever in the naga samādhi] Though one is set within the rolling red dust of the myriad appearances (fan xing), one nevertheless always abides in the dragon samādhi.

[The above is the transformation of consciousness into wisdom. The doctrinal schools say: “Transform the first five consciousnesses into the wisdom of perfect accomplishment; transform the sixth consciousness into the wisdom of wondrous observation; transform the seventh consciousness into the wisdom of equality; transform the eighth consciousness into the great mirror wisdom.” Though the sixth and seventh transform on the causal ground and the fifth and eighth transform on the fruition, only the name is changed, and not the substance.]

What has been said above is the transformation of consciousness into wisdom. The doctrinal schools say: “Transform the first five consciousnesses into the wisdom of perfect accomplishment; transform the sixth consciousness into the wisdom of wondrous observation; transform the seventh consciousness into the wisdom of equality; transform the eighth consciousness into the great mirror wisdom.” Though the sixth and seventh transform on the causal ground, and the fifth and eighth on the fruition ground, only their names and states are changed, and not their substance.

[Jiao zhong (among the doctrinal schools)] The Chan school calls itself the ‘school below’ (zong xia), and refers to all the schools that study sutras and teachings collectively as the ‘school of teaching’ (jiao xia). [Dan zhuan qi ming, er bu zhuan qi ti ye (only the name is changed, but not the substance)] This means that the eight consciousnesses and the four wisdoms are two states of one substance (the self-nature), just as ice and water appear altogether different, so there is the name ‘ice’ and the name ‘water’; but they are in fact only
H2O
in two states—one substance, two states. When ice melts into water the name changes, but the substance is still
H2O
, and so it is “only the name is changed, but not the substance.”

[Zhitong, awakening suddenly to the nature and the wisdom, presented a verse: The three bodies are from the beginning my substance; the four wisdoms are of the original mind’s illumination; body and wisdom merge without obstruction, responding to things and freely taking their forms. To begin to cultivate is all vain stirring; to guard and hold is not the true essence. The wondrous purport, because of the Master’s instruction, is at last known; finally the name of defilement is done away with.]

Zhitong, hearing the instruction, at once awakened to the three bodies and four wisdoms of the self-nature, and presented this verse: The three bodies are from the beginning the manifestation of my self-nature, and the four wisdoms are accomplished by the illumination of the original mind; the three bodies and four wisdoms merge without obstruction, responding to things and freely manifesting their forms. To set the mind to cultivation is all vain stirring; to guard the mind and hold it still is not the final truth. The wondrous purport of the three bodies and four wisdoms, because of the Master’s instruction, I now understand, and no longer work upon the defiled provisional names.

blocks.text: 8. The Original Mind and Original Nature

inline.s: [The monk Zhichang, a native of Guixi in Xinzhou, left home in childhood with the resolve to see his nature. One day he came to pay respects, and the Master asked him: Where have you come from, and what do you seek? He said: Your student recently went to Baitou Mountain in Hongzhou to pay respects to the Great Master Datong, and was shown the meaning of seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha, but I have not resolved my doubt, and so I have come from afar to bow to you, hoping the Master will compassionately instruct me. The Master said: What words did he say? Try to relate them.]

The monk Zhichang, a native of Guixi in Xinzhou, left home in his youth with the resolve to see his nature. One day he came to bow to the Sixth Patriarch. The Master asked: Where have you come from, and what do you seek? Zhichang replied: Your student recently went to Baitou Mountain in Hongzhou to pay respects to the Great Master Datong, and was shown the meaning of seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha. In my mind there is still some doubt, and I do not know whether it is so, and so I have come from afar to bow to you, hoping the Master will compassionately instruct me. The Master said: What words did he speak? Relate them to me.

[He said: Zhichang was there for three months in all, without receiving any instruction. Because of my earnestness for the Dharma, one evening I entered the abbot’s quarters alone to ask: What is this person’s original mind and original nature? Datong then said: Do you see the emptiness of space? I replied: I see it. He said: Do you see that space has any appearance? I replied: Space is formless—what appearance could it have?]

Zhichang said: Zhichang was there at the Great Master Datong’s place for more than three months without receiving any instruction. Your disciple’s mind was eager for the Dharma, and so one evening I went alone to the abbot’s quarters to ask: What are my original mind and original nature? The Great Master Datong then said: Do you see the emptiness of space? Your disciple replied: I see it. He said: Do you see that space has any appearance? Your disciple replied: Space is formless—how could it have an appearance!

[He said: Your nature is like space, with not a single thing visible—this is called right view; with not a single thing knowable—this is called true knowledge. With no blue, yellow, long or short, seeing only the original source pure and the awakened body perfectly bright, this is called seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha, and is also called the Tathagata’s knowledge and view.]

He said: Your nature is like space, with not a single thing visible—this is right view; with not a single thing knowable—this is true knowledge. The nature has no color and no form; seeing only the original source pure and the awakened body perfectly bright, this is seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha, and is also called the Tathagata’s knowledge and view.

[Though your student heard this explanation, he was still not resolved, and begs the Master to instruct him. The Master said: What that master spoke still retains views and knowledge, and so it left you unresolved. I will now show you a verse:]

Though your student heard his explanation, his mind still had unresolved doubt, and he begs the Master to instruct him. The Master said: What that master said still retains views and knowledge, and so you are still confused and unresolved. I will now give you a verse:

Because he still retains views and knowledge, it is not the final teaching. The Surangama Sutra, chapter five, says: “Within knowledge and view to establish knowledge—this is the root of ignorance; when knowledge and view are without view, this is nirvāṇa, the pure and undefiled true purity.”

[Not seeing a single thing yet holding a view of no-seeing—this is much like the drifting clouds that cover the sun; not knowing a single thing yet guarding an empty knowledge—this is still like lightning flashing in the great void. This knowledge and view rise in a flash, and being mistaken, how could it ever be the expedient understanding? You should, in a single thought, know that the self is wrong, and your own spiritual light will constantly appear.]

Not seeing a single thing yet holding a view of no-seeing is like the drifting clouds covering the sun so that the spiritual light does not appear; not knowing a single thing yet guarding an empty knowledge is still like lightning flashing in the great void (still not quiet). This knowledge (empty knowledge) and view (view of no-seeing) rise in a flash, and you still mistake them for true knowledge and right view—how, then, can you see your nature? When knowledge and view arise together, you should at once know this is wrong; when you let all knowledge and view subside, then your own spiritual light constantly appears.

Separate from mind-consciousness, the spiritual light bursts forth and one sees one’s own nature. The Surangama Sutra says: “Within knowledge and view to establish knowledge—this is the root of ignorance; when knowledge and view are without view, this is nirvāṇa.”

[Cuo ren he ceng jie fang bian (how could this mistake ever be the expedient understanding?)] This is indeed a mistake—how could it be an expedient understanding? “Jie fang bian” is an inverted construction, meaning the expedient understanding.

[Zhichang, hearing this verse, was at once opened, and composed a verse: For no reason knowledge and view arise, and one attaches to marks to seek bodhi. If one still holds the single thought of awakening, how can one surpass the delusion of old? The self-nature, the source of awakening, vainly flows along with the reflections; if one does not enter the Patriarch’s chamber, one is bewildered, running toward the two extremes.]

Zhichang, hearing this verse, was at once opened and clear, and so also composed a verse: For no reason knowledge (empty knowledge) and view (view of no-seeing) arise—this is to attach to marks and seek bodhi! If one still holds a single thought of ‘awakening,’ how can one emerge from the delusion of the past? The self-nature—this source of awakening—vainly flows along ceaselessly with knowledge and view, thought after thought. If one does not come to the gate of the Sixth Patriarch, one remains bewildered, now clinging to the existence of knowledge and view, now clinging to the non-existence of knowledge and view.
[One day Zhichang asked the Master: The Buddha spoke of the three vehicles, and also spoke of the supreme vehicle. Your disciple does not understand; I beg you to teach me.]

One day Zhichang asked the Master: The World-Honored One spoke of the three vehicles, and also spoke of a supreme vehicle. Your disciple has not understood its meaning, and begs the Master to explain it for me.

[San cheng (three vehicles)] The lesser vehicle, the middle vehicle, and the great vehicle. The lesser vehicle is the Vehicle of the Hearers, the middle vehicle is the Vehicle of the Solitary Buddhas, and the great vehicle is the Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas. [Zui shang cheng (supreme vehicle)] The unsurpassed teaching, that is, the perfect and sudden teaching, which is the single Buddha-vehicle.

[The Master said: Observe your own original mind; do not attach to the marks of dharmas outside the mind. The Dharma has no four vehicles; it is the minds of people that have their differences. Merely seeing, hearing, reciting and turning is the lesser vehicle; to awaken to the Dharma and understand its meaning is the middle vehicle; to cultivate in accordance with the Dharma is the great vehicle.]

The Master said: Observe your own original mind; do not attach to the marks of dharmas outside the mind. The Dharma originally has no four vehicles (lesser, middle, great, and supreme); it is only that the minds of people differ in delusion and awakening. Seeing, hearing, reciting, and turning the text is the lesser vehicle; awakening to the Dharma and understanding its meaning is the middle vehicle; cultivating in accordance with the Dharma is the great vehicle.

[Penetrating all dharmas and possessing all dharmas, defiled by nothing, free from all marks, attaining nothing—this is called the supreme vehicle. Vehicle means to practice; it does not lie in verbal disputes. You must cultivate yourself; do not ask me. At all times, the self-nature is free and at ease. Zhichang bowed in thanks and served him to the end of his life.]

Knowing that the self-nature penetrates all dharmas and possesses all dharmas, and so is defiled by nothing, free from all marks, and attains nothing—this is the supreme vehicle. “Vehicle” means to practice; it does not lie in verbal contention. The true meaning within it you must cultivate and realize for yourself; you need not ask me. In all times, do not seize upon marks, and remain unmoving. Zhichang bowed in gratitude, and from then on attended on the Master until the Master passed away.

[The monk Zhidao, a native of Nanhai in Guangzhou, asked for instruction: Your student, since leaving home, has read the Nirvāṇa Sutra for more than ten years but has not understood its main purport. I beg the Master to instruct me. The Master said: Where do you not understand? He said: “All compounded things are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.” I am in doubt about this.]

The monk Zhidao, a native of Nanhai in Guangzhou, asked the Master for instruction: Your student, since leaving home, has read the Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra for more than ten years without understanding its essential purport. I beg the Master to compassionately instruct me. The Master said: Where do you not understand? Zhidao said: The sutra says “All compounded things are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.” Your student is in doubt about this passage.

[Zhu xing (all compounded things)] “Xing” means flowing onward. “All compounded things” means that all things are within change (flowing on). [Zhu xing wu chang, shi sheng mie fa (all compounded things are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing)] All things change and are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. [Sheng mie mie yi (arising and ceasing have ceased)] The arising and ceasing of the thoughts of mind (including subtle thoughts) entirely cease. [Ji mie wei le (extinction is bliss)] Having broken the dream of ignorance, a peace and joy arising from within spontaneously well up; there is no longer the anxiety, fear, and affliction of worldly people (including emperors, the wealthy, and all who succeed and are happy).

“All compounded things are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.” This is the very famous “verse of impermanence,” also called the “Snow Mountain verse,” and is the great outline of the Buddha-Dharma. The first half, “all compounded things are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing,” is the cause of all suffering; the latter half, “when arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss,” is the path that ends suffering. The first half speaks of the dharmas of birth and death, the latter half speaks of the dharmas of nirvāṇa.
In the Great Parinirvāṇa Sutra, the World-Honored One describes an experience of his own in a past life in which he gave up his body in search of the Way:

At that time I was a brahmin, dwelling on the Snow Mountain and practicing the difficult ascetic penances. Then Sakra, lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven, and the gods saw such ascetic practice and were greatly astonished. Sakra then said: “The thought of bodhi is hard to arouse and easy to destroy.” So he changed himself into a rakshasa, of frightful appearance, and came to test me. He descended to the Snow Mountain, not far from me, and recited the first two lines of a verse spoken by the Buddhas of the past: “All compounded things are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing.” Hearing this half-verse, I was filled with joy, like one drowning in the sea who suddenly finds a boat. I went before him and asked for the latter half-verse. The rakshasa said he was tormented by hunger and thirst, and must eat the flesh and blood of a living person before he could go on. I said: I am willing to give up my body in offering to obtain it. The rakshasa said: “If you can thus give up your body, listen! Listen! I shall tell you the rest of the half-verse.” He then said: “When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.” Deeply pondering this meaning, I climbed a tall tree and threw myself down, giving up my body. Before I reached the ground, the rakshasa resumed the body of Sakra and caught me in mid-air, setting me down on the level ground. (For details, see
Annotations to the Snow Mountain Verse

[Luo cha (rakshasa)] A general term for evil ghosts; the male is called “rakshasa,” the female “rakshasika,” who either fly through the air or walk upon the earth, and delight in eating the flesh and blood of men. [Di shi (Sakra)] The lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven, Shakra-devamindra.

The meaning of this verse is: all things change and are impermanent, being illusions of arising and ceasing; when the arising and ceasing of the thoughts of mind (including subtle thoughts) entirely cease, and the great dream wakes, one realizes the state of extinction that is bliss of permanence, joy, self, and purity (nirvāṇa). Of these, “when arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss” refers to the state attained by the cultivator while still alive in the world. “Arising and ceasing have ceased” does not mean, as Zhidao says below, the destruction of the “form body,” and the “extinction” of “extinction is bliss” is also not what he calls “same as grass, trees, tiles, and stones,” but is the state without affliction and without birth and death. The Lankavatara Sutra says: “What I speak of is that the consciousness of false thought is extinguished; this is called nirvāṇa.”

[Ji mie (extinction)] When there is no affliction, this is called “quiet” (ji); when there is no birth and death, this is called “extinction” (mie). The state without affliction and without birth and death is nirvāṇa.

“dharmas of arising and ceasing” is the dream of ignorance: sentient beings, deluded and inverted, within the wholly unborn falsely see arising and ceasing. “When arising and ceasing have ceased” is to awaken from the dream of ignorance: the Buddhas, fully awakened, within the manifest arising and ceasing see only the unborn. “Extinction is bliss” is the ease and constant joy of the true self after waking from the dream. The final goal of practice is to awaken from the dream of ignorance.”

[The Master said: What are you doubting? He said: All sentient beings have two bodies, the form body and the Dharma body. The form body is impermanent, with arising and ceasing; the Dharma body is permanent, without knowledge and without awareness. The sutra says, “when arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss”; I do not know which body is extinguished and which body enjoys bliss. If it is the form body, then when the form body is extinguished the four elements are scattered, and it is entirely suffering—suffering cannot be called bliss. If the Dharma body is extinguished, then it is like grass, trees, tiles, and stones—who then would enjoy bliss?]

The Master said: Why are you in doubt? Zhidao said: All sentient beings have two bodies, namely the form body and the Dharma body. The form body is impermanent, with arising and ceasing; the Dharma body is permanent, without knowledge and without awareness. The sutra says “when arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.” I do not know which body is extinguished and which body enjoys bliss. If what is extinguished is the form body, then when the form body is extinguished the four elements are scattered, and it is all suffering—suffering cannot be called bliss. If what is extinguished is the Dharma body, then the Dharma body, without knowledge and awareness, is like grass, trees, tiles, and stones—how could it enjoy bliss?

[Again, the Dharma-nature is the substance of arising and ceasing, and the five aggregates are the function of arising and ceasing; one substance with five functions, and arising and ceasing are constant. In arising, the substance rises to function; in ceasing, the function is gathered back into the substance. If you allow them to arise again, then sentient beings, in endless birth and death, are unbroken and unceasing. If you do not allow them to arise again, then they return forever to extinction, the same as insentient things; and in that case all dharmas would be suppressed by nirvāṇa, unable even to arise—what bliss would there be?]

Moreover, the Dharma-nature is the substance of arising and ceasing, and the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness) are the function of arising and ceasing; one substance with five functions (form, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness), and arising and ceasing are constant—in arising, the substance rises to function; in ceasing, the function is gathered back into the substance. If you let them arise again, then sentient beings, in endless birth and death, are unbroken and unceasing—how can one speak of extinction? If you do not let them arise again, then they return forever to extinction, the same as insentient things; and in that case all dharmas would be suppressed by nirvāṇa, unable even to arise—what bliss would there be?

[The Master said: You are a son of the Buddha—why do you cultivate the heretical views of annihilationism and eternalism, and yet speak of the supreme vehicle? According to what you say, apart from the form body there is another Dharma body that, separate from arising and ceasing, seeks extinction; and again you infer that the nirvāṇa of constant bliss requires a body to enjoy it. This is clinging to birth and death and delighting in worldly pleasures.]

The Master said: You are a son of the Buddha—why do you cultivate the heretical views of annihilationism and eternalism, and thereby discuss the supreme Buddha-vehicle? According to what you say, apart from the form body there is another Dharma body that, separate from arising and ceasing, seeks extinction; and you infer that the nirvāṇa of constant bliss must have a body to enjoy it. This is deludedly clinging to birth and death as really existing, loving life and hating death, and wallowing in the pleasures of the world.

[Duan chang xie jian (heretical views of annihilationism and eternalism)] These are the “two views of annihilation and eternity”: annihilationism and eternalism. To hold that after death everything is annihilated and no longer exists is annihilationism. To hold that after death there is a next life, and that one is reborn as a human being life after life, is eternalism. Annihilationism denies existence on the basis of what exists, and eternalism affirms existence on the basis of what exists. The truth is that from the beginning there was not a single thing, and birth and death are both illusions; hence annihilationism and eternalism are both heretical views.

[You should now know that the Buddha, for all those deluded people who take the conglomeration of the five aggregates to be a self-substance, discriminating all dharmas as marks of external dust, loving life and hating death, flowing on thought after thought, not knowing that dreams and illusions are false, vainly undergoing samsara, and who turn the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa into a mark of suffering, running about seeking all day long.]

You should know that the Buddha appeared in the world precisely because all deluded people mistakenly take the conglomeration of the five aggregates to be themselves, and discriminate all dharmas as external objects, loving life and hating death, flowing on thought after thought, not knowing that life is like a dream or an illusion, false and unreal, and so vainly undergo samsara. They even take the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa to be suffering, and run about all day seeking outside the mind after material pleasures.

[Because the Buddha pitied this, he revealed the true bliss of nirvāṇa. In an instant there is no mark of arising, in an instant there is no mark of ceasing, and there is no further arising-and-ceasing that can be ceased—thus extinction appears before one. When it appears, there is no measure of appearance, and this is called constant bliss. This bliss has no one who experiences it and no one who does not experience it. How could there be the name of one substance with five functions? Still less can you say that nirvāṇa suppresses all dharmas so that they never arise—this is slandering the Buddha and reviling the Dharma. Listen to my verse:]

The World-Honored One, pitying the ignorance of sentient beings, revealed the true bliss of nirvāṇa. When one realizes that in an instant there is no mark of arising, and in an instant there is no mark of ceasing, and there is no further arising-and-ceasing that can be ceased, then extinction appears before one. When extinction appears, one is not even aware of extinction appearing—this is constant bliss (no longer dreaming the dreams of ordinary birth-and-death and of transformation birth-and-death). This bliss has no one who experiences it and no one who does not experience it—how could there be the saying of one substance with five functions? Still less can you say that nirvāṇa suppresses all dharmas so that they never arise—that is truly slandering the Buddha and reviling the Dharma. Listen to my verse:
[The supreme great nirvāṇa is brightly complete, constantly still and constantly illumining; common fools call it death, and heretics grasp it as annihilation.]

The supreme great nirvāṇa is brightly complete, constantly still and constantly illumining; common and ignorant people call this death, and heretics deludedly grasp it as annihilation (that nothing at all remains).
[Those who seek the two vehicles take it to be non-action; all of this belongs to what is reckoning in emotion, and is the root of the sixty-two views.]

Those seeking nirvāṇa in the two vehicles take nirvāṇa to be non-action. “Death,” “annihilation,” and “non-action” all belong to the false reckoning of emotional clinging, and are the very root of the sixty-two views.

[Liu shi er jian (sixty-two views)] These are the sixty-two heretical views that arise when heretics take the five aggregates of form, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness as their object.
[Falsely setting up unreal names, what real meaning is there? Only the person beyond measure can penetrate to non-grasping and non-rejecting.]
These are all fictitiously established false names—have they ever really existed? Only one who surpasses worldly views can penetrate the true meaning of nirvāṇa without grasping or rejecting.
[Falsely setting up unreal names, what real meaning is there?] Only a name without reality, like the “horn of a rabbit,” which is not really existent but is only a provisional name.
[With this one knows the five aggregates and the self within the aggregates, and the various forms manifested outside and the marks of every sound.]
Hence one knows the five aggregates, and the self within the aggregates, and the manifold forms manifested outside, and the marks of every sound.
[All are equal as a dream or illusion; one does not raise the view of common or sage, and does not form an interpretation of nirvāṇa; the two extremes and the three times are cut off.]

In fact these are all matters of a dream, illusions, with no difference at all. And so one does not raise the view of common or sage, does not form an interpretation of nirvāṇa, and the two extremes (existence and non-existence) and the three times (past, present, and future) all vanish.

[Ping deng ru meng huan (all are equal as a dream or illusion)] This explains the principle of the Heart Sutra that “all dharmas are empty marks, not arising, not ceasing, not defiled, not pure, not increasing, not decreasing”: all dharmas are illusory, and how could illusions have real arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease? When one realizes this principle, one can regard everything with equanimity, without love or hate, gain or loss, and be no longer burdened.
[Constantly respond to the functions of the faculties without raising a thought of function; discriminate all dharmas without raising a thought of discrimination.]

Constantly, in response to conditions, one uses the six faculties, yet does not raise a thought of using; clearly perceiving the difference of all dharmas, yet does not raise a thought of discrimination. (The Lankavatara Sutra of the Great Vehicle says: “When the consciousness of discriminated objects is extinguished, this is called nirvāṇa.”)
[When the kalpa-fire burns the bottom of the sea, and the wind-stirred mountains crash together, the true and constant bliss of extinction—such is the mark of nirvāṇa.]

Then, even when “the kalpa-fire dries up the bottom of the sea and the wind of disaster rushes the mountains to collide,” at the very time the world is about to be destroyed, one can still maintain the true and constant bliss of extinction; such is the mark of nirvāṇa.

[The kalpa-fire burning the bottom of the sea and the wind-stirred mountains crashing together] These are the great fire catastrophe and great wind catastrophe that arise when the world is about to be destroyed. [Jie huo (kalpa-fire)] One of the three great catastrophes (water, wind, and fire), namely the great fire that occurs at the kalpa of destruction, burning up to the first meditation heaven, so that everything is turned to ashes.
[I now labor with words to make you abandon heretical views; do not follow the words to understand, and I grant that you know a small part.]

I now labor to describe in words this state that cannot be spoken, to make you abandon heretical views. Do not give rise to understanding by following the words, but realize the wondrous purport beyond the words; then I grant that you know a small portion of nirvāṇa.
[Zhidao, hearing the verse, greatly awakened; he leapt up with joy, made obeisance, and withdrew.]
Zhidao, hearing the verse, greatly awakened; he leapt up with joy, bowed respectfully, and withdrew.

[The Chan master Xingsi was born into the Liu family of Ancheng in Jizhou. Hearing that the Dharma seat of Caoxi flourished and transformed countless people, he came directly to pay his respects and asked: What should one do so as not to fall into stages? The Master said: What have you been doing? He said: Even the noble truth I do not do. The Master said: Then into what stage do you fall? He said: If I do not even do the noble truth, what stage could there be? The Master greatly esteemed him and made him lead the assembly.]

The Chan master Xingsi was born into the Liu family of Ancheng in Jizhou. Hearing that the Dharma seat of the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi flourished and transformed countless people, he came directly to pay his respects to the Master. He asked for instruction: What should one do so as not to pass through the various stages (not fall into stages)? The Master said: What have you been doing? Xingsi said: I do not even do the noble truth. The Master said: Then on what stage (into what stage) do you fall? Xingsi said: If I do not even do the noble truth, what stage could there be? The Master greatly esteemed him and made him the first seat to lead the assembly.
[Fa xi (Dharma seat)] The seat for spreading the Dharma. [Sheng di (noble truth)] The truth seen by the sages, that is, suffering, accumulation, extinction, and the path.

[One day the Master said to him: You should go and transform one region; do not let [the teaching] be cut off. Xingsi, having obtained the Dharma, returned to Qingyuan Mountain in Jizhou to spread the Dharma and carry on the work.]

One day the Master said to him: You should share in the transformation of a region, and do not let the Sudden Teaching be cut off. Xingsi, having already obtained the Dharma, returned to Qingyuan Mountain in his home region of Jizhou to carry on and spread the Sudden Teachings; disciples gathered in clouds and the Chan wind greatly flourished.

blocks.text: 12. To Say It Resembles a Thing

inline.s: [The Chan master Huairang was the son of the Du family of Jinzhou. At first he went to pay respects to the National Master An of Song Mountain, and An sent him to Caoxi to investigate. When Huairang arrived, he bowed. The Master said: Where have you come from? He said: Song Mountain. The Master said: What thing has come like this? He said: To say it resembles a thing is not right. The Master said: Can it still be cultivated and realized? He said: Cultivating and realizing is not without it; being defiled is not to attain it.]

The Chan master Huairang was the son of the Du family of Jinzhou. At first he went to Song Mountain to pay respects to the National Master Hui’an, and the National Master Hui’an sent him to Caoxi to study. When Huairang arrived at Caoxi and bowed to the Sixth Patriarch, the Master said: Where have you come from? Huairang said: Song Mountain. The Master said: What thing has come thus? Huairang said: To say it resembles a thing is already not right (the self-nature is originally nothing, so how could it be any thing). The Master said: Can it still be cultivated and realized? Huairang said: Cultivation and realization are not without it (to cultivate the illusory with the illusory); but to be defiled is not to attain it (“from the beginning not a single thing; where could dust settle?”).

[National Teacher Anguo] This is Chan Master Hui’an, whom Empress Wu Zetian honored as National Teacher. From princes and high ministers down to the common people of the capital, all vied to come and pay their respects, prostrating themselves in the dust, as many as ten thousand each day. [Can-kou (seeking and inquiring)] Also written “can-kou” (can-kou: “to deliberate and inquire”).

[The Master said: Just this “non-defilement” is what all Buddhas keep in mind and protect. Since you are thus, I am also thus. Prajnatara of the Western Land prophesied that from beneath your feet a horse colt would emerge—one that would trample the whole world of sentient beings. Keep this in your heart; there is no need to speak of it in haste.]

The Great Master gave his seal of confirmation: Just this “non-defilement” is what all Buddhas keep in mind and protect. Since you are thus, I am also thus. The Venerable Prajnatara of the Western Land (the teacher of Bodhidharma, the twenty-seventh patriarch of the Western Lineage) prophesied that from beneath your door a fine horse would emerge (referring to Chan Master Mazu Daoyi), whose dharma heirs would spread across the world. Keep this in your heart; there is no need to speak of it too early.

[Western Land] Tianzhu (ancient India) lies to the west of China, and was therefore called the Western Land. The Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs says: “Seeking the Dharma in the Western Land; translating the scriptures in the Eastern Land.”

Later, Chan Master Huairang indeed had a dharma-heir, Chan Master Daoyi (because his lay surname was Ma, he was known throughout the world as Patriarch Ma). His inner-chamber disciples numbered one hundred and thirty-nine, each serving as a patriarch of his own region, teaching and transforming the world. Among them Xitang Zhizang, Baizhang Huaihai, and Nanquan Puyuan were the most renowned, acclaimed as the Three Great Masters of the Hongzhou school. From the line of Baizhang Huaihai there arose the Linji lineage and the Weiyang lineage.

[Huairang suddenly and fully awakened to the meaning, and thereafter attended upon the Master, serving him on his left and right for fifteen years, growing daily in the profound and mysterious depths of the doctrine. Later he went to the Southern Peak and greatly proclaimed the Chan lineage.]

Huairang was thereupon utterly and thoroughly enlightened, and so attended upon the Sixth Patriarch on his left and right for fifteen years, day by day coming to fully understand the profound and secret purport of the Sudden Teaching. Later he went to Mount Heng, the Southern Peak, and energetically propagated the Chan lineage.

[Chan Master Yongjia Xuanjue, a son of the Dai family of Wenzhou. In his youth he studied the sutras and treatises, and became deeply versed in the calm-and-insight (śamatha-vipaśyanā) method of the Tiantai school. Because he read the Vimalakirti Sutra, he awakened to the mind-ground. It happened that the Master’s disciple Xuance came to visit him; they talked at length together, and his words subtly matched the intent of the patriarchs.]

Chan Master Yongjia Xuanjue was the son of the Dai family of Wenzhou. From youth he studied the sutras and treatises, and was thoroughly versed in the calm-and-insight method of the Tiantai school. Through reading the Vimalakirti Sutra, he attained awakening. The Sixth Patriarch’s disciple Xuance happened to visit him, and they conversed freely; his words unobtrusively matched the intent of the patriarchs.

[Chan Master Yongjia Xuanjue] A native of Yongjia, his lay surname was Dai. Having left the household life, he explored the three collections of the canon, and was thoroughly versed in Tiantai’s calm-and-insight. Later he came to the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi, and on hearing a single word awakened, departing after a single night. At the time he was called “the One-Night Awakening.” The next day he came down the mountain and returned to Wenjiang. Scholars gathered about him in great numbers, and he was honored with the title Great Master Zhenjue. He entered stillness in the first year of the Xiantian era (712) under Emperor Ruizong of the Tang, and was posthumously granted the title Master Wuxiang (No-Marks). He composed a single Song of Certifying the Way. His Yongjia Collection also flourished in the world.
[Fucou (as spokes converge to a hub)] A phrase describing many people gathering together from all directions, just as the spokes of a wheel converge upon its hub.

[Xuance said: Good man, in whom have you attained the Dharma? He replied: I have listened to the Vaipulya sutras and treatises, and each has its own line of transmission; later, through the Vimalakirti Sutra, I awakened to the Mind Lineage of the Buddha, but no one has yet verified me. Xuance said: Before the time of King Bhadraśrī it could be allowed; but after the time of King Bhadraśrī, one who is self-awakened without a teacher is nothing but a naturalist heretic.]

Xuance asked: Under which teacher have you attained the Dharma? Xuanjue replied: I have listened to the Mahayana sutras and treatises, and each has its own line of transmission. Later, through the Vimalakirti Sutra, I awakened to the essential purport of the Chan lineage, but no one has yet verified me. Xuance said: Before the Buddha King Bhadraśrī appeared in the world, one might speak of a person self-awakened without a teacher; but after King Bhadraśrī appeared, whoever claims to be self-awakened without a teacher is nothing but a naturalist heretic.

[Vaipulya sutras] The general name for the Mahayana sutras. [Mind Lineage of the Buddha] Also called the Mind Lineage—that is, the Chan lineage. [King Bhadraśrī] That is, the Buddha King Bhadraśrī, the first Buddha of the past kalpa of adornment. [Before King Bhadraśrī] A term used in the Chan groves; the Garden of Patriarchal Deeds says: “Before King Bhadraśrī, it points to the ground of ultimate reality; after King Bhadraśrī, it is within the sphere of Buddha-affairs.” [Before the time of King Bhadraśrī it could be allowed; but after, one self-awakened without a teacher is a naturalist heretic] This is to say that one who has awakened without a teacher must seek verification from a clear-eyed person; otherwise he will mistake a play of light and shadow for the state of awakening.

[He said: I beg the good man to verify me. Xuance said: My words carry little weight. At Caoxi there is the Sixth Patriarch, to whom people gather from all four directions, and all of them receive the Dharma. If you wish to go, I will go with you.]

Xuanjue said: Then please verify me. Xuance said: My person is insignificant and my words carry little weight. At Caoxi there is the Sixth Patriarch; students gather there from all directions, and all receive instruction in the true Dharma. If you wish to go, I will go with you.

[Xuanjue then came with Xuance to pay his respects, walked around the Master three times, shook his staff, and stood still. The Master said: One who is a śramaṇa should possess the three thousand deportments and the eighty thousand subtle practices. Great Worthy, from whence have you come that you entertain such great conceit? Xuanjue said: The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Master said: Why not realize the unborn, and understand that there is no swiftness? He replied: Realization is itself the unborn; understanding is in its origin free from swiftness. The Master said: Just so! Just so!]

Xuanjue thereupon came with Xuance to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch. He walked around the Master three times, then shook his staff and stood before him. The Master said: A śramaṇa should possess the three thousand deportments and the eighty thousand subtle practices. From whence has the Great Worthy come, that he shows such great arrogance? Xuanjue said: The matter of birth and death is vast; impermanence is swift. The Master said: Why not grasp the unborn, and realize that there is no haste? Xuanjue replied: To grasp is itself the unborn; to realize is, in its origin, free from haste. (This was Xuanjue’s statement of the state he himself had already certified.) The Master confirmed: Just so! Just so!

[The three thousand deportments and the eighty thousand subtle practices] Among the four deportments of a bhikṣu—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—the subtle practices that ought to be observed. [Deportments (weiyi)] The majestic virtue and rules that should accompany walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. [The matter of birth and death is great] Where one will be reborn after death is a question of the utmost importance. The Great Master Chewu says: “Of all the heavy sufferings in this world, none exceeds birth and death. If birth and death is not ended, then after death there is birth, and after birth there is death, birth upon birth, death upon death; leaving one womb, entering another womb; casting off one bag of skin, taking up another bag of skin—the suffering is already unbearable. Moreover, while still within the wheel of samsara, one cannot avoid falling. Into the womb of a pig, the womb of a dog—what womb will one not bore into? The bag of skin of a donkey, the bag of skin of a horse—what will one not take up? This human body is the most difficult to obtain and the easiest to lose. With a single false thought, one falls into the evil realms. The three lower paths are easy to enter and difficult to escape; the hells are long in duration and heavy in suffering. Since the seven Buddhas, still as ants (beasts are foolish and always cling to their physical bodies as being so, and therefore remain for a very long time in the animal realm. When the corner wall of Jeta Grove monastery was being dug, the Buddha saw a nest of ants, and said to the elder Sudatta: these ants have been ants ever since the seven Buddhas). After eighty thousand kalpas, not yet free of the body of a pigeon (one day the Buddha saw a pigeon, and at once said to his disciples: this pigeon’s karma, even after eighty thousand kalpas, would still be a pigeon). The duration of the animal realm is already extreme; the duration of the ghost and hell realms is still further doubled. Through long ages past, when is there an end, when a rest? A myriad sufferings press upon one, with no refuge, no rescue.” (From the recorded sayings of the Great Master Chewu.) [Impermanence is swift] In the twinkling of an eye impermanence comes to claim one’s life; this refers to the brevity of human life. [The unborn] All things, in their origin, were never born, and therefore are also never extinguished. The Buddha said: “Birth is in its origin without birth; extinction is in its origin without extinction. All things are also thus.” (The Bodhisattva Garland Sutra

Chapter Thirteen.) [Realization is itself the unborn; understanding is in its origin free from swiftness] The Buddha said: “All things without exception are false and unreal.” (The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, Chapter Forty
the Kaundinya chapter.)

[Xuanjue then, with proper deportment, bowed to the Master, and after a while took his leave. The Master said: Are you not returning a little too swiftly? He said: In its origin there has never been motion; how could there be any swiftness? The Master said: Who is it that knows there is no motion? He said: The good man himself has given rise to discrimination. The Master said: You have grasped well the meaning of the unborn. He said: Does the unborn then have a meaning? The Master said: If there is no meaning, who then discriminates? He said: Discrimination, too, is not the work of the mind.]

At this Xuanjue, with full deportment, bowed to the Master, and then took his leave. The Master said: Is it not too swift to return like this? Xuanjue said: In its origin there has never been motion; how could there be anything swift or slow? The Master said: Who knows that in its origin there is no motion? Xuanjue said: It is the good man’s own mind that has given rise to discrimination. The Master said: You grasp well the meaning of neither birth nor extinction. Xuanjue said: Where then does the unborn have a meaning? The Master said: If there is no meaning, who is there to discriminate? Xuanjue said: Discrimination also is not the doing of the mind. (Earlier the Sixth Patriarch’s verse said: “Discriminate all things, yet give rise to no discriminating thought.”)

[Deportments (weiyi)] The majestic virtue and rules that should accompany walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. [Discrimination is not the work of the mind] To know the objects before one clearly without giving rise to deliberation.
The two exchanges above are the sharp, pointed words of Ch’an encounter; the two men were each testing the other’s state of attainment.

[Jifeng (the sharp point of a triggerman)] A term in the Chan school, referring to replies that are swift and keen, leaving no trace, and laden with profound meaning. The original sense of “jifeng” is the trigger-catch and the arrow-point of a crossbow, which the Chan school uses as a metaphor for quick and deep argument and speech. Those of the Chan school often use such sharp words, testing in the exchange the other’s degree of awakening.
[The Master said: Well done! Stay for a single night. At the time he was called “the One-Night Awakening.” Later he composed the Song of Certifying the Way, which flourished in the world.]
The Master said: Very good! Stay a single night. The people of the time called him “the One-Night Awakening.” Xuanjue afterwards wrote the Song of Certifying the Way, which flourished in the world.

Stay for a single night”—this was the Master’s skillful means, letting him awaken fully, wherefore the people of the time praised him as “the One-Night Awakening.” Although Xuanjue’s time with the patriarch was brief, it was the pivotal turning point on the bodhi path; he often said: At last I have gained my mind at Caoxi. In his Song of Certifying the Way he also said: “Since I came to know the Caoxi road, I realize that birth and death no longer concern me.”

[The Ch’an practitioner Zhihuang, having first called on the Fifth Patriarch, regarded himself as having already obtained right concentration (samādhi). He dwelt in a hermitage and sat long, for twenty years. The Master’s disciple Xuance, wandering on foot, came to the region north of the Yellow River. Hearing of Zhihuang’s fame, he went to his hut and asked: What are you doing here? Zhihuang replied: Entering concentration.]

The Ch’an practitioner Zhihuang, when he first called upon the Fifth Patriarch Hongren, already regarded himself as having obtained samādhi (right concentration). He dwelt alone in a thatched hut and sat long, for twenty years. The Sixth Patriarch’s disciple Xuance, wandering to the region north of the Yellow River, heard of the master of concentration Zhihuang, and went to his hut to visit him, asking: What are you doing here? Zhihuang answered: Entering concentration.

[Right concentration (zhengshou)] The meditative concentration in which all thought of the mind is stilled and all deliberating reflection perishes; it is also called samādhi. [Wandering on foot (youfang)] Traveling round to the monasteries of the various regions, studying and seeking the Way. [The region north of the Yellow River (hebei)] A general name for the area north of the Yellow River. [Zao] To go to, to visit; for example, “to pay a visit.”

[Xuance said: You speak of entering concentration. Do you enter it with a mind, or without a mind? If you enter without a mind, then all the mindless things—plants, trees, tiles, and stones—should attain concentration; if you enter with a mind, then all sentient beings endowed with mind should also attain concentration.]

Xuance said: You speak of entering concentration—is it entering with a mind, or without a mind? If it is without a mind, then all the mindless things — grasses, trees, tiles, and stones — are all without mind, and all should attain concentration; if it is with a mind, then all sentient beings possess mind, and all should also attain concentration.
[Endowed with consciousness (hanshi)] Those who possess the knowing mind; that is, sentient beings.

[Zhihuang said: At the very time I am entering concentration, I do not see any mind of “having” or “not having.” Xuance said: If you do not see any mind of “having” or “not having,” that is constant concentration. Where, then, is there any coming out or entering? If there is coming out and entering, that is not great concentration. Zhihuang was silent, with no reply.]

Zhihuang said: At the very time I am entering concentration, I see no mind that has or does not have. Xuance said: Since you see no “mind that has or does not have,” that is constant concentration—at all times within concentration; where then is there any emerging from, or entering into, concentration? (This refers to the words above, “Zhihuang said: Entering concentration.”) If concentration has coming out and entering, it is not great concentration. Zhihuang had no words in reply.

[After a long while he asked: Of whom does the master take up the succession? Xuance said: My teacher is the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi. Zhihuang said: What does the Sixth Patriarch take as concentration? Xuance said: What my teacher says is this: the wondrously profound, round and still nature, in which essence and function are as-they-are (tathata); the five aggregates originally empty, the six objects of sense non-existent; without going out or coming in, without concentration or distraction. The nature of Ch’an abides nowhere, and so is apart from the stillness of abiding; the nature of Ch’an is unborn, and so is apart from thoughts of birth. The mind is like empty space, yet it does not even possess the measure of empty space.]

Silent for a long while, Zhihuang asked: Pray, of whom is your teacher the successor? Xuance said: My teacher is the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi. Zhihuang said: Then what does the Sixth Patriarch take as meditation-concentration? Xuance said: My teacher says that the nature is wondrously profound, round and still, essence and function both as-they-are; the five aggregates (that is, the aggregates of body and mind) are originally empty, the six objects of sense (referring to outer and inner states) are non-existent; there is neither going out nor coming in, neither concentration nor distraction. The nature of Ch’an abides nowhere, so it does not dwell in the stillness of abiding; the nature of Ch’an is unborn, so it does not give rise to thoughts of birth. The mind is like empty space, yet does not even have the notion of empty space (it does not cling to the emptiness-view).
This is to say: that which is not deluded by objects, still and as-it-is, having extinguished both “having” and “not having”—only this is true concentration.

[As-it-is (ruru)] Abiding in thusness (zhenru). This is the state of the self-nature, which is non-dual and equal, free from inverted discrimination. [Thusness (zhenru)] “True” means the true aspect; “thus” means as-it-is; true aspects being thus, it is named “thusness”—that is, the real aspect of all things.

[Zhihuang, hearing this, went straight to call upon the Master. The Master asked: Good man, what brings you here? Zhihuang set forth fully the former circumstances. The Master said: Indeed, as has been said. You need only make your mind like empty space, without clinging to the emptiness-view; function without obstruction, in motion and stillness have no mind, forget the feelings of common and holy, both object and subject extinguished, nature and marks as-it-is—then there is no time when you are not in concentration.]

Zhihuang, having heard this teaching, went straight to call upon the Sixth Patriarch. The Sixth Patriarch asked: Good man, what is the occasion of your coming? Zhihuang related in full his meeting with Xuance. The Sixth Patriarch said: The principle of concentration is indeed as Xuance has said. You need only make your mind like empty space, without clinging even to emptiness, function without obstruction, in motion and stillness keep the mind without a mind, not giving rise to the views of the common or the holy (forget the feelings of common and holy), both subject and object extinguished, principle and phenomena interfused without obstruction—then naturally there is no time when you are not in concentration.

[Subject and object (nengsuo)] The initiating force is called “subject”; the passive force is called “object.” For example, in the contact of the six sense-bases with the six objects, the six sense-bases are the perceiving subject (neng), and the six objects are the perceived object (suo).

Concerning the great concentration in which there is neither going out nor coming in, Mr. Wang Xianglu says in his Discourse on the Process of Realizing the Essence and Setting It to Function: “When objects come and you do not attend to them, nor give rise to thoughts, yet without cutting off—this is concentration in stillness. When you are not deluded by objects but still cope with them, moving yet unmoved—this is concentration in motion. When you reach the point where motion and stillness are one, and there is nothing you can or cannot do—then it is great concentration.”

This sutra says: “What is called meditation-concentration? To be apart from marks on the outside is Ch’an, to be unconfused within is concentration. If one clings to marks outside, the mind within is confused; if one is apart from marks outside, the mind is not confused. The self-nature is originally pure and originally concentrated; it is only because one sees objects and thinks about them that it is confused. If one sees all the objects without the mind being confused, that is true concentration.”

[Zhihuang then had a great awakening, and the mind that he had gained in twenty years left not a trace. That very night, the common people of the region north of the Yellow River heard a voice in the sky say: Master Zhihuang attained the Way today! Later Zhihuang took leave with due ceremony and returned north of the Yellow River, teaching and converting the four assemblies.]

Zhihuang thereupon had a great awakening, and the mind he had gained through twenty years of long sitting in concentration vanished without a trace. That very night, the people north of the Yellow River heard a voice in the sky proclaim (a celestial being’s praise): Master Zhihuang attained the Way today! Later Zhihuang took leave of the Sixth Patriarch and returned north of the Yellow River, teaching and converting the four assemblies of monks and laypeople.

A bright teacher removes clinging and loosens bonds: For many years Zhihuang still clung to attaining concentration and entering concentration; now that the clinging and bond are gone, the sky is vast and the sea wide, and there is no time at all when he is not in concentration.

blocks.text: 15. He Does Not Understand the Dharma

inline.s: [A certain monk asked the Master: The purport of Huangmei (the Fifth Patriarch)—who has obtained it? The Master said: One who understands the Dharma obtains it. The monk said: Has the master obtained it or not? The Master said: I do not understand the Dharma.]

A certain monk asked the Sixth Patriarch: The purport of the Sudden Teaching of the Fifth Patriarch of Huangmei—who has obtained it? The Master said: One who understands the Dharma has obtained it. The monk said: Have you, master, obtained it? The Master said: I do not understand the Dharma.
[Purport (yizhi)] That to which the meaning points.
The Sixth Patriarch’s answer, cut and decisive, was like a thunderbolt from a clear sky, startling the dreamer within dreams awake!
The Diamond Sutra says: “Subhuti! What is spoken of as the Buddha-Dharma is not the Buddha-Dharma, and so is called the Buddha-Dharma.”

Emperor Wu of the Liang asked Bodhidharma: What is the highest meaning of the holy truths? Bodhidharma replied: Vastly empty, nothing holy. The emperor said: Who is it that faces me? Bodhidharma answered: I do not know.

In former times Master Gaofeng, citing the kōan of the Sixth Patriarch’s “I do not understand the Dharma,” composed a verse: “The patriarch does not understand the Ch’an; the scholar does not know a single word. Striking a stone head, bang! bang! he speaks of actual matters.”
[Purport (yizhi)] That to which the meaning points. [Vastly empty (kuoran)] The aspect of empty stillness.

[One day the Master wished to wash the robe transmitted to him, but there was no fine spring. He therefore went to a place some five li behind the monastery, where he saw the mountain forest luxuriant and beneficent vapors swirling.
