The Master shook his staff and struck the ground; a spring gushed forth at the touch of his hand, and pooled into a pond. He then knelt on a rock to wash the robe.]

One day the Master wished to wash the robe transmitted by the Fifth Patriarch, but there was no sweet spring. So he went to a place some five li behind the monastery, where he saw the mountain forest luxuriant and beneficent vapors swirling. The Master thereupon shook his staff and struck the ground; the spring gushed forth at the touch of his hand and pooled into a pond. He then knelt upon a rock to wash the robe.

[All at once a monk came to pay homage, saying: Fangbian, a native of Western Shu. Yesterday, in Southern Tianzhu, I saw the Patriarch Bodhidharma, who charged me to hasten to the Land of Tang, saying: “The right Dharma-eye treasury that I transmitted and the kashaya robe, now passed through six generations to Shaozhou Caoxi—go there and pay reverent homage.” Fangbian has come from afar, and wishes to see the robe and bowl transmitted by my teacher. The Master then showed them to him.]

All at once a monk came forward to pay homage, saying: Your disciple Fangbian is a native of Western Shu. Some days ago in Southern Tianzhu I saw the Patriarch Bodhidharma, who charged your disciple to hasten to the Land of Tang, saying: “The mind-dharma of the Ch’an lineage (the right Dharma-eye treasury) transmitted by me in the Land of Tang, together with the great robe (kashaya), has now passed to the sixth generation, at Shaozhou Caoxi—go there and pay it reverent homage.” Your disciple has come from afar, and wishes to see the robe and bowl transmitted by my teacher. The Master then showed him the robe and bowl.

[Yesterday (zuo)] Broadly, a past day; the past. For example: “I now see that what I did before was wrong.” (Returning Home, from the ode by Tao Yuanming.) [Southern Tianzhu] Tianzhu is India; Southern Tianzhu is one of the five Tianzhu. The divisions of Tianzhu into five regions, the southern being called Southern Tianzhu. [Mahakashyapa] That is, Mahakashyapa. One day at Vulture Peak the World-Honored One picked up a heavenly flower and showed it to the assembly. All the hundreds of thousands of humans and gods did not grasp his meaning; only Kashyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: “I have the right Dharma-eye treasury, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the real aspect with no marks, the subtle Dharma-gate, established without words, transmitted apart from the teaching—this I entrust to Mahakashyapa.” This was the World-Honored One first transmitting the Ch’an lineage. [Right Dharma-eye treasury] The Buddha’s mind-eye penetratingly sees the right Dharma, and thus is called the “right Dharma-eye”; deep and vast, containing countless virtues, it is called the “treasury.” [Kashaya (sengjiali)] The great robe of a monk.

[He then asked: What is the venerable one’s profession? Fangbian replied: I am skilled at sculpting. The Master, with a serious countenance, said: Try to sculpt something! Fangbian was at a loss. After several days he sculpted a likeness, seven inches high, wholly capturing its wonder. The Master laughed, and said: You understand only the plasticity of forms, not the Buddha-nature. The Master put out his hand and rubbed the crown of Fangbian’s head, saying: Forever be a field of merit for humans and gods. The Master then gave him a robe in return.]

The Master then asked: In what is the venerable one skilled? Fangbian said: I am skilled at making statues. The Master, with a stern countenance, said: Sculpt one to see! Fangbian, alarmed, knew not what to do. After several days, Fangbian sculpted the likeness of the Sixth Patriarch, about seven inches high, wholly capturing its wonder. The Master laughed and said: You understand only the plasticity of forms, not the Buddha-nature. Putting out his hand, he rubbed the crown of Fangbian’s head, saying: Forever be a field of merit for humans and gods. He then gave Fangbian a robe as a reward.

Question: The Sixth Patriarch was just washing the transmitted robe when he met Fangbian. The text says “the Master then gave him a robe in return.” Does this mean the Sixth Patriarch rewarded Fangbian with the robe transmitted by the Fifth Patriarch?

Answer: No. Would the faith-robe transmitted by the patriarchs be used to reward others? In Chapter Ten it says: “On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, I carried the spirit-shrine together with the transmitted robe and bowl back.” This proves that the faith-robe was still present.

[Fangbian took the robe and divided it into three parts: one to drape over the statue, one to keep for himself, and one to wrap in palm-fiber and bury in the ground. He made a vow, saying: Should anyone later obtain this robe, that will be the time of my coming forth into the world, to preside here and rebuild the halls.]

Fangbian divided the robe given by the Sixth Patriarch into three parts: one part he draped over the statue; one part he kept for himself; and one part he wrapped in palm-fiber and buried in the earth. He made a vow, saying: Should anyone in future, digging in the ground, obtain this robe, that will be the time of my coming forth into the world, to be abbot of this place and rebuild the halls.

[Zong] The same as “zong” (palm-fiber). [Yi] Read “yi,” to bury, to inter. [Rebuilding the halls (chongjian dianyu)] According to records: In the eighth year of the Jiayou era of the Song (1063), a monk named Weixian, repairing the halls and digging the ground, obtained the robe as fresh as new. The image is in Gaoyuan Monastery, and prayers to it were always answered.
[A monk cited the verse of Ch’an Master Wolun: Wolun has his skill—he can cut off the hundred thoughts; when objects come, his mind does not arise, and bodhi grows day by day.]

A certain monk, citing the verse of Ch’an Master Wolun, consulted the Sixth Patriarch. The verse said: “Wolun has his skill; he can cut off the hundred thoughts; when objects come, his mind does not arise, and bodhi grows day by day.”

Judging from this verse, Ch’an Master Wolun “can cut off the hundred thoughts; when objects come, his mind does not arise,” and moreover his afflictions grow lighter day by day while bodhi (awakening) grows—this is a rather good state. He took this, however, to be the ultimate, and so said with self-satisfaction, “Wolun has his skill.”

There are two stages in the work of practice: guarding (bao) and letting-be (ren). Wolun’s work was at the guarding stage; he already possessed the power to subdue random thoughts, accomplishing “not giving rise to the mind that dwells in form, not giving rise to the mind that dwells in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharma (when objects come, the mind does not arise).” What should be noted is that “cutting off the hundred thoughts” means not continuing a thought once it arises, and not suppressing thought so that it does not arise; “when objects come, the mind does not arise” means not giving rise, upon encountering objects, to a mind that clings and dwells.

No-thought is a matter of great importance in study and practice. It must be especially noted that one cannot use suppression of thought so that it does not arise in order to reach no-thought. For “to suppress thought so that it does not arise” is to use the power of will to crush thoughts; even if one can suppress them on the cushion, off the cushion they become only the more active; at times one can suppress them, at times they become all the more active. More importantly, the method of “suppressing thought so that it does not arise” can never in the end reach the state where “the six consciousnesses go out through the six gates, and in the midst of the six objects of sense they are undefiled and untangled, coming and going freely, functioning universally without obstruction.” Hence the Sixth Patriarch especially pointed out: “If one merely does not think of the hundred things, wiping thought away entirely—the moment a single thought is cut off, one dies and is reborn elsewhere—this is a great error.”

The correct no-thought is to not give rise to thought upon thought, clinging and dwelling. The Sixth Patriarch instructed: “No-thought means, within thought, to be without thought.” This is also what the layman Pang meant: “Good snowflakes, flake by flake, falling nowhere else.” Concerning practice in no-thought, the Sixth Patriarch instructed: “What is called no-thought? If, on seeing all things, the mind is not defiled or attached, this is no-thought. In function it pervades every place, and yet is attached to no place. One needs only purify the original mind, causing the
six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousnesses) to go out through the six gates (that is, the six sense-bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind)

—in the midst of the six objects of sense (form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharma)—to be undefiled and untangled, coming and going freely, functioning universally without obstruction. This is the samādhi of prajñā, the freedom of self-mastery, called the practice of no-thought.”

[The Master, hearing this, said: This verse has not yet understood the mind-ground. If one practices in accordance with it, one adds bonds to oneself. He thereupon showed a verse: Huineng has no skill; he does not cut off the hundred thoughts; when objects come, his mind rises again and again—how then does bodhi grow?]

The Sixth Patriarch, hearing this, said: This verse has not yet understood the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground. If you practice in accordance with it, you add bonds to yourself (you will only be able to be great-dead, not great-alive), and sink clogged on the path. He thereupon showed a verse to loosen his bonds: Huineng has no skill; he does not cut off the hundred thoughts; when objects come his mind rises again and again (rising spontaneously, giving rise to the mind that abides nowhere—a living and lively wondrous function); how then can bodhi grow (as viewed in the light of the real aspect of all things)?

[The Dharma-gate of the mind-ground] When the mind is empty, the state is empty of itself; all things are without bondage, originally self-liberated. [He does not cut off the hundred thoughts] Here, “not cutting off the hundred thoughts” does not mean not cutting off random thoughts; it is the state of “giving rise to the mind that abides nowhere.” This is the state of concentration and wisdom maintained equally; it is also what the Vimalakirti Sutra

Chapter One, “The Buddha’s Land” says: “Being able to well discriminate the aspects of all dharmas, and yet abide unmoved in the first principle.” (Being able to clearly discern all things, while the mind is unmoved by these illusions.) [First principle (first truth)] The supreme principle, that is, the real aspect of all things. The Buddha said: “All dharmas are false and unreal; that which is their extinction is called real, is called the real aspect, is called the dharma-realm, is called ultimate wisdom, is called the truth of the first principle, is called the emptiness of the first principle.” (The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra
Chapter Forty

the Kaundinya chapter.) [When objects come, the mind rises again and again] The Sixth Patriarch’s mind rising again and again upon meeting objects is not dwelling on objects and giving rise to the mind; it is what was said earlier: “the six consciousnesses go out through the six gates, and in the midst of the six objects of sense they are undefiled and untangled, coming and going freely, functioning universally without obstruction.” Here, “not cutting off the hundred thoughts, when objects come the mind rises again and again” belongs to the letting-be (ren) stage, and the state is very high. If one lacked the guarding (bao) work of “cutting off the hundred thoughts, and when objects come the mind does not arise,” then “not cutting off the hundred thoughts, when objects come the mind rises again and again” would be the samsaric state of “not cutting off the hundred random thoughts, the mind following objects in confusion.”

Wolun’s problems are these: First, “Wolun has his skill” shows that he still had a mind that grasps at attainment. Second, “he can cut off the hundred thoughts; when objects come, his mind does not arise”—in terms of skill, this still belongs to the guarding (bao) stage; he has not reached the spontaneity of letting-be, able to be dead but not able to be alive. The seriousness of the matter lies in his not yet knowing that he had taken a phantom city for the treasure-ground, and so took a withered tree leaning on a cold cliff as the ultimate—fortunately the Sixth Patriarch pointed out the road. Third, Wolun was still attached to the mark of “bodhi grows day by day,” wherefore the Sixth Patriarch spoke in depth: “How then does bodhi grow?”—from the standpoint of the real aspect of all things, what bodhi is there, let alone bodhi growing day by day? He was to be brought from marks to return to the nature.

Practice is like a piece of wood drifting in a river: if it is not snagged, it naturally flows down to the great ocean. What makes a good teacher precious is precisely the ability to see what a student is snagged upon, and to remove the clinging and loosen the bonds. Therefore, in Chapter Eight, “Sudden and Gradual,” the Sixth Patriarch said: “If I were to say I have a Dharma to give to a person, I would be deceiving you; I only untie bonds according to the circumstances.” A monk asked Zhaozhou: “What is the mystery within the mystery?” Zhaozhou said: “How long have you been seeking the mystery?” The monk said: “I have long been seeking it.” Zhaozhou said: “If it had not been for this old monk, you would almost have been killed by the mystery!” (Comment: The patriarch’s single phrase, like the king’s jewel-sword of the Vajra, cuts off all knowledge-views of both common and holy!)

[Mystery within the mystery (xuanzhongxuan)] The Linji patriarch received students with the three mysteries and three essentials. The three mysteries are: the mystery in the phrase, the mystery in the essence, and the mystery within the mystery. The Record of the Lamp of Five Houses records: “The Chan Master Fayuan of Benjue Monastery in Xiuzhou, a son of the Shen family of Jiangyin. A monk asked: ‘What is the mystery in the phrase?’ The master said: ‘A Kunlun mount riding an elephant, drawn by a single lotus thread.’ He asked: ‘What is the mystery in the essence?’ The master said: ‘The shadow steeped in a cold pool, the moon in the sky.’ He asked: ‘What is the mystery within the mystery?’ The master said: ‘Sleeping with a sword on the long platform of the dormitory.’ He asked: ‘Is there anything further above this?’ The master said: ‘Put it down.’”
Question: Wherein lies the difference between Wolun’s verse and the Sixth Patriarch’s verse?

Answer: In working at the practice there are two stages, guarding (bao) and letting-be (ren). First, guarding: guard the self-mind, cutting off thought and deliberation, without following the objects of sense. Second, letting-be: the self-nature takes the lead, functioning spontaneously and freely, without following the objects of sense. The earliest stage is guarding the self-mind (not giving rise to the mind that dwells in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharma). When the guarding work has matured, one abandons the guarding, abandons the restraint, and does the letting-be work, letting the mind function spontaneously and freely, yet never overstepping the measure (giving rise to the mind that abides nowhere). Here “the measure” means: not greed, not anger, not delusion. To use the cure of drug-addiction as an analogy, the first stage is the guarding stage, and consists in deeply recognizing the harm of taking drugs and strictly isolating oneself from them. Those severely addicted may even need to train for a time in a rehabilitation facility, and under strict environment and discipline learn certain methods and gain a preliminary ability to resist drugs before going home to continue the guarding way of recovery. Once the guarding work has matured, one begins the second stage, the letting-be work. One should reach the point where, though the drug be at hand for the taking, one is not enticed, and goes about one’s work and life normally. Again, for example, Confucius said: “Subdue the self and return to propriety (restraining oneself so that words and actions conform to propriety).” He also said: “Follow what the heart desires, yet without overstepping the measure.” Here “subdue the self and return to propriety” is the guarding work, and “follow what the heart desires without overstepping the measure” is the letting-be stage. By doing the work of “subduing the self and returning to propriety,” and after the struggle of several decades, at the age of seventy Confucius reached the state of “following what the heart desires without overstepping the measure.”
The Diamond Sutra says:

“All the bodhisattva-mahasattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind that dwells in form, nor a mind that dwells in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharma; they should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.”

Wolun’s verse is not giving rise to a mind that dwells in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharma—this is the guarding (bao) stage. The Sixth Patriarch’s verse is giving rise to the mind that abides nowhere—this is the letting-be (ren) stage, as the saying goes, “Passing through a hundred flowers, and not a single leaf clings to the body.” The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “Good man! All obstructions are precisely the ultimate awakening; thoughts gained and thoughts lost are none other than liberation; the Dharma accomplished and the Dharma destroyed are alike called nirvāṇa; wisdom and ignorance are equally prajñā; the Dharma achieved by bodhisattvas and by heretics is the same bodhi; ignorance and thusness are not two, but a single state; all the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, together with desire, anger, and delusion, are all pure conduct. The world of living beings and the lands of the Buddhas share one Dharma-nature; the hells and the heavenly palaces are all Pure Land; those with nature and those without nature equally perfect the Buddha-way; all afflictions are in the end liberation. The ocean-wisdom of the Dharma-realm, illuminating all marks, is like empty space. This is called the Tathagata’s accord with the nature of awakening. Good man! But so long as bodhisattvas and the beings of the last age, in all times, do not give rise to random thoughts (not giving rise to the mind that dwells in the six objects of sense), and also do not extinguish these random thoughts (giving rise to the mind that abides nowhere), dwelling in the realm of random thought without adding deliberate understanding, and in non-understanding not discriminating real or false—those beings, hearing this Dharma-gate, believing, understanding, receiving, and holding it, without fear or alarm, are called accordant with the nature of awakening. Good man! You should know that such beings have already worshipped hundreds of thousands of millions of Ganges-sands of Buddhas and great bodhisattvas, planting the roots of all virtues; the Buddha says such a person is named as one perfecting the knowledge of all aspects.”

[Ocean-wisdom of the Dharmarealm (fajie haihui)] The great wisdom that contemplates the equal nature of the Dharmarealm, deep and vast as the ocean, whence its name. [Knowledge of all aspects (yiqie zhongzhi)] Also called the knowledge of all marks; this is the Buddha’s wisdom that penetrates both the universal aspect of all dharmas (the real aspect of all dharmas) and their particular aspects.

blocks.text: Chapter Eight: The Sudden and the Gradual
1. Huineng in the South, Shenxiu in the North

inline.s: [At that time the Patriarch dwelt at Baolin Monastery at Caoxi, and the Great Master Shenxiu was at Yuquan Monastery in southern Jingzhou. At that time the two schools both flourished in their teaching, and everyone called them “Huineng in the South, Shenxiu in the North.” Hence there was the division of the Southern and Northern schools into Sudden and Gradual, and yet the students did not know the central purport of these schools.]

At that time the Sixth Patriarch dwelt at Baolin Monastery at Caoxi, and the Great Master Shenxiu was at Yuquan Monastery in the south of Jingzhou. At that time both schools were flourishing in teaching and transformation, and everyone said “Huineng in the South, Shenxiu in the North.” Hence there was the division of the Southern and Northern schools into Sudden and Gradual, and yet the students all did not know the central purport of these two schools.
[Yuquan Monastery] Located at the southeastern foot of Yuquan Mountain in Dangyang County, Hubei. [Central purport (zongqu)] The purpose and direction of a school.

Question: Shenxiu’s verse, “The body is the bodhi tree; the mind is like a bright mirror’s stand. Time and again, diligently wipe it, letting no dust gather upon it,” I feel great benefit from reading. But Huineng’s verse, “Bodhi is originally no tree; the bright mirror likewise is no stand. Originally there is not a single thing—where can dust gather?”—I feel I cannot put it to use. What is the reason?

Answer: With regard to any one Dharma, one must personally have the power to practice it before one can receive real benefit. Therefore one must choose a method of practice that accords with oneself. As the saying goes, “Medicine does not distinguish precious from cheap; what suits the ailment is excellent. The Dharma does not distinguish high from low; what accords with the student is wondrous.” Since you feel benefit from Shenxiu’s verse, practice in accordance with this verse. When your afflictions have grown thin, and the light of prajñā shines through more and more, you will of yourself come to understand the excellence of Huineng’s verse, and at that time you will have the power to carry it out. The Great Master Hanshan says: “As to what is called sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, this means that one has first awakened thoroughly, but there are still habitual tendencies not yet wholly purified. In all circumstances of environment, one raises the power of contemplation in the light of the principle one has awakened to, passing through the states and testing the mind. Melt away one measure of state, and realize one measure of the Dharmakaya; dissolve away one measure of random thought, and reveal one measure of original wisdom.” (From the Dream Wandering Collection,
in answer to Zheng Kunyan, Director of the Censorate.)
[Original wisdom (benzhi)] The unobstructed wisdom of liberation.

[The Master said to the assembly: The Dharma is in its origin a single school, but people are of the South and the North. The Dharma is a single kind, but the seeing is quick or slow. What is meant by Sudden and Gradual? The Dharma has no Sudden or Gradual; people have keen and dull faculties, and therefore it is called Sudden and Gradual.]

The Master said to the assembly: The Buddha-Dharma originally has a single purpose, but people are divided into South and North. The Dharma is a single kind, but the seeing of the Way is quick or slow. Why are there Sudden and Gradual? The Buddha-Dharma has no Sudden or Gradual; it is people’s faculties that are keen or dull—and so, teaching according to capacity, there arise the Sudden and the Gradual.

[Yet Shenxiu’s followers often ridiculed the patriarch of the Southern school, saying: He does not know a single word—what talent does he have? Shenxiu said: He has obtained the wisdom of one without a teacher, and deeply awakened to the Supreme Vehicle. I am not his equal! And my teacher the Fifth Patriarch personally transmitted to him the robe and the Dharma—how could this be without reason! I regret that I cannot journey far to draw near him; I am vainly receiving the imperial favor. Do you, all of you, not linger here, but go to Caoxi to seek resolution.]

Yet Shenxiu’s followers often ridiculed the patriarch of the Southern school, Huineng, saying: He cannot read a single word—what talent could he have? Shenxiu said: Huineng has obtained the wisdom of one self-awakened without a teacher, and deeply awakened to the Supreme Vehicle. I am not his equal! And my teacher the Fifth Patriarch personally transmitted to him the robe and the Dharma—how could that be without reason! I regret that I cannot journey far to Caoxi to draw near him, hear the Dharma, and receive instruction; here I am instead vainly receiving the imperial favor. Do you, all of you, not linger here any longer—go to Caoxi to study and resolve your doubts.

Shenxiu had read widely in the scriptures and served as a teaching master; the expectations of the assembly rested upon him. Yet because of Huineng he lost the transmission of the Dharma and the patriarch’s seat, and moreover held a position different from Huineng’s on Sudden and Gradual. Even so, he openly said to his disciples: “He has obtained the wisdom of one without a teacher, and deeply awakened to the Supreme Vehicle. I am not his equal! And my teacher the Fifth Patriarch personally transmitted to him the robe and the Dharma—how could this be without reason! I regret that I cannot journey far to draw near him; I am vainly receiving the imperial favor,” and urged his disciples: “Do not linger here—go to Caoxi to seek resolution.” Here the lofty integrity of Shenxiu is evident!

According to records: After the Fifth Patriarch passed into stillness, Shenxiu went to Yuquan Monastery at Dangyang Mountain in Jiangling (today the southeast of Dangyang County, Hubei), and there greatly opened up the Ch’an Dharma. Over more than twenty years his fame resounded throughout the four seas. Empress Wu heard of him, summoned him to the capital, bore him up in a chair to the hall, and personally knelt in homage to him—at that time he was already past ninety. When Emperor Zhongzong came to the throne, he received even greater veneration. In the second year of the Shenlong era (706), he passed into stillness at Tiangang Monastery, and was posthumously titled the Great Master Datong. He lived over a hundred years (“Shenxiu was born at the end of the Sui; he was over a hundred years old, but never spoke of it, so no one knew his age”), and his years as a monk numbered eighty.
[Monk’s years (sengla)] Also called Dharma-years or precept-years; the number of years since a monk or nun received the complete precepts.

[One day he commanded his disciple Zhicheng, saying: You are bright and full of wisdom; you may go for me to Caoxi to hear the Dharma. Whatever you hear, take it earnestly to heart and record it, and return to tell it to me.]

One day Shenxiu commanded his disciple Zhicheng, saying: You are bright and full of wisdom; go for me to the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi to hear the Dharma. Whatever you hear, take it earnestly to heart, and return to tell it to me.
An open mind like a valley—the bearing of a true master.

[Zhicheng, receiving the command, went to Caoxi. He followed the assembly in its visits and requests, but did not say where he came from. At that time the Patriarch said to the assembly: There is now a person who steals the Dharma, secretly present in this assembly. Zhicheng then came out and bowed, and related the matter fully. The Master said: You come from Yuquan, so you must be a spy. He replied: I am not! The Master said: How can you not be? He replied: Before I spoke, I was one; now that I have spoken, I am not.]

Zhicheng, receiving the command, arrived at Caoxi. He followed the assembly in paying respects and seeking edification, but did not say where he came from. At that time the Sixth Patriarch said to the assembly: There is a person robbing the Dharma, hidden in this assembly. Zhicheng then came forward, bowed, and related in detail how he had received his teacher’s command to come to Caoxi and hear the Dharma. The Master said: You come from Yuquan Monastery of the Northern school—you must be a spy. Zhicheng replied: I am not! The Master said: How can you not be? Zhicheng replied: Before I spoke of my origin, I was one; now that I have stated my origin, I am not.
[Spy (xizuo)] A secret agent; a spy.

[The Master said: How does your teacher instruct the assembly? He replied: He constantly directs and instructs the assembly to dwell the mind and contemplate stillness, and to sit long without lying down. The Master said: To dwell the mind and contemplate stillness is a sickness, not Ch’an; to sit long with a cramped body—what benefit is that to the principle?]

The Master said: How does your teacher instruct the assembly? Zhicheng replied: My teacher constantly guides and instructs the assembly to gather the mind and contemplate stillness, and to sit long without lying down (never eating lying down, but sitting). The Master said: To gather the mind and contemplate stillness is a sickness, not Ch’an; to sit long with a cramped body—what benefit is this to the awakening to the Way?
[Never lying down (budao dan)] Sitting cross-legged, without distinction of day or night.
The Sixth Patriarch said:

“When the true-such self-nature gives rise to thought, though the six sense-organs see, hear, know, and perceive, they are not defiled by all the states, and the true nature is ever self-possessed. Therefore the sutra says: Being able to well discriminate the aspects of all dharmas, and yet abide unmoved in the first principle.”

When the true-such self-nature gives rise to thought, one works at prajñā contemplation—when evil comes, one crosses over by the right; when delusion comes, one crosses over by awakening; when ignorance comes, one crosses over by wisdom; when the bad comes, one crosses over by the good—until both extremes are abandoned and the false, random mind-thought is done away with. This is the method of practice of the Sixth Patriarch’s Ch’an.
The Sixth Patriarch said:

“Rise without false and deceitful thoughts; use your own true-such nature, and with the wisdom of contemplation, in regard to all dharmas neither grasp nor reject—this is to see the nature and accomplish the Buddha-way.”
[Hear my verse: In life, one sits and does not lie down; in death, one lies down and does not sit. A single putrid bag of bones—what lesson is to be set upon it?]
Hear my verse: In life, one can sit and not lie down; in death, one lies down and does not sit. Such a putrid bag of bones—how can one use it to do one’s practice?

blocks.text: 2. The Dharma of Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom

inline.s: [Zhicheng bowed again, saying: Your disciple studied the Way for nine years at the Great Master Shenxiu’s place, but could not attain accord and awakening. Now, hearing the master’s single exposition, I have attained accord with the original mind. Your disciple’s matter of birth and death is great; may the master, in his great compassion, give me further instruction.]

Zhicheng bowed again, saying: Your disciple studied the Way for nine years at the Great Master Shenxiu’s place, without attaining accord and awakening. Today, hearing the master’s exposition, I have at once attained accord and awakening with the original mind. Your disciple’s matter of birth and death is great—I pray the master, in his great compassion, to give me further instruction and guidance.

[The Master said: I hear that your teacher instructs students in the Dharma of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. I do not know how your teacher speaks of precepts, concentration, and wisdom—what is their aspect in action? Tell me and let me see. Zhicheng said: The Great Master Shenxiu says: “To do no evil is called precepts; to perform all good is called wisdom; to purify one’s own mind is called concentration.” He speaks thus—I do not know what Dharma the master uses to teach people?]

The Master said: I hear that your teacher instructs students in the Dharma of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. I do not know how your teacher explains precepts, concentration, and wisdom? Tell me about it. Zhicheng said: The Great Master Shenxiu says: “To do no evil is called precepts; to perform all good is called wisdom; to purify one’s own mind is called concentration.” He says it thus—I do not know how the master teaches people?
[Aspect in action (xingxiang)] The form and manner of one’s performance.

[The Master said: If I were to say I have a Dharma to give to a person, I would be deceiving you. I only untie bonds according to the circumstances, and provisionally name it samādhi. The precepts, concentration, and wisdom that your teacher speaks of are truly inconceivable; but the precepts, concentration, and wisdom that I see are different. Zhicheng said: Precepts, concentration, and wisdom ought to be one thing—how can they differ?]

The Master said: If I were to say there is a Dharma I give to people, that would be deceiving you. I only remove clinging and loosen bonds according to the circumstances, and provisionally give it the name samādhi. The precepts, concentration, and wisdom that your teacher speaks of are indeed profound and subtle; but my view of precepts, concentration, and wisdom is yet different. Zhicheng said: Precepts, concentration, and wisdom should be a single thing—how can they differ?

[Removing clinging and loosening bonds (qu nian jie fu)] To remove the clinging and bonds on the body; in the Ch’an groves it is transferred to mean dissolving the attachment to afflictions, in order to reach the state of ease and freedom from obstruction.

[The Master said: Your teacher’s precepts, concentration, and wisdom take in the Mahayana people; my precepts, concentration, and wisdom take in the people of the Supreme Vehicle. If the understanding differs, the seeing is quick or slow. Listen to my exposition, and see whether it is the same as his. The Dharma I speak never departs from the self-nature. To speak the Dharma apart from the essence is called speaking of marks, and the self-nature remains ever deluded. You must know that all the myriad things function from the self-nature—this is the true Dharma of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.]

The Master said: The precepts, concentration, and wisdom your teacher speaks of lead in the Mahayana people; the precepts, concentration, and wisdom I speak of lead in the people of the Supreme Vehicle. If the understanding differs, the seeing of the Way is quick or slow. Listen to my exposition, and see if it is the same as his. The Dharma I speak never departs from the self-nature; to speak the Dharma apart from this essence is called speaking of marks (speaking the Dharma attached to marks), and the self-nature remains ever deluded. You must know that all the myriad things arise their aspects and functions from the self-nature—only this is the true Dharma of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

[Hear my verse: The mind-ground with no wrong is the self-nature’s precepts; the mind-ground with no delusion is the self-nature’s wisdom; the mind-ground with no confusion is the self-nature’s concentration; neither increasing nor decreasing, itself the diamond; the body going, the body coming—originally samādhi.]

Hear my verse: The mind-ground giving rise to no dispute of right and wrong, self and other, is the self-nature’s precepts; the mind-ground not deluded and inverted is the self-nature’s wisdom; the mind-ground not dull and scattered is the self-nature’s concentration; neither increasing nor decreasing, firm as a diamond; in coming and going, everything is samādhi.

[Mind-ground (xindi)] The mind has no form or aspect, so the earth is used as a metaphor for the mind. Moreover, the mind is like the earth. The earth has the meaning of generating, and the mind too has the meaning of generating. All the forests and plants grow from the earth, and likewise all the dharmas of good and evil, the fruiting bodies of the six realms and the four sages, all arise from the self-mind. The earth has the meaning of providing support, and the mind too has the meaning of providing support. The earth supports minerals, plants, and animals, and the mind supports the five aggregates, the six sense-bases, the eighteen realms, the dharmas of world and beyond-world, and the dharmas of outflows and without outflows. Hence mind and earth are combined into one name, and called the mind-ground. [The mind-ground with no wrong is the self-nature’s precepts] “The mind-ground with no wrong” means, in all times and all places, not giving rise to discrimination, without love or hate, without like or dislike. Master Huiming says in his Records of Instruction: “What is called precepts? The mind-ground with no wrong is the self-nature’s precepts. Precepts are divided into those with marks and those without marks; the with-marks is called bodily precepts, the without-marks is called mind-precepts. Those who study the mind-ground Dharma-gate should strictly uphold the mind-precepts. Everyone now sitting in meditation is doing the work of the mind-precepts. Why? Because after ascending the seat, one concentrates on holding the mantra, and by the power of the mantra locks up all random thoughts; in time random thoughts do not arise, and this is the state of the mind-ground with no wrong. Not only is it so on the seat; it is also so after the seat. In all times and all places, one gives rise to no discrimination and no affliction; naturally motion and stillness are one, and only then is the precept of the mind-ground with no wrong completed.”

[Zhicheng, hearing the verse, repented and gave thanks, and offered a verse: The five aggregates make up an illusory body—how can the illusory be ultimate? Turning back to seek thusness, the Dharma is still not pure.]

Zhicheng, hearing the verse, repented and gave thanks, and likewise offered a verse: The five aggregates are falsely combined into an illusory body—how could the illusory body be ultimate? Even turning back with this to seek thusness, still clinging to Dharma-marks, it is not yet pure.

[Repentance and thanks (huixie)] Earlier Zhicheng held that “precepts, concentration, and wisdom ought to be one thing,” and only through the Sixth Patriarch’s instruction realized that he himself was wrong, wherefore he repented and gave thanks. [Turning back to seek thusness, the Dharma is still not pure] To use the Dharma of “to do no evil is called precepts; to perform all good is called wisdom; to purify one’s own mind is called concentration” in order to turn back and seek thusness—still clinging to Dharma-marks, it is not yet pure. What Shenxiu transmitted was precepts, concentration, and wisdom with marks; what the Sixth Patriarch transmitted was precepts, concentration, and wisdom without marks. The Records of Instruction of Master Huiming says: “What is called precepts? The mind-ground with no wrong is the self-nature’s precepts. Precepts are divided into those with marks and those without marks; the with-marks is named bodily precepts, the without-marks is named mind-precepts.”

[The Master approved. He then said to Zhicheng: Your teacher’s precepts, concentration, and wisdom exhort the people of small faculties; my precepts, concentration, and wisdom exhort the people of great faculties. If one awakens to the self-nature, one does not set up bodhi and nirvāṇa, nor the liberation of knowledge and views, nor a single Dharma obtainable—only then can one establish the myriad dharmas. If one understands this meaning, it is also called the Buddha-body, also called bodhi and nirvāṇa, also called the liberation of knowledge and views. A person who has seen the nature may set these up or not set them up; coming and going, free, without obstruction or hindrance. In function, responding as one acts; in words, responding as one answers; everywhere manifesting the transformation-body, without departing from the self-nature, at once attaining the autonomous transcendental powers, playing in samādhi—this is called seeing the nature.]

The Master gave his approval. He then said to Zhicheng: The precepts, concentration, and wisdom your teacher speaks of instruct the people of small faculties; the precepts, concentration, and wisdom I speak of instruct the people of great faculties. If one has awakened to one’s own nature, one does not set up bodhi and nirvāṇa, nor the liberation of knowledge and views, nor a single Dharma obtainable—only then can one establish the myriad dharmas with the true-such original nature. (Chapter Four says: “When the true-such self-nature gives rise to thought, though the six sense-organs see, hear, know, and perceive, they are not defiled by all the states, and the true nature is ever self-possessed.”) If one understands this meaning, it is called the Buddha-body, also called bodhi and nirvāṇa, also called the liberation of knowledge and views. A person who has seen the nature may set up these names and marks, or not set them up; coming and going, free, without obstruction or hindrance. In function, responding as one acts; in words, responding as one answers; manifesting all transformation-bodies, without departing from one’s own nature, at once attaining the autonomous transcendental powers, playing in samādhi—this is called seeing the nature.
[Everywhere manifesting the transformation-body (pujian huashen)] Here the character “jian” (to see) is, in ancient usage, the same as “xian” (to manifest).

The two kinds of precepts, concentration, and wisdom spoken of by Shenxiu and the Sixth Patriarch are in fact two stages of work, applied respectively to the people of small faculties and the people of great faculties. What is called small faculties and great faculties is not fixed and unchangeable. If one cannot get a start on practicing the “mind-ground with no wrong, no delusion, and no confusion,” it shows the foundation is insufficient; one should then follow Shenxiu’s method and work hard. After a few years one will naturally come to grasp the excellence of “the mind-ground with no wrong, no delusion, and no confusion,” and be able to practice along this path.
In the passage above, the Sixth Patriarch said: “A person who has seen the nature may set up, or not set up.” Therefore Zhicheng asked further: What is the meaning of not establishing?

[Zhicheng again inquired of the Master: What is the meaning of not establishing? The Master said: The self-nature has no wrong, no delusion, no confusion; thought after thought in prajñā contemplation, ever apart from the marks of dharmas, free and self-possessed, whatever you do is wholly attained—what is there to establish? The self-nature is awakened of itself; sudden awakening, sudden cultivation, with no graded sequence—therefore one does not establish all dharmas. All dharmas are quiescent and extinct—what sequence is there? Zhicheng bowed, and wished to serve as attendant, never slackening by day or night.]

Zhicheng again inquired of the Master: What is the meaning of “not establishing”? The Master said: The self-nature has no wrong, no delusion, no confusion (the self-nature’s precepts, concentration, and wisdom); thought after thought in prajñā contemplation, knowing illusion and at once leaving it (ever apart from the marks of dharmas); free and self-possessed, whatever you do is wholly attainable (free in every direction)—what is there to establish? The self-nature is awakened of itself; sudden awakening and sudden cultivation, with no graded sequence—therefore one does not establish all dharmas. All dharmas are quiescent and extinct—what sequence is there? Zhicheng bowed, and wished to be his attendant, never slackening by day or night.

[Marks of dharmas (faxiang)] The aspects and forms manifested by all dharmas. [Free in every direction, wholly attained (zongheng jinde)] “Zongheng” means without restraint; “jinde” means all attainable. Therefore “zongheng jinde” here means: whatever one does is all right—in every place, never departing from the Way. [Sudden awakening and sudden cultivation (dunwu dunxiu)] Sudden awakening is awakening to the real aspect of all things: originally there is not a single thing. Sudden cultivation is: “Knowing illusion, at once leaving it, without resort to expedient means; apart from illusion, at once awakened, with no graded sequence.” (The Complete Enlightenment Sutra.) “All things forever left, cold and without smoke.” (The Buddha-Store Sutra.) Sudden awakening and sudden cultivation are very effective for the people of the supreme faculties, but for those beneath, though they know in principle that “all marks are false and unreal,” upon seeing illusion they cannot at once awaken to it as illusion; or knowing in principle that it is illusion, in actual fact they cannot leave it—“seeing it clearly, yet unable to endure”—and then they must practice gradual cultivation to remove the habitual tendencies; as the saying goes, “the principle may be suddenly awakened, but the actual practice must be gradually eliminated.”

Question: Zhicheng originally accepted his teacher’s command, came to Caoxi to hear the Dharma, and was then to return and report. Why, after hearing the Dharma, did he not return? This is to betray his teacher’s kindness!

Answer: This is exactly “rely on the Dharma, not on the person”—“I love my teacher, but I love truth yet more.” The deluded ones under the Northern school, through discrimination of love and hate, had developed into hatred; not only did they at one time set fire to the mountain, but even now they had sent a swordsman to assassinate the Sixth Patriarch (see below). Zhicheng had now come to recognize that the Southern school was the true transmission. If he went back and spoke the truth plainly (and if he did not speak truthfully, harboring a crafty mind, how could he practice?), he would certainly not be accepted, and moreover his life would be in danger. He therefore could only send a letter of report and remain himself.

[The monk Zhiche, a native of Jiangxi, originally of the Zhang family, named Xingchang, in his youth a knight-errant. Since the division of the South and the North, though the two school-masters were without “self” and “other” in their hearts, their followers vied in rising love and hate. At that time the followers of the Northern school set up Master Shenxiu as the Sixth Patriarch, and jealous that the robe transmitted to the patriarch had become known to the world, they instructed Xingchang to come and assassinate the Master.]

The monk Zhiche, a native of Jiangxi, originally of the Zhang family, named Xingchang, was in his youth a knight-errant. Since the two schools of South and North had divided, although the two school-masters, Huineng and Shenxiu, were without “self” and “other” in their hearts, their disciples vied in rising love and hate. At that time the followers of the Northern school set up Master Shenxiu as the sixth patriarch, and afraid lest the matter of the robe and bowl transmitted to Master Huineng become known to the world, they dispatched Xingchang to come and assassinate the Master. (Truly shocking! What Buddhism is this? The bitterness of practice is precisely for the sake of birth and death—when jealousy arises, one falls into hell! Therefore the Platform Sutra repeatedly warns the cultivator not to harbor jealousy.)

[The Master, with his mind’s transcendental power, knew beforehand of this matter, and so placed ten taels of gold at his seat. When evening fell, Xingchang entered the patriarch’s chamber and was about to harm him; the Master stretched out his neck to receive the blow. Xingchang swung the blade three times, but not the least harm was done.]

The Master had the power of knowing the minds of others, and knew beforehand of this matter, so he placed ten taels of gold at the side of his seat. At nightfall, Xingchang stole into the Sixth Patriarch’s chamber and was about to harm him; the Master stretched out his neck to let him strike. Xingchang swung his knife and struck three times, but the Master was not injured in the least.

[Power of knowing the minds of others (taxintong)] One of the six transcendental powers, the supernatural ability to know the thoughts of others. [Six transcendental powers (liutong)] The transcendental power obtained by the sages of the three vehicles (the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, the vehicle of the bodhisattva), of six kinds: the power of the heavenly eye, the heavenly ear, the knowledge of others’ minds, the knowledge of former lives, the power of spiritual legs (miracle-working), and the extinction of outflows. They are also called the six supernatural powers.

[The Master said: A righteous sword is not evil; an evil sword is not righteous. I owe you only gold, not your life! Xingchang, startled, fell to the ground, and only after a long while came to himself. He begged for mercy, repenting of his fault, and at once wished to leave the household life. The Master then gave him the gold, saying: Go away for now—I fear the assembly may turn and harm you. You may come another day in changed guise, and I will receive you. Xingchang, receiving the master’s command, fled by night, and later took refuge with a monk, left the household life, received the complete precepts, and practiced with vigor.]

The Master said: The knight’s righteous sword should not be put to evil use; a sword put to evil use is not the act of an upright man. In a former life I owed you only gold, not your life! Xingchang, greatly startled, fell unconscious to the ground, and only after a long while came to himself. He begged the Master, repenting of his fault, and made the vow to leave the household life and follow the Sixth Patriarch. The Master thereupon gave him the ten taels of gold, saying: Go away for the time being. In this guise of a night-traveling swordsman, if the assembly saw you, they would turn and harm you. You may come another day in changed dress, and I will take you as a disciple. Xingchang, receiving the master’s command, fled by night, and later took refuge with a monk and left the household life, received the complete precepts, and practiced with vigor.
[Receive with compassion (shezhou)] To take in and protect beings with a compassionate heart.

blocks.text: 5. The Meaning of Eternal and Impermanent

inline.s: [One day, recalling the Master’s words, he came from far to pay his respects. The Master said: I have long thought of you—why have you come so late? He said: The other day I received the master’s forgiveness of my offense. Now though I have left the household life and practice austerities, I can in the end hardly repay your virtue; perhaps only by transmitting the Dharma and liberating beings! Your disciple often reads the Nirvāṇa Sutra, but does not understand the meaning of eternal and impermanent. I beg the master, in his compassion, to explain it briefly.]

One day, recalling the Master’s words (“You may come another day in changed guise, and I will receive you”), Xingchang came from afar to pay his respects. The Master said: For a long time I have been thinking of you—why have you come only now? Xingchang said: That day I received the master’s forgiveness of my offense. Now, though I have left the household life and practice austerities, I can in the end hardly repay the master’s great kindness. Having thought it over, only by spreading the Dharma and liberating beings could I repay it! Your disciple often reads the Nirvāṇa Sutra, but does not understand the meaning of eternal and impermanent. I beg the master, in his compassion, to explain it briefly.
[Jin (to pay respects)] Read “jin,” meaning to have an audience, to pay respects.
[The Master said: What is impermanent is precisely the Buddha-nature; what is eternal is precisely all the dharmas of good and evil and the discriminating mind.]
The Master said: What is called impermanent is precisely the Buddha-nature; what is called eternal is all the dharmas of good and evil and the discriminating mind.

[He said: What the master says greatly contradicts the sutra text. The Master said: I transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal—how would I dare to contradict the Buddha’s teachings? He said: The sutra says the Buddha-nature is eternal, yet the master says it is impermanent; the dharmas of good and evil, and even the bodhi-mind, are all impermanent, yet the master says they are eternal. This is contradictory, and makes those who study the school all the more doubtful.]

Xingchang said: What the master says greatly contradicts the sutra text. The Master said: I transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal—how would I dare to contradict the Buddha’s sutras? Xingchang said: The sutra says the Buddha-nature is eternal, yet the master says it is impermanent; the dharmas of good and evil, and even the bodhi-mind, are all impermanent, yet the master says they are eternal. This contradicts the sutra, and makes those who study all the more doubtful.

[Mind-seal (xinyin)] “Mind” is the Buddha-essence; “seal” means to affirm, or to fix with a seal. The Chan school does not establish words, does not rely on speech, but transmits mind to mind only, sealing the minds of beings with the Buddha-mind, and certifying the non-dual aspect. The Garden of Patriarchal Deeds says: “Bodhidharma came from the West, establishing no words, single-transmitting the mind-seal, pointing directly to the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha.” [Buddha-mind] The Buddha’s own inner realization, inexpressible in words or speech, is called the Buddha-mind. To print the Buddha-mind directly on the mind of beings is called transmitting mind to mind.

[The Master said: As for the Nirvāṇa Sutra, in the past I heard the nun Wujin Cang recite it once, and I thereupon explained it, without a single word or meaning disagreeing with the sutra text; and even now, speaking for your sake, I have never had two ways of speaking. Xingchang said: The student’s knowledge and capacity are shallow and dull; I pray the master to instruct me fully and in detail.]

The Master said: As for the Nirvāṇa Sutra, in the past I heard the nun Wujin Cang recite it once, and I thereupon explained it for her, without a single word or meaning disagreeing with the sutra text; and even now, explaining it for your sake, there is still no difference. Xingchang said: Your disciple’s understanding is shallow and dull; I pray the master to instruct me fully and penetratingly.

[The Master said: Do you know? If the Buddha-nature were eternal, what would there be to say of the dharmas of good and evil? Even throughout countless kalpas, there would not be a single person who gave rise to the bodhi-mind. Therefore my speaking of it as impermanent is precisely the Buddha’s own teaching of the true-eternal Way.]

The Master said: Do you know? The Buddha-nature is the source of all things. If the Buddha-nature were eternal, without change, how could there still be the dharmas of good and evil? Even through countless kalpas, there would not be a single person who gave rise to the bodhi-mind (because “arising” is a turning from non-being to being). Therefore my speaking of the Buddha-nature as impermanent, as changing, is precisely the true-eternal principle the Buddha taught.

[Give rise to the bodhi-mind (fa puti xin)] To give rise to the great mind aspiring upward to the Buddha-way and transforming beings below; that is, to give rise to the mind that seeks the perfect awakening and becomes a Buddha.

[Again, if all dharmas were truly impermanent, then each thing would possess its own self-nature that receives and contains birth and death, and the true-eternal nature would be without a place it does not reach. Therefore my speaking of them as eternal is precisely the Buddha’s teaching of the true-impermanent meaning. Because ordinary people and heretics cling to a false eternal, and the two vehicles count the eternal as impermanent, together forming the eight inversions, the Buddha—in the sutra of the ultimate teaching on nirvāṇa—broke through those biased views, and revealed and expounded the true Eternal, true Bliss, true Self, and true Purity. You now cling to the words and turn your back on the meaning, taking the impermanence of extinction (the view of the two vehicles) and a fixed dead eternity (the view of the ordinary and the heretic) alike, and so misinterpret the Buddha’s final, perfectly subtle words. Though you read it a thousand times, what benefit is there?]

Furthermore, if all dharmas were truly impermanent, then every thing would possess its own essence that receives and contains birth and death, and the true-eternal Dharma-nature would be without a place it does not reach. Therefore my speaking of the dharmas as eternal is precisely the Buddha’s teaching of the true-impermanent meaning. Because ordinary people and heretics cling to a false eternal, and the two vehicles grasp the true-eternal as impermanent (the two vehicles count the eternal as impermanent), together forming the eight inversions; so in the sutra of the ultimate teaching on nirvāṇa, the Buddha broke through their biased views and revealed and expounded the true Eternal, true Bliss, true Self, and true Purity. You now cling to the words and sentences and turn your back on the true meaning, taking the impermanence of extinction (the view of the two vehicles) and a fixed dead eternity (the view of the ordinary and the heretic) alike, and so misinterpret the Buddha’s final, perfectly subtle and profound instruction. Even reading the Nirvāṇa Sutra a thousand times—what benefit is there?

[Eight inversions (badao)] Ordinary people and heretics cling to marks: taking suffering as bliss, impermanence as eternal, non-self as self, impurity as purity. The eternal, bliss, self, and purity they falsely cling to are the four inversions. The two vehicles, breaking through marks, hold that all dharmas are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure (not knowing that there is also the true Eternal, true Bliss, true Self, and true Purity)—such false holding is another four inversions; altogether eight inversions. [Teaching of the ultimate meaning (liaoyi jiao)] Any teaching that directly, completely, and fully reveals and exhausts the principle of the Buddha-Dharma is called a “teaching of the ultimate meaning.” If, in accordance with the capacity of beings, it does not directly reveal the meaning but gradually leads by expedient methods, it is called a “teaching of the provisional meaning.” [The Buddha’s final, perfectly subtle words (fos zhi yuanmiao zuihou weiyan)] The Nirvāṇa Sutra was spoken by the World-Honored One before he entered nirvāṇa, and so is called “the Buddha’s final, perfectly subtle words.”

[Xingchang all at once had a great awakening, and spoke a verse: Because one holds to an impermanent mind, the Buddha spoke of an eternal nature; one who does not know this is an expedient means, is like one picking up pebbles in a spring-pond. Now I, without exerting effort, have the Buddha-nature appear before me; it was not that the teacher gave it to me, nor did I obtain anything.]

Xingchang all at once had a great awakening, and spoke a verse: Because there is a mind that holds to impermanence, the Buddha spoke of an eternal Buddha-nature; not knowing this is an expedient for breaking the impermanent mind, one then goes and holds to the eternal, like one who picks up broken stones and tiles in a spring-pond and takes them for gems. Now I, without exerting effort in bitter practice, have the Buddha-nature appear before me of itself; in fact, the teacher transmitted nothing, and I have obtained nothing.

[Like one picking up pebbles in a spring-pond] The Record of the Ancestral Mirror says: “Obtaining the true gem within a spring-pond, the pebbles picked up are all false.” The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says: “You should know that the contemplation of impermanence and suffering you formerly practiced is not real. For example, in springtime a number of people, bathing in a great pond and riding about on a boat in play, lost a lapis lazuli gem, which sank in the deep water. Then all those people together went into the water to search for the gem. Vying to grab tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, and pebbles, each took himself to have found a lapis lazuli bead, and joyfully brought it out—and only then knew it was not real.” [It was not that the teacher gave it to me, nor did I obtain anything] This is spoken from the standpoint of the ultimate on principle. For the teacher’s giving and my obtaining are both illusions; although one is using illusion to leave illusion, still one is in the midst of illusion, and so it is said: “It was not that the teacher gave it to me, nor did I obtain anything.” This is the same principle as “the Tathagata said nothing” in the Diamond Sutra.

Note: Surveying the exchange between the Sixth Patriarch and Xingchang, as well as the verse Xingchang spoke after his great awakening, one sees that the Buddha-nature being eternal or impermanent are both expedient teachings, spoken in order to remove biased clinging. What then is the ultimate teaching? To speak ultimately, the Buddha-nature transcends the eternal and the impermanent. In Chapter One, “Lineage of Practice,” the Sixth Patriarch instructed Yinzong: “The Buddha-nature is neither eternal nor impermanent.”

Concerning the Buddha-nature there is also a very famous kōan: “A monk asked Zhaozhou: Does a dog have the Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: Nothing (Wu).” As everyone knows, all sentient beings have the Buddha-nature. Why did Zhaozhou say “Nothing”? The Essentials of Mind-Transmission says: “If you are a true man, look into a kōan. A monk asked Zhaozhou: ‘Does a dog have the Buddha-nature or not?’ Zhaozhou said: ‘Nothing.’ Simply, throughout the twelve hours, look into this word ‘Nothing.’ Contemplate it by day, contemplate it by night, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, when putting on clothes and eating, when passing excrement and urine—keeping mind fixed upon mind, rousing your finest spirit, guarding this word ‘Nothing.’ As the days grow long and the months deepen, hammer it into one mass. All at once the flower of the mind bursts into bloom, and you awaken to the auspicious device of the Buddhas and patriarchs; you will no longer be misled by the tongues of the old masters of the world, and you will be able to open your mouth wide and say: ‘Bodhidharma came from the West, raising waves without wind; the World-Honored One, twirling the flower, was a whole confession of defeat.’ Arriving here, what is there to say of King Yama? Even the thousand sages can do nothing to you! Don’t you believe it—there is truly such subtlety! Why so? Because the matter concedes to the resolute mind! A verse says: ‘Breaking free from the dust and toil is no common thing; gripping hard the cow-rope, make a single mighty struggle. Without one bout of cold piercing to the bone, how could one get the plum-blossom’s fragrance to fill the nostrils?’” We ourselves may examine this kōan. If there comes a place of awakening, one will be able to savor the subtlety of the Sixth Patriarch’s dialogue with Xingchang.
[The Master said: Now you have awakened wholly. You should be named Zhiche. Zhiche bowed, gave thanks, and withdrew.]
The Master said: Now you have awakened thoroughly. You should be named Zhiche. Zhiche bowed to the Master, gave thanks, and withdrew.

blocks.text: 6. Shenhui Comes to Pay His Respects

inline.s: According to records: Shenhui was studious from youth. Hearing that the Great Master at Caoxi in Lingnan was greatly proclaiming the Way of Ch’an, he emulated the boy Sudhana in his fifty-three visits, and came from far across a thousand li to pay respects to the Sixth Patriarch. His feet were broken and he had no shoes, so he tore his robe and wrapped his feet to walk. After meeting the patriarch, he attended upon him throughout, and in the end fully obtained the Sudden Teaching. The Sixth Patriarch praised him, saying: “The young Master Shenhui, who has attained the equality of good and not-good, unmoved by praise or blame, giving rise to neither sorrow nor joy.” (Chapter Ten, “The Transmitted Teachings.”)

After Shenxiu passed into extinction, his senior disciple Puji continued to expound the style of his school, which flourished for a time. The people of the time called him “Dharma-master of the two capitals, teacher of the three emperors” (“the two capitals” refers to the western capital Chang’an and the eastern capital Luoyang; “the three emperors” refers to Wu Zetian, Emperor Zhongzong, and Emperor Ruizong). Between the two capitals, almost all followed Shenxiu. Puji also made Shenxiu the true dharma-heir of Bodhidharma’s lineage, established him as the Sixth Patriarch, and called himself the Seventh.

In order to protect the true Dharma, Shenhui entered the capital Luoyang, and, heedless of threats to his life, made a lion’s roar, greatly propagating the Ch’an Dharma of Caoxi. He held a great open assembly at Dayun Monastery at Huatai in Henan, where he publicly debated with Master Chongyuan of the Shenxiu line—who was at the time “famous in both capitals and known across the sea”—on the right and wrong and the true and false of the Southern and Northern Ch’an schools. He attacked the Northern school’s “lineage of transmission as collateral, its Dharma-gate as gradual,” and wrote the Treatise on Revealing the Lineage, fixing the Southern Huineng as the Sudden lineage (confirming the southern Huineng as the Sudden school), and the Northern Shenxiu as the Gradual teaching (the northern Shenxiu as the Gradual school). He established the principles of the Southern school, causing the Sudden Teaching to spread greatly in Luoyang and to circulate through the world—a bright lamp held high, transforming generation after generation.

[Heeding no threat to his life, making a lion’s roar] According to the Record of Determining Right and Wrong of the Southern School, at that time Chongyuan threatened Shenhui, saying: “The name of Chan Master Puji fills the country; the whole world has heard of him, and every mouth passes on the tale—an inconceivable thing. In condemning him thus, are you not at enmity with your own body and life?” Shenhui replied: “Chan Master Puji’s school differs from the Southern school; I myself am sorting out right and wrong, and fixing its principles. I now mean to propagate the Mahayana and establish the true Dharma, so that all beings may know of it—how could I begrudge my body and life?” Chongyuan asked again: “In acting thus, are you not seeking fame and profit?” Shenhui replied: “When I do not begrudge even my life, how could I give it a thought for fame and profit?” This shows well the spirit of Shenhui, who forgot the body for the sake of the Dharma. For this, Shenhui suffered the utmost ostracism and harm from the Northern school. The censor Lü Yi, currying favor with Puji, falsely accused Shenhui of gathering disciples, suspecting the beginnings of mischief. According to the Great Commentary on the Complete Enlightenment Sutra, in less than two years Shenhui was forced to move four times: “In the twelfth year of the Tianbao era, being slandered for gathering the masses, he was ordered banished to Yiyang Commandery, and then moved to Wudang Commandery. In the thirteenth year, by imperial grace he was moved to Xiangzhou. In the seventh month he was again ordered moved to Kaiyuan Monastery in Jingzhou. All these were the persecutions of the followers of the Northern school.” In the third year of Shenhui’s banishment, the situation suddenly changed—the An Lushan rebellion broke out, and Lü Yi was killed by the rebels, and only then did the persecution stop. [The unhindered assembly (wuzhe hui)] Such a dharma-assembly makes offerings universally, like the people of today holding a thousand-monk feast to form ten thousand karmic ties; anyone may take part, with no one barred or restricted.

[There was a boy named Shenhui, a son of the Gao family of Xiangyang, thirteen years old, who came from Yuquan to pay his respects. The Master said: Good teacher, you have come far and suffered hardship. Have you brought the fundamental nature? If you have the fundamental nature, you should recognize the master of it—try and speak of it. Shenhui said: I take non-abiding as the fundamental nature; seeing is itself the master.]

There was a boy named Shenhui, the son of the Gao family of Xiangyang, thirteen years old, who came from Yuquan Monastery in Jingzhou (Shenxiu’s place) to pay respects to the Master. The Master said: Good teacher, you have come from afar and suffered hardship (the Master saw that he had traveled wearily, in torn robe with bound feet)—have you awakened to the fundamental nature? If you have, you should recognize the master of the house—do speak of it! (The Master’s kindly countenance was gracious.) Shenhui, thinking the Master was asking about “the fundamental” and “the master,” answered at once: I take non-abiding as the fundamental nature; right seeing is itself the master.

[The Master said: How can this novice speak so carelessly? Shenhui then asked: Master, as you sit in Ch’an, do you see or not see? The Master struck him three times with his staff, saying: When I strike you, is it painful or not painful? He replied: It is both painful and not painful. The Master said: I both see and do not see. Shenhui asked: What is “both seeing and not seeing?”

The Master said: How can you novice speak so rashly? Seeing the Master’s scolding, Shenhui wanted to test the Master, and so asked in turn: Master, as you sit in Ch’an, do you see the state, or do you not see the state? (The little novice was keen and mischievous.) The Master struck him three times with his staff, saying: When I strike you, is it painful, or not painful? (The Master’s skillful means subdued him.) Shenhui answered: It is both painful and not painful. The Master said: I both see and do not see. Shenhui asked: What is “both seeing and not seeing?”

[Novice (shami)] One who has left the household life and received the ten precepts. The ten precepts are: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to commit sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to drink wine; sixth, not to adorn the body with perfumes and flowers; seventh, not to delight in music, song, and dance; eighth, not to sit or lie on a high, broad, and magnificent bed; ninth, not to eat at the wrong time; tenth, not to hoard gold, silver, and wealth. [Zhenghe] How thus. [Quci] Carelessly; rashly.]

[The Master said: As to my seeing: I constantly see the faults of my own mind, and do not see the right and wrong, the likes and dislikes, of others—therefore I both see and do not see. As to your “both painful and not painful”—how is this? If you were not painful, you would be the same as wood and stone; if you were painful, you would be the same as an ordinary person, and would give rise to anger and hatred. What you asked before, “seeing and not seeing,” is the two extremes; “painful and not painful” is arising and ceasing. You have not yet seen your own self-nature, and still you dare to toy with people! Shenhui bowed, repented, and gave thanks.]

The Master said: As to my seeing—I constantly see the faults of my own mind; as to my not-seeing—I do not see the right and wrong, the likes and dislikes, of others; thus I say I both see and do not see. As to your saying “both painful and not painful”—what does this mean? If you were not painful, you would be the same as wood and stone, without consciousness; if you were painful, you would be the same as an ordinary person, and would give rise to anger and hatred. The “seeing and not seeing” you asked about before is the two extremes; “painful and not painful” is arising and ceasing—this shows you have not yet seen the nature. You have not yet seen your own nature, yet you dare to toy with people in this way! Shenhui bowed, repented, and confessed his fault.

[The Master again said: If your mind is deluded and you do not see (the nature), ask a good teacher for the road; if your mind has awakened, you then see the nature yourself, and practice the Dharma accordingly. You are yourself deluded and do not see your own mind, yet you come to ask me about seeing and not seeing. My seeing, I know myself—how could it replace your delusion? If you see it yourself, neither can you replace my delusion. Why do you not know and see for yourself, but ask me about seeing and not seeing? Shenhui again bowed more than a hundred times, begging forgiveness for his offenses, and thereafter served diligently as attendant, never leaving the Master’s side.]

The Master again said: If your mind is deluded and does not see the nature, you should ask a good teacher to seek the road to seeing the nature; if your mind has already awakened, you then see the nature yourself, and should practice the Dharma accordingly. (From this one knows too that what the Sixth Patriarch transmitted was a sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation.) You are yourself deluded and do not see the nature, yet you come to ask me whether I see or not. As for my seeing the nature, I know it myself—how could it replace your delusion? If you see the nature yourself, neither can it replace my delusion. Why do you not know and see for yourself, and instead ask me whether I see or not? Shenhui again made more than a hundred prostrations, begging the Master to forgive his offenses, and from then on served the Master diligently, never leaving his side.

[One day the Master said to the assembly: I have a certain thing, without head and without tail, without name and without title, without back and without face. Do you all recognize it? Shenhui came forward, saying: It is the source of all Buddhas, Shenhui’s Buddha-nature.]

One day the Master said to the assembly: I have a certain thing, with no head and no tail, no name and no title, no back and no face. Do you all still recognize it? Shenhui came forward, saying: It is the source of all Buddhas, Shenhui’s Buddha-nature.

[The Master said: I told you it has no name and no title, yet you call it “source” and “Buddha-nature.” In the future you will have a thatched roof to cover your head, yet you will only be a follower of intellectual understanding.]

The Master said: I have already told you it has no name, yet you call it “source” and “Buddha-nature.” Later you will have a single place of refuge, yet you will only become a Ch’an person who knows and understands.

[Mao] That is, “thatch.” [A thatched roof to cover one’s head] To have a thatched hut to shelter one’s body; here it is a metaphor for establishing one’s own gate and household. [Follower of the lineage (zongtu)] A Ch’an person—one who takes Ch’an as his lineage.]

The Sixth Patriarch asked: “Do you all recognize it?” His meaning was: Have you experienced it?—not, in terms of knowledge, whether you are aware of it. Hence he rebuked Shenhui’s answer: one must work hard in practice and awakening; otherwise, even if the gate and household flourish, one only becomes a Ch’an person who knows and understands (a follower of intellectual understanding). The master and the student—one question, one answer, one rebuke—were alike full of boundless compassion.

[After the patriarch passed into extinction, Shenhui entered the capital Luoyang, and greatly propagated the Sudden Teaching of Caoxi. He wrote the Treatise on Revealing the Lineage, which flourished in the world.]

After the Sixth Patriarch passed into extinction, Shenhui entered the capital Luoyang, and greatly propagated the Sudden Teaching of Caoxi, writing the Treatise on Revealing the Lineage, which flourished in the world.

The Sudden Teaching of Caoxi spread throughout the four seas, and its benefit reached later ages; Shenhui’s merit was like a mountain. The deeds of Shenhui’s “entering the capital Luoyang and greatly propagating the Sudden Teaching of Caoxi” are as follows:

After the Sixth Patriarch passed into extinction, Shenxiu, because he was revered by Wu Zetian, had his teaching flourish greatly in the north, and it was called the “Northern school.” After Shenxiu passed into extinction, his disciple Chan Master Puji continued to expound the style of his school, with an exceedingly high reputation, flourishing for a time; he claimed that Shenxiu was the orthodox transmission of Bodhidharma, the sixth patriarch of the Chan lineage, and that he himself was Shenxiu’s successor. (Li Yong’s Stele of the Great Master Dazhao (Puji) records that Puji, at his death, instructed his disciples, saying: “I received the charge from my late teacher, and transmit this secret seal. From far, Bodhidharma the Bodhisattva guided Hui Ke; Hui Ke advanced to Seng Can; Seng Can focused upon Dao Xin; Dao Xin transmitted to Hong Ren; Hong Ren bestowed it upon Datong (Shenxiu); Datong left it to me—now seven generations.”) At that time the Shenxiu line was of great power and prestige, and the lineage they established no one dared to question.

(When Shenxiu entered the capital, Empress Wu Zetian, leading Emperor Zhongzong, Emperor Ruizong, and the assembled ministers, knelt to welcome him, showing the utmost respect and honor. She even specially decreed that Shenxiu might ride up to the hall in a shoulder-bearer, straight to the front of the hall; and when meeting the emperor, he need not perform the rites, but only sat cross-legged to see the sovereign. Whenever Shenxiu went out, the prefects of the various regions, and officials and ladies of every rank, heard the news and came, raising embroidered banners and offering incense and flowers, lining the road to greet him—sometimes so many of them that the roads were blocked. Many princes, nobles, and kinsmen of the court, scholars, commoners, monks, nuns, and laymen came from far across ten thousand li to pay their respects, prostrating themselves in the dust, numbering by tens of thousands daily. When Emperor Zhongzong came to the throne, he showed Shenxiu even greater reverence; and thereafter Emperor Ruizong also held Shenxiu in the deepest esteem. When Shenxiu died, the whole city of Chang’an wept; the monks and laymen who sent off the funeral numbered more than a hundred thousand. The court also built three great monasteries to commemorate him: one in the western capital Chang’an; one establishing the Dumen Monastery at Dangyang Mountain in Jingzhou; and one establishing the Baoen Monastery at Weishi in Chenliu, the place of his birth. The Mirror and Thread of the Buddhas and Patriarchs says: “Shenxiu dwelt in the eastern capital, and the world called him ‘Dharma-master of the two capitals, teacher of the three emperors.’ In the second month of the second year of the Shenlong era he passed into extinction, and was posthumously titled Datong. Shenxiu was born at the end of the Sui, lived over a hundred years, and never spoke of it, so no one knew his age.” After Shenxiu, his disciple Chan Master Puji led the assembly; princes, nobles, scholars, and commoners vied in coming to pay respects, held in high esteem by the imperial house. At that time a saying went round: “Under the Northern school’s gate, its power reaches the very heavens.” In such a situation, Shenhui dared to challenge single-handedly—this shows his exceptional courage and insight, the spirit that forgets the body for the Dharma.)
