When Shenhui arrived at the capital Luoyang and saw the Northern school’s Ch’an Dharma flourishing, claiming to be the orthodox transmission of Bodhidharma, he put forward that the Northern school’s “lineage of transmission is collateral, its Dharma-gate is gradual”; that the Sudden Teaching of the Southern school is superior to the Gradual teaching of the Northern school; that the true marrow of Bodhidharma’s Ch’an is preserved in the Sudden Teaching of the Southern school; and that Huineng is the true orthodox transmission of the Chan lineage since Bodhidharma, with the robe and bowl as proof.

On the fifteenth day of the first month of the twelfth year of the Kaiyuan era (724), Shenhui held an unhindered assembly (a dharma-assembly in which monks and laypeople, high and low, might all take part) at Dayun Monastery at Huatai (today Huaxian County, Henan), and engaged in fierce debate with the then-renowned scholar Master Chongyuan of Dayun Monastery, establishing the principles of the Southern school while refuting the then most prestigious Chan Master Puji. Shenhui said: “(Bodhidharma) transmitted a single kashaya robe as the token of the Dharma to Hui Ke; Hui Ke transmitted it to Seng Can; Seng Can to Dao Xin; Dao Xin to Hong Ren; Hong Ren to Huineng—six generations succeeding one another, unbroken and unceasing.” “When Master Shenxiu was alive, he pointed to the sixth-generation transmitted Dharma-robe as being at Shaozhou, but did not call himself the sixth generation. Now Chan Master Puji calls himself the seventh generation, and wrongly sets up the elder (Shenxiu) as the sixth—this is not allowed.” At that time Master Chongyuan threatened: Chan Master Puji’s fame fills the world; in criticizing him thus, do you not fear for your life? Shenhui said calmly: I am here to discriminate right and wrong and to decide the principles, to propagate the Mahayana and establish the true Dharma—how can I begrudge my body and life? His resolute stance and incisive words startled those who took part in the assembly. Because of Shenhui’s victory in debate and his propagation, the “Southern school” thereupon began gradually to replace the “Northern school” and became the orthodox transmission of Chinese Ch’an, causing the Sudden-awakening Dharma-gate of Caoxi to spread greatly in Luoyang and to circulate through the world.

In the twelfth year of the Tianbao era (753), the censor Lu Yi of the Northern school, a follower of Puji, falsely accused Shenhui of gathering disciples with intent to harm the court. Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang thereupon summoned him to the capital; because he reasoned and spoke plainly, he was merely banished to Yiyang Commandery in Jiangxi, and before long moved to Wudang Commandery in Hubei. In the spring of the thirteenth year of the Tianbao era (754), he was moved again to Xiangzhou, and in the seventh month he was ordered moved to Kaiyuan Monastery in Jingzhou. Though Shenhui, owing to the Northern school’s retaliation, lived a life of banishment, shifting through four places in two years, his reputation did not decline.

In the third year of Shenhui’s banishment, the fourteenth year of the Tianbao era (755), An Lushan rebelled, raised troops, and captured Luoyang, drawing near to Chang’an; Emperor Xuanzong fled in haste to western Shu. The deputy marshal Guo Ziyi led troops to suppress the rebellion; because military pay was lacking, following the temporary proposal of the Right Attendant Pei Mian, an order was sent throughout the commanderies and prefectures to set up precept-platforms to ordain monks, collecting a certain tax money (incense-water money) to help the military needs. At this time Shenhui was still in banishment in Jingzhou; Lü Yi, who had falsely accused him, had been killed by the rebels, and the assembled councilmen invited him out to preside over the setting up of platforms and ordaining of monks, and so he returned to Luoyang. In the first year of the Zhide era (756), Shenhui was already eighty-nine. The monasteries of Luoyang had by then been destroyed in the fires of war; he thereupon temporarily established a monastery, building a square platform in the middle, and gave all the income from the ordinations to support the military expenses—playing a great part in the recovery of the two capitals by Emperor Daizong and Guo Ziyi.

After the rebellion of An Lushan had been put down, Emperor Suzong commanded him to enter the palace for offerings, and decreed the building of Ch’an halls in Heze Monastery where he had once stayed; wherefore the people of the time called the Ch’an learning he propagated the Heze school.

On the thirteenth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Shangyuan era (760), Shenhui passed into stillness at Heze Monastery in Luoyang, at the age of ninety-three. A stupa was built for him at Baoying Monastery in Luoyang, and he was posthumously titled Great Master Zhenzong.

[The Master saw that the various schools, in their difficult questioning, all gave rise to evil minds. He gathered them together before his seat, and said with compassion: “Those who study the Way should wholly remove all good thoughts and all evil thoughts. There is no name that can be named; it is named in the self-nature. The nature without duality is called the true nature. Upon the true nature one establishes all the gates of teaching, and at once upon a word one must see it for oneself.” The people, hearing this, all made obeisance, and asked to serve him as their teacher.]

The Master saw that the various schools were mutually confronting and reproaching one another, and all gave rise to evil minds. He thereupon gathered them together before his seat, and said with compassion: “Those who study the Way should wholly remove all good thoughts and all evil thoughts; one can neither name it good nor name it evil, but name it in the self-nature. This nature without duality is called the true nature. The gates of teaching established upon the true nature—at once upon a word one must see the nature for oneself.” The people, hearing this instruction, were as if awakened from a dream, and all devoutly prostrated themselves, requesting to serve the Sixth Patriarch as their teacher.

blocks.text: Chapter Nine: The Protecting of the Dharma

inline.s: This chapter tells of the emperor’s imperial summons to the Sixth Patriarch, and how, because the Patriarch pointed out and gave the Tathagata’s knowledge and vision, the emperor “suddenly awakened to the Supreme Vehicle, gratefully acknowledging the master’s kindness, and holding it above his head without end”! This is the protection and upholding of the Sudden Teaching, and so the chapter is named “The Protecting of the Dharma.”

blocks.text: 1. The Racing Summons and the Welcome

inline.s: [On the Festival of the First Full Moon of the first year of the Shenlong era, Zetian and Zhongzong issued an edict saying: “We have invited the two masters, Hui’an and Shenxiu, to be offered in the palace, that in the leisure from Our myriad affairs We may constantly investigate the One Vehicle. The two masters decline in favor, saying: ‘In the south there is Master Huineng, who secretly received the robe and Dharma of Master Hong Ren and transmits the Buddha’s mind-seal; We may invite him to ask.’ Now We dispatch the palace attendant Xue Jian, bearing the racing edict to invite you. We pray the Master, in his compassionate regard, to hasten to the Upper Capital.” The Master sent up a memorial declining on the ground of illness, wishing to end his days in the forest and the hills.]

On the fifteenth day of the first month of the first year of the Shenlong era (705, when the Sixth Patriarch was sixty-seven), Empress Dowager Zetian and Emperor Zhongzong of the Tang issued an edict saying: “We have invited the two masters, Hui’an and Shenxiu, to be offered in the palace, so that in the leisure from the many tangled affairs of government We may constantly investigate the One Buddha-Vehicle. The two masters decline in favor, saying: ‘In the south there is Master Huineng, who secretly received the robe and Dharma of the Great Master Hong Ren and transmits the Buddha’s mind-seal; We may invite him to be offered in the palace.’ Now We specially dispatch the palace attendant Xue Jian, riding, bearing the edict to invite you. We pray the Master, in his compassionate regard, to hasten to the Upper Capital.” The Master sent up a memorial, declining on the grounds of illness, wishing to end his old age in the mountain forest.

Shenxiu’s patriarchal seat had been “taken,” and his purpose differed from Huineng’s, and he well knew that Huineng surpassed himself; yet now, when the emperor invited him to the palace for offerings, he still declined in favor of Huineng. Truly a shining model of a cultivator of the Way!

[Festival of the First Full Moon (shangyuan)] The name of a festival. By custom, the fifteenth day of the first lunar month is the Shangyuan Festival, and its night is the Shangyuan night, also called the “Lantern Festival.” [Wu Zetian] Wu Zetian (

), named Zhao (the same as “shining”; this was a character made for her own name), a native of Wenshui in Bingzhou (today east of Wenshui, Shanxi). At fourteen she was selected into the palace by Emperor Taizong of the Tang as a consort of the fifth rank; after Taizong’s death she became a nun. Before long she was summoned as a secondary consort by Emperor Gaozong, and in the year
she was made empress, gradually controlling the government, and was called together with Gaozong “the Two Sages.” Later she deposed Emperor Zhongzong and Emperor Ruizong in succession, and in
proclaimed herself the Emperor Sheng Shen, changing the name of the dynasty to Zhou—known in history as the Zhou of Wu. In

Emperor Zhongzong was restored to the throne, and honored her with the title “Zetian, the Great Holy Emperor”; later generations commonly called her Wu Zetian. [Zhen] The emperor’s self-designation. [The two masters, An and Xiu] The two masters Hui’an and Shenxiu. For Chan Master Hui’an, see the note in Chapter Seven, “The Accumulation of Opportunities.” [Myriad affairs (wanji)] That is, “wanji,” referring to the numerous and tangled affairs of state that the sovereign manages daily. [The One Vehicle] Also called the One Buddha-Vehicle, the only teaching that can lead one to Buddhahood.

blocks.text: 2. Sitting in Ch’an and Practicing Concentration

inline.s: [Xue Jian said: The Ch’an worthies of the capital all say: “If one wishes to comprehend the Way, one must sit in Ch’an and practice concentration; for one to attain liberation without relying on meditative concentration—there has never been such a thing.” I do not know how the Master speaks of the Dharma?]

Xue Jian asked: The Ch’an great masters of the capital all say: “If one wishes to enter the Way, one must sit in Ch’an and practice concentration; to attain liberation without relying on meditative concentration—that is impossible.” I do not know what the Master’s view is?

[The Master said: The Way is awakened by the mind—how could it be in sitting? The sutra says: “If one says the Tathagata sits or lies down, he is practicing a wrong path. Why? Because he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.” Unborn and unextinguished: this is the Tathagata’s pure Ch’an. All dharmas empty and still: this is the Tathagata’s pure sitting. Ultimately there is no realization—how much less is there any sitting!]

The Master said: The Way is awakened by the mind—how could it be in sitting? The sutra says: “If anyone thinks the Tathagata sits or lies down, he is practicing a wrong path, and cannot see the Tathagata.” Why? Because the Tathagata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. Unborn and unextinguished—this is the Tathagata’s pure Ch’an. All dharmas empty and still—this is the Tathagata’s pure sitting. To speak ultimately, the very matter of realizing the fruit does not exist—how much less sitting!

In the Diamond Sutra, the Buddha said: “If anyone says the Tathagata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I say. Why? Because the Tathagata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere—therefore he is called thus-come.”

[Xue Jian said: When your disciple returns to the capital, the sovereign will surely ask. I pray the Master, in his compassion, to point out the essential mind, that I may transmit and report it to the two palaces and the students of the Way in the capital. It is like a single lamp that lights a hundred thousand lamps: the dark ones all become bright, and brightness without end.]

Xue Jian said: When your disciple returns to the capital, the Empress Dowager and the Emperor will surely ask what the Master has instructed. I pray the Master, in his compassion, to point out the essential mind, that I may transmit and report it to the Empress Dowager and the Emperor (the two palaces), and inform all the students of the Way in the capital. This is like a single lamp (a metaphor for the Master’s instruction) lighting hundreds and thousands of lamps: the dark ones all become bright; passing the light on in turn, lighting ever the unlit lamps, transmitting without end (brightness without end).

[The Master said: The Way has no bright or dark; bright and dark are the meaning of alternating succession. Brightness without end is also one day at an end, because names are established in mutual dependence. The Vimalakirti Sutra (the Jingming Sutra) says: “The Dharma has no comparability, because it has nothing to stand against.”]

The Master said: The Way has no bright or dark; bright and dark are the meaning of alternating change. To say brightness without end—in the end it does come to an end, because the concepts of bright and dark arise only in mutual dependence; if there were no dark, about what would one speak of bright? The Vimalakirti Sutra (the Jingming Sutra) says: “The Dharma has no comparability, because it has nothing to stand against.”

[The Dharma has no comparability, because it has nothing to stand against] The Buddha-Dharma is without mutual dependence, and so has no comparability. This is to clarify that “the Way has no bright or dark.”

[Xue Jian said: Bright is a metaphor for wisdom; dark is a metaphor for affliction. If the cultivator of the Way does not use wisdom to illumine and break through affliction, how can he escape the birth and death of the beginningless? The Master said: Affliction is precisely bodhi—neither two nor different. If one uses wisdom to illumine and break through affliction, this is the view of the two vehicles, those of the faculties of the goat and the deer; the wise of supreme wisdom and great faculties are all not thus.]

Xue Jian said: Bright is a metaphor for wisdom; dark is a metaphor for affliction. If the cultivator of the Way does not use wisdom to illumine and break through affliction, how can he escape the birth and death of the wheel of samsara that has been without beginning? The Master said: In the light of the real aspect of all dharmas, affliction is precisely bodhi—the two are not different. If one uses wisdom to illumine and break through affliction, that is the view of the faculties of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha); those of supreme wisdom and great faculties are all not thus.

[The faculties of the goat and the deer (yang lu deng ji)] The faculties of the two vehicles. The Lotus Sutra uses the goat-cart and the deer-cart as metaphors for those of the two vehicles. [Affliction is precisely bodhi—neither two nor different] This is speaking of the real aspect of all dharmas. “Affliction is precisely bodhi, neither two nor different” means that affliction and bodhi are both illusions, affairs of a dream—how can there be any actual difference between them? This is the non-dual Dharma-gate. Hence the passage below says: “Bright and non-bright: the ordinary person sees them as two; the wise, penetrating them, find their nature non-dual.” The real aspect of all dharmas revealed here by the Sixth Patriarch is the principle of the Heart Sutra: “These are the empty marks of all dharmas, neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increased nor diminished.” This principle is explained in detail in the Elucidation of the Heart Sutra.

[Xue Jian said: What is the Mahayana view? The Master said: Bright and non-bright: the ordinary person sees as two; the wise, penetrating them, find their nature non-dual. The nature without duality is the true nature. As for the true nature: dwelling among the ordinary and the dull, it does not diminish; among the wise and the holy, it does not increase; abiding in affliction, it is not confused; dwelling in meditative concentration, it is not still; not cut off, not eternal; not coming, not going; not in the middle, nor within or without; neither born nor extinguished; nature and marks as-they-are, ever abiding and unchanging—this is named the Way.]

Xue Jian said: Then what is the Mahayana view? The Master said: Bright and non-bright—the ordinary person, deluded by marks, takes them as two different things; the wise, awakening and penetrating them, find their essence non-dual. This nature without duality is the true nature (the true nature of all dharmas). As for the true nature: dwelling among the ordinary and the dull, it does not diminish; among the wise and the holy, it does not increase; abiding in affliction, it is not confused; dwelling in meditative concentration, it is not still; not cut off, not eternal; not coming, not going; not in the middle, nor within nor without; neither born nor extinguished; nature and marks one-as-they-are, never changing (ever abiding, not shifting)—this is called the Way.

[True nature (shixing)] The true nature, that is, the real aspect. All dharmas are illusions, so their essence is non-dual (wholly identical). Yongjia’s Song of Certifying the Way says: “The true nature of non-bright is precisely the Buddha-nature; the illusory empty body is precisely the Dharmakaya.”

The essential meaning of the non-dual Dharma-gate is: not to be turned by marks (because “all marks are false and unreal”). The ordinary person, seeing two, is turned by marks; the wise, penetrating the emptiness and stillness of the Dharma-nature, are free from marks and self-possessed.

[Xue Jian said: The Master speaks of neither birth nor extinction—how does this differ from the heretics? The Master said: What the heretics say of neither birth nor extinction is to use extinction to stop birth, and to use birth to make extinction manifest; extinction is still not extinction, and birth speaks of not being born. What I say of neither birth nor extinction is that in its origin there is no birth, and now also no extinction—and therefore it differs from the heretics.]

Xue Jian said: The Master speaks of neither birth nor extinction—what is the difference between this and the heretics? The Master said: What the heretics say of neither birth nor extinction is to use extinction to stop birth, and to use birth to make extinction manifest; in this way, extinction is as if not extinction, and birth, being spoken of, is still not born. But what I say of neither birth nor extinction is that in its origin there never was being (“originally there is not a single thing”), and hence no extinction either—and so it differs from the heretics.

What the heretics call “neither birth nor extinction” means eternal existence; what the Sixth Patriarch calls “neither birth nor extinction” means that all things are illusory, and in fact never existed.

[Neither birth nor extinction (busheng bumie)] What the Platform Sutra says by “neither birth nor extinction” is this: all dharmas never existed (originally never born, and hence also never extinguished)—this is the real aspect of all dharmas (the actual condition of all things). The Buddha-Store Sutra

Chapter Two, “On Buddha-Recitation,” says: “What is called the real aspect of all dharmas? That is to say, all dharmas are ultimately empty, with nothing at all.” The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “All beings, within the unborn, falsely see birth and extinction; therefore they are said to revolve in the wheel of birth and death.” The Sutra of the Most Victorious King says: “The unborn is real; birth is false. Foolish people are drowned in birth and death; the Tathagata embodies the real, with no falsity, and this is called nirvāṇa.” The Benevolent King Sutra says: “All dharmas are by nature truly empty, neither coming nor going, neither born nor extinguished, the same as ultimate reality, equal to the Dharma-nature.”
In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

Chapter Two Hundred Ninety-six, the Buddha said: “Subhuti, in this great treasure-store of prajñāpāramitā, not a single dharma is spoken of as having birth or extinction, defilement or purity, grasping or relinquishing. Why? Because there is not a single dharma that can arise or cease, be defiled or purified, be grasped or relinquished.” The Heart Sutra says: “These are the empty marks of all dharmas: neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increased nor diminished.”

Therefore, what the Buddha-Dharma calls “neither birth nor extinction” is the real aspect of all dharmas—originally there is not a single thing; how can there be any birth or extinction to speak of? The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

Chapter Eleven, “The Chapter on Illusion,” says: “The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? Does illusion have defilement or purity? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti! What do you think? Does illusion have birth or extinction? No, World-Honored One.”

[If you wish to know the essential mind, only refrain from thinking of all good and all evil, and naturally you will enter the pure body of mind, still and serene, ever serene, with the wondrous functions of the Ganges’ sands.]

If you wish to know the essential mind, only do not think of all good and evil (apart from marks within marks), and naturally you will enter the pure body of mind (the original nature), still and serene, ever serene, with wondrous functions without end, as many as the sands of the Ganges.

If you wish to know the essential mind, only refrain from thinking of all good and all evil, and naturally you will enter the pure body of mind, still and serene, ever serene, with the wondrous functions of the Ganges’ sands.”—This is the dotting of the eye on the painted dragon, the utmost crux of it all!

Here, “do not think of all good and evil” is not “not to think of the hundred things, and to cut off thought altogether”; it means not to discriminate and deliberate, giving rise to the feelings of love and hate, grasping and relinquishing. The Third Patriarch of the Chan school, Seng Can, says in his Faith-mind Inscription: “The supreme Way is not difficult—it simply dislikes picking and choosing. Only do not love and hate, and it is clear and transparent. A hair’s-breadth of difference, and heaven and earth are separated.” The Fourth Patriarch of the Chan school, Master Daoxin, says: “The objects of the environment are neither good nor bad; good and bad arise in the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, from whence do the false feelings arise? Since the false feelings do not arise, the true mind knows all in freedom.”

All beings without exception possess the nature of awakening, numinous, bright, empty, and still, no different from the Buddha. But because from beginningless kalpas they have never awakened, they falsely cling to the body and mind (form, feeling, thought, volition, and consciousness) as self (the mark of a self), and so give rise to the feelings of love and hate, grasping and relinquishing. Thereupon they create karma according to their feelings, and receive retribution according to their karma—birth, old age, sickness, and death, revolving in the wheel of samsara through long kalpas.
[Xue Jian, having received the Master’s instruction, suddenly and greatly awakened. He bowed, took leave, and returned to the palace, presenting in a memorial what the Master had said.]

Xue Jian, having received the Master’s instruction, was as if the stuffing were suddenly removed from his mind, suddenly and greatly awakened. He bowed, took leave, and returned to the court, presenting the Master’s words in a memorial to the Empress Dowager and the Emperor.

[On the third day of the ninth month of that year, an edict praised the Master, saying: The Master, declining on the grounds of age and illness, cultivates the Way for Us—he is the country’s field of merit. The Master is like Vimalakirti (Jingming), who, feigning illness in Vaisali, expounded the Mahayana, transmitted the mind of all Buddhas, and spoke the non-dual Dharma. Xue Jian transmitted the Master’s instruction in the Tathagata’s knowledge and vision. We, by Our accumulated good and its surplus blessing, having sown good roots in former lives, were so fortunate as to meet the Master’s coming forth in the world, and suddenly awakened to the Supreme Vehicle, gratefully acknowledging the Master’s kindness and holding it above Our head without end! And We offer a fine-wool kashaya robe and a crystal bowl, and command the Prefect of Shaozhou to repair the monastery halls, and bestow the Master’s former dwelling as the Guoen (National Grace) Monastery.]

On the third day of the ninth month of that year, the emperor again issued an edict praising the Master: “The Master, declining the summons on the grounds of age and illness, cultivates the Way for Us at Caoxi—he is the country’s field of merit. The Master is like the layman Vimalakirti (Jingming), who, in the city of Vaisali (Piye), took illness as a pretext, and expounded the Mahayana, transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal, and spoke the non-dual Dharma-gate. Xue Jian returned to the palace and reported the Tathagata’s knowledge and vision that the Master had instructed. We, through accumulated good and its surplus blessing, having sown good roots in a former age, were so fortunate as to meet the Master’s coming forth in the world, and suddenly awakened to the One Buddha-Vehicle (the Supreme Vehicle). Gratefully acknowledging the Master’s kindness, We hold it above Our head without end! And We offer the fine-wool kashaya robe presented by the kingdom of Goryeo, and a crystal bowl, and command the Prefect of Shaozhou to build and repair the monastery halls, and bestow the Master’s former dwelling in Xinzhou as the Guoen (National Grace) Monastery.”

[Yú qìng: the virtue bequeathed to later generations; a household that accumulates goodness will surely be left with a surplus of blessing.] [Dǐng dài: to carry an image of the Buddha, a scripture, and other such things upon the crown of the head, a gesture of the utmost reverence.] [Mó nà: the name of a kind of robe (kasaya), produced in the land of Goryeo.]

blocks.text: 1. Teaching You How to Preach the Dharma

inline.s: [One day the Master called the disciples Fahai, Zhicheng, Fada, Shenhui, Zhichang, Zhitong, Zhiche, Zhidao, Fazhen, Faru and others, and said: you are not like the rest of the people; after my passage into nirvaṇa, each of you will become a teacher of one region.]

One day the Master summoned the disciples Fahai, Zhicheng, Fada, Shenhui, Zhichang, Zhitong, Zhiche, Zhidao, Fazhen, Faru and others, and said to them: you are unlike other people; after my passing, each of you will be a teacher in your own region.

[I now teach you how to preach the Dharma so that you will not lose the fundamental purport of our school. First you must raise the three categories of the Dharma-gate and employ the thirty-six pairs; whether emerging or withdrawing, you should be free of the two extremes, and when speaking of all dharmas do not depart from self-nature. Should someone suddenly ask you about the Dharma, let your words always be paired, all taken from opposites, with coming and going mutually conditioning each other; in the end the two [opposing] dharmas are completely eradicated, leaving nothing further to cleave to.]

I now teach you to preach the Dharma in this way, and only then will you not lose the essential purport of our school (the Sudden Teaching). When expounding the Dharma you must first raise the three categories of the Dharma-gate and employ the thirty-six pairs; in coming and going be free of the two extremes, and in speaking of all dharmas do not depart from self-nature. If someone suddenly asks you about the Dharma, speak of both sides when you talk, keeping every utterance paired and all of it drawn from opposites, each conditioning the other as cause; in the end the two opposing sides are done away with altogether, and there is no other place to abide — this is the Middle Way.

[Three categories (sān kē): all dharmas are divided into the five aggregates (skandhas, also translated as the five heaps), the twelve sense-fields (āyatanas, also translated as the twelve entrances), and the eighteen realms (dhātus); by observing self and the external world from these three aspects one may break the erroneous view of a self and realize the principle of non-self.] [Thirty-six pairs: thirty-six kinds of relative concepts. Whenever the thirty-six pairs are employed, whether emerging or withdrawing one should at once be free of the two extremes, so as to keep others from being caught by words and from clinging to meaning, thereby transcending duality — this is called the Middle Way.] [Middle Way: not leaning toward emptiness nor toward existence; neither empty nor existent, both empty and existent, not falling into either extreme, perfectly fused and unobstructed — this is called the Middle Way.]

blocks.text: 2. The Three Categories of the Dharma-Gate

inline.s: [By the three categories of the Dharma-gate are meant the skandha, the realm, and the entry. The skandha is the five skandhas: form, feeling, thought, volition, and consciousness. The entry is the twelve entries: the six outer sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas) and the six inner sense-doors (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). The realm is the eighteen realms: the six sense-objects, the six sense-doors, and the six consciousnesses.]

The three categories of the Dharma-gate are: the skandha, the realm, and the entry. The skandha is the five skandhas: form, feeling, thought, volition, and consciousness. The entry is the twelve entries: the six outer sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas) and the six inner sense-doors (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). The realm is the eighteen realms: the six sense-objects, the six sense-doors, and the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness).

[Yin, jie, ru: also called "aggregates, realms, and sense-fields," that is, the five skandhas, the eighteen realms (the six sense-bases, the six sense-objects, and the six consciousnesses), and the twelve sense-fields (the six sense-bases and the six sense-objects).] [Five yin: also called the five aggregates, namely form, feeling, thought, volition, and consciousness. "Yin" means to veil and conceal: they can obscure the true suchness of the intrinsic nature and give rise to manifold afflictions.] [Six sense-doors: that is, the six sense-bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.] [Six consciousnesses: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. These are the discriminating functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, feeling, and reflecting that arise when the six sense-bases (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind) meet the six sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, dharmas).]

[Self-nature can contain all dharmas, and so is named the storehouse consciousness. If thinking and reflection arise, this becomes the transforming consciousness, which produces the six consciousnesses, issues from the six sense-doors, and perceives the six sense-objects; thus these eighteen realms are all functions arising from self-nature. If self-nature is deviant, it produces the eighteen deviant functions; if self-nature is upright, it produces the eighteen upright functions. If the functions are evil, they are the functions of a sentient being; if good, they are the functions of a Buddha. From what do the functions come? They come from self-nature.]

Self-nature can contain all dharmas, and is therefore called the storehouse consciousness (the intrinsic nature). When self-nature gives rise to thinking and reflection, it becomes the transforming consciousness (consciousness-nature), producing the six consciousnesses (eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness). The six consciousnesses issue from the six sense-doors (the six sense-bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and perceive the six sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas). Thus these eighteen realms (the six consciousnesses, six sense-bases, and six sense-objects) are all functions of self-nature. If self-nature is deviant, these eighteen realms produce eighteen deviant functions; if self-nature is upright, these eighteen realms produce eighteen upright functions. If the functions are evil, they are the functions of a sentient being; if good, they are the functions of a Buddha. Where do the functions come from? They come from self-nature.

[If thinking and reflection arise, then it becomes the transforming consciousness] Master Dixian, in his Commentary on Mahāyāna Cessation and Contemplation (Dàchéng Zhǐguān Shùjì), says: "Why is it that this pure mind (self-nature) has been covered since time without beginning by the defiling dharmas of ignorance? Because from the outset it was never enlightened; although its essence remains unchanging, it follows the conditions of defilement. Thus it is said that when thought indistinctly arises ("if thinking and reflection arise"), ignorance comes to be. The arising of thought becomes a state of agitation, which goes against original stillness; and ignorance becomes a state of darkness, which goes against original illumination. Thereupon the whole essence of the mind is taken up as the ālayavijñāna (ālaya consciousness), which is named the karmic mark ("this is the transforming consciousness"). From this the whole of truth turns into falsity, and within falsity subject and object are parted." The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: "The mind is born from the ālaya, the [seventh] consciousness arises depending on the manas; the ālaya gives rise to all the mind-functions, as the ocean gives rise to waves." This means the manas (the will) is born from the ālayavijñāna, and the first six consciousnesses (eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness) in turn arise depending on the manas; thus the first seven consciousnesses are all derived from the ālayavijñāna, which is therefore often used as a general term for the totality of the eight consciousnesses (consciousness-nature).
In this passage the Sixth Patriarch gives an extremely important exposition of self-nature:

First, the original state of self-nature is the storehouse consciousness (the intrinsic nature); when thinking arises (delusion), its transforming state is the spiritual consciousness (consciousness-nature). Therefore, it is self-nature that transmigrates, it is self-nature that gains liberation, and it is self-nature that attains Buddhahood. Patriarch Linji says: "Just watch the puppet dancing on the stage — the pulling and the tugging all depend on the one behind it." This means the physical body is the puppet, and the one manipulating this physical body is self-nature. Again he says: "Upon this lump of red flesh there sits a true person without rank; the very one now preaching and the very one now listening." So it is self-nature that preaches, and it is self-nature that listens.

Second, when self-nature gives rise to thinking, it produces the six consciousnesses, issues from the six sense-doors, and perceives the six sense-objects. Therefore thinking is the root of ignorance. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: "To establish knowledge upon knowledge is the very root of ignorance; when knowledge no longer sees, this is nirvāṇa, the true purity free of outflows." The Essence of the Transmission of Mind (Chuanxin Fayao) says: "Still the thoughts and let go of deliberation, and the Buddha naturally appears before you."

Third, if self-nature is deviant, it produces the eighteen deviant [realms], and the six consciousnesses, six sense-bases, and six sense-objects are all deviant; if self-nature is upright, it produces the eighteen upright [realms], and the six consciousnesses, six sense-bases, and six sense-objects are all upright. If the functions are evil, they are the functions of a sentient being; if good, they are the functions of a Buddha. Whether deviant or upright, good or evil, it is always self-nature that is functioning.

[Opposite dharmas. There are five pairs in the insentient outer world: heaven paired with earth, sun paired with moon, brightness paired with darkness, yin paired with yang, water paired with fire — these are the five pairs.]
Within the thirty-six pairs, the insentient outer world has five pairs: heaven and earth, sun and moon, brightness and darkness, yin and yang, water and fire — five pairs in all.

[Twelve pairs in dharmas, marks, and language: speech paired with dharma, existence paired with non-existence, the formed paired with the formless, the marked paired with the markless, the out-flowing paired with the outflow-free, form paired with emptiness, movement paired with stillness, clarity paired with turbidity, the ordinary paired with the holy, the monk paired with the layman, old paired with young, large paired with small — these are the twelve pairs.]

There are twelve pairs in dharmas, marks, and language: speech and dharma, existence and non-existence, form and formlessness, marks and marklessness, the out-flowing and the outflow-free, form and emptiness, movement and stillness, clarity and turbidity, the ordinary and the holy, the monastic and the lay, old and young, large and small — twelve pairs in all.

[Nineteen pairs of the functioning of self-nature: long paired with short, deviant paired with upright, delusion paired with wisdom, foolishness paired with intelligence, turmoil paired with concentration, compassion paired with cruelty, precepts paired with transgression, straight paired with crooked, real paired with unreal, treacherous paired with level, affliction paired with bodhi, eternal paired with impermanent, pity paired with harm, joy paired with anger, renunciation paired with miserliness, advancing paired with retreating, arising paired with ceasing, dharmakāya paired with the physical body, nirmāṇakāya paired with saṃbhogakāya — these are the nineteen pairs.]

There are nineteen pairs in the functioning of self-nature: long and short, deviant and upright, delusion and wisdom, foolishness and intelligence, turmoil and concentration, compassion and cruelty, precepts and transgression, straight and crooked, real and unreal, treacherous and level, affliction and bodhi, eternal and impermanent, pity and harm, joy and anger, renunciation and miserliness, advancing and retreating, arising and ceasing, dharmakāya and the physical body, nirmāṇakāya and saṃbhogakāya — nineteen pairs in all.

[The Master said: These thirty-six pairs of dharmas, if you understand how to use them, will enable the Way to run through all the scriptures and dharmas, so that in coming and going you are free of the two extremes. When self-nature functions and you converse with others, outwardly be free of marks while among marks, and inwardly be free of emptiness while in emptiness. If you cling entirely to marks, you grow in deviant views; if you cling entirely to emptiness, you grow in ignorance.]

The Master said: These thirty-six pairs of dharmas, if you know how to employ them, will let the Way run through all scriptures and dharmas, so that in coming and going you are free of the two extremes. Self-nature must function, and when you speak with others, outwardly you must be free of marks while among marks and inwardly free of emptiness while in emptiness. If you cling entirely to marks, deviant views grow; if you cling entirely to emptiness, ignorance grows.

[Those who cling to emptiness may even slander the scriptures, declaring outright that words and letters are not needed. Since they say words and letters are not needed, people should not even use language, for this very speech is itself the mark of words and letters. Again they say: "The direct way sets up no words or letters." But even these two words, "set up no," are themselves words and letters. Seeing what others say, they at once slander them for being attached to words and letters. You should know that it is one thing to be deluded yourself, but quite another to slander the Buddhist scriptures. Do not slander the scriptures — the offenses are numberless!]

Those who cling to emptiness may even slander the scriptures, declaring positively that words and letters are not needed. Since they say words and letters are not needed, people should not even use language, for language is itself the mark of words and letters. Again they say that the way which points directly to the mind sets up no words or letters. But even the two words "set up no" are themselves words and letters. Seeing someone preach, they at once slander him for clinging to the mark of words and letters. You should know that to be deluded yourself is one thing, yet this is to slander the Buddhist scriptures as well; by all means do not slander the scriptures, for that creates immeasurable and boundless offenses.

Master Hanshan says: "The patriarchs of old all taught people to investigate Chan. Although their talk transcended the Buddha and surpassed the patriarchs, their real intent was to lead people to become Buddhas and patriarchs. There has never been one who sought to become a Buddha or a patriarch yet failed to honor the words and teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs. To set aside the teaching and speak only of practice is to throw away the compass and the square while seeking the round and the square." (From the Mengyou anthology, "Instructing Liuru Kungong")

[If one clings to outer marks and engages in contrived practices in search of the truth, or sets up many practice grounds while discoursing on the faults of existence and non-existence, such a person will not see the nature even after many kalpas. Just listen and practice in accordance with the Dharma; but neither should you think of nothing at all, which obstructs the nature of the Way. If you only listen and do not practice, it causes people to give rise to deviant thoughts. Simply practice in accordance with the Dharma and give the Dharma-gift without dwelling on marks. If you awaken, then speak in this way, use in this way, practice in this way, and act in this way, and you will not lose the fundamental teaching of our school.]

If one clings to marks outside the mind and engages in contrived practices in search of truth, or builds many practice grounds while discoursing on the faults of existence and non-existence, such a person will not see the nature even after countless kalpas. Having heard the teaching, you should practice in accordance with the Dharma; but neither should you think of absolutely nothing (think of nothing at all), which obstructs the nature of the Way. If you hear the teaching and do not practice, it causes people to give rise to deviant thoughts. Therefore practice in accordance with the Dharma, giving the Dharma-gift without dwelling on marks. If you awaken to this principle, then speak in this way, use in this way, practice in this way, and act in this way, and you will not lose the essential purport of our school (the Sudden Teaching).
[Dharma-gift (fǎ shī): to expound to others the Buddha-Dharma one has heard and known.]

[If someone asks you about the meaning, answer an inquiry about existence with non-existence, an inquiry about non-existence with existence, an inquiry about the ordinary with the holy, and an inquiry about the holy with the ordinary. The two paths conditioning each other give rise to the meaning of the Middle Way. Just as one question is met with one answer, so should all remaining questions be handled in this way, and you will not lose the principle.]

If someone asks you about the meaning of the Dharma, answer an inquiry about existence with non-existence, an inquiry about non-existence with existence, an inquiry about the ordinary with the holy, and an inquiry about the holy with the ordinary. Since the two extremes condition each other as cause, the meaning of the Middle Way arises. Just as one question is met with one answer, so should all remaining questions be answered in this way, and you will not lose the principle of the Middle Way.
[Meaning of the Middle Way: the subtle principle that is free of the two mutually opposed extremes and, moreover, has no need even of the middle, utterly transcending all duality.]

[Suppose someone asks, "What is called darkness?" You answer: "Brightness is the cause and darkness the condition; when brightness vanishes there is darkness. Brightness reveals darkness and darkness reveals brightness, coming and going mutually conditioned, and so the meaning of the Middle Way is realized." Answer all other questions in this way. When you transmit the Dharma in the future, teach one another in this manner, and do not lose the essential purport!]

If someone asks, "What is called darkness?" you answer: "Brightness is the cause and darkness the condition; when light vanishes, there is darkness. Because there is the concept of "brightness" there is the concept of "darkness," and because there is the concept of "darkness" there is the concept of "brightness"; brightness and darkness mutually condition each other, and this is the meaning of the Middle Way." Answer all other questions in this way. When you transmit the Dharma in the future, teach one another accordingly, and do not lose the essential purport of the Sudden Teaching!

[In the renzi (water-ox) year of the Taiji era, in the seventh month of the Yanhe period, the Master ordered the disciples to go to the Guo'en Monastery in Xinzhou to build a pagoda, and urged them to hasten the work. The following year, at the end of summer, it was completed. On the first day of the seventh month he gathered the assembly and said: "By the eighth month I shall leave this world. If any of you have doubts, you must ask me early, and I will resolve your doubts and bring your delusion to an end. Once I have gone, there will be no one to teach you!" Hearing this, Fahai and the others all wept, but only Shenhui remained unmoved in spirit, without a single tear.]
In the renzi year of the Taiji era of Emperor Ruizong of Tang (the year

, when the reign title was changed to "Yanhe"), in the seventh month, the Master ordered the disciples to go to the Guo'en Monastery in Xinzhou (his former residence) to build a pagoda, and urged them to finish it quickly (for the Master already knew his time had come). The pagoda was completed at the end of summer of the following year (

). On the first day of the seventh month the Master gathered the assembly and said: By the eighth month I shall leave this world. If there is anything you do not understand, ask me early, so that I may resolve your doubts and end your confusion. Once I have gone, there will be no one to teach you! Hearing this, Fahai and the rest all wept in sorrow, and only Shenhui remained unmoved in spirit, shedding no tears.

[Renzi: the renzi year. This is the ancient Chinese method of reckoning years by pairing the heavenly stems (jia, yi, bing, ding, wu, ji, geng, xin, ren, gui) with the earthly branches (zi, chou, yin, mao, chen, si, wu, wei, shen, you, xu, hai).] [Ordering the disciples to go to the Guo'en Monastery in Xinzhou to build a pagoda: The Guo'en Monastery was the Master's former residence. See 'Chapter Nine, Protecting the Dharma,' where the emperor "commanded the prefect of Shaozhou to repair the monastery and bestowed the Master's old residence as the Guo'en Monastery."]

[The Master said: Shenhui, though a young monk, has already attained the evenness of good and non-good, unmoved by slander and praise, untouched by sorrow and joy. The rest of you have not attained this; after so many years in the mountains, what Way have you actually been cultivating? Why do you weep now? What is it that grieves you? If you worry that I am going to an unknown place, know that I know my own destination; if I did not know my destination, I would not have told you of it beforehand. Your weeping is because you do not know where I am going; if you knew, you would not weep. The Dharma-nature is originally without arising or ceasing, without coming or going.]

The Master said: Although Shenhui is young, he has already realized the undiscriminating mind that treats good and non-good as equal, unmoved by slander and praise, untouched by sorrow and joy. The rest of you have not realized this; after so many years in the mountains, what Way have you been cultivating after all? Why do you weep now? What is it that worries you? If you worry that I do not know my destination, I know my own destination; if I did not know my destination, I could not have told you in advance when I would leave this world. You weep because you do not know my destination; if you knew my destination, you would not weep. Know that the essence of all dharmas is this: originally unborn, therefore unceasing, without coming and without going.

[Never would I have told you beforehand: a year earlier the Master had urged that a pagoda be built, which was his foreknowledge of the coming time; now he again informed the disciples a month in advance.] [The Dharma-nature is originally without arising or ceasing, without coming or going: this means all dharmas are illusory. All dharmas have never arisen, and so have never ceased; only with ignorance do arising and ceasing appear. The Buddha says in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, chapter forty, the section on Kaundinya: "All dharmas are false and unreal." The Sutra of Complete Enlightenment says: "Perfect enlightenment shines universally, quiescent and non-dual. Within it, hundreds of millions of asamkhyeyas of ineffable Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky, rising in confusion and ceasing in confusion."]
Question: Where does a cultivator of the Way go at the end of life?

Answer: Minister Wencao once asked: When a person who has realized the principle reaches the end of this life, what does he rely upon? Guifeng (the Chan Master Zongmi, fifth patriarch of the Huayan school of the Tang) replied: "If false thoughts arise and you do not follow them, then at the moment of death your old karma naturally cannot bind you. Although there is the intermediate state, you are free to go where you will, alighting at will in the heavens or among men. If the thoughts of love and aversion have already vanished, you will no longer receive a body of allotted portions, and can naturally exchange the short for the long and the coarse for the subtle. If the subtle streaming are all utterly quenched and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment remains alone and clear, then you respond to circumstances and manifest hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies to ferry sentient beings of karmic affinity — this is called a Buddha." (See the Jingde-era Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

[Intermediate state (zhōng yīn): after death and before entering a new womb, a transformation body formed of subtle matter sustains life; this transformation body is the intermediate-state body. During the first forty-nine days this intermediate state passes through a birth and a death every seven days, undergoing seven such cycles, awaiting the ordering of karmic conditions before it takes rebirth. The Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: "At the time of death, kinsfolk weep. The person is frightened and cannot hold himself together. The good and evil of a whole life all appear before his eyes. Once the warm breath is spent, the five aggregates of the past cease and the intermediate state of the present is born. After entering the womb, the present intermediate state ceases and the five aggregates of the future are born. It is like a lamp being lit and darkness vanishing, or the lamp going out and darkness returning — a continuous, unbroken succession."]
For a fuller discussion of life and death, the Direct Explanation of the True Mind (Zhenxin Zhishuo) says — for the detailed commentary one may consult the article
On Life and Death

Someone says: I have heard that one who sees the nature escapes from birth and death. Yet the patriarchs of old, who were all seers of the nature, still underwent birth and death; and now in this world we plainly see that cultivators of the Way have the matter of birth and death. How then can it be said that they escape from birth and death?

The answer: Birth and death are originally non-existent; it is through false calculation that they are taken to be real. It is like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the empty sky. Or one without such an ailment (or without diseased eyes) says: there are no flowers in the sky. The one who is afflicted (the sick-eyed person) does not believe it. Once the disease of the eye is gone, the sky-flowers naturally vanish, and only then does he believe there were no flowers. While the flowers have not yet vanished, those flowers too are empty; it is only the sick one who falsely holds them to be flowers — they are not real in essence. Just so, a person falsely takes birth and death to be real; or one free of birth and death tells him: originally there is no birth and death. If that person one day puts an end to his falsity, birth and death are naturally removed, and only then does he know that birth and death were originally nothing. While birth and death have not yet ceased, they too are not real — because he falsely holds them to be real. The sutra (the Sutra of Complete Enlightenment) says: "Good man, all sentient beings from time without beginning have been utterly deluded, like a lost man who mistakes the four directions. They falsely take the four great elements to be their own body and the shadowy traces of the six sense-objects to be their own mind — like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky. Moreover, just as the many sky-flowers vanish in the empty sky, it cannot be said that there is a fixed place where they cease; why? Because there is no place of their arising. All sentient beings, amid what is unborn, falsely see arising and ceasing, and so they are said to revolve in birth and death." Based on this passage, one may be certain that one who reaches and awakens to the true mind of perfect enlightenment is originally without birth and death. Now, to know there is no birth and death yet not be able to escape it — that is because one's practice has not yet reached the point. Hence the teaching says: The lady Ambapali asked Manjushri, "I know clearly that birth is a dharma which is not born; why then am I carried along by birth and death?" Manjushri replied, "Because one's power is not yet sufficient." Later, a mountain master asked Master Xiu, "I know clearly that birth is a dharma which is not born; how is it that I am still carried along by birth and death?" Xiu replied, "A bamboo shoot will after all become a bamboo; but can you use it now as a strip?" So it is: to know there is no birth and death is not equal to realizing no birth and death; to realize no birth and death is not equal to awakening to no birth and death; to awaken to no birth and death is not equal to using no birth and death. Today people do not even know there is no birth and death, much less realize it, awaken to it, or use it. Therefore, is it not fitting that those who hold to birth and death do not believe in the Dharma of no birth and death!"

blocks.text: 5. The Verse on True and False, Motion and Stillness

inline.s: [All of you sit down, and I will give you a verse called the Verse on True and False, Motion and Stillness. If you recite and take up this verse, your intent will be the same as mine, and practicing accordingly you will not lose the essential purport!]

The Master said: Sit down, all of you, and I will give you a verse called the Verse on True and False, Motion and Stillness. If you recite and hold to this verse, your mind will be at one with mine, and practicing accordingly you will not lose the essential purport of the Sudden Teaching!

The passage above said, "The Dharma-nature is originally without arising or ceasing, without coming or going." How then should one treat all dharmas? The Master next spoke the Verse on True and False, Motion and Stillness. In this verse he gives a penetrating teaching on the common pitfalls of practice, "true and false" and "motion and stillness."
[The monks made obeisance and asked the Master to compose a verse. The verse says:]
The monks respectfully made obeisance and asked the Master to recite a verse. The verse says:
[Among all things there is nothing true; do not take what you perceive to be true. If you take what you perceive to be true, then all such perception is utterly not true.]
Among all dharmas there is nothing true; do not take direct perception as true. If you take direct perception to be true, then such perception is entirely not true.
[Utterly not true: such perception is wholly not a true perception. The Diamond Sutra says: "All marks whatsoever are all false and vain."]
[If you can possess the true yourself, then apart from the false the mind is at once true. If your own mind does not leave the false, where is there any truth to be found?]
If you would possess the true yourself, then apart from illusion the mind is at once true (knowing as it really is); if your mind does not leave illusion, where can the true be seen?

[If the mind does not leave the false, where is there any truth: if the mind does not leave falsehood, then it is dwelling upon illusion — where can the true reality be seen? The Diamond Sutra says: "If you see that all marks are no marks, then you see the Tathagata."]
[Sentient beings know motion; insentient things do not move. If you cultivate the practice of non-movement, you become the same as insentient things that do not move.]
Sentient beings move and act; insentient things do not move. If you cultivate a practice of non-movement, you become the same as insentient things, stiff and unmoving.
[If you seek true non-movement, there is non-movement upon movement; non-movement as mere non-movement — insentient things have no Buddha-seed.]
If you seek the true non-movement, there is non-movement upon movement; if non-movement is merely non-movement, it is like tiles and stones, which have no Buddha-seed.

[Non-movement upon movement: although there is seeing, hearing, knowing, and feeling, with thoughts, words, and actions, it is nonetheless alive and free, unstained by the myriad realms, forever at ease. This is what the Diamond Sutra means: "You should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; you should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere." The Sutra of Complete Enlightenment says: "At all times do not give rise to false thoughts; and over these various false thoughts, neither do you suppress them." Only this is the true non-movement that is non-movement upon movement.]
[To be able to distinguish the marks well, while unmoved in the ultimate sense; if you hold such a view, this is the functioning of true suchness.]
Being able to distinguish the marks of all dharmas while unmoved in the ultimate sense; if you hold such a view, this is the arising function of true suchness.

[Ultimate sense (dì yī yì): the supreme principle, namely the supreme truth of the Middle Way, which is neither empty nor existent, both genuinely empty and wondrously present. The Buddha says in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, chapter forty, the section on Kaundinya: "All dharmas are false and unreal; what they cease along with is named the real, is named the real mark, is named the dharma-realm, is named ultimate wisdom, is named the ultimate truth, is named the ultimate emptiness."]

This sutra, Chapter Four on Concentration and Wisdom, says: "True suchness and self-nature give rise to thought; although the six sense-bases have seeing, hearing, knowing, and feeling, they are not stained by the myriad realms, and the true nature is forever at ease. Hence the sutra says: to be able to distinguish the marks of all dharmas while unmoved in the ultimate sense."
[I tell all who study the Way: strive diligently and apply the mind; do not, at the gate of the Great Vehicle, cling to the wisdom of birth and death.]

I tell all who study the Way: when doing the practice you must apply the mind (the manas); do not, though what you cultivate is the gate of the Great Vehicle, do the practice with a calculating, discriminating mind.

[Mind (yì): that is, the manas. The characteristic of the manas is its constant, deliberate reflection, giving rise to the discriminating mind.] [Strive diligently and apply the mind: the manas constantly and deliberately reflects, clings to the objects of mind, and from it the discriminating mind and false thoughts constantly arise. Therefore to investigate Chan is to investigate with the manas, to dam up the stream of false thoughts so that it no longer flows; and right there where it does not flow, to look and see the original face.] [The wisdom of birth and death: the calculating, discriminating mind.] [Calculating mind: the mind that grasps at realms and deliberates over things.]
[If your words accord, then together discuss the Buddhist meaning; if they truly do not accord, then press your palms together and let the other be pleased.]

If at the word your views accord, then together investigate the essential meaning of the Buddha-Dharma; if your views truly do not accord, then press your palms together and withdraw, letting the other be pleased (not angering the other).
[This school is originally without contention; to contend is to lose the meaning of the Way. If you insist on disputing over Dharma-gates, self-nature enters birth and death.]

Because the Sudden school is originally without contention; contention means being turned by illusion and contradicting the Way. If one does not go along but argues over which Dharma-gate is superior or inferior, self-nature falls into the cycle of birth and death.
[Zheng: to dispute, to contend.] [Ni: not to go along with, to oppose.]

In the Platform Sutra the Master admonishes us again and again to be without contention, because fondness for disputing — especially over which Dharma-gate is right or wrong, superior or inferior — is an ingrained bad habit of cultivators, and unless this habit is removed one cannot put an end to birth and death.

[At that time, having heard the verse, the assembly all made obeisance. They comprehended the Master's intent and each gathered in their minds, practiced in accordance with the Dharma, and no longer dared to dispute.]

At that time, having heard the Master finish this verse, the disciples all made obeisance, honoring him with praise and gratitude. They took in the Master's intent, each gathered in their minds, and practiced in accordance with the Master's teaching, no longer daring to dispute.

[Then the assembly knew the Master would not long remain in the world. The elder Fahai bowed again and asked: After the Master enters nirvaṇa, to whom will the robe and the Dharma be entrusted? The Master said: Since I preached the Dharma at the Mahābrahmā Monastery up to the present, all of it has been transcribed and circulated; the title I give it is the "Jewel-Dharma Platform Sutra." You should guard it, handing it down from one to another, to ferry the many kinds of sentient beings. Only by preaching in accordance with it is it called the true Dharma.]

Then everyone knew the Master would soon leave the world. The elder Fahai again bowed to the Master and respectfully asked: After the Master enters nirvaṇa, to whom will the robe and the Dharma be entrusted? The Master said: From my preaching at the Mahābrahmā Monastery down to the present, all of it has been transcribed and circulated. The title I bestow on this Dharma is the Jewel-Dharma Platform Sutra. You should guard this sutra, passing it on from generation to generation, to ferry the many kinds of sentient beings; only by preaching in accordance with this sutra is it called the true Dharma.
[Entering nirvaṇa (rù miè): to realize and enter nirvāṇa, also called perfect stillness, a euphemism for the passing of a sage.] [Mu: title, name.]

[Today I transmit the Dharma to you, but I do not give you the robe. Because your root of faith is fully mature, firmly settled, and free of doubt, you are fit for the great matter. Yet according to the meaning of the verse which the ancestral Master Bodhidharma transmitted, the robe should no longer be handed down.]

Today I transmit the Dharma to you but no longer pass on the robe. Because your root of faith is fully mature, firmly settled without doubt, and fit for the great matter of spreading the Dharma, therefore I transmit the Dharma to you. And according to the meaning of the verse transmitted by the ancestral Master Bodhidharma, the ancestral robe should not be handed down further.

[Yet according to the meaning of the verse which the ancestral Master Bodhidharma transmitted, the robe should not be handed down: the verse of the ancestral Master Bodhidharma below says, "One flower opens into five leaves," prophesying that after the Sixth Patriarch the Chan school would flourish greatly, dividing the lamp into five houses, with Dharma heirs spread throughout the world; and since there was only a single ancestral robe, it should not be transmitted any further.]
[The verse says: I originally came to this land, transmitting the Dharma to save those lost in delusion; one flower opens into five leaves, and the fruit naturally ripens.]

The verse of the ancestral Master Bodhidharma says: My original intent in coming to this land was to transmit the Dharma and save sentient beings lost in delusion; one flower opens into five leaves, and the fruit naturally ripens.

[One flower opens into five leaves: the "one flower" refers to the Sixth Patriarch Huineng; the "five leaves" refer to the five houses of Caodong, Linji, Yunmen, Weiyang, and Fayen. This was the cryptic prophecy of the ancestral Master Bodhidharma concerning the division of the school into five houses.]
One mark: there is only the one mark of no-marks. One practice: there is only the practice of the single, pure upright mind.
[No-marks (wú xiāng): the Buddha-Store Sutra

first chapter on the real mark of all dharmas, says: "The marks of all dharmas are all one mark, namely no-marks." The Sutra of Complete Enlightenment says: "The ocean-like wisdom of the dharma-realm illumines all marks, as if it were empty space."]

[The Master again said: Good knowing ones! Each of you should purify your minds and listen to my preaching. If you wish to bring to perfection the wisdom of all the seeds, you must penetrate the samādhi of one mark and the samādhi of one practice.]

The Master again said: Good knowing ones (in this manner of address the Master expresses his earnest expectation of these future masters of the Dharma, and his prophecy for them)! Each of you should purify your minds and listen to my preaching. If you wish to perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood (to bring to perfection the wisdom of all the seeds), you must penetrate the samādhi of one mark and the samādhi of one practice.

[Wisdom of all the seeds (zhǒng zhì): that is, the wisdom of all the seeds, the Buddha's wisdom that knows all the manifold dharmas.] [Bringing to perfection the wisdom of all the seeds: the perfect realization of the fruit of Buddhahood.]

[If in every place you do not dwell on marks, and amid those marks give rise to neither aversion nor affection, with no taking and no rejecting, not thinking of matters of gain and loss, accomplishment and ruin, but at ease and serene, empty and open, still and content — this is called the samādhi of one mark.]

If in every place you do not dwell on marks, and amid those marks give rise to neither aversion nor affection, nor any taking or rejecting, not thinking about matters of gain and loss, accomplishment and ruin, but at ease and serene, empty and open, tranquil and content — this is called the samādhi of one mark.

[Not thinking of matters of gain and loss, accomplishment and ruin: when you see it, do it; having done it, let it go. Once it is done, what is there that is not done? As long as it is done with awareness, the present moment is itself complete.]

[If in every place, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you maintain the pure single upright mind, then this is the unmoving bodhimanda and the true Pure Land — this is called the samādhi of one practice.]

If in every place, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you maintain the pure single upright mind, then this is the unmoving bodhimanda and the true Pure Land — this is called the samādhi of one practice. (Please refer to the section on the samādhi of one practice in Chapter Four on Concentration and Wisdom.)
[Upright mind (zhí xīn): the straightforward mind without flattery or crookedness. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra

first scroll says: "The Tathagatas of the ten directions, being of a single path, all leave birth and death through the upright mind." The Vimalakīrti Sutra says: "The upright mind is the bodhimanda; the upright mind is the Pure Land."] [Unmoving bodhimanda: "unmoving" means neither arising nor ceasing. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra

second scroll says: "If you can turn things, then you are the same as the Tathagata. With body and mind perfectly illumined, in the unmoving bodhimanda, upon the tip of a single hair you can contain all the lands of the ten directions."]
[If a person is endowed with these two samādhis, it is like a seed within the ground, which is stored and nurtured until it ripens its fruit; so too is it with the one mark and the one practice.]

If a person is endowed with these two samādhis, it is like a seed beneath the ground, which after being stored and nourished will surely blossom and bear fruit; so too with one who holds to the samādhi of one mark and the samādhi of one practice — given time, he will surely accomplish it.

[My preaching today is like the timely rain, moistening all the great earth; your Buddha-nature is like these seeds, which, meeting this generous wetting, all sprout and grow. Those who take up my purpose will surely gain bodhi; those who practice in accordance with my teaching will surely realize the wondrous fruit.]

My preaching today is like the timely rain, moistening the whole great earth; your Buddha-nature is like the seeds, which, meeting this abundant sweet rain, all sprout and grow. Those who take up my purpose will surely gain bodhi; those who practice in accordance with my teaching will surely realize the wondrous fruit.

[Your Buddha-nature is like the seeds, which, meeting this generous wetting, all sprout and grow: the sprouting and growing of the Buddha-nature means that the Buddha-nature begins to function.] [Wondrous fruit (miào guǒ): the supremely wondrous fruit, that is, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.]

The Sixth Patriarch says: "Those who take up my purpose will surely gain bodhi; those who practice in accordance with my teaching will surely realize the wondrous fruit." Who else could speak such words? Reflect on it! Reflect on it!

[Listen to my verse: The ground of the mind holds all the seeds; the universal rain makes them all sprout. Once you awaken suddenly and the flower's passion is gone, the fruit of bodhi is naturally accomplished.]

Listen to my verse: The ground of the mind holds the seeds of Buddhahood; the rain of the Dharma moistens them and all sprout. Suddenly enlightened, the passion of the empty flower is extinguished, and the fruit of bodhi is naturally accomplished.

[Having spoken the verse, the Master said: "The Dharma is non-dual, and the mind is so as well. The Way is pure, and has no marks. Be careful not to contemplate stillness or to empty the mind; this mind is originally pure, with nothing to take and nothing to reject. Each of you strive on, and go well according to circumstances!" At that time the assembly made obeisance and withdrew.]

Having spoken the verse, the Master said again: The Buddha-Dharma is non-dual, and the mind is non-dual as well. The Way is originally pure, and has no marks (all marks are illusory). You should not contemplate stillness or empty the mind; this mind is originally unmoving and pure, and agitation and defilement are only illusions seen by the deluded — so there is no stillness to be seized and no defilement to be removed. (The Master here speaks of the gate of sudden enlightenment and sudden practice.) Each of you should strive on, and go well according to circumstances. At that time the assembly bowed to the Master and withdrew.

blocks.text: 8. The Falling Leaf Returns to Its Root

inline.s: [On the eighth day of the seventh month the Master suddenly said to the disciples: "I wish to return to Xinzhou; you should quickly prepare the boats and oars." The assembly entreated him to stay earnestly and firmly, but the Master said: "Even the Buddhas, when they appear in the world, still show forth nirvāṇa; where there is coming, there must be going — this is the constant principle. This body of mine must also have its place to return."]

On the eighth day of the seventh month the Master suddenly said to the disciples: I wish to return to Xinzhou; you should quickly prepare the boats and oars. Knowing that the Master was about to leave the world, the assembly all earnestly entreated him to remain. The Master said: Even the Buddhas who appear in the world still show forth nirvāṇa; where there is coming there must be going, and this is the necessary principle. This physical body of mine likewise must have its place of return.
[I wish to return to Xinzhou: a year earlier the Master had ordered the disciples to go to the Guo'en Monastery in Xinzhou to build a pagoda, and urged them to hasten the work.]

[The assembly said: When the Master goes from here, when will he come back? The Master said: The falling leaf returns to its root; when I come again, I shall have no mouth. They asked again: The treasury of the true Dharma eye — to whom will it be entrusted? The Master said: The one who has the Way attains it; the one without a mind penetrates it.]

The assembly asked: When the Master goes to Xinzhou from here, when will he return? The Master said: My going back to Xinzhou is the body's return to its root; when I come again, there will be no physical body. The assembly asked again: The treasury of the true Dharma eye (the mind-seal of the Chan school) — to whom will it be entrusted? The Master said: The one who has the Way attains this mind-seal; the one without a mind penetrates it.

[The falling leaf returns to its root: this refers to what was said above, "This body of mine must also have its place to return."] [When I come again, I shall have no mouth: when he comes again, he will no longer be a physical body.] [The treasury of the true Dharma eye (zhèng fǎ yǎn zàng): a name for the virtue of the Buddha-mind, the mind-seal transmitted separately outside the doctrine in the Chan school. The Accounts of the Śākyamuni Era says: "The Buddha was on Vulture Peak when the great Brahma king offered him a golden udumbara flower. The World-Honored One twirled the flower and showed it to the assembly; the hundred thousand devas and men were all bewildered, and only Kashyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, which I entrust to Kashyapa."] [Without a mind (wú xīn): to be free of false thoughts is called being without a mind. The Diamond Sutra says: "Do not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor on sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; you should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere."]

[They asked again: Will there be any calamity later? The Master said: Five or six years after my passing, a man will come to take my head. Listen to my prophecy: To nourish a parent on the head, and the mouth must needs be fed; the calamity of meeting the one Full (Man); with Yang (Willow) and Liu (Poplar) as the officials.]

The assembly asked again: Will there be any misfortune afterward? The Master said: Eleven (five plus six) years after my passing, a person will come to steal my head. Remember my words: To nourish a parent on the head, and the mouth must needs be fed; the calamity of meeting the one Full (Man); with Yang (Willow) and Liu (Poplar) as the officials. (This means: on the head were parents needing filial support, and the mouth needed food to offer [them]; when Zhang Jingman committed the offense, Yang and Liu were the two officials.)

The case of the stolen head was as follows: Zhang Jingman, a man of Ruzhou, was by nature wholly filial, yet had no food to nourish his parents. A monk of the Silla kingdom (Korea) named Jindabei (Great Compassion) wished to take the Sixth Patriarch's head back to his country for worship, and hired Zhang Jingman with two thousand coins to commit the theft. When the deed failed and he was arrested, the prefect of Shaozhou was Liu Wutian and the magistrate of Qujiang county was Yang Kan. Because the monks of the monastery set forth the Master's prophecy, Zhang Jingman was judged innocent and released.

[Again he said: Seventy years after my departure, two bodhisattvas will come from the east, one a monk and one a layman, who at the same time will spread the saving transformation, establish my school, repair and build monasteries, and make the Dharma lineage flourish.]

The Master said again: Seventy years after I am gone, two bodhisattvas will come from the east, one a monk (referring to the Chan Master Mazu Daoyi) and one a layman (referring to the layman Pangyun). At the same time they will make the Dharma of the Buddha flourish and transform beings, establish the Chan school, build and repair monasteries, and cause the gate of the Sudden Teaching to prosper.

[Pang Yun (Pangyun), courtesy name Daoxuan, a native of Hengyang in Hunan, was a famous lay Chan practitioner of the Tang. He studied Chan under Mazu Daoyi and Shitou Xiqian, and associated frequently with the renowned Chan masters of his day, such as Danxia Tianran, Yaoshan Weiyan, Bailing, Damei Fachang, Luopu, and Yangshan Huiji. His realization was very high, and later generations praised him as the Vimalakīrti of China, ranking him alongside the Layman Fu. The world also called him the Layman Pang, the Old Man Pang, and the Great Layman Pang of Xiangyang.] [Layman Fu: his surname was Fu, his personal name Xi, and his courtesy name Xuanfeng. At twenty-four he met an Indian monk, Song the ascetic, who told him of his past causes; he built a hermitage between the twin catalpa trees on Pine Mountain and named himself the Great Layman Shanyu of the Coming Liberation. After seven years of ascetic practice, while sitting in calm meditation he saw the three Buddhas, Śākyamuni, Jinsu, and Dingguang, after which he showed supernatural powers.
