Emperor Wu of the Liang honored him and often called him the Layman Fu.] [Great layman (dà shì): a common term for a bodhisattva.] [Shanyu (Good Wisdom): refers to the ninth of the ten bodhisattva stages, the stage of Good Wisdom.] [Monastery (qié lán): a shortening of saṃghārāma, the grounds and residence where the monks dwell, a general term for a temple.] [Dharma heir (fǎ sì): one who succeeds to the purport [of the lineage].] [Establish my school, repair and build monasteries, and make the Dharma lineage flourish: this refers to Mazu's founding of the community monasteries. Before this the Chan school had no dedicated practice places; the monks mostly lodged in Vinaya temples, which made practice and study inconvenient. After Mazu established the monasteries (Chan temples, hence also called Chan groves) and Baizhang laid down the pure rules, the Chan monks from then on dwelt together in community, forming a system, and the Chan school flourished greatly.]
Question: The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Jingde era

in the section on the Layman Pangyun, says: "(Pangyun) asked Mazu, "What kind of person is the one who is not a companion to the myriad dharmas?" Mazu said: "When you have gulped up the water of the Western River in a single mouthful, then I will tell you."" May I ask: what does "gulping up the water of the Western River in a single mouthful" mean?

Answer: "The one who is not a companion to the myriad dharmas" refers to the intrinsic nature. "Gulping up the water of the Western River in a single mouthful" refers to cutting off the stream of false thoughts. When the Layman Pang asked "what kind of person is the one who is not a companion to the myriad dharmas," his meaning was: how does one see the nature? When Mazu answered "When you have gulped up the water of the Western River in a single mouthful, then I will tell you," his meaning was: above all, cut off the stream of false thoughts. The Record of the Patriarchal Hall records that when the Layman Pang heard Mazu's answer, "he was greatly enlightened. He went at once to the keeper of the storehouse, borrowed a brush and an inkstone, and composed a verse: The ten directions are one assembly, each one studies the non-doing; this is the place where the Buddha is chosen; with the mind empty, one passes the examination and returns." Therefore, it is only when the mind is empty that one can pass the examination.
[Passing the examination (jí dì): to be selected in the examinations of the imperial-exam era.]

blocks.text: 9. The Blood Lineage of the Chan School

inline.s: [Blood lineage (xuè mài): the system of transmission of the successive patriarchs.]
[The disciples asked: We do not know, since the Buddhas and patriarchs of old manifested and appeared, how many generations have been transmitted? We beg you to bestow instruction.]
The disciples asked again: We do not know, since the Buddhas and patriarchs manifested in the world, how many generations have been transmitted in all? We beg your instruction.
[Manifesting in response (yìng xiàn): the Buddha, responding to the occasion, manifests a body.]

[The Master said: The Buddhas of old who appeared in the world are already without number and beyond reckoning. Now, beginning with the seven Buddhas: in the past kalpa of Adornment there were the Buddha Vipashyin, the Buddha Shikhin, and the Buddha Vishvabhu; in the present kalpa of the Wise there were the Buddha Krakucchanda, the Buddha Kanakamuni, the Buddha Kashyapa, and the Buddha Śākyamuni — these are the seven Buddhas.]

The Master said: The ancient Buddhas who appeared in the world are countless and boundless, beyond calculation. Now, taking the seven Buddhas nearest to us: in the past kalpa of Adornment there were the Buddha Vipashyin, the Buddha Shikhin, and the Buddha Vishvabhu; in the present kalpa of the Wise there were the Buddha Krakucchanda, the Buddha Kanakamuni, the Buddha Kashyapa, and the Buddha Śākyamuni — these are what are called the seven Buddhas.

[Kalpa of Adornment (zhuāng yán jié): the past great kalpa is called the kalpa of Adornment. In any great kalpa there are four intermediate kalpas of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, and in the twenty small kalpas of the kalpa of abiding a thousand Buddhas appear. In the kalpa of Adornment the Buddha of Flower Light appeared first, and the last three Buddhas were Vipashyin, Shikhin, and Vishvabhu.] [Kalpa of the Wise (xián jié): the past great kalpa is called the kalpa of Adornment, the future great kalpa is called the kalpa of Constellations, and the kalpa of the Wise is the present great kalpa, in which a thousand Buddhas appear. The first four Buddhas are Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kashyapa, and Śākyamuni.] [Śākyamuni Buddha (shì jiā wén fó): that is, Śākyamuni Buddha.]

[Śākyamuni Buddha first transmitted [the Dharma] to the venerable Mahakashyapa; second, to the venerable Ānanda; third, to the venerable Shanavasika; fourth, to the venerable Upagupta; fifth, to the venerable Dhitika; sixth, to the venerable Micchaka; seventh, to the venerable Vasumitra; eighth, to the venerable Buddhanandi; ninth, to the venerable Buddhamitra; tenth, to the venerable Bhadrata; eleventh, to the venerable Punyayasas; twelfth, to the great master Ashvaghosha; thirteenth, to the venerable Kapimala; fourteenth, to the great master Nagarjuna; fifteenth, to the venerable Kanadeva; sixteenth, to the venerable Rahulata; seventeenth, to the venerable Sanghanandi; eighteenth, to the venerable Gayasata; nineteenth, to the venerable Kumarata; twentieth, to the venerable Jayata; twenty-first, to the venerable Vasubandhu; twenty-second, to the venerable Manorhita; twenty-third, to the venerable Haklenayasas; twenty-fourth, to the venerable Simha; twenty-fifth, to the venerable Basiasita; twenty-sixth, to the venerable Punyamitra; twenty-seventh, to the venerable Prajnatara; twenty-eighth, to the venerable Bodhidharma; twenty-ninth, to the great master Huike; thirtieth, to the great master Sengcan; thirty-first, to the great master Daoxin; thirty-second, to the great master Hongren; and Huineng is the thirty-third patriarch. All the patriarchs above each had their own transmission. In the future you must pass it down from generation to generation, and do not let it go awry!]

The blood lineage of the Chan school is: Śākyamuni Buddha first transmitted [the Dharma] to the ancestral founder, the venerable Mahakashyapa; the second patriarch, the venerable Ānanda; the third, the venerable Shanavasika; the fourth, the venerable Upagupta; the fifth, the venerable Dhitika; the sixth, the venerable Micchaka; the seventh, the venerable Vasumitra; the eighth, the venerable Buddhanandi; the ninth, the venerable Buddhamitra; the tenth, the venerable Bhadrata; the eleventh, the venerable Punyayasas; the twelfth, the great master Ashvaghosha; the thirteenth, the venerable Kapimala; the fourteenth, the great master Nagarjuna; the fifteenth, the venerable Kanadeva; the sixteenth, the venerable Rahulata; the seventeenth, the venerable Sanghanandi; the eighteenth, the venerable Gayasata; the nineteenth, the venerable Kumarata; the twentieth, the venerable Jayata; the twenty-first, the venerable Vasubandhu; the twenty-second, the venerable Manorhita; the twenty-third, the venerable Haklenayasas; the twenty-fourth, the venerable Simha; the twenty-fifth, the venerable Basiasita; the twenty-sixth, the venerable Punyamitra; the twenty-seventh, the venerable Prajnatara; the twenty-eighth, the venerable Bodhidharma; the twenty-ninth, the great master Huike; the thirtieth, the great master Sengcan; the thirty-first, the great master Daoxin; the thirty-second, the great master Hongren; and I am the thirty-third patriarch. The patriarchs above each had their own transmission. In the future you too must pass it down generation after generation, without error!

[Śākyamuni Buddha first transmitted [the Dharma] to the venerable Mahakashyapa: The Sutra of the Great Brahma King's Questions on the Buddha's Ultimate Meaning says: The Brahma king came to Vulture Peak and offered a golden udumbara flower to Śākyamuni Buddha, asking the Buddha to preach the Dharma. The World-Honored One twirled the flower and showed it to the assembly, without speaking. At that time the hundred thousand devas and men one and all failed to understand his meaning; only the venerable Kashyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the real mark that is without marks, the subtle Dharma-gate, not established in words or letters, transmitted separately outside the doctrine. I entrust it to Mahakashyapa. This was the beginning of the Chan school.] [Venerable (zūn zhě): an honorific title for an arhat.] [Great layman (dà shì): a common term for a bodhisattva.]

[In the guichou (water-ox) year of the Xiantian era of Emperor Xuanzong, on the third day of the eighth month, after the meal at the Guo'en Monastery, the Master said to the assembly of disciples: Each of you take your seats according to your rank; I am taking leave of you.]
In the guichou (water-ox) year of the Xiantian era of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang (the year

), on the third day of the eighth month, after the meal at the Guo'en Monastery in Xinzhou (the Guo'en Monastery was built at the site of the Sixth Patriarch's former residence, bestowed by imperial command; see the section on "A Decree of Imperial Praise"), the Master said to all the disciples: Each of you take your seats according to your rank; I am taking leave of you.
[Xiantian second year: the year
, that is, the first year of the Kaiyuan era, for in this year the reign title was changed to "Kaiyuan."] [Guichou year: the guichou year.]

[Fahai said: What teaching does the Master leave behind, so that the deluded people of later generations may see the Buddha-nature? The Master said: Listen attentively! In later generations, deluded people — if they recognize this sentient being, that is the Buddha-nature; if they do not recognize this sentient being, then for ten thousand kalpas they will search for the Buddha and rarely encounter him. I now teach you: recognize the sentient being in your own mind, and see the Buddha-nature of your own mind.]

At that time Fahai respectfully asked: What teaching does the Master leave behind, so that the deluded people of later generations may see the Buddha-nature? The Master said: Listen attentively! You deluded people of later generations must recognize that the sentient being is the deluded Buddha-nature; if you do not recognize that the sentient being is the deluded Buddha-nature, and instead seek the Buddha outside the mind, then for ten thousand kalpas you will hardly meet him. I now teach you: recognize this deluded sentient being in your own mind, and see the Buddha-nature of your own mind.

[If you wish to see the Buddha, simply recognize the sentient being; for it is the sentient being that is deluded and turns away from the Buddha, not the Buddha that is deluded and turns away from the sentient being. If self-nature awakens, the sentient being is a Buddha; if self-nature is deluded, the Buddha is a sentient being. If self-nature is equal, the sentient being is a Buddha; if self-nature is deviant and dangerous, the Buddha is a sentient being.]

If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, simply recognize that deluded sentient being; for it is the sentient being that is deluded and inverted, turning away from the Buddha-nature, and not the Buddha-nature that is deluded and inverted, turning away from the sentient being. If self-nature awakens, the sentient being is a Buddha; if self-nature is deluded, the Buddha is a sentient being. If self-nature is equal, the sentient being is a Buddha; if self-nature is deviant and dangerous, the Buddha is a sentient being.

[If your minds are dangerous and crooked, then the Buddha is hidden among sentient beings; with a single thought of evenness and uprightness, that is the sentient being becoming a Buddha. My own mind has the Buddha; one's own Buddha is the true Buddha. If one's own mind has no Buddha-mind, where can one seek the true Buddha? Your own mind is the Buddha; do not be at all doubtful. Outside [the mind] there is not a single thing that can be established; all is the ten thousand dharmas born of the original mind. Hence the sutra says: "When the mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all kinds of dharmas cease."]

If your minds are sinister and crooked, then the Buddha-nature lies hidden in these evil minds and does not reveal itself; with a single thought of brightness and uprightness, these evil minds are transformed into the Buddha-nature. (The Song of Realizing the Way says: "The real nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature.") One's own mind originally has the Buddha; the self-Buddha is the true Buddha. If one has no mind to become a Buddha, where can one go to seek the true Buddha? Your own mind is the Buddha — by no means harbour any further doubt. Outside the mind there is not a single thing that can be established; the ten thousand dharmas are all born of the original mind. Hence the sutra says: "When the mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all kinds of dharmas cease."

[All is the ten thousand dharmas born of the original mind: this sutra, in "Chapter Ten, The Entrustment," says: "Self-nature can contain all dharmas, and is therefore called the storehouse consciousness (the intrinsic nature); if thinking and reflection arise, it becomes the transforming consciousness (consciousness-nature). The consciousness-nature produces the six consciousnesses, issues from the six sense-doors (the six sense-bases), and perceives the six sense-objects." This means: when self-nature gives rise to thinking (the mind arising), the intrinsic nature turns into the consciousness-nature and produces the six consciousnesses, issues from the six sense-doors (the six sense-bases), and perceives the six sense-objects, thereby illusorily seeing the ten thousand dharmas. "Chapter Six on Repentance" says: "The nature of people is originally pure; the ten thousand dharmas arise from self-nature. To think about all evil matters causes evil actions to arise; to think about all good matters causes good actions to arise."]

blocks.text: 11. The Verse on the True Buddha of Self-Nature

inline.s: [The Verse on the True Buddha of Self-Nature: this verse sets forth that the intrinsic nature of sentient beings is the true Buddha, and warns them not to seek to become a Buddha outside. Its central thought is: "With right view, the three poisons cease of themselves; the devil is transformed into the Buddha, true and not false." This verse is the key to understanding the entire sutra.]

[I now leave a verse to take leave of you, called the Verse on the True Buddha of Self-Nature. If people of later generations grasp the meaning of this verse, they will see their own original mind and of themselves accomplish the Way of the Buddha. The verse says:]

I now leave a verse to take leave of you, called the Verse on the True Buddha of Self-Nature. If people of later generations grasp the purport of this verse, they will see their own original mind and of themselves accomplish the Way of the Buddha. The verse says:

[True suchness and self-nature are the true Buddha; deviant views and the three poisons are the devil king. In the time of deviant delusion the devil is in the house; in the time of right view the Buddha is in the hall.]

True suchness and self-nature (the intrinsic nature) are the true Buddha; deviant views and the three poisons (greed, anger, and delusion) are the devil king. When deluded by deviant views, the devil dwells in the house of the mind; when right view is present, the Buddha is in the hall of the mind.

[When deviant views arise within the nature, the three poisons are born — that is the devil king coming to dwell in the house. With right view, the mind of the three poisons is removed of itself, and the devil becomes a Buddha, true and not false.]

When deviant views arise in self-nature, the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion arise of themselves — that is the devil king coming to dwell in the mind's house. When self-nature gives rise to right view, the mind of the three poisons is removed by itself, and the devil is truly transformed into the true Buddha.

[The dharmakāya, the saṃbhogakāya, and the nirmāṇakāya — these three bodies are originally one body; if within the nature you can see them yourselves, that is the bodhi-cause of attaining Buddhahood.]

The dharmakāya, the saṃbhogakāya, and the nirmāṇakāya — these three bodies are originally one body (self-nature); if you can see these three bodies within self-nature, that is the bodhi-cause of attaining Buddhahood.

[Originally it is from the nirmāṇakāya that the pure nature is born; the pure nature is ever present within the nirmāṇakāya. The nature causes the nirmāṇakāya to walk the true path, and in the future it is perfected, true and endless.]

Originally it is from the nirmāṇakāya that the pure nature is born; the pure nature is ever present within the nirmāṇakāya. The pure nature causes the nirmāṇakāya to walk the true path, and in the future the merit of the saṃbhogakāya is perfected, true and endless.

In "Chapter Six," the Sixth Patriarch says: "What is called the hundred-thousand-million nirmāṇakāya? If you do not think of the myriad dharmas, the nature is originally like empty space. A single thought of reflection is called transformation. To think of evil matters is to transform into the hells; to think of good matters is to transform into the heavens; cruelty and harm transform into dragons and serpents; compassion transforms into a bodhisattva; wisdom transforms into the higher realms; and stupidity transforms into the lower regions. The transformations of self-nature are very many, but the deluded cannot awaken to them. When in every thought evil arises, one constantly walks the evil paths; with a single thought turned back to good, wisdom is born. This is called the nirmāṇakāya Buddha of self-nature."

[The nature of lust is originally the cause of the pure nature; to remove lust is itself the body of the pure nature. If within the nature each one is free of the five desires, then in an instant of seeing the nature, that is the true.]

The nature of lust (evil) is originally the cause of the pure nature; to remove lust (evil) is itself the body of the pure nature. If within the nature each is freed of desire for form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, then in an instant one truly sees the Buddha-nature.

[Lust (yín): evil.] [Five desires (wǔ yù): form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful appearances; sound to pleasing sounds; smell to fragrant odors; taste to delicious flavors; and touch to agreeable sensations. Because these five can cause people to give rise to a mind of greed and desire, they are called the five desires.]

[If in this life you meet the gate of the Sudden Teaching, and suddenly awaken to self-nature and see the World-Honored One; if you wish to cultivate and seek to become a Buddha — do you know where you intend to seek the true?]

If in this life you encounter the gate of the Sudden Teaching and suddenly awaken to your own nature, you will see the Tathagata face to face; if instead you wish to cultivate merit and pursue Buddhahood outwardly, do you know where you intend to seek the true Buddha?

[If within the mind you can see the true yourselves, then having the true is itself the cause of attaining Buddhahood; if you do not see self-nature and seek the Buddha outside, whatever thought you rouse makes you a great fool.]

If within your own mind you can see that self-nature is originally pure, this is the cause of attaining Buddhahood; if you do not see your own nature but seek to become a Buddha outside, then whoever rouses such a thought is a great fool.
[True (zhēn): self-nature is originally pure.]

[The Dharma-gate of the Sudden Teaching is now left with you; to save and ferry the people of the world, you must cultivate yourselves. I tell you, beings who will study the Way in the future: not to hold this view is a great error.]

The Dharma-gate of the Sudden Teaching is now left with you; to save and ferry the people of the world, you must first cultivate yourselves. I tell you who in the future will study the Way: if you do not hold the view this verse sets forth, that is an utterly absurd error.
[Great error (yōu yōu): absurd; for example, "such absurd talk should be kept from the mouth of a wise man."]

blocks.text: 12. Causing You to See the Nature

inline.s: [Having spoken the verse, the Master told them: Abide well! After my passing, do not engage in the worldly sorrow of weeping and raining tears. If you receive condolences and wear mourning clothes, you are not my disciple, and it is not the true Dharma.]

Having spoken the verse, the Master told the assembly: Conduct yourselves well! After my passing, do not weep raining tears like the worldly. If you receive condolences and wear mourning garments, you are not my disciples, and it is not the true Dharma.

[Just recognize your own original mind, and see your own original nature — without movement and without stillness, without arising and without ceasing, without coming and without going, without right and without wrong, without abiding and without moving on. I fear that your minds are deluded and will not grasp my meaning, so now I enjoin you again, to cause you to see the nature. After my passing, practice in accordance with this, as when I was in the world; if you go against my teaching, then even though I am still in the world, it will do you no good.]

Just recognize your own original mind, and you will see that your own original nature is without movement and without stillness, without arising and without ceasing, without coming and without going, without right and without wrong, without abiding and without moving on. I merely fear that your minds are deluded and cannot grasp my meaning, so now I enjoin you once more, to cause you to see the nature. After my passing, practice in accordance with this, as you did when I was in the world; if you go against my teaching, then even though I am still in the world, it will be of no benefit.
In this sutra the Sixth Patriarch teaches "recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature" as many as three times, which shows how important it is.
[Again he spoke a verse: Continually, without cultivating merit; ceaselessly, without doing evil; silent and still, cutting off seeing and hearing; vast and open, the mind with no attachment.]
The Master again spoke a verse: Toiling on without cultivating merit; surging on without doing evil; in stillness cutting off seeing and hearing; with the mind empty and no attachment.

[Wu wu: the appearance of diligent, weary toil; for example, "toiling on through the whole year."] [Teng teng: to churn and roll without ceasing.] [Cutting off seeing and hearing: when seeing, just see; when hearing, just hear, without rousing a thought or giving rise to a single idea.] [Mind empty: in the mind, no affairs; in affairs, no mind.]

This verse is the Master reaffirming the essential of the mind. In "Chapter Nine, Protecting the Dharma," the Sixth Patriarch says: "If you wish to know the essential of the mind, then simply do not think about any good or evil; you will naturally enter the pure mind-essence, serene and ever still, its wondrous function vast as the sands of the Ganges." Its core is: be free of all marks! The Śūraṅgama Sūtra

fifth scroll, the Buddha says: "To establish knowledge upon knowledge is the root of ignorance; when knowledge no longer sees, this is nirvāṇa, the true purity free of outflows." The whole of the Platform Sutra is saying: you are the Buddha — awaken at once!
Question: Why "continually without cultivating merit"?

Answer: The Essence of Mind-Cultivation (Xiu Xin Jue) says: "Only awaken to the one mind; there is not the least dharma to be obtained — this is the true Buddha." "If you are not certain, and do not believe that this is the Buddha, but wish to practice while clinging to marks in order to seek merit and function, all of this is false thought and runs contrary to the Way." "Doing evil or doing good are both clinging to marks. Clinging to marks and doing evil, one vainly undergoes the round of birth and death; clinging to marks and doing good, one vainly undergoes toil and suffering. In the end it is not as good as, upon these very words, directly recognizing the original Dharma." The Buddha's Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters says: "The Buddha said: The shramana who has left home cuts off desire and puts away love, recognizes the source of his own mind, penetrates the deep principle of the Buddha, and awakens to the unconditioned Dharma. Inwardly there is nothing attained; outwardly there is nothing sought; the mind is not tied to the Way, nor does it bind karma; without thought and without doing, without practice and without realization. Passing through no stages, yet itself most noble, this is called the Way."

blocks.text: 13. The White Rainbow Touching the Earth

inline.s: Having spoken the verse, he sat upright until the third watch of the night, when he suddenly said to the disciples: "I am going!" And at once he passed away. At that time a rare fragrance filled the chamber, a white rainbow touched the earth, the trees and woods turned white, and the birds and beasts cried out in sorrow.]

Having spoken the verse, the Master sat upright until the third watch of the night, when he suddenly said to the disciples: I am going! And at once he showed forth his passing. At that time a rare fragrance filled the chamber, a white rainbow stretched from the sky to the earth, the trees and woods turned white, and the birds and beasts cried out in sorrow.
[Suddenly (yǎn rán): all at once.] [Passing away (qiān huà): refers to the showing forth of a monk's passing.]

[In the eleventh month, the officials of the three prefectures of Guangzhou, Shaozhou, and Xinzhou, together with the disciples, monks, and lay people, vied to welcome the true body [of the Master], and could not decide where it should go. So they burned incense and prayed: "Wherever the incense smoke points, there shall be the Master's homecoming!" At that time the incense smoke went straight toward Caoxi. On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, they moved the spirit-shrine, together with the transmitted robe and bowl, and returned.]

In the eleventh month of that year, the officials of the three prefectures of Guangzhou, Shaozhou, and Xinzhou, together with the disciples, both monks and lay people, vied to welcome the Master's true body in order to make offerings, and could not decide where it should go. So they burned incense and prayed: Wherever the incense smoke points, there shall be the Master's homecoming! At once the incense smoke went straight toward Caoxi. On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, the people moved the spirit-shrine where the Master had sat in meditation, together with the robe and bowl transmitted by the Fifth Patriarch, back to the Baolin Monastery at Caoxi for offerings.

[The following year, on the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month, [the body] was taken out of the shrine, and the disciple Fangbian coated it with fragrant clay. The disciples recalled the prophecy of the head being taken, and so first bound the Master's neck firmly with iron plate and lacquered cloth before placing it in the pagoda. Suddenly within the pagoda a white light appeared, rising straight up into the sky, and only dispersed after three days. This was reported to the court, and an imperial decree ordered a stele to be erected recording the Master's way and conduct.]

On the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month of the following year, the Master’s body was taken out of the shrine, and the disciple Fangbian coated it with fragrant clay. The disciples recalled the Master’s prophecy that “someone would steal the head,” so they first wrapped the Master’s neck firmly with iron plate and lacquered cloth, and then placed the body within the pagoda. At that moment a white light suddenly appeared inside the pagoda, rising straight up into the sky, and it was only after three days that it dispersed. The prefect of Shaozhou reported this to the court, and the emperor ordered a stele to be erected recording the Master’s way and virtue.
[Tie ye: iron plate.] [Ji: to record

[The Master lived to the age of seventy-six. At twenty-four he received the transmission of the robe, at thirty-nine he shaved his head, and for thirty-seven years he taught the Dharma for the benefit of living beings. Those who attained the essential purport and succeeded to the Dharma numbered forty-three persons; those who awakened to the Way and rose beyond the ordinary could not be counted.]
The Master’s lifespan was seventy-six years (

). At twenty-four he received the robe of the Fifth Patriarch, at thirty-nine he shaved his head, and for thirty-seven years he taught the Dharma for the benefit of living beings. Those who attained the essential purport of the Sudden Teaching and inherited the Master’s Dharma lineage numbered forty-three, while those who awakened and passed beyond the three realms could not be counted.

[The faith robe transmitted by Bodhidharma, the precious bowl and kasaya bestowed by Emperor Zhongzong, and the true image of the Master sculpted by Fangbian, together with his implements and so forth, are placed in the pagoda by the attendant in charge of the pagoda, to forever guard the Baolin monastery. The Platform Sutra was transmitted to reveal the essential purport. All of this flourishes the Three Jewels and benefits all beings.]

The faith robe transmitted by the Patriarch Bodhidharma, the cotton kasaya and crystal bowl bestowed by Emperor Zhongzong of the Tang, and the Master’s likeness sculpted by Fangbian, together with the implements used by the Master, were all placed within the pagoda by the attendant in charge of the pagoda, to forever guard the Baolin monastery. Moreover, the Platform Sutra was transmitted to the world to make known the essential purport of the Sudden Teaching. All of this is the flourishing of the Three Jewels and the benefit of all beings!
[Faith robe: also called the patriarch’s robe, the kasaya that signifies the proof of Dharma transmission.] [Shi zhi: here ‘shi’ means to take charge, to oversee, to arrange.]
